children.note: Holocrine glands opening into hair follicles (pilosebaceous unit); absent on palms and soles; androgen-driven in acne.

manas.q: Where are sebaceous glands absent, and what drives them?

children.note: Found over almost all skin, most dense on palms and soles; cool the body; sympathetic nerves using acetylcholine.

manas.q: Which neurotransmitter drives eccrine sweating?

children.note: In axillae and anogenital skin; open into follicles; active from puberty; odour comes from bacterial breakdown.

manas.q: Where are apocrine glands and when do they become active?

children.note: Hard keratin plate made by the nail matrix; toenails grow slower, so toenail changes take longer to clear.

manas.q: Which part of the nail makes the nail plate?

children.note: Why skin failure is dangerous.
Stops water loss and entry of microbes, chemicals and UV; damaged barrier underlies dry, eczematous skin.

manas.q: What does the skin barrier protect against?

children.note: Sweating and changes in dermal blood flow (dilation or constriction) control heat loss.

manas.q: How does skin regulate temperature?

children.note: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the epidermis to vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol).

manas.q: How does the skin make vitamin D?

children.note: Widespread skin loss or erythroderma causes fluid and protein loss, hypothermia and infection risk.

manas.q: What are the dangers of acute skin failure?

children.note: Lesions that arise first (beyond macule, papule, vesicle, bulla).
Raised, flat-topped lesion over 1 cm wide, often from merging papules; classic in psoriasis.

manas.q: What is a plaque?

children.note: Solid raised lesion over 1 cm, usually reaching deeper into dermis or subcutis.

manas.q: What is a nodule?

children.note: Itchy, short-lived swelling from dermal oedema; each one usually fades within 24 hours (urticaria).

manas.q: What is a wheal and how long does each one last?

children.note: Visible collection of pus; may be infected or sterile (as in pustular psoriasis).

manas.q: Is a pustule always infected?

children.note: Bleeding into skin that does not blanch: petechiae are pinpoint; purpura larger; ecchymosis is a bruise.

manas.q: What distinguishes petechiae, purpura and ecchymosis?

children.note: Small dilated superficial blood vessels visible in the skin.

manas.q: What is telangiectasia?

children.note: Burrow: thin track made by the scabies mite. Comedone: plugged follicle (blackhead or whitehead) in acne.

manas.q: What do a burrow and a comedone indicate?

children.note: Changes that develop from primary lesions or scratching.
Visible flakes of shed stratum corneum, as in psoriasis or tinea.

manas.q: What is scale?

children.note: Dried serum, blood or pus on the surface; golden 'honey' crusts suggest impetigo.

manas.q: What does a honey-coloured crust suggest?

children.note: Erosion: loss of epidermis only, heals without a scar. Ulcer: loss into dermis or deeper, may scar.

manas.q: What is the difference between an erosion and an ulcer?

children.note: Excoriation: scratch mark, implying itch. Fissure: linear crack, e.g. on dry hands or heels.

manas.q: What are excoriation and fissure?

children.note: Thinning of skin: shiny, wrinkled, see-through, with visible vessels; e.g. after potent topical steroid overuse.

manas.q: What does skin atrophy look like and what can cause it?

children.note: Keloid spreads beyond the original wound; hypertrophic scar stays within it. Keloids are commoner in darker skin.

manas.q: How does a keloid differ from a hypertrophic scar?

children.note: Arrangement often points to the diagnosis.
Ring with a clearer centre, e.g. tinea corporis or granuloma annulare.

manas.q: Give two causes of annular lesions.

children.note: Concentric rings with a dusky centre; typical of erythema multiforme.

manas.q: Which condition gives target lesions?

children.note: Confined to one nerve segment on one side, as in herpes zoster.

manas.q: Which infection gives a dermatomal rash?

children.note: Clustered blisters on a red base; typical of herpes simplex.

manas.q: What does a cluster of vesicles on a red base suggest?

children.note: In a line: Koebner response along a scratch, or contact with a plant or object.

manas.q: Name causes of linear lesions.

children.note: Flexures (elbow and knee creases): atopic eczema beyond infancy. Extensor surfaces (elbows, knees): psoriasis.

manas.q: Which conditions favour flexural vs extensor sites?

children.note: Face, V of neck, backs of hands; shaded areas such as under the chin are spared.

manas.q: How do you recognise a photo-exposed distribution?

children.note: Quick tests that sharpen the diagnosis.
Firm rubbing shears off epidermis; positive in pemphigus vulgaris, SJS/TEN and staphylococcal scalded skin.

manas.q: In which conditions is Nikolsky sign positive?

children.note: Pinpoint bleeding when psoriatic scale is scraped off, from capillaries near the surface.

manas.q: What is the Auspitz sign?

children.note: Press a glass slide on the lesion: redness that fades is vasodilation; colour that stays is purpura.

manas.q: How does diascopy separate erythema from purpura?

children.note: Rubbing a lesion makes it swell and redden from mast cell release; seen in mastocytosis.

manas.q: What is Darier sign?

children.note: A system so nothing is missed.
Good light, full exposure with a chaperone as needed; include scalp, nails, mouth and genitals.

manas.q: Which areas are often missed in a skin examination?

children.note: Feel texture, warmth, tenderness, depth and mobility; check if the lesion blanches.

manas.q: What should you feel for when palpating a lesion?

children.note: Skin scraping with KOH for fungi, swab for culture, Wood's lamp, and punch biopsy for histology.

manas.q: Name simple bedside investigations in dermatology.

children.note: A handheld lit magnifier that shows structures not seen by the naked eye; aids pigmented lesions and more.

manas.q: What is dermoscopy used for?

children.note: Skin of colour is the norm for most Kenyan patients; textbooks often show lighter skin.
Inflammation may look violet, dusky, brown or grey rather than red; use warmth, swelling and tenderness too.

manas.q: How may inflammation look in darker skin?

children.note: Post-inflammatory hyper- or hypopigmentation is common and slow to fade in darker skin; warn patients.

manas.q: What often follows inflammation in darker skin?

children.note: Six types (I to VI) based on tendency to burn or tan; types V and VI are darker skin.

manas.q: What does the Fitzpatrick scale classify?

children.note: High-yield contrasts.
Pemphigus: intraepidermal, flaccid blisters, erosions, mouth involved. Pemphigoid: subepidermal, tense blisters, elderly.

manas.q: Contrast pemphigus vulgaris and bullous pemphigoid.

children.note: Blanching redness is vasodilation; non-blanching spots are bleeding and may signal sepsis or low platelets.

manas.q: Why does a non-blanching rash matter?

children.note: Only damage reaching the dermis scars; epidermal loss heals completely.

manas.q: Why does an erosion heal without a scar?

children.note: Papers read 2026-10-19.
Survey of 196 dermatologists in 24 African countries: about half used dermoscopy; main barriers were lack of training and dermatoscopes.

manas.q: What limits dermoscopy use by dermatologists in Africa?

children.note: US review: dark skin is under-shown in textbooks and training, which contributes to missed or late diagnoses.

manas.q: Why does poor skin-of-colour teaching matter?

maps.title: HME 602 · In depth: Rational prescribing and the EML

nodeData.topic: Rational prescribing and the EML in depth
nodeData.note: From choosing a drug to stopping it: EML concepts, dosing, special groups, ADRs and interactions. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Key terms behind the course bubble.
Patients get medicines suited to their clinical need, in doses fitting them, for the right length of time, at the lowest cost to them and society.

manas.q: What is the WHO definition of rational use of medicines?

children.note: The WHO conference of experts that framed rational drug use met in Nairobi, Kenya, in 1985.

manas.q: Where and when did the WHO conference on rational drug use meet?

children.note: Medicines that meet a population's priority health needs, chosen on disease burden, evidence of efficacy and safety, and cost-effectiveness.

manas.q: What are essential medicines and how are they selected?

children.note: Too many drugs per patient, antibiotics for viral illness, injections when oral would do, ignoring guidelines, and self-medication.

manas.q: Give examples of irrational medicine use.

children.note: The template for national lists such as Kenya's.
First published in 1977; WHO revises it every two years.

manas.q: When was the first WHO Model List published and how often is it revised?

children.note: Core: minimum medicines for a basic health system. Complementary: need specialist care, tests or training.

manas.q: What is the difference between the core and complementary lists?

children.note: A separate Model List for children (EMLc) has existed since 2007.

manas.q: Since when has WHO published an essential medicines list for children?

children.note: Access (first/second choice, lower resistance risk), Watch (higher resistance risk, limit use) and Reserve (last resort).

manas.q: What do the three AWaRe antibiotic groups mean?

children.note: Using the current Kenya Essential Medicines List (KEML) at the bedside and in supply.
In public facilities, choose listed generics suited to your level of care so the drug is stocked and affordable.

manas.q: Why should public-sector prescribers choose from the KEML?

children.note: Write the international non-proprietary name: cheaper, avoids brand confusion and allows substitution.

manas.q: Why prescribe by generic name?

children.note: Pharmacy and Poisons Board registers medicines and runs pharmacovigilance; KEMSA supplies public facilities.

manas.q: What are the roles of the Pharmacy and Poisons Board and KEMSA?

children.note: The KEML is meant to be used with national clinical guidelines that set first-line treatments.

manas.q: What should the KEML be used together with?

children.note: WHO Guide to Good Prescribing (1994) method.
Be clear what you are treating and what the treatment should achieve before picking a drug.

manas.q: What two things come first when choosing a P-drug?

children.note: List effective groups and compare them on efficacy, safety, suitability and cost.

manas.q: On which four criteria are drug groups compared?

children.note: Choose the drug within the group, then dosage form, dose schedule and duration.

manas.q: After choosing a group, what else must be decided?

children.note: Confirm the P-drug suits this patient: allergies, interactions, pregnancy, kidney and liver function, cost.

manas.q: What must be checked before giving your P-drug to an individual?

children.note: The best P-treatment may be advice or no drug at all.

manas.q: Is a drug always needed in rational treatment?

children.note: Kinetics that drive dose choice.
Reached after about 4–5 half-lives of regular dosing; same rule for wash-out after stopping.

manas.q: How long does a drug take to reach steady state?

children.note: Loading dose = target concentration × volume of distribution; used when steady state would take too long.

manas.q: What determines the loading dose?

children.note: Depends on clearance: maintenance rate = clearance × target concentration.

manas.q: What determines the maintenance dose?

children.note: Small gap between effective and toxic levels: digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, warfarin, aminoglycosides; monitor closely.

manas.q: Name drugs with a narrow therapeutic index.

children.note: Adjust for the patient in front of you.
Reduce or avoid renally cleared drugs (e.g. aminoglycosides, metformin) by eGFR or creatinine clearance; avoid NSAIDs.

manas.q: How should prescribing change in kidney impairment?

children.note: No single test guides dosing; take care with sedatives and opioids that can tip patients into encephalopathy.

manas.q: Which drugs need special care in liver disease?

children.note: Avoid known teratogens such as warfarin, ACE inhibitors, valproate, isotretinoin, methotrexate and tetracyclines.

manas.q: Name drugs to avoid in pregnancy because of fetal harm.

children.note: Dose by weight (or body surface area), use child formulations; avoid aspirin (Reye syndrome).

manas.q: Why is aspirin avoided in children?

children.note: Lower kidney function and higher drug sensitivity: start low, go slow, review often.

manas.q: What is the prescribing principle for older adults?

children.note: Check whether the drug passes into milk and could affect the baby before prescribing.

manas.q: What must be checked before prescribing in breastfeeding?

children.note: Beyond the basic contents.
Record drug allergies and the reaction type before prescribing.

manas.q: What should be recorded before writing any prescription?

children.note: State dose form, route, frequency and duration or total quantity so the dispenser need not guess.

manas.q: What details stop dispensing errors?

children.note: Opioids and some sedatives are controlled under Kenya's Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (Control) Act; extra rules apply.

manas.q: Which Kenyan law controls opioid prescribing?

children.note: Explain effect, how to take it, common side effects, warning signs and when to return.

manas.q: What should a patient be told about a new medicine?

children.note: Recognise, classify and report.
Predictable, dose-related extension of the drug's action and common, e.g. bleeding on warfarin.

manas.q: What is a type A adverse drug reaction?

children.note: Unpredictable, not dose-related, often immune: anaphylaxis, SJS/TEN. Usually requires stopping the drug.

manas.q: What is a type B adverse drug reaction?

children.note: C chronic (long use), D delayed (e.g. teratogenesis), E end-of-use (withdrawal), F failure of therapy.

manas.q: What do ADR types C, D, E and F stand for?

children.note: Suspected adverse reactions and poor-quality medicines are reported to Kenya's Pharmacy and Poisons Board.

manas.q: Where are suspected ADRs reported in Kenya?

children.note: Pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic.
Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital and St John's wort lower levels of other drugs.

manas.q: Name common enzyme-inducing drugs.

children.note: Macrolides (e.g. clarithromycin) and azole antifungals (e.g. fluconazole) raise levels of other drugs.

manas.q: Name common enzyme-inhibiting drugs.

children.note: Rifampicin makes hormonal contraceptives less reliable; advise a method not affected, such as an IUD or injectable.

manas.q: Why does rifampicin matter for contraception?

children.note: Drugs with added effects, e.g. two sedatives, or two QT-prolonging drugs.

manas.q: Give an example of a pharmacodynamic interaction.

children.note: The last WHO step in depth.
Decide in advance what to check (effect, toxicity, levels) and when.

manas.q: What should a monitoring plan include?

children.note: Planned reduction or stopping of drugs where harm now outweighs benefit, agreed with the patient.

manas.q: What is deprescribing?

children.note: Benzodiazepines, steroids, beta-blockers and antidepressants need tapering to avoid withdrawal or rebound.

manas.q: Name drug classes that need tapering when stopped.

children.note: Simple once-daily regimens, clear counselling and checking cost help patients take medicines as intended.

manas.q: How can adherence be improved?

children.note: Rational prescribing applied to antibiotics.
Right drug, dose, route and duration; take cultures when possible; review at 48–72 hours.

manas.q: What are the core steps of antibiotic stewardship?

children.note: Most upper respiratory infections are viral; antibiotics add harm and drive resistance.

manas.q: Why avoid antibiotics for the common cold?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then where others differ.
Current KEML with national clinical guidelines; PPB regulates medicines; KEMSA supplies public facilities.

manas.q: Which documents and bodies guide prescribing in Kenya?

children.note: Model List for adults and children, updated every two years, with AWaRe guidance for antibiotics.

manas.q: What WHO tools support rational prescribing?

children.note: The BNF and BNF for Children are the standard prescribing references; NICE gives guidance.

manas.q: What is the standard prescribing reference in the UK?

children.note: Publishes its own National List of Essential Medicines (latest 2022).

manas.q: What is India's essential medicines list called?

children.note: Beers criteria (American Geriatrics Society) and STOPP/START (Europe) flag risky drugs in older people.

manas.q: Name two tools for spotting inappropriate drugs in older adults.

children.note: High-yield points.
A is common, dose-related, predictable; B is rare, not dose-related, unpredictable.

manas.q: Contrast type A and type B ADRs.

children.note: Adding an inducer can make the other drug fail; stopping it can cause toxicity.

manas.q: Why can stopping an enzyme inducer cause toxicity?

children.note: Rational drug use was defined at a WHO meeting in Nairobi in 1985.

manas.q: Which Kenyan city hosted the 1985 rational drug use meeting?

children.note: Papers read 2026-10-19.
Review of 74 studies: 16 used the WHO 6-step model; effect was mostly judged by satisfaction or tests, rarely by behaviour or patient outcomes.

manas.q: How is rational prescribing teaching usually evaluated?

children.note: 11 of 12 studies found medical students wrote better prescriptions after added teaching; formal teaching and assessment advised.

manas.q: Does extra prescription-writing teaching help medical students?

children.note: Most trials used medication reviews in primary care; just over half beat usual care on at least one main outcome.

manas.q: How did deprescribing trials in older adults perform?

maps.title: HOS 600 · In depth: Nonunion and chronic osteomyelitis

nodeData.topic: Nonunion and chronic osteomyelitis in depth
nodeData.note: Why fractures fail to heal, how bone infection persists, and how both are investigated and reconstructed. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Healing is taking longer than expected for that bone and injury, but is still progressing and may unite without new intervention.

manas.q: What is delayed union?

children.note: Healing has stopped and will not complete without intervention. A widely quoted (FDA) cut-off: at least 9 months after injury with no progress for 3 months.

manas.q: How is fracture nonunion defined?

children.note: A long-standing nonunion in which a fibrous or synovium-lined false joint forms between the fragments, allowing painless or painful movement.

manas.q: What is a pseudarthrosis?

children.note: Persistent or relapsing bone infection, typically beyond about 6 weeks; its hallmark is dead (necrotic) bone harbouring bacteria.

manas.q: What is the hallmark of chronic osteomyelitis?

children.note: Infection of a fracture site, with or without implants. Confirmed by a sinus or wound breakdown reaching bone/implant, pus, same organism in ≥2 deep samples, or organisms on histology.

manas.q: Which findings confirm a fracture-related infection?

children.note: Key terms for failed healing and persistent bone infection.
Healing needs osteogenic cells, an osteoconductive scaffold, osteoinductive growth signals, mechanical stability and an adequate blood supply. Nonunion means one or more is missing.

manas.q: What are the elements of the 'diamond concept' of fracture healing?

children.note: Absolute stability (compression plating) gives direct healing without callus; relative stability (nails, casts, bridging plates) heals by callus.

manas.q: Which fixation gives primary bone healing and which gives callus healing?

children.note: Tissue formed depends on strain at the gap: under about 2% bone forms, 2–10% cartilage, above 10% only granulation tissue — too much movement blocks union.

manas.q: What does Perren's strain theory predict?

children.note: Bacteria stuck to dead bone or implants live in a protective matrix that resists antibiotics and immune cells — why chronic infection needs surgical removal.

manas.q: Why can antibiotics alone rarely cure chronic osteomyelitis?

children.note: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause; Salmonella is a classic cause in sickle cell disease; open fractures add Gram-negatives and mixed flora.

manas.q: Which organisms commonly cause chronic osteomyelitis?

children.note: What bone needs to unite, and why infection persists.
Little or no callus but viable bone ends — often from displacement or a gap; needs reduction and contact, sometimes graft.

manas.q: What is an oligotrophic nonunion?

children.note: Nonunion with infection: treat both — remove dead bone and implants as needed, control infection, then stabilise and reconstruct.

manas.q: What are the principles of treating an infected nonunion?

children.note: I medullary, II superficial (cortex surface), III localised full-thickness but stable, IV diffuse and mechanically unstable.

manas.q: What are the four Cierny–Mader anatomic types of osteomyelitis?

children.note: A: healthy host. B: local and/or systemic compromise (e.g. diabetes, smoking, poor skin). C: treatment would harm more than the disease.

manas.q: What are the Cierny–Mader host classes?

children.note: Types of nonunion and staging of osteomyelitis.
Smoking, diabetes, obesity, malnutrition and long-term steroids all impair healing; optimise them before reconstruction.

manas.q: Which patient factors predispose to nonunion?

children.note: Open and high-energy fractures, bone loss, soft-tissue stripping, infection, inadequate stability or a residual gap.

manas.q: Which injury and surgical factors predispose to nonunion?

children.note: Scaphoid waist/proximal pole, distal-third tibia, femoral neck and proximal fifth metatarsal metadiaphysis (Jones) — all have precarious blood supply.

manas.q: Name four fracture sites prone to nonunion.

children.note: Patient, injury and surgical factors.
Ongoing pain at the fracture, pain on loading, abnormal movement or deformity, and broken or loosening implants.

manas.q: How does a nonunion present?

children.note: Discharging sinus, recurrent flares of pain and swelling, bone thickening and tenderness; fever is often absent between flares.

manas.q: How does chronic osteomyelitis present?

children.note: Late presentation, untreated childhood haematogenous infection and poorly managed open fractures drive much of the burden.

manas.q: Why is chronic osteomyelitis common in low-resource settings?

children.note: How these patients present.
Persistent fracture line, rounded sclerotic bone ends, absent or non-bridging callus; in infection, periosteal reaction, lytic areas and dense sequestra.

manas.q: What X-ray signs suggest nonunion?

children.note: Tibial union score: each of 4 cortices on AP and lateral films scores 1–3 (line visible, callus, bridged); total 4–12.

manas.q: How is the RUST score calculated?

children.note: CT confirms bridging and shows sequestra; MRI maps marrow spread, abscesses and sinus tracts.

manas.q: What do CT and MRI add in nonunion and osteomyelitis?

children.note: FBC, ESR and CRP; normal values do not exclude low-grade infection. In unexplained atrophic nonunion check glucose, vitamin D, calcium and thyroid.

manas.q: Do normal ESR and CRP exclude an infected nonunion?

children.note: Take several deep samples with separate instruments at surgery; avoid sinus swabs, which grow colonisers. Withhold antibiotics beforehand if clinically safe.

manas.q: How should samples be taken to diagnose bone infection?

children.note: Imaging, bloods and sampling.
Stop smoking, control diabetes, correct nutrition and vitamin D deficiency before or alongside surgery.

manas.q: What host measures support nonunion surgery?

children.note: For aseptic femoral/tibial shaft nonunion after nailing: ream and insert a larger nail, or add a plate around the nail.

manas.q: How is aseptic shaft nonunion after nailing managed?

children.note: Iliac crest autograft is the gold standard: it is osteogenic, osteoinductive and osteoconductive.

manas.q: Why is autograft the gold standard bone graft?

children.note: Stage 1: debride and fill defect with cement spacer; a membrane forms over weeks. Stage 2: remove spacer, pack the membrane with bone graft.

manas.q: Describe the Masquelet induced-membrane technique.

children.note: Circular frame with corticotomy and gradual distraction (distraction osteogenesis) grows new bone to fill defects and corrects deformity.

manas.q: How does Ilizarov bone transport fill a bone defect?

children.note: Fix the mechanics, fix the biology, fix the host.
Orthopaedic, plastic surgery, microbiology and infectious diseases together: debride, manage dead space, stabilise, cover soft tissue, target antibiotics.

manas.q: What are the five steps of surgical management of bone infection?

children.note: Remove all dead bone until punctate cortical bleeding (the 'paprika sign') shows healthy bone.

manas.q: What is the 'paprika sign'?

children.note: Antibiotic-loaded PMMA beads/spacers (must be removed later) or absorbable carriers such as calcium sulphate; muscle flaps also fill space.

manas.q: What options exist for dead space management?

children.note: Early infection with a stable implant: debridement, antibiotics and implant retention (DAIR). Late infection or loose implant: remove or exchange.

manas.q: When can an infected fracture implant be retained?

children.note: Long courses, culture-directed: often about 6 weeks if implants removed and up to 12 weeks if retained.

manas.q: How long are antibiotics given for fracture-related infection?

children.note: Considered when the limb cannot be salvaged, the host is class C, or the patient prefers a faster return to function.

manas.q: When is amputation considered in chronic osteomyelitis?

children.note: Surgery first; antibiotics support it.
Pathological fracture, limb shortening or angular deformity (physeal damage in children), joint stiffness and chronic pain.

manas.q: What local complications follow chronic osteomyelitis?

children.note: Long-standing suppuration can cause AA amyloidosis, presenting with proteinuria and renal failure.

manas.q: Which systemic complication can follow years of bone suppuration?

children.note: Infection can flare years or decades later, so follow-up is long and 'arrest' is preferred to 'cure'.

manas.q: Why is chronic osteomyelitis described as arrested rather than cured?

children.note: Long-term consequences.
Screen every nonunion for infection before reconstruction — an occult infection will make grafting fail.

manas.q: Why must infection be excluded in every nonunion?

children.note: Appears denser (whiter) than surrounding bone because it is dead and not remodelled.

manas.q: Why does a sequestrum look dense on X-ray?

children.note: Adding stability alone will not heal an atrophic nonunion — it also needs graft or biological stimulation.

manas.q: Why does rigid fixation alone fail in atrophic nonunion?

children.note: High-yield points.
The Kenya MoH Clinical Guidelines for Level 4–6 hospitals are the national reference for hospital care; check them for local antibiotic and referral advice.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline is the national reference for Level 4–6 hospital care?

children.note: WHO global SSI guidance advises against prolonging antibiotic prophylaxis after the operation ends.

manas.q: Does WHO advise continuing prophylactic antibiotics after surgery?

children.note: International expert group that set the confirmatory and suggestive criteria for fracture-related infection used worldwide.

manas.q: Who defined the criteria for fracture-related infection?

children.note: A 2022 review found FRI consensus authors were mostly from high-income countries; core principles still apply, but infrastructure limits standardisation.

manas.q: How applicable are FRI consensus guidelines to low-income settings?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then international consensus.
Papers read 2026-10-19.
Meta-analysis of 30 studies (38,465 patients): infection raised odds about 7-fold; open fracture, smoking, diabetes and obesity also linked. Evidence mostly low quality.

manas.q: Which risk factor most raised nonunion odds after operated shaft fractures?

children.note: Review of 42 studies (1,605 adults): pooled cure 91% for long-bone chronic osteomyelitis with no clear difference between single- and two-stage surgery.

manas.q: Is two-stage surgery better than single-stage for long-bone chronic osteomyelitis?

children.note: No low-income country authors on FRI consensus papers; diagnosis approach and team working are achievable, but local evidence is lacking.

manas.q: Which parts of FRI consensus are achievable in low-resource settings?

maps.title: HPS 600 · In depth: Psychiatric emergencies

nodeData.note: Safety first, medical causes next: agitation, suicide, delirium, alcohol withdrawal and drug reactions. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What counts as an emergency and the first steps.
An acute disturbance of mood, thought or behaviour carrying an immediate risk of harm to self or others, or of serious medical deterioration.

manas.q: What is a psychiatric emergency?

children.note: Never interview a potentially violent patient alone; keep a clear exit for both of you, know the alarm and remove potential weapons.

manas.q: How do you make the interview setting safe?

children.note: Check airway, vital signs and blood glucose early: an 'acute psychiatric' presentation may be hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, infection or intoxication.

manas.q: Which bedside checks come first in any behavioural emergency?

children.note: Calm words before medicines, medicines before restraint.
One calm staff member speaks; respect personal space, listen, acknowledge feelings, set clear limits and offer real choices (e.g. oral medicine, food, quiet room).

manas.q: Name key verbal de-escalation techniques.

children.note: Last resort: least restrictive, shortest time, trained staff, avoid pressure on chest/neck, continuous observation and full documentation.

manas.q: What are the safety rules for physical restraint?

children.note: After rapid tranquillisation check pulse, BP, temperature, respiratory rate, SpO2 and consciousness regularly until the patient is fully alert and active.

manas.q: What must be monitored after rapid tranquillisation?

children.note: Benzodiazepines: respiratory depression (flumazenil reverses). Haloperidol: acute dystonia, QT prolongation and arrhythmia — get an ECG when possible.

manas.q: What are the main risks of IM benzodiazepines and haloperidol?

children.note: Assess, then make safe.
Asking openly about suicidal thoughts does not plant the idea or raise risk; it often brings relief and opens help.

manas.q: Does asking about suicide increase suicide risk?

children.note: Previous attempt (strongest predictor), depression and other mental disorder, substance misuse, chronic illness or pain, recent loss, isolation and access to means.

manas.q: What is the strongest single predictor of suicide?

children.note: Thoughts, plans, intent, preparations, access to means, lethality of any attempt, hopelessness, and protective factors such as family and faith.

manas.q: What elements make up a suicide risk assessment?

children.note: If risk is imminent: do not leave alone, remove means (pesticides, drugs, sharps), supervised setting, involve family, safety plan and arrange follow-up.

manas.q: What immediate steps protect a patient at imminent suicide risk?

children.note: Medical stabilisation comes first — e.g. pesticide (organophosphate) poisoning, a common method in rural low-income settings.

manas.q: Which self-poisoning is common in low-income rural settings?

children.note: Exclude an organic cause before labelling psychosis.
Acute onset, fluctuating course, inattention and altered consciousness, disorientation, often worse at night; hallucinations are often visual.

manas.q: What are the core features of delirium?

children.note: First episode in later life, sudden onset, abnormal vital signs, disorientation, visual or tactile hallucinations, focal neurology or recent head injury.

manas.q: Which features suggest an organic cause of acute psychosis?

children.note: Hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, sepsis, cerebral malaria, meningitis/encephalitis, HIV-related CNS infection, intoxication or withdrawal, electrolyte, liver or renal failure, drugs.

manas.q: List important organic causes to exclude in acute confusion.

children.note: Glucose, FBC, electrolytes, renal and liver tests, calcium, malaria test, HIV test, urinalysis; CT and lumbar puncture when indicated.

manas.q: What basic tests screen for organic causes of acute behaviour change?

children.note: Treat the cause, reorient, keep family near, good lighting and sleep; low-dose antipsychotic only for severe distress or danger. Avoid benzos unless alcohol/benzo withdrawal.

manas.q: How is delirium managed?

children.note: Can cause vivid dreams, insomnia, mood change and occasionally psychosis — check ARV history in people living with HIV.

manas.q: Which antiretroviral is known for neuropsychiatric side effects?

children.note: From tremor to delirium tremens.
Tremor, sweating and anxiety from 6–24 h after the last drink; seizures mostly 12–48 h; delirium tremens usually from 48–72 h.

manas.q: What is the timeline of alcohol withdrawal?

children.note: Confusion, vivid visual or tactile hallucinations, marked autonomic overactivity and fever; potentially fatal medical emergency.

manas.q: What are the features of delirium tremens?

children.note: First-line: long-acting benzodiazepine (chlordiazepoxide or diazepam); lorazepam if liver failure. CIWA-Ar score can guide symptom-triggered dosing.

manas.q: What is first-line treatment of alcohol withdrawal?

children.note: Confusion, eye signs (nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia) and ataxia; full triad often absent. Give parenteral thiamine before glucose.

manas.q: What is the classic triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy?

children.note: Chronic amnestic state after thiamine deficiency: severe new-learning deficit with confabulation.

manas.q: What characterises Korsakoff syndrome?

children.note: Building on NMS, serotonin syndrome and lithium basics.
High-potency or depot antipsychotics, rapid dose increase, dehydration, agitation and restraint.

manas.q: What raises the risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

children.note: Rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury, aspiration, DVT/PE and seizures; check CK, renal function and urine for myoglobin.

manas.q: What are the major complications of NMS?

children.note: Wait at least 2 weeks after recovery, then a lower-potency or second-generation antipsychotic at a low dose, titrated slowly with close monitoring.

manas.q: How should antipsychotics be restarted after NMS?

children.note: Combinations of SSRIs/SNRIs with tramadol, MAOIs, linezolid, triptans or other serotonergic drugs, or overdose.

manas.q: Which drug combinations trigger serotonin syndrome?

children.note: Diagnosis centres on clonus (spontaneous, inducible or ocular) with agitation, sweating, tremor, hyperreflexia or fever after a serotonergic drug.

manas.q: Which sign is central to the Hunter criteria for serotonin syndrome?

children.note: Stop serotonergic drugs, supportive care and benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist) in moderate cases; ICU for hyperthermia.

manas.q: How is serotonin syndrome treated?

children.note: Coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, then seizures and coma.

manas.q: What are the features of lithium toxicity?

children.note: Dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and thiazide diuretics raise lithium levels.

manas.q: Which drugs and states precipitate lithium toxicity?

children.note: Take 12 h after the last dose. Usual target about 0.4–1.0 mmol/L; toxicity becomes likely above 1.5 mmol/L.

manas.q: When should a lithium level be taken, and what level suggests toxicity?

children.note: Early extrapyramidal emergencies.
Within hours to days of starting antipsychotics (especially haloperidol), commoner in young men: torticollis, oculogyric crisis, tongue protrusion, trismus.

manas.q: What is acute dystonia and who gets it?

children.note: Rare but life-threatening: stridor and airway compromise — treat urgently.

manas.q: Which form of acute dystonia threatens life?

children.note: Parenteral anticholinergic (e.g. procyclidine, benztropine or biperiden) or diphenhydramine; usually resolves within minutes.

manas.q: How is acute dystonia treated?

children.note: Inner restlessness with inability to sit still; often mistaken for worsening agitation and linked to impulsivity and suicidality.

manas.q: Why is akathisia dangerous to miss?

children.note: A treatable motor syndrome.
Stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, staring, echolalia and echopraxia; rated with the Bush–Francis scale.

manas.q: What are the features of catatonia?

children.note: Mood disorders (commonest), schizophrenia, autism, and medical causes such as encephalitis (including anti-NMDA receptor) and metabolic disease.

manas.q: What conditions cause catatonia?

children.note: A benzodiazepine trial is both diagnostic and first-line treatment; a clear response supports catatonia.

manas.q: What is the first-line treatment of catatonia?

children.note: Used when benzodiazepines fail and urgently in malignant catatonia.

manas.q: When is ECT used for catatonia?

children.note: Catatonia with fever and autonomic instability — overlaps with NMS; avoid antipsychotics and treat as an emergency.

manas.q: What is malignant catatonia?

children.note: Dehydration, malnutrition, DVT/PE, pressure sores, aspiration pneumonia and contractures.

manas.q: What medical complications occur in catatonia?

children.note: High-yield points.
Clonus and hyperreflexia point to serotonin syndrome; lead-pipe rigidity with slow reflexes points to NMS.

manas.q: Which examination finding separates serotonin syndrome from NMS?

children.note: In malnourished or alcohol-dependent patients give thiamine before or with glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke's.

manas.q: Why give thiamine before glucose in alcohol-dependent patients?

children.note: New visual hallucinations suggest delirium, intoxication or withdrawal until proven otherwise.

manas.q: What do new visual hallucinations suggest?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then where other guidance differs.
Kenya's National Clinical Guidelines for Management of Common Mental Disorders are the local reference for acute care pathways.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers common mental disorders?

children.note: The mhGAP Intervention Guide supports non-specialists to manage self-harm/suicide, psychosis and substance withdrawal, with explicit emergency steps.

manas.q: What does WHO mhGAP provide for non-specialist health workers?

children.note: UK rapid tranquillisation: IM lorazepam alone, or IM haloperidol with IM promethazine, chosen by history and ECG.

manas.q: Which IM options does NICE NG10 give for rapid tranquillisation?

children.note: Advises against using risk tools or scales to predict suicide or to decide who gets treatment; focus on needs and safety planning.

manas.q: What does NICE 2022 say about suicide risk prediction tools?

children.note: British Association for Psychopharmacology consensus guideline on catatonia: benzodiazepines and ECT central; based mainly on small observational studies.

manas.q: On what evidence is the 2023 BAP catatonia guideline mostly based?

children.note: Papers read 2026-10-19.
Traditional suicide prediction has repeatedly failed; authors propose treating all patients as possibly at risk with person-centred formulation and joint safety plans.

manas.q: Why do authors argue against suicide risk prediction?

children.note: Network meta-analysis of 149 trials: several fixed-schedule benzos cut withdrawal seizures, but only fixed-schedule diazepam cut delirium tremens.

manas.q: Which drug alone reduced delirium tremens in a 149-trial network meta-analysis?

children.note: BAP consensus covers benzodiazepines, ECT and malignant catatonia; trials are rare, so advice rests mainly on small observational studies, case series and reports.

manas.q: What evidence underpins catatonia treatment recommendations?

maps.title: HSU 600 · In depth: The acute abdomen

nodeData.note: Pain mechanisms, causes by site, tests, resuscitation and when to operate. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What counts as an acute abdomen and what can mimic it.
Sudden-onset abdominal pain (hours to a few days) from a condition that may need urgent surgery or other urgent intervention.

manas.q: What is meant by the 'acute abdomen'?

children.note: DKA, inferior myocardial infarction, lower-lobe pneumonia, sickle cell crisis, acute porphyria and herpes zoster can all present with abdominal pain.

manas.q: Name medical conditions that can mimic a surgical acute abdomen.

children.note: How abdominal pain is generated and why its site changes.
Dull, poorly localised, felt in the midline; comes from stretch or ischaemia of an organ's wall via autonomic afferents.

manas.q: What are the features of visceral abdominal pain?

children.note: Foregut organs hurt in the epigastrium, midgut in the periumbilical area, hindgut in the suprapubic area.

manas.q: Where is visceral pain from foregut, midgut and hindgut organs felt?

children.note: Sharp, well localised and worse on movement or coughing; arises when inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum.

manas.q: What causes sharp, well-localised abdominal pain worse on movement?

children.note: Early periumbilical visceral pain shifts to the right iliac fossa once the inflamed appendix irritates parietal peritoneum.

manas.q: Why does appendicitis pain move from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa?

children.note: Colicky pain suggests obstruction of a hollow tube (gut, ureter); constant pain suggests inflammation, ischaemia or peritonitis.

manas.q: What does colicky abdominal pain usually indicate?

children.note: Recognising the common patterns.
Inspiratory arrest on palpating the right upper quadrant suggests acute cholecystitis.

manas.q: What is Murphy's sign and what does it suggest?

children.note: Severe constant epigastric pain radiating to the back, often eased by leaning forward; gallstones and alcohol are the main causes.

manas.q: How does acute pancreatitis pain typically present?

children.note: Sudden severe epigastric pain that rapidly becomes generalised peritonitis; may follow NSAID use.

manas.q: What is the classic presentation of a perforated peptic ulcer?

children.note: Tenderness at McBurney's point; Rovsing's sign (left iliac pressure causes right-sided pain); psoas and obturator signs for retrocaecal/pelvic sites.

manas.q: Which signs support acute appendicitis on examination?

children.note: Colicky pain, vomiting, abdominal distension and absolute constipation (no stool or flatus).

manas.q: What are the four cardinal features of intestinal obstruction?

children.note: Small bowel obstruction: early vomiting, less distension. Large bowel obstruction: early distension and constipation, late vomiting.

manas.q: How does small bowel obstruction differ clinically from large bowel obstruction?

children.note: Adhesions after surgery and obstructed hernias are leading causes; sigmoid volvulus is an important cause of large bowel obstruction in East Africa.

manas.q: What are common causes of intestinal obstruction in Kenyan adults?

children.note: Colicky pain with drawing up of legs, vomiting, a sausage-shaped mass and redcurrant-jelly stool.

manas.q: What are the classic features of intussusception in an infant?

children.note: Older patient with abdominal or back pain, a pulsatile mass and shock; go straight to theatre if unstable.

manas.q: How does a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm present?

children.note: Tests in order, from bedside to imaging.
Urine dipstick (infection, blood in stones), capillary glucose and ketones (DKA), ECG (inferior MI).

manas.q: Which bedside tests should be done in every acute abdomen?

children.note: FBC, urea and electrolytes, LFTs, amylase or lipase, lactate, blood gas, and group and crossmatch if surgery is likely.

manas.q: Which blood tests are routine in an acute abdomen?

children.note: A level over three times the upper limit of normal, with typical pain, supports acute pancreatitis.

manas.q: What amylase or lipase level supports acute pancreatitis?

children.note: Dilated if small bowel >3 cm, colon >6 cm, caecum >9 cm.

manas.q: What is the 3-6-9 rule on abdominal X-ray?

children.topic: Small bowel vs colon on X-ray
children.note: Small bowel: central, valvulae conniventes cross the full width. Colon: peripheral, haustra cross only part of the width.

manas.q: How do you tell dilated small bowel from colon on X-ray?

children.note: A large inverted-U loop arising from the pelvis on abdominal X-ray suggests sigmoid volvulus.

manas.q: What does the coffee-bean sign on abdominal X-ray suggest?

children.note: Ultrasound is first choice for gallstones, cholecystitis and gynaecological causes, and avoids radiation in pregnancy and children.

manas.q: For which suspected causes is ultrasound the first imaging test?

children.note: Contrast CT is the most informative test for many adult causes, e.g. perforation, obstruction level and ischaemia, if the patient is stable.

manas.q: What is the most informative imaging test in a stable adult with an acute abdomen?

children.note: Migration, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, RIF tenderness (2), rebound, fever, leucocytosis (2), left shift. Total 10; ≥7 makes appendicitis likely.

manas.q: What are the components of the Alvarado score for appendicitis?

children.note: Resuscitate first, then decide on theatre.
ABC, IV access and crystalloid, analgesia, nil by mouth, catheter to monitor urine output, antibiotics if peritonitis or sepsis.

manas.q: What are the first steps in managing a sick patient with an acute abdomen?

children.note: Trials show early opioid analgesia does not reduce diagnostic accuracy or worsen management decisions; do not withhold it awaiting surgical review.

manas.q: Should analgesia be withheld until the surgeon examines the patient?

children.note: Decompresses the stomach in obstruction or persistent vomiting and reduces aspiration risk.

manas.q: Why insert a nasogastric tube in bowel obstruction?

children.note: Generalised peritonitis, free gas with peritonitis, strangulated obstruction, or haemodynamic instability from intra-abdominal bleeding.

manas.q: What are indications for urgent laparotomy?

children.note: Without signs of strangulation, a trial of conservative care (drip and suck) is usual; operate if it fails or strangulation appears.

manas.q: How is uncomplicated adhesive small bowel obstruction first managed?

children.note: If bowel is viable: endoscopic detorsion and a flatus tube, then planned sigmoid colectomy because recurrence is common. Gangrene needs resection.

manas.q: How is sigmoid volvulus managed?

children.note: Usually closure with an omental patch, then H. pylori eradication and acid suppression.

manas.q: What is the usual operation for a perforated peptic ulcer?

children.note: What goes wrong and who does worse.
Pain becomes constant, with fever, tachycardia, localised tenderness or peritonism, rising WBC and lactate.

manas.q: Which features suggest strangulated bowel obstruction?

children.note: Sepsis, intra-abdominal abscess, wound infection or burst abdomen, anastomotic leak, fistula, AKI and later adhesions.

manas.q: List complications after emergency abdominal surgery.

children.note: Elderly, immunosuppressed, steroid-treated and diabetic patients may have few signs despite serious pathology.

manas.q: Which patients may show few abdominal signs despite serious disease?

children.note: High-yield points for wards and exams.
Always examine hernial orifices and the external genitalia; an obstructed hernia or testicular torsion is easily missed.

manas.q: Which areas must be examined in every acute abdomen?

children.note: Amylase can also rise in perforated ulcer, mesenteric ischaemia and ruptured ectopic, so interpret it with the clinical picture.

manas.q: Name non-pancreatic causes of a raised serum amylase.

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
Follow the MoH Clinical Guidelines for Level 4–6 hospitals, linked below, and your local surgical protocol.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers hospital care of surgical emergencies?

children.note: WHO recommends typhoid conjugate vaccine in endemic countries, which should cut typhoid and its perforations.

manas.q: What WHO-recommended vaccine can reduce typhoid perforation?

children.note: The World Society of Emergency Surgery issues appendicitis (Jerusalem) and adhesive obstruction (Bologna) guidelines.

manas.q: Which society publishes the Jerusalem and Bologna guidelines?

children.note: The UK National Emergency Laparotomy Audit tracks outcomes and promotes formal risk assessment before emergency laparotomy.

manas.q: What does the UK National Emergency Laparotomy Audit do?

children.note: Papers read 2026-10-19.
Cochrane (13 RCTs): about 31% of antibiotic-treated patients needed appendicectomy within a year (very uncertain); wound infections may be fewer (low certainty).

manas.q: In the 2024 Cochrane review, what share of antibiotic-treated patients needed appendicectomy in a year?

children.note: Pooled patient data (5 studies): emergency POCUS had about 83% sensitivity and 93% specificity for SBO; less sensitive with residents and at BMI ≥30.

manas.q: How accurate is point-of-care ultrasound for small bowel obstruction?

children.note: Meta-analysis of 3 RCTs (570 patients): early routine CT gave more correct diagnoses at 24 h and lower 6-month mortality than selective CT.

manas.q: What did RCTs show for early routine CT in acute abdominal pain?

children.note: Review of 32 studies (Francophone Africa): typhoid perforation caused a median 35% of peritonitis cases; median mortality 16%; mostly young people.

manas.q: What share of peritonitis did typhoid perforation cause in the 2024 African review?

maps.title: HSU 603 · In depth: Diabetic retinopathy

nodeData.note: Staging, mechanism, signs, imaging, laser, anti-VEGF and screening worldwide. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: How diabetic eye disease is named and staged.
Progressive damage to the retinal small vessels caused by chronic hyperglycaemia; a microvascular complication of diabetes.

manas.q: What is diabetic retinopathy?

children.note: Non-proliferative (mild, moderate, severe) and proliferative, defined by new vessel growth.

manas.q: What are the two main stages of diabetic retinopathy?

children.note: Diabetic macular oedema is graded separately and can occur at any stage of retinopathy.

manas.q: Can diabetic macular oedema occur without proliferative retinopathy?

children.note: Oedema involving the central fovea threatens reading vision and is the main target for anti-VEGF treatment.

manas.q: Why does centre-involving macular oedema matter?

children.note: From high glucose to new vessels.
Hyperglycaemia causes pericyte loss and basement membrane thickening, weakening capillary walls and forming microaneurysms.

manas.q: Which cellular changes cause microaneurysms in diabetic retinopathy?

children.note: A broken blood–retinal barrier lets fluid and lipid leak out, giving retinal thickening (oedema) and hard exudates.

manas.q: What causes hard exudates and macular oedema?

children.note: Capillaries close, the retina becomes ischaemic and releases VEGF.

manas.q: What links retinal ischaemia to new vessel growth?

children.note: Fluffy white patches from infarcts of the nerve fibre layer, where axoplasmic flow stops; a sign of ischaemia.

manas.q: What are cotton wool spots?

children.note: New vessels grow onto the retina, disc or iris; they bleed easily and pull on the retina as fibrous tissue contracts.

manas.q: Why are new vessels in proliferative retinopathy dangerous?

children.note: Often silent until late.
Vision is usually normal until macular oedema or bleeding occurs, which is why screening is essential.

manas.q: Why is screening needed in diabetic retinopathy?

children.note: Gradual blurring (macular oedema), sudden floaters or painless vision loss (vitreous haemorrhage), a curtain (retinal detachment).

manas.q: What symptoms suggest vision-threatening diabetic eye disease?

children.note: Haemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 or more, or IRMA in 1 or more quadrant.

manas.q: What is the 4-2-1 rule for severe non-proliferative retinopathy?

children.note: Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities: dilated shunt vessels within the retina near closed capillaries; they signal severe ischaemia.

manas.q: What are IRMA?

children.note: New vessels on the iris can block the drainage angle and cause painful neovascular glaucoma.

manas.q: What is rubeosis iridis and what can it cause?

children.note: Examining the eye and the patient.
Dilate the pupils (e.g. tropicamide) and examine the retina, including the macula and periphery.

manas.q: How should the retina be examined for diabetic retinopathy?

children.note: Digital retinal photographs, graded by trained staff or AI, are the basis of screening programmes.

manas.q: What is the main tool of diabetic eye screening programmes?

children.note: Optical coherence tomography measures retinal thickness and detects and monitors macular oedema.

manas.q: Which test best detects and monitors diabetic macular oedema?

children.note: Shows leakage, capillary non-perfusion and new vessels; used when planning treatment.

manas.q: What does fluorescein angiography show in diabetic retinopathy?

children.note: Used when vitreous haemorrhage blocks the view, to check for retinal detachment.

manas.q: When is B-scan ultrasound used in diabetic eye disease?

children.note: HbA1c, blood pressure, lipids, renal function and urine albumin; retinopathy and nephropathy often coexist.

manas.q: Which systemic tests matter in a patient with diabetic retinopathy?

children.note: Systemic control plus eye treatment.
Better glycaemic and blood pressure control slows onset and progression; joint care with the diabetes team.

manas.q: Which systemic measures slow diabetic retinopathy?

children.note: A rapid large fall in HbA1c can briefly worsen retinopathy; review the eyes when intensifying treatment.

manas.q: What can happen to retinopathy when HbA1c falls rapidly?

children.note: In type 2 diabetes, fenofibrate cut the need for laser (FIELD) and slowed retinopathy progression when added to a statin (ACCORD-Eye).

manas.q: Which lipid drug slowed retinopathy progression in type 2 diabetes trials?

children.note: Bevacizumab, ranibizumab and aflibercept are given by intravitreal injection for centre-involving DMO with reduced vision.

manas.q: Name intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs used for diabetic macular oedema.

children.note: Intravitreal dexamethasone is an option for DMO not responding to anti-VEGF, especially in pseudophakic eyes; watch for raised IOP and cataract.

manas.q: When are intravitreal steroids used for diabetic macular oedema?

children.note: Panretinal laser can reduce peripheral field and night vision and may worsen macular oedema.

manas.q: What are the side effects of panretinal photocoagulation?

children.note: The DRCR Protocol S trial found ranibizumab non-inferior to PRP for vision in PDR at 2 years, but it needs frequent visits.

manas.q: What did Protocol S show about anti-VEGF versus PRP for PDR?

children.note: For non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage and traction detachment threatening the macula.

manas.q: What are the indications for vitrectomy in diabetic retinopathy?

children.note: What leads to blindness.
Macular oedema, vitreous haemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment and neovascular glaucoma.

manas.q: What are the sight-threatening complications of diabetic retinopathy?

children.note: Retinopathy can progress quickly in pregnancy; examine early and in each trimester if retinopathy is present.

manas.q: How should retinopathy be monitored in pregnancy?

children.note: Can worsen retinopathy and macular oedema; control DMO before and monitor after surgery.

manas.q: How can cataract surgery affect diabetic eye disease?

children.note: Timely laser or anti-VEGF greatly lowers the risk of severe vision loss; late presentation is the main problem.

manas.q: What most improves visual prognosis in diabetic retinopathy?

children.note: High-yield points.
Hypertensive: arteriolar narrowing, AV nipping, flame haemorrhages, disc swelling if severe. Diabetic: microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages.

manas.q: How do hypertensive and diabetic retinopathy differ on fundoscopy?

children.note: Proliferative retinopathy can be present with 6/6 vision; never skip fundoscopy because acuity is normal.

manas.q: Can a patient with 6/6 vision have proliferative retinopathy?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
Follow the MoH National Clinical Guidelines on Management of Diabetes (2024), linked on the course map, for local eye screening and referral.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline sets diabetic eye screening?

children.note: The International Council of Ophthalmology gives resource-graded diabetic eye care guidance for low- and high-resource settings.

manas.q: Which international body gives resource-graded diabetic eye care guidance?

children.note: Screen type 1 within 5 years of onset, type 2 at diagnosis; every 1–2 years if no retinopathy and good control; approved AI systems are an option.

manas.q: How often does ADA allow screening if there is no retinopathy?

children.note: Annual retinal photography from age 12, now extended to two-yearly for low-risk people with no retinopathy on two screens.

manas.q: How has UK diabetic eye screening changed for low-risk people?

children.note: Papers read 2026-10-19.
Meta-analysis of 30 studies (18 countries): about 1 in 4 adults with diabetes had DR; East Africa was highest at about 32%.

manas.q: About what share of adults with diabetes in sub-Saharan Africa have retinopathy?

children.note: 34 real-world studies: AI grading of fundus photos had about 94% sensitivity and 89% specificity for DR on gradable images.

manas.q: How accurate is AI diabetic retinopathy screening in real-world studies?

children.note: 81 LMIC studies: AI accuracy was generally high, but evidence on cost, regulation and patient outcomes was thin.

manas.q: What is missing from the evidence on AI retinopathy screening in LMICs?

children.note: Real-world DMO results lag trials due to undertreatment and poor follow-up; LMICs also face cost and travel barriers.

manas.q: Why are real-world anti-VEGF results for DMO worse than in trials?

maps.title: HCH 400 · In depth: Concepts of health and disease

nodeData.topic: Concepts of health and disease in depth
nodeData.note: Defining health, models, causation, natural history, prevention, measurement and health frameworks. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Beyond the 1948 wording.
'Complete' wellbeing is unattainable and hard to measure, and it can label most people, especially those with chronic disease, as unhealthy.

manas.q: Give two criticisms of the WHO 1948 definition of health.

children.note: Huber and colleagues (BMJ 2011) proposed health as the ability to adapt and self-manage in the face of challenges.

manas.q: What alternative definition of health did Huber et al. propose in 2011?

children.note: Physical, mental and social are core; emotional, spiritual and vocational dimensions are often added.

manas.q: List the commonly described dimensions of health.

children.note: Health and disease are a spectrum from positive health through unrecognised disease to severe illness and death.

manas.q: Why is health described as a continuum rather than two states?

children.note: Three views of being unwell.
A biological abnormality of structure or function, as defined by the clinician.

manas.q: What is meant by 'disease' in contrast to illness?

children.note: The person's subjective experience of feeling unwell; one can have disease without illness and vice versa.

manas.q: What is 'illness'?

children.note: The social role given to an unwell person; Parsons' sick role exempts duties but expects seeking help and wanting to recover.

manas.q: What are the rights and duties of Parsons' sick role?

children.note: Ways of explaining health and disease.
Disease is a fault in body parts caused by agents; strong for treatment but ignores social and psychological factors.

manas.q: What is the main weakness of the biomedical model?

children.note: Engel (1977): biological, psychological and social factors interact to cause and shape illness.

manas.q: Who proposed the biopsychosocial model, and when?

children.note: Health reflects balance between people and their environment; links to the agent–host–environment triad.

manas.q: What does the ecological model of health stress?

children.note: Combines all the above and treats the whole person within their community.

manas.q: What is the holistic model of health?

children.note: Antonovsky asked what creates health rather than disease; his key idea is the 'sense of coherence'.

manas.q: What is the central concept of Antonovsky's salutogenesis?

children.note: From single causes to webs.
Organism found in every case, isolated, reproduces disease when inoculated and is recovered again; fails for carriers and unculturable agents.

manas.q: What are the limitations of Koch's postulates?

children.note: Chronic disease results from many interlinked factors; cutting one strand can still reduce disease.

manas.q: What does the 'web of causation' describe?

children.note: A necessary cause must be present (e.g. TB bacillus for TB); a sufficient cause inevitably produces disease.

manas.q: Distinguish a necessary from a sufficient cause.

children.note: Strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy (1965).

manas.q: List the Bradford Hill criteria for causation.

children.note: Of the Hill criteria, only temporality — cause before effect — is required.

manas.q: Which Bradford Hill criterion is essential for causation?

children.note: Phases used for planning interventions.
Before the agent affects the person: agent, host and environment interact; the target of primary prevention.

manas.q: Which phase of natural history does primary prevention target?

children.note: Starts when the agent enters the host: subclinical changes, then clinical disease, then recovery, disability or death.

manas.q: What are the stages of the pathogenesis phase?

children.note: Infections range from inapparent through mild and severe to fatal; inapparent cases sustain spread.

manas.q: Why do inapparent infections matter in disease control?

children.note: Leavell and Clark's five levels and beyond.
Health promotion and specific protection (primary); early diagnosis and treatment (secondary); disability limitation and rehabilitation (tertiary).

manas.q: What are Leavell and Clark's five levels of prevention?

children.note: Protecting patients from overmedicalisation and harm from unnecessary tests or treatment.

manas.q: What is quaternary prevention?

children.note: WHO (1968) screening principles: important problem, recognisable early stage, acceptable test, effective treatment, cost justified.

manas.q: Give key Wilson–Jungner criteria for screening.

children.note: Rose: most cases come from the many at modest risk, so a small population-wide shift prevents more cases than targeting the high-risk few, yet each person gains little.

manas.q: What is Rose's 'prevention paradox'?

children.note: Indicators and summary measures.
Crude death rate, infant mortality rate, maternal mortality ratio, under-5 mortality and life expectancy.

manas.q: Name common mortality indicators of population health.

children.note: Incidence counts new cases over time; prevalence counts existing cases; prevalence ≈ incidence × duration.

manas.q: How are prevalence, incidence and duration related?

children.note: Disability-adjusted life year = years of life lost (YLL) + years lived with disability (YLD); one DALY is one lost healthy year.

manas.q: What makes up a DALY?

children.note: Quality-adjusted life year weights years lived by quality of life (1 = full health, 0 = death); used in cost-effectiveness.

manas.q: What is a QALY used for?

children.note: Health-adjusted life expectancy: years a person can expect to live in full health.

manas.q: What does health-adjusted life expectancy (HALE) measure?

children.note: How causes of health are grouped.
Canada's 1974 Lalonde report grouped determinants as human biology, environment, lifestyle and health care organisation.

manas.q: What four fields did the Lalonde report describe?

children.note: WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health (chair Michael Marmot) reported 'Closing the gap in a generation' in 2008.

manas.q: What did the 2008 WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health report?

children.note: Health worsens step by step as social position falls, not just among the poorest.

manas.q: What is the social gradient in health?

children.note: Two or more long-term conditions in one person; shifts care away from single-disease thinking.

manas.q: How is multimorbidity defined?

children.note: Control, elimination, eradication.
Reducing incidence, prevalence or harm to a locally acceptable level with ongoing effort.

manas.q: What is meant by disease control?

children.note: Interrupting transmission in a defined area while the agent persists elsewhere.

manas.q: How does elimination differ from eradication?

children.note: Worldwide permanent removal of the agent; smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.

manas.q: Which human disease has been eradicated, and when was this declared?

children.note: Global declarations shaping public health.
Declared primary health care the key to 'Health for All by the year 2000'.

manas.q: What did the Alma-Ata Declaration of 1978 call for?

children.note: Five action areas: healthy public policy, supportive environments, community action, personal skills, reorienting health services.

manas.q: Name the five action areas of the Ottawa Charter.

children.note: Renewed the commitment to primary health care as the route to universal health coverage.

manas.q: What did the 2018 Astana Declaration reaffirm?

children.note: Human, animal and environmental health are linked and need joint action, e.g. zoonoses and antimicrobial resistance.

manas.q: What is the One Health approach?

children.note: Quick recall.
Screening finds disease early, so it is secondary prevention; immunisation is primary (specific protection).

manas.q: Is screening primary or secondary prevention?

children.note: The hidden base of the iceberg is what screening and surveys try to uncover.

manas.q: How does the iceberg phenomenon relate to screening?

children.note: How health is framed in law and policy; Kenya first.
The Constitution of Kenya 2010, Article 43, gives every person the right to the highest attainable standard of health, including reproductive health care.

manas.q: Which article of Kenya's 2010 Constitution guarantees the right to health?

children.note: Article 43 also states that no one shall be denied emergency medical treatment.

manas.q: What does Kenya's Constitution say about emergency medical treatment?

children.note: Under the Fourth Schedule, county governments run county health services; national government keeps health policy and national referral facilities.

manas.q: Who delivers county health services under Kenya's devolution?

children.note: Besides defining health, it states that the highest attainable standard of health is a fundamental right of every human being.

manas.q: What right does the WHO Constitution declare?

children.note: Sustainable Development Goal 3 aims to ensure healthy lives and wellbeing for all; target 3.8 is universal health coverage.

manas.q: Which SDG target covers universal health coverage?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-02.
Review: multimorbidity appears about a decade earlier in deprived communities and needs person-centred, coordinated care rather than single-disease guidelines.

manas.q: How much earlier does multimorbidity occur in deprived communities?

children.note: Review argues social connection (support, isolation, loneliness) is often missing from social-determinants work and proposes a cross-sector framework.

manas.q: Which social determinant does the 2022 Annual Review argue is often overlooked?

children.note: 59 studies, mostly high-income: yearly cost per person ranged I$800–150,000; few data from low- and middle-income countries.

manas.q: What range of annual per-person multimorbidity costs did the 2022 review find?

maps.title: HDR 400 · In depth: Imaging modalities overview

nodeData.note: How each modality makes a picture, what it shows best, contrast and radiation safety. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What medical imaging is and how a test is chosen.
Techniques that create pictures of structures inside the body to diagnose disease, stage it, monitor treatment or guide procedures.

manas.q: What is medical imaging used for?

children.note: Plain X-ray, fluoroscopy, CT and nuclear medicine (including PET) all expose the patient to ionising radiation.

manas.q: Which imaging modalities use ionising radiation?

children.note: Weigh the clinical question, diagnostic yield, radiation, cost, availability and patient factors such as pregnancy, renal function and implants.

manas.q: Which factors guide the choice of imaging test?

children.note: The basic principle behind each picture.
X-rays pass through the body and are absorbed differently by tissues; the detector records what gets through, giving a 2D shadow image.

manas.q: How is a plain radiograph produced?

children.note: From darkest to brightest: air (gas), fat, soft tissue/fluid, bone (calcium) and metal.

manas.q: List the five radiographic densities from dark to bright.

children.note: Continuous real-time X-ray imaging used for contrast studies (e.g. barium swallow) and guiding interventions; dose rises with screening time.

manas.q: What is fluoroscopy used for?

children.note: A rotating X-ray tube and detector ring acquire data that a computer reconstructs into thin cross-sectional slices.

manas.q: How does CT produce cross-sectional images?

children.note: CT density scale: water is 0, air about −1000; fat is negative, bone strongly positive.

manas.q: What are the Hounsfield values of water and air?

children.note: The same CT data are displayed with different settings (lung, soft tissue, bone, brain) to show different tissues best.

manas.q: Why are CT images viewed on different 'windows'?

children.note: A piezoelectric transducer sends high-frequency sound into tissue and builds an image from echoes reflected at tissue interfaces.

manas.q: How does ultrasound create an image?

children.note: Higher-frequency probes give better resolution but less depth; low-frequency probes reach deep organs with poorer detail.

manas.q: What is the trade-off between ultrasound frequency and depth?

children.note: Measures the frequency shift of echoes from moving blood to show flow direction and velocity, e.g. in DVT or carotid studies.

manas.q: What does Doppler ultrasound measure?

children.note: A strong magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses make hydrogen nuclei (protons) emit signals that are mapped into an image.

manas.q: What is the signal source in MRI?

children.note: On T1, fat is bright and fluid dark (good anatomy); on T2, fluid is bright (good for oedema and pathology).

manas.q: Which tissue is bright on T1 and which on T2 MRI?

children.note: A radiotracer is given and a gamma camera detects its emissions, showing organ function rather than just structure.

manas.q: What does nuclear medicine imaging mainly show?

children.note: Positron-emitting tracers, most often FDG (a glucose analogue), show metabolically active tissue such as many cancers; usually fused with CT.

manas.q: Which tracer is most used in PET and what does it show?

children.note: The right word for each modality.
Radiopaque (white) structures block X-rays; radiolucent (dark) ones let them through.

manas.q: What do radiopaque and radiolucent mean?

children.note: Hyperdense, hypodense or isodense compared with surrounding tissue; e.g. fresh blood in the brain is hyperdense.

manas.q: How does acute haemorrhage appear on non-contrast CT brain?

children.note: Hyperechoic (bright), hypoechoic (darker) and anechoic (black, e.g. simple fluid).

manas.q: What does 'anechoic' mean on ultrasound?

children.note: Gallstones cast a posterior acoustic shadow; fluid-filled cysts show posterior acoustic enhancement.

manas.q: Which ultrasound artefact is typical of gallstones?

children.note: Hyperintense (bright) and hypointense (dark) signal, always stating the sequence (T1, T2, etc.).

manas.q: Which words describe brightness on MRI?

children.note: What each modality does best and where it fails.
Cheap, quick and widely available; first-line for chest and suspected fractures, but structures overlap and soft-tissue contrast is poor.

manas.q: What are the main strengths and weaknesses of plain X-ray?

children.note: Fast and detailed for trauma, lungs, bone and the acute abdomen; drawbacks are radiation dose and iodinated contrast risks.

manas.q: Why is CT the workhorse for major trauma?

children.note: Portable, no radiation, real time, cheap; guides needles and drains and allows bedside FAST scans in trauma.

manas.q: Name advantages of ultrasound over CT.

children.note: Slow, costly, noisy and claustrophobic; some pacemakers, cochlear implants and metal foreign bodies (e.g. in the eye) can be contraindications.

manas.q: Name contraindications or drawbacks of MRI.

children.note: Bone scan for skeletal metastases, V/Q scan for pulmonary embolism and thyroid scan for nodules or hyperthyroidism.

manas.q: Give three common nuclear medicine scans and their uses.

children.note: Agents that make vessels, organs or bowel stand out.
Can cause allergy-like reactions and kidney injury; ask about previous reactions and check renal function in at-risk patients.

manas.q: What are the main risks of iodinated contrast?

children.note: Barium shows the gut well but avoid it if perforation is suspected (peritonitis); use water-soluble contrast instead.

manas.q: Why is barium avoided when perforation is suspected?

children.note: Linked to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in severe renal impairment and generally avoided in pregnancy.

manas.q: Which serious complication is linked to gadolinium in renal failure?

children.note: Protecting patients and staff.
Justification (benefit must outweigh risk), optimisation (ALARA: as low as reasonably achievable) and dose limits for workers and public.

manas.q: What are the three principles of radiation protection?

children.note: Deterministic effects (skin burns, cataract) have a threshold and worsen with dose; stochastic effects (cancer) have no threshold, only rising probability.

manas.q: How do deterministic and stochastic radiation effects differ?

children.note: A chest X-ray gives about 0.02 mSv; a CT gives many times that dose, so do not repeat CT without good reason.

manas.q: Roughly what effective dose does a chest X-ray give?

children.note: Growing tissues and long life ahead raise cancer risk per unit dose, so prefer ultrasound or MRI and child-sized CT settings.

manas.q: Why is radiation dose a bigger concern in children?

children.note: Ask about pregnancy (and test if unsure) in women of reproductive age before ionising imaging of the abdomen or pelvis.

manas.q: What must be checked before abdominopelvic X-ray or CT in a woman of childbearing age?

children.note: Staff cut exposure by minimising time near the source, standing further away and using lead aprons and screens.

manas.q: Name the three practical ways staff reduce radiation exposure.

children.note: Common first-line choices to know.
Abdominal ultrasound is first-line for gallstones and acute cholecystitis.

manas.q: What is the first-line imaging for suspected gallstones?

children.note: An erect chest X-ray may show free gas under the diaphragm; CT is more sensitive.

manas.q: Which plain film can show pneumoperitoneum?

children.note: CT pulmonary angiography is standard; a V/Q scan is an option when contrast must be avoided.

manas.q: What imaging is standard for suspected pulmonary embolism?

children.note: Compression duplex ultrasound of the leg veins is the usual test.

manas.q: Which test is used to confirm a suspected DVT?

children.note: Non-contrast CT of kidneys, ureters and bladder is usual in adults; ultrasound first in pregnancy and children.

manas.q: What is the usual imaging for adult renal colic?

children.note: Quick wins for OSCEs and viva.
Confirm patient name, date, projection and side markers before describing any finding.

manas.q: What should you check before describing a radiograph?

children.note: AP films magnify the heart, so cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio over 0.5) is judged on a PA film.

manas.q: Why is heart size not reliably assessed on an AP chest X-ray?

children.note: Assess rotation, inspiration and exposure before reading the lungs and mediastinum.

manas.q: Which three quality checks apply to a chest X-ray?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
The MoH Clinical Guidelines for Level 4–6 hospitals cover management and referral of common conditions; pick imaging using your hospital's radiology protocol.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guidance frames hospital care and referral, including imaging?

children.note: The Kenya Nuclear Regulatory Authority licenses and inspects facilities that use radiation sources, including X-ray units.

manas.q: Which Kenyan body regulates use of X-ray and other radiation sources?

children.note: The IAEA International Basic Safety Standards, co-sponsored by WHO, set global rules for protecting patients and staff.

manas.q: Which international standards cover radiation protection in medicine?

children.note: The International Commission on Radiological Protection sets the justification, optimisation and dose-limit framework most countries adopt.

manas.q: Which body framed justification, optimisation and dose limits?

children.note: The American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria and the UK Royal College of Radiologists' iRefer guide test choice.
