manas.q: Name referral guidance used in the US and UK to pick imaging tests.

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-02.
Review of 36 publications: midwives, nurses, clinical officers and others gave useful bedside scans after short training; barriers were training cost, internet and power.

manas.q: Can non-specialist primary care staff in LMICs perform useful POCUS?

children.note: 20 observational studies in low-resource settings: POCUS changed diagnosis in 15–52% and management in 17–87%, but none showed an effect on mortality.

manas.q: Has POCUS in low-resource settings been shown to reduce mortality?

children.note: Seven studies of children with congenital heart disease: cumulative doses 0.96–53.5 mSv, mostly from interventional cardiology; a significant number exceeded 20 mSv.

manas.q: Which procedures gave most radiation dose to children with congenital heart disease?

maps.title: HME 400 · In depth: Clinical history and examination

nodeData.topic: Clinical history and examination in depth
nodeData.note: Taking a focused history, examining system by system and turning findings into a plan. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Why history and examination matter and how to start well.
In most patients the history points to the diagnosis; examination and tests then confirm or refine it.

manas.q: Which part of the clinical assessment gives most diagnostic information?

children.note: Wash hands, introduce yourself and your role, confirm the patient's identity and get verbal consent before examining.

manas.q: What should you do before starting a history or examination?

children.note: Offer a chaperone for intimate examinations, use screens and expose only what is needed while keeping dignity.

manas.q: When should a chaperone be offered?

children.note: How to ask so patients tell you more.
Start open ('Tell me about…'), listen without interrupting, then narrow with closed questions to fill gaps.

manas.q: In what order should open and closed questions be used?

children.note: Questions that suggest the answer ('The pain spreads to your arm, doesn't it?') distort the history.

manas.q: Why should leading questions be avoided?

children.note: Explore the patient's Ideas, Concerns and Expectations about the illness.

manas.q: What does ICE stand for in history taking?

children.note: Summarise back to check accuracy and tell the patient when you change topic.

manas.q: Why summarise back to the patient during a history?

children.note: Use a trained interpreter where possible; relatives may filter information or limit what is disclosed.

manas.q: Why is a trained interpreter preferred over a relative?

children.note: A widely taught consultation framework: initiate, gather information, examine, explain and plan, close.

manas.q: Name the stages of the Calgary–Cambridge consultation model.

children.note: Getting each section right.
Record the main symptom in the patient's own words with its duration.

manas.q: How should the presenting complaint be recorded?

children.note: Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associated features, Time course, Exacerbating/relieving factors, Severity.

manas.q: What does SOCRATES stand for?

children.note: Ask about TB, HIV status, diabetes, hypertension, asthma, previous surgery and blood transfusions.

manas.q: Which past conditions are especially important to ask about in Kenya?

children.note: Include over-the-counter and herbal or traditional remedies; for each allergy record what reaction occurred.

manas.q: What should be recorded alongside a drug allergy?

children.note: Smoking in pack-years, alcohol, occupation, home and support, and recent travel (e.g. to malaria areas).

manas.q: Which items belong in the social history?

children.note: Packs (20 cigarettes) smoked per day multiplied by years smoked.

manas.q: How are pack-years calculated?

children.note: Ask last menstrual period, pregnancies and parity, and contraception; it changes diagnosis, drugs and imaging.

manas.q: Why ask about the last menstrual period?

children.note: Add pregnancy and birth history, immunisation, feeding and nutrition, and developmental milestones.

manas.q: Which extra sections are added in a paediatric history?

children.note: A brief screen of other systems catches symptoms the patient did not mention.

manas.q: What is the purpose of the systems review?

children.note: Look at the whole patient first.
Temperature, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation; respiratory rate is the one most often skipped.

manas.q: Which vital sign is most often omitted?

children.note: Weight, height and BMI (kg/m²); in children use weight-for-height and MUAC.

manas.q: How is BMI calculated?

children.note: Check mucous membranes, skin turgor, capillary refill (normally about 2 seconds or less) and postural BP.

manas.q: What is a normal capillary refill time?

children.note: Look for clubbing, koilonychia, leukonychia, splinter haemorrhages, palmar erythema and tremor.

manas.q: Which nail signs should you look for in the hands?

children.note: Spoon-shaped nails, classically from iron-deficiency anaemia.

manas.q: What does koilonychia suggest?

children.note: Small linear bleeds under the nail; can point to infective endocarditis but also occur after trauma.

manas.q: Which serious infection can cause splinter haemorrhages?

children.note: Look for jaundice in the sclera in daylight; pallor in conjunctivae, palms and nail beds.

manas.q: Where is jaundice best detected?

children.note: Central cyanosis shows on the tongue and lips (hypoxaemia); peripheral cyanosis only in fingers and toes (poor perfusion).

manas.q: How do you tell central from peripheral cyanosis?

children.note: Key steps per system beyond IPPA.
Pulse rate, rhythm and character, JVP, apex beat and heart sounds; radio-femoral delay suggests coarctation of the aorta.

manas.q: Which pulse sign suggests coarctation of the aorta?

children.note: Normally in the 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line; displaced in cardiomegaly.

manas.q: Where is the normal apex beat?

children.note: Trachea position, chest expansion, percussion, breath sounds and vocal resonance.

manas.q: What respiratory signs are checked on examination?

children.note: Stony dull suggests pleural effusion; hyperresonant suggests pneumothorax.

manas.q: What percussion note suggests pleural effusion?

children.note: Heard over consolidation, with increased vocal resonance.

manas.q: Where is bronchial breathing heard?

children.note: Patient lying flat; palpate starting away from any pain; feel for the liver from the right iliac fossa upward so a very large liver edge is not missed.

manas.q: Why start abdominal palpation in the right iliac fossa for the liver?

children.note: Dullness in the flanks that moves when the patient rolls over indicates ascites.

manas.q: Which sign confirms ascites on percussion?

children.note: Hernial orifices, external genitalia and, when indicated and consented, a rectal examination.

manas.q: What parts of abdominal examination are often forgotten?

children.note: Tone, power (MRC 0–5), reflexes, sensation and coordination, comparing both sides.

manas.q: Which scale grades muscle power?

children.note: Upper motor neurone: increased tone, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantar. Lower: wasting, fasciculation, reduced tone and reflexes.

manas.q: How do upper and lower motor neurone lesions differ?

children.note: From findings to a plan.
One or two sentences: who the patient is, key symptoms, key signs and relevant background.

manas.q: What goes into a case summary statement?

children.note: List active problems separately so none is missed, then rank differentials for each.

manas.q: Why make a problem list?

children.note: Investigations, treatment and monitoring linked to the differentials, plus what you will tell the patient.

manas.q: What should the management plan link to?

children.note: Write legibly with date, time, name, signature and designation; record negatives that matter.

manas.q: What must every clinical note include?

children.note: Common OSCE marks.
Always compare left with right; asymmetry is often the key sign.

manas.q: Why compare both sides during examination?

children.note: Report important absent findings (e.g. no neck stiffness in headache) as they narrow the differential.

manas.q: What is a pertinent negative?

children.note: Finish by thanking the patient, helping them dress and washing your hands.

manas.q: How should an examination be finished?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
The MoH Clinical Guidelines for Level 4–6 hospitals, linked below, frame assessment and referral of common conditions.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline frames hospital assessment of common conditions?

children.note: The Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Council regulates doctors, including standards on consent and confidentiality.

manas.q: Which Kenyan body regulates doctors' professional conduct?

children.note: Integrated Management of Childhood Illness gives a structured history, danger-sign check and examination for sick children.

manas.q: Which WHO approach structures assessment of sick children?

children.note: Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment helps staff spot emergency and priority signs in children on arrival.

manas.q: What is ETAT used for?

children.note: Common in the US and elsewhere: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan.

manas.q: What does SOAP stand for in clinical notes?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-02.
Meta-analysis (43 studies): most neuro signs are specific but insensitive for a central cause; in acute vestibular syndrome, HINTS by trained clinicians: sensitivity 92.9%, HINTS+ 99.0%.

manas.q: How sensitive is HINTS for a central cause of acute vestibular syndrome?

children.note: 64 studies: video-based exam components gave diagnostic accuracy similar to in-person exams, but interrater reliability varied; MMSE was reliable.

manas.q: How does video-based physical examination compare with in-person examination?

children.note: 18 studies (3 RCTs): chatbots can gather histories and improve engagement and satisfaction; need data security and to keep empathic contact.

manas.q: What benefits did studies report for chatbots in history-taking?

maps.title: HSU 604 · In depth: Complications of otitis media

nodeData.topic: Complications of otitis media in depth
nodeData.note: How middle-ear infection spreads, the complications it causes, and how to spot, scan and treat them. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What counts as a complication and how they are grouped.
Spread of middle-ear infection beyond the mucosa of the middle-ear cleft into bone, soft tissue, the inner ear, the facial nerve or the cranial cavity.

manas.q: What is meant by a complication of otitis media?

children.note: Within the temporal bone: mastoiditis, petrous apicitis, facial nerve palsy, labyrinthitis, labyrinthine fistula and hearing loss.

manas.q: Which complications of otitis media stay within the temporal bone?

children.note: Pus escaping the temporal bone: subperiosteal (postauricular), zygomatic and Bezold abscesses.

manas.q: Name abscesses that form outside the temporal bone in otitis media.

children.note: Meningitis, extradural abscess, subdural empyema, brain abscess, lateral (sigmoid) sinus thrombosis and otitic hydrocephalus.

manas.q: List the intracranial complications of otitis media.

children.note: Acute otitis media causes most mastoiditis in young children; chronic disease with cholesteatoma causes most complications in older children and adults.

manas.q: Which type of otitis media drives complications in adults?

children.note: How infection gets out of the middle ear.
Cholesteatoma and chronic osteitis destroy bone, opening a direct path to dura, sinus, labyrinth or facial canal.

manas.q: How does cholesteatoma lead to intracranial infection?

children.note: Infected small veins can carry infection through bone that still looks intact, so a complication can occur without visible erosion.

manas.q: How can infection spread from the ear through intact bone?

children.note: Round and oval windows, natural bony gaps, old fracture lines and previous surgery let infection pass without new erosion.

manas.q: Name preformed routes by which ear infection spreads.

children.note: The thin tegmen tympani roof separates the middle ear and antrum from the middle cranial fossa, so erosion here risks temporal lobe abscess.

manas.q: Erosion of the tegmen tympani puts which brain region at risk?

children.note: Behind the mastoid lie the sigmoid sinus and posterior fossa; spread this way causes sinus thrombosis or cerebellar abscess.

manas.q: Posterior spread from the mastoid threatens which structures?

children.note: The tympanic part of the facial nerve canal is often thin or dehiscent, so middle-ear inflammation can reach the nerve directly.

manas.q: Why can acute otitis media cause facial nerve palsy?

children.note: The lateral semicircular canal is the part of the labyrinth most often eroded by cholesteatoma, creating a fistula.

manas.q: Which semicircular canal is most often eroded by cholesteatoma?

children.note: Beyond the existing mastoiditis, Gradenigo and fistula bubbles.
Pus under pressure breaks down the thin bony walls between mastoid air cells, forming one cavity; it can then burst outwards or inwards.

manas.q: What happens to the mastoid air cells in coalescent mastoiditis?

children.note: Drooping of the posterosuperior bony meatal wall on otoscopy suggests pus in the mastoid antrum.

manas.q: What otoscopic sign suggests pus in the mastoid antrum?

children.note: In acute otitis media palsy is usually partial and recovers with antibiotics plus myringotomy; with cholesteatoma it needs urgent surgical exploration.

manas.q: How does management of facial palsy differ in acute versus chronic otitis media?

children.note: Toxins irritate the inner ear: vertigo and partial sensorineural loss that can recover if the cause is treated quickly.

manas.q: Is hearing loss from serous labyrinthitis reversible?

children.note: Bacteria enter the inner ear: severe vertigo, vomiting, nystagmus and a permanently dead ear; can spread to meningitis.

manas.q: What is the hearing outcome of suppurative labyrinthitis?

children.note: The sixth nerve runs in Dorello's canal close to the petrous apex, so apex infection weakens lateral gaze.

manas.q: Why does petrous apicitis cause a sixth nerve palsy?

children.note: Conductive loss from perforation or ossicle erosion (long process of incus most often); sensorineural loss when the labyrinth is involved.

manas.q: Which ossicle part is most often eroded in chronic otitis media?

children.note: Where mastoid pus points.
The most common mastoiditis abscess: pus collects under the periosteum behind the ear; fluctuant, with loss of the postauricular crease.

manas.q: What is the most common abscess complicating acute mastoiditis?

children.note: Pus tracking into air cells of the zygomatic root gives swelling in front of and above the ear.

manas.q: Where does a zygomatic abscess from mastoiditis appear?

children.note: Pus bursts through the medial side of the mastoid tip and runs deep to sternocleidomastoid, so it can spread into deep neck spaces.

manas.q: Why can a Bezold abscess spread into the deep neck?

children.note: Deeper detail on the life-threatening group.
Pus between bone and dura; often silent and found at surgery, sometimes with persistent headache or throbbing ear pain.

manas.q: Why is an otogenic extradural abscess often missed before surgery?

children.note: Pus spreads fast over the brain surface: high fever, seizures, focal weakness and falling consciousness; a neurosurgical emergency.

manas.q: Which otogenic intracranial complication causes rapid seizures and focal signs?

children.note: Local encephalitis, then a quiet latent stage while a capsule forms, then enlargement with raised pressure, then possible rupture.

manas.q: What are the stages of an otogenic brain abscess?

children.note: Contralateral upper quadrant field loss; nominal (word-finding) aphasia if on the dominant side; seizures.

manas.q: Which visual field defect suggests a temporal lobe abscess?

children.note: Same-side ataxia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia and nystagmus, with raised pressure features.

manas.q: What signs point to an otogenic cerebellar abscess?

children.note: Clot in the sigmoid sinus can extend into the internal jugular vein and shed septic emboli to the lungs.

manas.q: Where can septic emboli from lateral sinus thrombosis lodge?

children.note: On contrast CT a filling defect in the sinus with an enhancing rim suggests venous sinus thrombosis.

manas.q: What CT sign suggests venous sinus thrombosis?

children.note: Raised intracranial pressure with normal CSF, linked to sinus thrombosis: headache, vomiting, papilloedema, sixth nerve palsy; vision is at risk.

manas.q: What CSF findings are seen in otitic hydrocephalus?

children.note: Signs that a discharging ear is turning serious.
Atticoantral (squamous) disease: attic perforation or retraction pocket with scanty, foul-smelling discharge and cholesteatoma; prone to complications.

manas.q: What features make a chronically discharging ear 'unsafe'?

children.note: New earache, headache, fever, vomiting, vertigo, facial weakness or drowsiness in a patient with ear disease need urgent assessment.

manas.q: Which symptoms in chronic ear disease suggest a complication?

children.note: Partial or oral antibiotic courses can hide classic signs while the infection keeps eroding bone.

manas.q: Why can mastoiditis present with few signs after antibiotics?

children.note: Confirm the complication and find the source.
Contrast CT shows bone erosion, mastoid coalescence, abscesses and many sinus clots; usually the first scan.

manas.q: What is the usual first scan for a suspected otogenic complication?

children.note: Better for brain abscess, empyema, labyrinth involvement and venous sinus thrombosis.

manas.q: Which imaging best shows otogenic brain abscess and sinus thrombosis?

children.note: Only after imaging excludes abscess or mass effect, because of the risk of brain herniation.

manas.q: Why must imaging come before lumbar puncture in otogenic meningitis?

children.note: Ear pus swab and blood cultures before antibiotics where possible; full blood count and inflammatory markers.

manas.q: Which samples should be taken before antibiotics in complicated otitis media?

children.note: Tuning fork tests at the bedside, then pure tone audiometry when the patient is fit.

manas.q: How is hearing assessed in suspected labyrinth involvement?

children.note: Treat the complication, then remove the ear source.
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics that reach the CNS and cover anaerobes in chronic disease; adjust to culture results.

manas.q: What antibiotic cover is needed in otogenic intracranial complications?

children.note: Opening the eardrum drains the middle ear in acute otitis media complications; a ventilation tube may be inserted.

manas.q: What simple procedure drains the middle ear in acute complications?

children.note: Modified radical mastoidectomy removes cholesteatoma and diseased bone to make the ear safe.

manas.q: Which operation clears cholesteatoma causing complications?

children.note: Neurosurgical aspiration or excision with prolonged IV antibiotics; ear surgery when the patient is stable.

manas.q: How is an otogenic brain abscess treated?

children.note: Antibiotics plus mastoid surgery; anticoagulation is often added but practice varies between centres.

manas.q: How is otogenic lateral sinus thrombosis managed?

children.note: Outcomes and how to prevent them.
Intracranial complications, especially brain abscess and meningitis, still carry significant death and disability rates.

manas.q: Which otogenic complications carry the highest mortality?

children.note: Prompt treatment of acute otitis media and follow-up of chronic discharge reduce complications.

manas.q: How can complications of otitis media be prevented?

children.note: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is in Kenya's routine infant schedule; it reduces pneumococcal meningitis and other invasive disease and modestly reduces otitis media.

manas.q: Which routine infant vaccine helps prevent pneumococcal ear and brain infection?

children.note: Untreated hearing loss in children harms speech, learning and school progress, so screen and refer.

manas.q: Why does hearing loss from otitis media matter for children?

children.note: Quick points examiners like.
Central perforation with mucoid discharge is usually safe; attic/marginal perforation or cholesteatoma is unsafe.

manas.q: Which perforation sites indicate an unsafe ear?

children.note: The fistula test can be negative if the labyrinth is already dead or the fistula is blocked by cholesteatoma.

manas.q: When can the fistula test be falsely negative?

children.note: Upward through tegmen: temporal lobe. Backward through sinus plate: cerebellum and sigmoid sinus.

manas.q: Map the route of spread to the site of otogenic brain abscess.

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
Follow the MoH Clinical Guidelines for Level 4–6 hospitals, linked below, and refer suspected complications to ENT urgently.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers hospital ear infection care?

children.note: WHO's World Report on Hearing (2021) urges integrating ear and hearing care into primary care, including chronic ear infection.

manas.q: What 2021 WHO report covers ear and hearing care?

children.note: NICE's acute otitis media antimicrobial guidance favours no or delayed antibiotics for many children, with hospital referral if complications are suspected.

manas.q: How does UK NICE guidance approach antibiotics for acute otitis media?

children.note: The American Academy of Pediatrics 2013 guideline allows observation without antibiotics in selected children with non-severe disease.

manas.q: What option did the AAP 2013 guideline allow for mild acute otitis media?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-02.

CSOM is a leading cause of potentially preventable hearing loss, linked to deprivation; topical antibiotics are optimal for discharge, antiseptics where unavailable; surgery may help persistent disease.

manas.q: What is the preferred treatment for ear discharge in CSOM?

children.note: Pooled community studies estimated CSOM in 3.8% of people (about 297 million), with 85% in low- and middle-income countries.

manas.q: What global prevalence of CSOM did the 2025 systematic review estimate?

children.note: Across 23 studies (883 patients), surgically treated patients had larger reductions in complications than medically or conservatively managed ones.

manas.q: How did surgery compare with medical care in complicated acute mastoiditis?

children.note: In 312 children, the sinus had fully recanalised in 67% at median 8-month follow-up; bleeding was rare (0.3%), no deaths; 31% had suspected otogenic hydrocephalus, 3% needed permanent shunts.

manas.q: How often had otogenic venous sinus thrombosis fully recanalised in children at follow-up?

maps.title: HSU 605 · In depth: Rapid sequence induction

nodeData.note: Why RSI is done, how to prepare, drug choices, pitfalls and special cases. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What RSI is for.
After preoxygenation, an induction agent and a fast-acting muscle relaxant are given back to back so a cuffed tracheal tube can be placed quickly.

manas.q: What is rapid sequence induction?

children.note: Shorten the time between losing protective airway reflexes and sealing the trachea with a cuffed tube, to limit aspiration.

manas.q: What is the main aim of rapid sequence induction?

children.note: Classic RSI avoids mask ventilation before intubation; modified RSI allows gentle, low-pressure mask breaths in patients who desaturate quickly.

manas.q: How does modified RSI differ from classic RSI?

children.note: Why aspiration and desaturation are the twin threats.
Recent food, bowel obstruction, trauma, pain, opioids, labour, diabetic gastroparesis and reflux all raise aspiration risk.

manas.q: Name factors that make a patient a 'full stomach'.

children.note: Inhaled acidic gastric contents cause a chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome), first described in obstetric anaesthesia.

manas.q: What is Mendelson syndrome?

children.note: Oxygen replaces nitrogen in the functional residual capacity, creating a reservoir that lengthens safe apnoea time.

manas.q: How does preoxygenation lengthen safe apnoea time?

children.note: Obesity, pregnancy, young children, sepsis and lung disease shrink the oxygen reservoir or raise oxygen use, so saturation falls quickly.

manas.q: Which patients desaturate fastest during apnoea?

children.note: Nasal oxygen kept running during apnoea lets oxygen keep flowing into the alveoli, delaying desaturation.

manas.q: What is apnoeic oxygenation?

children.note: Plan before you push drugs.
Look externally, Evaluate 3-3-2, Mallampati, Obstruction, Neck mobility: a quick screen for difficult laryngoscopy.

manas.q: What does the LEMON airway assessment stand for?

children.note: Working suction, two laryngoscopes (video if available), tubes in two sizes, bougie, supraglottic airway, front-of-neck kit, capnography.

manas.q: What equipment must be ready before RSI?

children.note: Sniffing position; in obesity, ramp so the ear canal is level with the sternal notch; head-up tilt helps preoxygenation.

manas.q: How should an obese patient be positioned for RSI?

children.note: Assign roles and say plans A to D aloud before starting, so everyone knows the next step if intubation fails.

manas.q: Why should the team brief plans A–D before RSI?

children.note: Reliable IV access with fluid running, ECG, blood pressure, pulse oximetry and waveform capnography attached.

manas.q: What monitoring is essential during RSI?

children.note: Choices and cautions (no induction doses here).
Smooth, fast induction but drops blood pressure through vasodilatation and myocardial depression; reduce or avoid in shock.

manas.q: What is the main haemodynamic problem with propofol at induction?

children.note: Tends to keep blood pressure up via sympathetic stimulation and causes bronchodilation; useful in shock and asthma.

manas.q: Why is ketamine favoured for RSI in shocked or asthmatic patients?

children.note: The classic RSI agent: rapid onset; causes hypotension and is irritant if injected outside the vein or into an artery.

manas.q: What is a danger of extravascular thiopental?

children.note: Haemodynamically stable but suppresses adrenal steroid production.

manas.q: What endocrine side effect does etomidate cause?

children.note: Depolarising: fasciculations, then rapid paralysis; can cause bradycardia (repeat doses, children), potassium rise, myalgia.

manas.q: What are common side effects of suxamethonium?

children.note: Hyperkalaemia, malignant hyperthermia risk, known suxamethonium apnoea, and from about 24–48 h after major burns, crush or denervation injury (risk lasts months).

manas.q: When is suxamethonium contraindicated?

children.note: Low or abnormal plasma cholinesterase prolongs paralysis; keep the patient sedated and ventilated until it wears off.

manas.q: What causes prolonged paralysis after suxamethonium?

children.note: High-dose rocuronium acts fast but lasts long; without sugammadex you cannot wake the patient quickly if intubation fails.

manas.q: What is the drawback of rocuronium for RSI without sugammadex?

children.note: An opioid can blunt the pressor response in raised ICP or heart disease; have a vasopressor drawn up for post-induction hypotension.

manas.q: Why might an opioid be added at RSI in head injury?

children.note: Fine points of the sequence.
Do not start laryngoscopy until the relaxant has worked (fasciculations stop with suxamethonium); early attempts cause coughing and trauma.

manas.q: When should laryngoscopy start after giving the relaxant?

children.note: Press the cricoid, the only complete ring, back against the oesophagus; release if it worsens the view or blocks ventilation.

manas.q: Why is the cricoid cartilage used for cricoid pressure?

children.note: Release cricoid pressure if the patient actively vomits, to avoid oesophageal rupture; tilt head-down and suction.

manas.q: What should you do with cricoid pressure if the patient vomits?

children.note: A sustained waveform end-tidal CO2 trace is the gold standard; no trace means assume the tube is in the oesophagus.

manas.q: What is the gold standard for confirming tracheal tube placement?

children.note: Cricoid pressure is released only after the cuff is inflated and tube position is confirmed.

manas.q: When is cricoid pressure released during RSI?

children.note: What goes wrong and why.
Prolonged or repeated attempts cause desaturation; stop and oxygenate rather than persist.

manas.q: What should you do if saturation falls during intubation attempts?

children.note: Induction drugs reduce sympathetic tone and positive pressure ventilation cuts venous return; worse in shock.

manas.q: Why does blood pressure often fall after RSI?

children.note: Leads quickly to hypoxic cardiac arrest; prevented by routine waveform capnography.

manas.q: How is unrecognised oesophageal intubation prevented?

children.note: The patient may wake while still paralysed if the induction agent wears off, especially with long-acting rocuronium; start ongoing sedation.

manas.q: Why is awareness a risk after RSI with rocuronium?

children.note: Triggered by suxamethonium or volatile agents: rising end-tidal CO2, rigidity, tachycardia and fever; treat with dantrolene.

manas.q: What is the specific treatment for malignant hyperthermia?

children.note: Damage to teeth, lips, pharynx or larynx, more likely with multiple or forceful attempts.

manas.q: What makes airway trauma more likely during intubation?

children.note: Adapting RSI to the patient.
General anaesthesia for caesarean section is done as RSI, with left uterine displacement and antacid prophylaxis.

manas.q: Why is general anaesthesia for caesarean done as RSI?

children.note: Faster desaturation and bradycardia with suxamethonium; have atropine ready and size equipment carefully.

manas.q: What drug should be ready for bradycardia during paediatric RSI?

children.note: Avoid both hypoxia and hypotension, which worsen secondary brain injury; blunt the pressor response.

manas.q: What two insults must be avoided during RSI in head injury?

children.note: Resuscitate first where possible, reduce induction agent dose and prefer a haemodynamically stable agent.

manas.q: How should RSI be adapted in a shocked patient?

children.note: Care continues once the tube is in.
Start sedation and analgesia promptly to prevent awareness while paralysed.

manas.q: Why must sedation start promptly after RSI?

children.note: Confirm tube depth on chest X-ray, pass a gastric tube and set ventilation; watch blood pressure closely.

manas.q: What checks follow successful intubation?

children.note: Extubate fully awake with protective reflexes back, often head-up or on the side.

manas.q: How should a full-stomach patient be extubated?

children.note: Quick points examiners like.
Can't intubate, can't oxygenate: declare it and move to emergency front-of-neck access.

manas.q: What is the response to a can't intubate, can't oxygenate situation?

children.note: DAS approach: scalpel through the cricothyroid membrane, bougie into the trachea, then a small cuffed tube over it.

manas.q: Describe the scalpel–bougie–tube technique.

children.note: A flat capnograph after intubation means oesophageal intubation until proven otherwise, even in cardiac arrest.

manas.q: What does a flat capnograph after intubation mean?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
Use the MoH Clinical Guidelines for Level 4–6 hospitals and your hospital's anaesthesia protocol.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers hospital emergency and anaesthesia care?

children.note: Before induction the WHO checklist asks whether there is a difficult airway or aspiration risk and if help and equipment are ready.

manas.q: What airway question does the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist ask before induction?

children.note: The Difficult Airway Society publishes adult intubation algorithms; with the OAA it issued 2015 obstetric failed intubation guidance.

manas.q: Which UK bodies issued obstetric failed intubation guidance in 2015?

children.note: The American Society of Anesthesiologists published updated difficult airway management practice guidelines in 2022.

manas.q: In which year did the ASA publish its updated difficult airway guidelines?

children.note: Use of cricoid pressure differs between countries and units; follow your local protocol.

manas.q: Is cricoid pressure used the same way everywhere?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-02.
A 20-member SCCM panel used GRADE on 10 questions, giving one strong recommendation, seven conditional suggestions and two best-practice statements.

manas.q: How many strong recommendations did the SCCM 2023 RSI guideline make?

children.note: Seven RCTs (2384 adults): ketamine probably caused more peri-intubation instability but less adrenal suppression, and probably no effect on first-attempt success (moderate certainty).

manas.q: How did ketamine compare with etomidate for first-attempt success in RSI?

children.note: An ED review found aspiration happened with or without cricoid pressure and too little evidence to judge its effect on success or aspiration.

manas.q: What did the 2022 ED review conclude about cricoid pressure?

children.note: DAS 2025 keeps plans A–D, stresses continuous oxygen, first-attempt success and waveform capnography; 65 recommendations include RSI.

manas.q: Which four plans does the DAS 2025 algorithm keep?

maps.title: HSU 606 · In depth: Oral anatomy and dentition

nodeData.topic: Oral anatomy and dentition in depth
nodeData.note: Oral cavity layout, tongue, palate, salivary glands, tooth development, eruption, notation and common disorders. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: The two parts of the mouth and their boundaries.
The slit between the lips/cheeks and the teeth and gums; the parotid duct opens into it.

manas.q: What is the oral vestibule?

children.note: Space inside the dental arches: roof is the hard and soft palate, floor is mainly the tongue resting on mylohyoid.

manas.q: What forms the roof and floor of the oral cavity proper?

children.note: The mouth opens into the oropharynx at the palatoglossal arches; the palatine tonsil sits between palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.

manas.q: Where does the palatine tonsil lie?

children.note: Muscles, nerves and surface features.
All tongue muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (XII) except palatoglossus, supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus.

manas.q: Which tongue muscle is not supplied by the hypoglossal nerve?

children.note: With a lower motor neurone XII lesion the protruded tongue deviates towards the weak side, because the healthy genioglossus pushes unopposed.

manas.q: Which way does the tongue deviate in a hypoglossal nerve lesion?

children.note: General sensation via the lingual nerve (V3); taste via the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (VII).

manas.q: Which nerves carry touch and taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?

children.note: Both general sensation and taste are carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).

manas.q: Which nerve carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue?

children.note: Circumvallate papillae lie just in front of the sulcus terminalis; filiform papillae are the most numerous and have no taste buds.

manas.q: Which tongue papillae have no taste buds?

children.note: Tip drains to submental nodes, the sides to submandibular nodes, the back to deep cervical nodes; central tumours may spread to both sides.

manas.q: Where does lymph from the tip of the tongue drain first?

children.note: Hard and soft palate.
Formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae in front and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones behind.

manas.q: Which bones form the hard palate?

children.note: All supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus except tensor veli palatini, which is supplied by V3.

manas.q: Which soft palate muscle is supplied by the mandibular nerve?

children.note: The uvula is pulled away from the side of a vagus nerve lesion when the patient says 'aah'.

manas.q: Which way does the uvula deviate in a unilateral vagus lesion?

children.note: Greater palatine nerve supplies most of the hard palate mucosa; the nasopalatine nerve supplies the area behind the upper incisors.

manas.q: Which nerves supply the mucosa of the hard palate?

children.note: Ducts, nerves and stones.
Stensen's duct crosses masseter, pierces buccinator and opens opposite the upper second molar.

manas.q: Where does the parotid duct open into the mouth?

children.note: Parasympathetic fibres from IX relay in the otic ganglion and reach the gland with the auriculotemporal nerve.

manas.q: Which ganglion relays secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland?

children.note: Wharton's duct opens on the sublingual papilla beside the lingual frenulum; secretomotor fibres come via chorda tympani and the submandibular ganglion.

manas.q: Where does the submandibular duct open?

children.note: Its saliva is more mucous and alkaline and the duct runs upwards against gravity, so most salivary stones form here.

manas.q: Why are salivary stones commonest in the submandibular gland?

children.note: Adults secrete roughly 1–1.5 L a day; saliva contains amylase, lysozyme and IgA and buffers plaque acid.

manas.q: About how much saliva does an adult produce per day?

children.note: How a tooth forms (odontogenesis).
Enamel comes from ectoderm (ameloblasts); dentine, pulp and cementum come from neural-crest-derived mesenchyme.

manas.q: Which germ layer gives rise to enamel?

children.note: The enamel organ passes through bud, cap and bell stages before enamel and dentine are laid down.

manas.q: Name the stages of tooth development.

children.note: Ameloblasts are lost once the tooth erupts, so lost enamel is never replaced, whereas dentine can be added throughout life.

manas.q: Why can enamel not repair itself after eruption?

children.note: A tooth is held in its socket by the periodontal ligament, a fibrous joint called a gomphosis.

manas.q: What type of joint holds a tooth in its socket?

children.note: Formulae, timing and mixed dentition.
Per quadrant: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 molars; there are no premolars in the primary set.

manas.q: What is the dental formula of the primary dentition?

children.note: Per quadrant: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars; premolars replace the primary molars.

manas.q: Which permanent teeth replace the primary molars?

children.note: From about 6 to 12 years primary and permanent teeth are present together.

manas.q: Over roughly what ages is the dentition mixed?

children.note: Wisdom teeth usually erupt in late teens to early twenties and are often impacted or absent.

manas.q: When do third molars usually erupt?

children.note: Teeth present at birth, usually lower central incisors; may be loose and pose an aspiration risk.

manas.q: Which teeth are most often present at birth as natal teeth?

children.note: Consider hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism, rickets, Down syndrome and cleidocranial dysplasia.

manas.q: Name systemic causes of delayed tooth eruption.

children.note: How teeth are named in records.
First digit is the quadrant (1–4 permanent, 5–8 primary, clockwise from upper right); second digit counts back from the midline.

manas.q: How does the FDI two-digit tooth notation work?

children.note: 11 = upper right permanent central incisor; 36 = lower left first permanent molar.

manas.q: In FDI notation, which tooth is 36?

children.note: What doctors meet in and around the teeth.
Plaque bacteria, chiefly Streptococcus mutans, ferment sugars into acid that demineralises enamel then dentine.

manas.q: Which organism is chiefly linked to dental caries?

children.note: Fluoride forms acid-resistant fluorapatite and aids remineralisation; excess during enamel formation causes fluorosis.

manas.q: How does fluoride protect teeth?

children.note: Mottled, brown-stained enamel is common where groundwater fluoride is high, notably parts of the Rift Valley.

manas.q: Why is dental fluorosis common in parts of Kenya's Rift Valley?

children.note: Gingivitis is reversible gum inflammation; periodontitis destroys attachment and bone, loosening teeth; diabetes worsens it.

manas.q: What separates gingivitis from periodontitis?

children.note: Spreading cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces, usually from a lower molar infection; airway emergency.

manas.q: What is Ludwig's angina and why is it dangerous?

children.note: White plaques that wipe off leaving a red base; in an adult without obvious cause, test for HIV.

manas.q: What should oral thrush in an otherwise well adult prompt?

children.note: Rapid gangrene of the mouth and face, mainly in malnourished young children; it starts as gum ulceration.

manas.q: Which children are most at risk of noma?

children.note: Replant at once or store in milk and see a dentist urgently; primary teeth are not replanted.

manas.q: How should a knocked-out permanent tooth be handled?

children.note: Looking at the mouth well.
Use a good light and tongue depressor: lips, vestibule, gums, teeth, tongue (including underside), floor, palate, tonsils.

manas.q: List the areas to inspect in an oral examination.

children.note: One finger in the floor of mouth, other hand under the jaw, to feel submandibular gland and stones.

manas.q: How is the submandibular gland palpated?

children.note: A panoramic radiograph showing all teeth and both jaws on one film; used for impaction, infection and jaw fractures.

manas.q: What does an orthopantomogram show?

children.note: Quick recall.
20 primary teeth have no premolars; the 32 permanent include 8 premolars and 12 molars.

manas.q: How many premolars and molars are in the permanent dentition?

children.note: Lingual nerve carries touch but the chorda tympani (VII) carries taste for the front of the tongue.

manas.q: Which nerve carries taste fibres within the lingual nerve?

children.note: How oral health is framed; Kenya first.
Use the MoH Clinical Guidelines for Level 4–6 hospitals and refer dental problems to county dental services.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline should guide hospital care?

children.note: The WHO Global Oral Health Status Report (2022) estimated that oral diseases affect close to 3.5 billion people.

manas.q: About how many people does WHO estimate have oral diseases?

children.note: WHO added noma to its list of neglected tropical diseases in 2023.

manas.q: When did WHO list noma as a neglected tropical disease?

children.note: FDI notation is used internationally; the UK often uses Palmer notation and the USA the Universal 1–32 system.

manas.q: Which tooth-numbering systems are used in the UK and USA?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-02.
Expert consensus: plan caries care from each patient's risk assessment and lesion activity, aiming to control progression and restore function, with personalised follow-up.

manas.q: What guides caries treatment plans in the 2022 expert consensus?

children.note: ECC may raise the risk of new caries in both dentitions; advice: improve parents' oral health, set up an early dental home and treat minimally invasively.

manas.q: What approach to early childhood caries does the 2022 consensus advise?

children.note: Meta-analysis in adults 45 and over: pooled prevalence 22% for edentulism and 45% for dental caries, varying widely by country.

manas.q: What pooled edentulism and caries prevalence did the 2022 meta-analysis find?

maps.title: HOS 400 · In depth: Orthopaedic history and examination

nodeData.topic: Orthopaedic history and examination in depth
nodeData.note: Taking a targeted history, examining joints and spotting limb- and life-threatening problems. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What a good orthopaedic assessment must achieve.
Make a diagnosis, judge how much function is lost, and spot anything that threatens life or limb.

manas.q: What are the three goals of an orthopaedic assessment?

children.note: Expose the joint fully and always compare with the normal limb; subtle swelling, wasting or lost movement shows up side by side.

manas.q: Why should both limbs be exposed and compared?

children.note: Ask where it hurts first and watch the patient's face while you examine; never cause unnecessary pain.

manas.q: What should you do before palpating a painful joint?

children.note: Questions that point to the diagnosis.
Site, onset, character, radiation, timing, aggravating and relieving factors and severity; night or rest pain needs extra thought.

manas.q: Which features of musculoskeletal pain should be recorded?

children.note: Ask how the force was applied and how strong it was; high-energy trauma means looking hard for other injuries.

manas.q: Why is the mechanism of injury important?

children.note: Inflammatory: long morning stiffness easing with activity. Mechanical: pain worse with use and better with rest.

manas.q: How does inflammatory stiffness differ from mechanical pain?

children.note: True locking suggests a loose body or torn meniscus blocking movement; giving way suggests instability or pain inhibition.

manas.q: What do locking and giving way of the knee suggest?

children.note: Record hand dominance, job, walking distance and daily tasks; treatment goals depend on what the patient needs to do.

manas.q: Why record hand dominance and occupation?

children.note: Fever, weight loss and night sweats raise concern for infection (including TB) or malignancy.

manas.q: Which systemic symptoms point to infection or tumour?

children.note: Ask about diabetes, HIV, sickle cell disease, steroid use and anticoagulants; each changes the differential or the risks.

manas.q: Which comorbidities and drugs matter in an orthopaedic history?

children.note: Going deeper than the basic order.
Skin (scars, sinuses, redness), shape (swelling, deformity, wasting) and the resting position or attitude of the limb.

manas.q: What three things do you inspect under 'Look'?

children.note: Use the back of the hand for temperature, then palpate bony landmarks and joint line for tenderness and check for effusion.

manas.q: How do you assess joint temperature?

children.note: Test active movement first, then passive; record ranges in degrees from the neutral zero position.

manas.q: In what order are active and passive movements tested?

children.note: Passive range full but active reduced suggests weakness, tendon rupture or pain; both reduced suggests a joint block or stiffness.

manas.q: What does reduced active but full passive movement suggest?

children.note: Watch the patient walk; an antalgic gait has a shortened stance phase on the painful side.

manas.q: What is an antalgic gait?

children.note: True: ASIS to medial malleolus. Apparent: fixed midline point (e.g. umbilicus) to medial malleolus; differs with pelvic tilt.

manas.q: How are true and apparent leg length measured?

children.note: Knee in slight flexion (about 20–30°); excess anterior tibial translation with a soft end-point suggests an ACL tear.

manas.q: What does the Lachman test assess?

children.note: Quick screen for locomotor problems.
Gait, Arms, Legs and Spine: a rapid screen to find which area needs a full regional examination.

manas.q: What does GALS stand for?

children.note: Any pain or stiffness in muscles, joints or back? Can you dress fully without difficulty? Can you manage stairs?

manas.q: What are the three GALS screening questions?

children.note: Hands behind head, hands out palms down then up, make a fist, pinch each finger to thumb, squeeze across the MCP joints.

manas.q: Which manoeuvres screen the arms in GALS?

children.note: Check knee effusion, flex hip and knee with hip rotation, and squeeze across the MTP joints for tenderness.

manas.q: Which manoeuvres screen the legs in GALS?

children.note: Inspect from behind and side for curves, ear towards shoulder for neck, and touch toes to watch lumbar flexion.

manas.q: How is the spine screened in GALS?

children.note: A paediatric version (pGALS) adapts the screen for school-age children.

manas.q: What is the paediatric version of GALS called?

children.note: Check distal function every time.
Pulses, colour, temperature and capillary refill (normally under 2 seconds) distal to the injury.

manas.q: What is a normal capillary refill time?

children.note: Light touch in nerve territories, motor power graded 0–5 (MRC scale) and reflexes where relevant.

manas.q: How is muscle power graded?

children.note: Humeral shaft: radial nerve (wrist drop). Shoulder dislocation: axillary nerve. Fibular neck: common peroneal nerve (foot drop).

manas.q: Which nerve is at risk with a humeral shaft fracture?

children.note: Check the radial pulse, hand perfusion and median nerve including its anterior interosseous branch (OK sign).

manas.q: Which nerve branch is tested with the OK sign?

children.note: Findings that must not be missed.
History of cancer, fever or immunosuppression, weight loss, major trauma, steroid use, constant night pain and progressive neurology.

manas.q: List red flags in low back pain.

children.note: Treat as septic arthritis until proven otherwise; aspirate (ideally before antibiotics) and refer urgently.

manas.q: How should a hot, swollen single joint be treated until proven otherwise?

children.note: Back pain with gibbus, systemic symptoms or TB contact suggests spinal TB (Pott disease); check neurology.

manas.q: Which features suggest spinal tuberculosis?

children.note: Decide who needs an X-ray after injury.
Rule-out tools for alert adults: a negative rule makes a fracture unlikely, reducing unnecessary X-rays.

manas.q: What is the purpose of the Ottawa rules?

children.note: Ankle X-ray if malleolar-zone pain plus bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the distal 6 cm of either malleolus, or unable to bear weight four steps.

manas.q: When does the Ottawa ankle rule call for an X-ray?

children.note: Foot X-ray if midfoot pain plus tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal or navicular, or unable to bear weight four steps.

manas.q: Which bony points are checked in the Ottawa foot rule?

children.note: Knee X-ray if age 55+, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, cannot flex to 90°, or cannot bear weight four steps.

manas.q: List the five criteria of the Ottawa knee rule.

children.note: Inability to take four steps both straight after the injury and when examined, regardless of limping.

manas.q: How is inability to bear weight defined in the Ottawa rules?

children.note: Surgical emergency of the lumbar nerve roots.
Nerve roots below the conus (around L1–L2) are compressed, most often by a large central lumbar disc prolapse.

manas.q: What most commonly causes cauda equina syndrome?

children.note: Saddle or perianal numbness, bladder or bowel change, bilateral or alternating sciatica, sexual dysfunction and leg weakness.

manas.q: What are the symptoms of cauda equina syndrome?

children.note: Test perianal and saddle sensation, lower-limb power and reflexes; DRE for anal tone; bladder scan for post-void residual.

manas.q: What should be examined if cauda equina syndrome is suspected?

children.note: CES-I has altered bladder sensation without retention; CES-R has painless retention and generally a worse outlook.

manas.q: How does CES-I differ from CES-R?

children.note: Urgent MRI of the lumbar spine and urgent spinal surgical referral for decompression.

manas.q: What is the key investigation in suspected cauda equina syndrome?

children.note: Raised pressure in a closed fascial space.
Pressure in a closed fascial compartment rises until tissue perfusion fails; muscle and nerve become ischaemic.

manas.q: What is the mechanism of compartment syndrome?

children.note: Tibial and forearm fractures, crush injury, reperfusion after vascular repair and tight casts or bandages.

manas.q: Which injuries carry high risk of compartment syndrome?

children.note: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the muscles in the compartment.

manas.q: What are the earliest signs of compartment syndrome?

children.note: Distal pulses are usually still present; a lost pulse is a late sign, so never wait for it.

manas.q: Does a palpable pulse exclude compartment syndrome?

children.note: Split casts and dressings down to skin, keep the limb at heart level, and arrange urgent fasciotomy.

manas.q: What is the immediate management of suspected compartment syndrome?

children.note: Used when clinical signs are unreliable (e.g. unconscious): delta pressure = diastolic BP minus compartment pressure; under 30 mmHg is a common fasciotomy threshold.

manas.q: What delta pressure threshold is commonly used for fasciotomy?

children.note: Life before limb.
Airway with cervical spine protection, Breathing, Circulation with bleeding control, Disability, Exposure with warmth.

manas.q: What are the steps of the ATLS primary survey?

children.note: Direct pressure first; a tourniquet for life-threatening limb haemorrhage that pressure cannot stop.

manas.q: How is life-threatening limb haemorrhage controlled?

children.note: For suspected pelvic fracture with shock, apply a binder centred over the greater trochanters; avoid repeated pelvic springing.

manas.q: Where should a pelvic binder be centred?

children.note: Allergies, Medications, Past history and pregnancy, Last meal, Events and environment of the injury.

manas.q: What does AMPLE stand for?

children.note: Head-to-toe exam once stable; a repeat (tertiary) survey later catches injuries missed early.

manas.q: Why is a tertiary survey done in trauma?

children.note: Photograph, cover with a saline-moistened dressing, splint, give early IV antibiotics and tetanus cover.

manas.q: What are the first steps for an open fracture?

children.note: Quick wins in OSCEs.
Wash hands, consent, expose adequately with dignity, and ask about pain before starting.

manas.q: What should you do at the start of every MSK OSCE?

children.note: End with neurovascular status, joints above and below, and which imaging you would request.

manas.q: How should you close an orthopaedic examination station?

children.note: Name deformity by the position of the distal part relative to the proximal (varus, valgus, rotation, angulation).

manas.q: How is a deformity described?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
Use the MoH Clinical Guidelines for Level 4–6 hospitals and your hospital trauma and referral protocols.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers hospital trauma care?

children.note: WHO and ICRC teach a Basic Emergency Care course built on the ABCDE approach for low-resource settings.

manas.q: Which WHO course teaches the ABCDE approach for low-resource settings?

children.note: The American College of Surgeons runs ATLS, the source of the primary and secondary survey structure.

manas.q: Which body runs the ATLS course?

children.note: NICE has low back pain and sciatica guidance; the British Orthopaedic Association issues BOAST trauma standards.

manas.q: What are BOAST standards?

children.note: Guidelines worldwide agree that suspected cauda equina syndrome needs urgent MRI.

manas.q: What do international guidelines agree on for suspected CES?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-04.
15 studies (8560 adults): sensitivity about 0.91 but specificity only about 0.25; a good rule-out tool that cuts X-rays, with many false positives.

manas.q: How sensitive was the Ottawa ankle rule in the 2022 meta-analysis?

children.note: Cochrane (14 studies): most single red flags screened poorly; older age, trauma and steroid use were more informative, and combinations may help.

manas.q: Which red flags were most informative for vertebral fracture in the 2023 Cochrane review?

children.note: All nine guidelines named saddle sensory change and bladder or bowel dysfunction as red flags and advised urgent MRI; DRE and residual volume still matter.

manas.q: Which two red flags appeared in all CES guidelines reviewed?

children.note: Nursing text on fracture types and care.
Nursing text on spinal conditions.

maps.title: HPS 400 · In depth: Psychiatric interview

nodeData.note: Structuring the history, mental state exam, risk, cognition, collateral and capacity. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Safety, privacy and rapport first.
Sit with clear access to the exit for both of you, know how to call for help, and tell staff where you are.

manas.q: How should a room be arranged for a psychiatric interview?

children.note: Explain that what is said stays confidential unless there is serious risk to the patient or others.

manas.q: What are the limits of confidentiality in a psychiatric interview?

children.note: Introduce yourself, explain the purpose, show empathy, listen actively and notice non-verbal cues.

manas.q: Which skills help build rapport in a psychiatric interview?

children.note: Interview in the patient's preferred language; use a trained interpreter rather than a relative where possible.

manas.q: Why avoid using relatives as interpreters?

children.note: Periodically summarise what you heard and check it is correct; this shows listening and corrects errors.

manas.q: Why summarise during a psychiatric interview?

children.note: Deeper detail on each heading.
Record the main problem in the patient's own words, and how and why they came for help now.

manas.q: How should the presenting complaint be recorded in psychiatry?

children.note: Onset, duration, course, triggers, symptoms by syndrome (mood, psychosis, anxiety) and the effect on daily functioning.

manas.q: What should the history of presenting illness cover?

children.note: Previous episodes, diagnoses, admissions, treatments and response, and any past self-harm or suicide attempts.

manas.q: What does the past psychiatric history include?

children.note: Epilepsy, HIV, thyroid disease, head injury; current drugs, adherence and side effects of past psychotropics.

manas.q: Which medical conditions matter in a psychiatric history?

children.note: Alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, khat (miraa) and other drugs: amount, pattern, dependence features and last use.

manas.q: Which substances should be asked about in a Kenyan psychiatric history?

children.note: Mental illness, suicide and substance use in relatives, plus family relationships and support.

manas.q: What does the family history cover in psychiatry?

children.note: Birth, milestones, schooling, work record, relationships, psychosexual history and major life events or trauma.

manas.q: What is included in the personal history?

children.note: Arrests, charges or violence; housing, income, dependants and social support.

manas.q: Why is forensic history taken in psychiatry?

children.note: A snapshot of the mind at interview (ASEPTIC).
Appearance and behaviour, Speech, Emotion (mood and affect), Perception, Thought, Insight and judgement, Cognition.

manas.q: What does the ASEPTIC mnemonic stand for?

children.note: Dress, hygiene, eye contact, rapport, psychomotor activity, abnormal movements and level of arousal.

manas.q: What is observed under appearance and behaviour?

children.note: Rate, volume, tone and amount; pressured speech suggests mania, poverty of speech suggests depression or psychosis.

manas.q: What does pressured speech suggest?

children.note: Mood is the patient's sustained, self-described emotion; affect is the observed expression, judged for range and congruence.

manas.q: What is the difference between mood and affect?

children.note: How thoughts link: flight of ideas, loosening of associations, thought block, circumstantiality or tangentiality.

manas.q: Give examples of abnormal thought form.

children.note: Delusions, overvalued ideas, obsessions, preoccupations, and thoughts of self-harm or harming others.

manas.q: What is assessed under thought content?

children.note: A fixed false belief held despite contrary evidence and not explained by the person's cultural or religious background.

manas.q: What is a delusion?

children.note: Hallucination: a perception with no external stimulus. Illusion: misreading a real stimulus.

manas.q: How does a hallucination differ from an illusion?

children.note: Does the patient see they are unwell, accept a need for treatment, and make safe decisions?

manas.q: What does insight in the MSE assess?

children.note: Suicide, harm to others, self-neglect.
Move from passive wishes to die to active thoughts, intent, plan, access to means and any preparations.

manas.q: Which elements of suicidal thinking should be explored?

children.note: Planning, precautions against discovery, a note or final acts, and regret at surviving point to high intent.

manas.q: Which features of an attempt suggest high suicidal intent?

children.note: Previous attempt, mental illness, substance misuse, male sex, chronic illness or pain, isolation and recent loss.

manas.q: Name risk factors for completed suicide.

children.note: Family support, children, religious or moral beliefs, hope for the future and engagement with care.

manas.q: Name protective factors against suicide.

children.note: Thoughts of harm, a named target, past violence, command hallucinations, persecutory beliefs and intoxication.

manas.q: Which features raise concern about risk to others?

children.note: Poor eating, hygiene or shelter, missed treatment, exploitation, and risk to children or dependants.

manas.q: What does self-neglect risk include?

children.note: Combine findings into a risk formulation and a safety plan; screening scores alone do not predict who will die by suicide.

manas.q: Why shouldn't risk scales alone guide suicide management?

children.note: Bedside tools, not diagnoses.
A 30-point test of orientation, registration, attention, recall, language and copying a figure.

manas.q: How many points is the MMSE scored out of?

children.note: A 30-point test adding executive tasks (trail-making, clock drawing); more sensitive for mild cognitive impairment.

manas.q: Why is the MoCA more sensitive than MMSE for mild impairment?

children.note: Low schooling, language and unfamiliar tasks lower scores; the MoCA adds a point for 12 years' education or less.

manas.q: How does MoCA adjust for low education?

children.note: Delirium: sudden onset, fluctuating course and inattention. Dementia: gradual decline with clear consciousness early on.

manas.q: What features distinguish delirium from dementia?

children.note: Examine physically and consider glucose, FBC, electrolytes, thyroid tests, HIV and syphilis serology as indicated.

manas.q: Which tests help exclude organic causes of psychiatric symptoms?

children.note: Information from others.
Family, friends, teachers, employers, previous clinicians and referral notes.

manas.q: Who can give a collateral history?

children.note: Onset and course of change, behaviour at home, risk incidents, substance use and premorbid personality.

manas.q: What should a collateral history explore?

children.note: Seek the patient's consent; you may listen to informants without disclosing the patient's information.

manas.q: Can you take a collateral history without breaching confidentiality?

children.note: Decision-specific judgement.
Adults are presumed to have capacity unless shown otherwise; mental illness alone does not remove it.

manas.q: Does a psychiatric diagnosis mean a patient lacks capacity?

children.note: Capacity is judged for one decision at one time and may return as the illness improves.

manas.q: Why is capacity described as decision-specific?

children.note: Can the person understand the information, retain it, use or weigh it, and communicate a choice?

manas.q: What four abilities make up the functional test of capacity?

children.note: A decision you disagree with does not by itself show lack of capacity.

manas.q: Does an unwise decision prove lack of capacity?

children.note: Kenya's Mental Health Act sets the rules for involuntary admission and treatment; learn your unit's forms.

manas.q: Which Kenyan law governs involuntary psychiatric admission?

children.note: Pulling it together.
Explains the problem using biological, psychological and social factors rather than a diagnosis alone.

manas.q: What is a biopsychosocial formulation?

children.note: Predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors organise the formulation.

manas.q: What are the 4 Ps in a psychiatric formulation?

children.note: State the likely diagnosis, differentials, risk level, investigations and an immediate management plan.

manas.q: What should follow the formulation in a case presentation?

children.note: OSCE tips.
Ask about suicide and harm to others in every station; it does not plant the idea.

manas.q: Does asking about suicide increase risk?

children.note: Quote the patient for mood; describe affect from what you see.

manas.q: How should mood and affect be recorded differently?

children.note: Summarise, check concerns, agree a follow-up and a crisis contact before ending.

manas.q: How should a psychiatric interview end?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
Use Kenya MoH mental health guidance and your hospital protocols; WHO mhGAP-based training supports assessment by non-specialists in primary care.

manas.q: What guides psychiatric assessment in Kenyan practice?

children.note: The mhGAP Intervention Guide (version 2.0, 2016) helps non-specialists assess and manage priority mental, neurological and substance conditions.

manas.q: What is the WHO mhGAP Intervention Guide for?

children.note: WHO's LIVE LIFE (2021) suicide prevention approach includes limiting access to means and early identification and follow-up.

manas.q: What is WHO's LIVE LIFE initiative about?

children.note: NICE advises against using risk tools or scales alone to predict suicide or decide on care after self-harm.

manas.q: What does NICE 2022 say about suicide risk scales?

children.note: WHO's ICD-11 (in use from 2022) and the APA's DSM-5-TR (2022) set diagnostic criteria.

manas.q: Which two diagnostic classification systems are used in psychiatry?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-04.
Review: a good interview builds a working alliance; empathic listening and noticing non-verbal cues, behaviour and appearance improve diagnosis.

manas.q: Which interview skills does the 2024 review say improve emergency psychiatric diagnosis?

children.note: Screening finds those at risk; a positive screen leads to full assessment. Tools are limited, so clinical judgement matters; many may not need admission if support and safety plans are workable.

manas.q: What should follow a positive suicide risk screen?

children.note: 803 memory clinic patients plus 19 studies: MoCA scores ran lower than MMSE; converting MoCA to MMSE was the more accurate direction.

manas.q: Which score tends to be lower, MoCA or MMSE?

children.note: Nursing text on suicide risk.
Nursing text on delirium.

maps.title: HSU 400 · In depth: Wound healing and wound care

nodeData.topic: Wound healing and wound care in depth
nodeData.note: How wounds heal, what delays them, assessment, dressings, infection, chronic ulcers and scars. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What a wound is and how wounds are described.
A break in the continuity of skin or other tissue, caused by trauma, surgery, pressure, heat or disease.

manas.q: What is a wound?

children.note: An acute wound moves through the healing phases on time; a chronic wound fails to heal in the expected time, often stuck in inflammation.

manas.q: How does a chronic wound differ from an acute wound?

children.note: Incised (clean cut), laceration (torn, ragged edges), abrasion (graze), puncture (deep, narrow), contusion and crush injury.

manas.q: Name the main types of mechanical wound.

children.note: Cells and molecules behind each phase.
Vessels constrict, platelets plug and fibrin forms a clot; platelets release growth factors such as PDGF and TGF-beta that call in repair cells.

manas.q: Which growth factors do platelets release to start repair?

children.note: Neutrophils arrive within hours and clear bacteria and debris; macrophages follow over the next days and become the dominant cell.

manas.q: Which white cell arrives first in a fresh wound?

children.note: Macrophages clear debris and release growth factors that drive fibroblasts and new vessels; healing fails without them, unlike without neutrophils.

manas.q: Which cell is essential for normal wound healing?

children.note: Fibroblasts lay down type III collagen and matrix while new capillaries grow in, giving red, granular, easily bleeding tissue.

manas.q: What is granulation tissue made of?

children.note: Keratinocytes migrate from wound edges (and hair follicles) across a moist bed to cover the defect.

manas.q: Where do new epithelial cells come from in wound healing?

children.note: Myofibroblasts pull wound edges inward, shrinking open wounds; strong in secondary intention and can cause contractures.

manas.q: Which cell causes wound contraction?

children.note: Type III collagen is replaced by stronger type I and cross-linked; scar strength rises but never fully matches normal skin (about 80% at best).

manas.q: What collagen change occurs in remodelling?

children.note: Choosing primary, secondary or delayed closure.
Little granulation is needed; epithelium bridges the thin gap within about 1–2 days, giving a fine linear scar.

manas.q: Why does primary intention give a small scar?

children.note: Large or infected defects fill from the base with granulation, then contract and epithelialise; slower and leaves a wider scar.

manas.q: Which processes fill a wound healing by secondary intention?

children.note: A contaminated wound is cleaned, left open and reviewed, then closed once clean and free of infection.

manas.q: What is tertiary (delayed primary) closure?

children.note: Heavily soiled, late-presenting or infected wounds, and many bite wounds, are usually not closed primarily.

manas.q: Which wounds should usually not be closed primarily?

children.note: Group them as local and systemic for exams.
Infection, foreign body, dead tissue, haematoma, poor blood supply, tension, oedema, movement, previous radiation.

manas.q: List local factors that delay wound healing.

children.note: Diabetes, malnutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc), steroids, cytotoxics, smoking, old age, HIV/immunosuppression, jaundice, uraemia, anaemia.

manas.q: List systemic factors that delay wound healing.

children.note: High glucose impairs neutrophil function, small-vessel disease lowers perfusion, and neuropathy lets unnoticed injury continue.

manas.q: Give three ways diabetes delays wound healing.

children.note: Steroids blunt inflammation and collagen synthesis; vitamin A is classically taught to partly counter this effect.

manas.q: Which vitamin is taught to partly reverse steroid-impaired healing?

children.note: Nicotine causes vasoconstriction and carbon monoxide lowers oxygen delivery, raising wound breakdown and infection.

manas.q: How does smoking impair wound healing?

children.note: History, examination and tests.
Mechanism, time since injury, contamination, foreign body, tetanus immunisation status, diabetes/HIV, drugs (steroids, anticoagulants).

manas.q: What should the history of a wound include?

children.note: Site, size (length, width, depth), edges, base, exudate, odour, surrounding skin and any tracking or undermining.

manas.q: Which features describe a wound on examination?

children.note: Red: healthy granulation. Yellow: slough. Black: necrotic eschar. Green or foul: suspect infection.

manas.q: What do red, yellow and black wound beds indicate?

children.note: Before giving local anaesthetic, test distal pulses, sensation and tendon function; explore for nerve, tendon or vessel injury.

manas.q: Why test sensation before infiltrating local anaesthetic?

children.note: Spreading redness, warmth, swelling, increasing pain, pus, offensive smell, wound breakdown, fever.

manas.q: What are the signs of wound infection?

children.note: Glucose, FBC; swab only clinically infected wounds; X-ray for foreign body, fracture or osteomyelitis; biopsy a non-healing edge.

manas.q: Which investigations help in a poorly healing wound?

children.note: Principles, not product lists.
Wash out with plenty of saline or clean drinking-quality water to remove debris and lower bacterial load.

manas.q: What fluid can be used to irrigate a wound?

children.note: Remove dead tissue, slough and foreign material that feed bacteria and block healing.

manas.q: Why is wound debridement done?

children.note: Surgical/sharp (fastest), autolytic (moist dressings let own enzymes work), mechanical, enzymatic and biological (sterile larvae).

manas.q: Name methods of wound debridement.

children.note: A moist, warm, protected bed lets cells migrate faster than under a dry scab; avoid both drying and soaking.

manas.q: Why are moist dressings preferred over letting wounds dry?

children.note: Dry wound: add moisture (hydrogel). Heavy exudate: absorb (alginate, foam). Infected: antimicrobial (iodine, silver).

manas.q: How do you choose a dressing for a dry versus a wet wound?

children.note: A sealed foam dressing on suction removes exudate, reduces oedema and encourages granulation in large open wounds.

manas.q: What does negative pressure wound therapy do?

children.note: Definition, types, risk and prevention.
Infection of the incision or operated organ/space within 30 days of surgery, or longer when an implant was left in.

manas.q: What time frame defines a surgical site infection?

children.note: Superficial incisional (skin, subcutis), deep incisional (fascia, muscle) and organ/space (e.g. intra-abdominal abscess).

manas.q: What are the three levels of surgical site infection?

children.note: Dirty wound class, long operation, diabetes, obesity, smoking, malnutrition, hypothermia, razor shaving, poor technique.

manas.q: Name risk factors for surgical site infection.

children.note: Clip not shave, alcohol-based skin prep, antibiotic prophylaxis within 120 min before incision (WHO; many protocols say 60 min), keep patient warm, control glucose.

manas.q: Name key measures that prevent surgical site infection.

children.note: Staphylococcus aureus dominates in clean surgery; gut Gram-negatives and anaerobes after bowel surgery.

manas.q: Which organism most often causes SSI after clean surgery?

children.note: Open the wound and drain pus, debride, dress; give antibiotics if cellulitis spreads or the patient is systemically unwell.

manas.q: What is the main treatment of a superficial SSI with pus?

children.note: Recognise the ulcer type, then treat the cause.
Gaiter area, often above the medial malleolus; shallow, sloping edges, wet, with varicose veins, brown staining and hard skin.

manas.q: Describe the typical site and look of a venous ulcer.

children.note: Check ABPI first, then graduated compression and leg elevation; treat underlying venous reflux where possible.

manas.q: What is the mainstay of venous ulcer treatment?

children.note: Toes, heel or shin; punched-out, painful (worse on elevation), pale base, cold foot, weak or absent pulses.

manas.q: How does an arterial ulcer present?

children.note: Below 0.9 suggests arterial disease; full compression is usually avoided below about 0.8, so seek specialist advice. Calcified vessels in diabetes can read falsely high.

manas.q: Why can ABPI be falsely high in diabetes?

children.note: Usually neuropathic: painless, under pressure points such as metatarsal heads, ringed by callus; may also be ischaemic.

manas.q: Where do neuropathic diabetic foot ulcers typically occur?

children.note: Offload pressure, debride callus, treat infection, assess blood supply, control glucose; bone felt on probing suggests osteomyelitis.

manas.q: What does probing to bone in a diabetic ulcer suggest?

children.note: Tissue death from sustained pressure and shear over bony points: sacrum, heels, hips, ischium, occiput in lying patients.

manas.q: Which sites are commonest for pressure ulcers?

children.note: Stage 1 non-blanching redness, 2 partial-thickness, 3 full-thickness skin loss, 4 exposed bone/tendon/muscle; plus unstageable.

manas.q: How are pressure ulcers staged?

children.note: Risk-assess on admission, turn regularly, use pressure-relieving surfaces, keep skin clean and dry, feed well.

manas.q: How are pressure ulcers prevented?

children.note: Beyond keloid vs hypertrophic basics.
Collagen deposition outpaces breakdown during remodelling, leaving a raised, firm scar.

manas.q: What is the basic cause of hypertrophic and keloid scars?

children.note: Earlobes (e.g. after piercing), front of chest, shoulders and upper back.

manas.q: Where do keloids commonly form?

children.note: Common after burns and wounds under tension or across joints; appears within weeks and often softens over months.

manas.q: In which wounds are hypertrophic scars common?

children.note: Silicone sheets or gel, pressure garments, intralesional steroid; keloid excision alone often recurs, so combine with adjuvant therapy.

manas.q: Why is keloid excision combined with adjuvant therapy?

children.note: A shortened scar across a joint limits movement, classically after burns; prevent with splints and physio; release with Z-plasty or grafts.

manas.q: How are scar contractures prevented?

children.note: Every wound: ask about tetanus.
Spore-forming anaerobe in soil and dung; its toxin blocks inhibitory nerve signals, causing lockjaw and muscle spasms.

manas.q: How does tetanus toxin cause muscle spasm?

children.note: Puncture or soil/manure-contaminated wounds, devitalised tissue, burns, open fractures and wounds with delayed surgery.

manas.q: Which wounds are tetanus-prone?

children.note: Clean and debride; give tetanus toxoid if immunisation is not up to date; add tetanus immunoglobulin for prone wounds in unknown/incomplete cover.

manas.q: When is tetanus immunoglobulin added to toxoid?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
Use the MoH Clinical Guidelines for Level 4–6 hospitals and your hospital protocol for wound care and surgical prophylaxis.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers hospital surgical and wound care?

children.note: WHO global SSI guidance favours alcohol-based chlorhexidine skin prep, avoiding razors, and not prolonging prophylaxis after surgery.

manas.q: What does WHO advise about continuing antibiotic prophylaxis after surgery?
