children.note: The International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot publishes international guidelines on prevention, offloading and infection.

manas.q: Which body publishes international diabetic foot guidelines?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-04.
Review: repair needs coordinated migration, matrix deposition, angiogenesis and inflammation; immune cells influence keratinocytes, fibroblasts, vessels, fat and nerves.

manas.q: Which skin cell types do immune cells influence during repair?

children.note: Review: chronic wounds are rising and costly; newer evidence-based care is replacing outdated standards, but gaps remain in cutting limb loss and death.

manas.q: What gaps remain in chronic wound care per the 2022 review?

children.note: Review: S. aureus and Pseudomonas use virulence factors, and biofilms with mixed microbes help them evade immunity and resist antimicrobials.

manas.q: How do biofilms help wound bacteria survive?

children.note: High-yield points for vivas and MCQs.
Sloping: venous/healing. Punched-out: arterial or neuropathic. Rolled: basal cell carcinoma. Everted: squamous cell carcinoma.

manas.q: What does an everted ulcer edge suggest?

children.note: Never apply compression to a leg ulcer before excluding significant arterial disease.

manas.q: What must be checked before compressing a leg ulcer?

children.note: In any wound viva, state tetanus status and prophylaxis — examiners expect it.

manas.q: Which preventive step must be addressed in every wound?

children.note: Free textbook chapter on wound care and dressings.
Free textbook chapter on common skin disorders.

maps.title: HSU 403 · In depth: Anatomy of the eye and orbit

nodeData.topic: Eye and orbit anatomy in depth
nodeData.note: Bony orbit, openings, muscles, globe, aqueous flow, visual pathway, lids, blood supply and clinical links. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Shape and the four walls.
A four-sided pyramid: base at the orbital rim, apex behind at the optic canal; seven bones: frontal, zygomatic, maxilla, ethmoid, sphenoid, lacrimal, palatine.

manas.q: Name the seven bones forming the orbit.

children.note: Orbital plate of frontal bone plus lesser wing of sphenoid; the anterior cranial fossa lies above.

manas.q: Which bones form the orbital roof?

children.note: Zygomatic bone and greater wing of sphenoid; the thickest, strongest wall.

manas.q: Which is the strongest orbital wall?

children.note: Mainly maxilla, with zygomatic and palatine; roofs the maxillary sinus and carries the infraorbital groove and nerve.

manas.q: Which sinus lies below the orbital floor?

children.note: Maxilla, lacrimal, ethmoid (paper-thin lamina papyracea) and sphenoid body; the thinnest wall, beside the ethmoid air cells.

manas.q: Which part of the medial orbital wall is paper-thin?

children.note: What passes where.
In the lesser wing of sphenoid; carries the optic nerve (CN II) and ophthalmic artery.

manas.q: What passes through the optic canal?

children.note: Between greater and lesser wings of sphenoid; carries CN III, IV, VI, the three V1 branches and the superior ophthalmic vein.

manas.q: Which nerves pass through the superior orbital fissure?

children.note:
Lacrimal, Frontal, Trochlear (outside the tendinous ring); Superior III, Abducens, Nasociliary, Inferior III (inside the ring).
Mnemonic: Live Frankly To See Absolutely No Insult

manas.q: What mnemonic lists superior orbital fissure nerves?

children.note: Origin of the four recti; encircles CN II, ophthalmic artery, both divisions of III, nasociliary and VI. Lacrimal, frontal and IV pass outside.

manas.q: Which SOF nerves pass outside the common tendinous ring?

children.note: Between greater wing of sphenoid and maxilla; carries the infraorbital and zygomatic nerves and venous links to the pterygoid plexus.

manas.q: Which nerve passes through the inferior orbital fissure?

children.note: Seven muscles, three nerves.
Four recti (superior, inferior, medial, lateral), two obliques (superior, inferior) and levator palpebrae superioris.

manas.q: Name the seven extraocular muscles.

children.note: MR adducts, LR abducts. SR elevates, adducts, intorts. IR depresses, adducts, extorts.

manas.q: What are the actions of superior rectus?

children.note: SO depresses (best in adduction), intorts, abducts. IO elevates (best in adduction), extorts, abducts.

manas.q: What are the actions of the superior oblique?

children.note: Test SR and IR with the eye abducted; test the obliques with the eye adducted. SO: look down and in.

manas.q: In which gaze is the superior oblique tested?

children.note: Superior division: SR and levator. Inferior: MR, IR, IO, plus parasympathetic fibres to the ciliary ganglion for pupil and accommodation.

manas.q: Which muscles does the superior division of CN III supply?

children.note: Smooth muscle in the upper lid supplied by sympathetic fibres; its loss causes the mild ptosis of Horner syndrome.

manas.q: Why is there ptosis in Horner syndrome?

children.topic: Layers of the globe in depth
children.note: Beyond the three coats.
Clear, avascular, densely supplied by V1; gives most of the eye's focusing power. Five layers from epithelium to endothelium.

manas.q: Which structure provides most of the eye's refractive power?

children.note: Touching the cornea makes both eyes blink: afferent V1 (nasociliary), efferent VII to orbicularis oculi.

manas.q: What are the afferent and efferent nerves of the corneal reflex?

children.note: Tough white collagen coat; meets the cornea at the limbus; perforated at the back by optic nerve fibres (lamina cribrosa).

manas.q: What is the limbus?

children.note: Sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic, CN III) constricts; dilator pupillae (sympathetic) dilates.

manas.q: Which nerve supply constricts the pupil?

children.note: Ciliary muscle changes lens shape for near focus; ciliary processes secrete aqueous humour.

manas.q: What are the two jobs of the ciliary body?

children.note: Vascular layer between sclera and retina; nourishes the outer retina including photoreceptors.

manas.q: Which layer nourishes the photoreceptors?

children.note: Neurosensory retina lies on the pigment epithelium; detachment separates these two layers.

manas.q: Between which layers does retinal detachment occur?

children.note: Spaces of the eye and the drainage route.
Anterior (cornea to iris), posterior (iris to lens) and vitreous (behind the lens, filled with gel).

manas.q: Name the three chambers of the eye.

children.note: Ciliary processes → posterior chamber → through pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork at the angle → Schlemm's canal → veins.

manas.q: Trace the flow of aqueous humour.

children.note: Roughly 10–21 mmHg, set by balance of aqueous production and outflow.

manas.q: What is the normal range of intraocular pressure?

children.note: Focusing for near.
Biconvex, clear, avascular; capsule, cortex and nucleus; hung from the ciliary body by zonules.

manas.q: What holds the lens in place?

children.note: Ciliary muscle contracts → zonules slacken → lens rounds up → more power for near vision.

manas.q: What happens to the zonules during accommodation?

children.note: Accommodation, convergence and pupil constriction occur together on looking at a near object.

manas.q: What three things make up the near response?

children.note: Presbyopia: lens stiffens with age, near focus fails from the 40s. Cataract: lens opacity.

manas.q: What causes presbyopia?

children.note: Fundus landmarks.
Rods: dim light, mainly peripheral. Cones: colour and fine detail, packed at the fovea.

manas.q: Which photoreceptors give colour vision?

children.note: Lies temporal to the optic disc; its centre is the fovea.

manas.q: Which side of the optic disc is the macula?

children.note: Where ganglion cell axons leave the eye; no photoreceptors, so it forms the physiological blind spot.

manas.q: Why does the optic disc cause a blind spot?

children.note: Central retinal artery and vein branch from the disc; arterioles are narrower and lighter than venules.

manas.q: How do retinal arterioles differ from venules on fundoscopy?

children.note: Lesion site predicts field defect.
Retina → optic nerve → chiasm → optic tract → lateral geniculate body → optic radiation → occipital visual cortex.

manas.q: Trace the visual pathway from retina to cortex.

children.note: Nasal retinal fibres (temporal fields) cross; pituitary tumour pressing the chiasm gives bitemporal hemianopia.

manas.q: Which visual field defect does a pituitary tumour cause?

children.note: Optic tract, radiation or cortex lesions give contralateral homonymous hemianopia; occipital lesions may spare the macula.

manas.q: What field defect follows a right optic tract lesion?

children.note: Temporal (Meyer loop) lesion: contralateral upper quadrant loss. Parietal lesion: contralateral lower quadrant loss.

manas.q: A temporal lobe lesion causes which quadrant defect?

children.note: Afferent CN II → pretectal area → both Edinger–Westphal nuclei → CN III → both pupils constrict (direct and consensual).

manas.q: Why does light in one eye constrict both pupils?

children.note: Protection and tears.
Skin, orbicularis oculi, tarsal plate with meibomian glands, then conjunctiva; the orbital septum runs from rim to tarsus.

manas.q: Where does the orbital septum attach?

children.note: Closing: orbicularis oculi (CN VII). Opening: levator (CN III) helped by Müller muscle (sympathetic).

manas.q: Which nerve supplies orbicularis oculi?

children.note: In the upper outer orbit; secretomotor parasympathetic fibres come via the facial nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion.

manas.q: Which nerve carries secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland?

children.note: Puncta → canaliculi → lacrimal sac → nasolacrimal duct → inferior meatus of the nose.

manas.q: Trace the drainage of tears.

children.note: Outer lipid (meibomian glands), middle aqueous (lacrimal gland), inner mucin (conjunctival goblet cells).

manas.q: What are the three layers of the tear film?

children.note: Arteries in, veins to the cavernous sinus.
First major branch of the internal carotid; enters the orbit through the optic canal with the optic nerve.

manas.q: From which artery does the ophthalmic artery arise?

children.note: Runs inside the optic nerve to the disc; an end artery, so blockage gives sudden painless loss and a cherry-red spot.

manas.q: What fundus sign follows central retinal artery occlusion?

children.note: Supply the choroid and optic nerve head; a cilioretinal branch, when present, may spare central vision in CRAO.

manas.q: What do the posterior ciliary arteries supply?

children.note: Superior and inferior ophthalmic veins drain to the cavernous sinus and lack valves, so infection can spread backwards.

manas.q: Where do the ophthalmic veins drain?

children.note: Anatomy that explains signs.
Floor fracture: trapped inferior rectus limits upgaze with diplopia, enophthalmos, numb cheek and upper lip (infraorbital nerve).

manas.q: Why is the cheek numb after an orbital floor fracture?

children.note: Eye down and out, ptosis; a dilated pupil suggests compression (e.g. aneurysm), while pupil-sparing suits microvascular causes like diabetes.

manas.q: What does pupil involvement in a CN III palsy suggest?

children.note: IV: vertical diplopia worse reading or going downstairs. VI: cannot abduct, horizontal diplopia; may be a false localising sign of raised ICP.

manas.q: Why can a sixth nerve palsy be a false localising sign?

children.note: The septum is the barrier. Orbital: proptosis, painful or limited eye movement, reduced vision or colour vision, RAPD. Preseptal: lid only.

manas.q: Which signs separate orbital from preseptal cellulitis?

children.note: Usually from ethmoid sinusitis through the lamina papyracea; valveless veins can carry it to the cavernous sinus.

manas.q: Why can orbital cellulitis cause cavernous sinus thrombosis?

children.note: Open-angle: outflow resistance at the meshwork, painless field loss. Angle-closure: iris blocks the angle, painful red eye, hazy cornea.

manas.q: How does angle-closure glaucoma differ from open-angle?

children.note: Eye health context; Kenya first.
Follow MoH clinical guidelines and your hospital eye unit protocols; refer orbital cellulitis and sight-threatening eyes urgently.

manas.q: Which eye conditions should be referred urgently?

children.note: WHO published its World report on vision in 2019, calling for eye care integrated into universal health coverage.

manas.q: In which year did WHO publish the World report on vision?

children.note: Trachoma scars the tarsal conjunctiva, turning lashes inward (trichiasis); still endemic in parts of Kenya. WHO uses the SAFE strategy.

manas.q: How does trachoma damage the eyelid?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-04.
US cohort of 220 children: MSSA was the commonest organism, MRSA uncommon; 39.5% had surgery; steroids not linked to failure; ≤2-week courses rarely failed.

manas.q: Which organism was most common in the 2022 paediatric orbital cellulitis cohort?

children.note: Review: assess for orbital compartment syndrome first; CT brain and orbits with and without contrast finds abscess or intracranial spread; ultrasound cannot exclude intracranial spread.

manas.q: Which imaging is key for complications of orbital cellulitis?

children.note: High-yield points.
Only two structures: optic nerve and ophthalmic artery; most other nerves and vessels pass via the orbital fissures.

manas.q: Which two structures pass through the optic canal?

children.note: Pupillary fibres run on the outside of the nerve, so compression dilates the pupil early.

manas.q: Why does compression of CN III dilate the pupil early?

children.note: Bitemporal hemianopia localises to the optic chiasm.

manas.q: Where is the lesion in bitemporal hemianopia?

children.note: Free textbook chapter on the visual pathway.
Free textbook chapter linking aqueous flow to glaucoma drugs.

maps.title: HCP 300 · In depth: Beta-lactams and glycopeptides

nodeData.note: Classes, how they kill, why they fail, side effects, allergy, monitoring and stewardship. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: The families to know, with typical members.
Benzylpenicillin (injected) and phenoxymethylpenicillin (oral): narrow, mainly streptococci and Treponema pallidum.

manas.q: Name the two natural penicillins and their main targets.

children.note: Amoxicillin and ampicillin: add some Gram-negatives (e.g. H. influenzae) and cover Enterococcus faecalis and Listeria.

manas.q: Which penicillins cover Listeria and Enterococcus faecalis?

children.note: Piperacillin, given with tazobactam: broad Gram-negative cover including Pseudomonas, plus anaerobes.

manas.q: Which penicillin covers Pseudomonas?

children.note: Broadly, later generations gain Gram-negative cover; examples by generation below.

manas.q: How does spectrum change across cephalosporin generations?

children.note: Cefalexin (oral), cefazolin (IV): mainly Gram-positive cocci; cefazolin is a common surgical prophylaxis choice.

manas.q: Give two first-generation cephalosporins.

children.note: Cefuroxime: more H. influenzae and Gram-negative cover than first generation.

manas.q: Name a second-generation cephalosporin.

children.note: Ceftriaxone, cefotaxime: strong Gram-negative cover and CSF entry; ceftazidime adds Pseudomonas.

manas.q: Which third-generation cephalosporin covers Pseudomonas?

children.note: Cefepime (4th) covers Pseudomonas; ceftaroline (5th) binds PBP2a so is active against MRSA.

manas.q: Which cephalosporin is active against MRSA?

children.note: Meropenem, imipenem (given with cilastatin), ertapenem: widest beta-lactam spectrum; ertapenem misses Pseudomonas.

manas.q: Which carbapenem does not cover Pseudomonas?

children.note: Aztreonam: Gram-negative aerobes only, including Pseudomonas; no useful Gram-positive or anaerobic activity.

manas.q: What is the spectrum of aztreonam?

children.note: Clavulanate, tazobactam, sulbactam and the newer avibactam protect the partner drug; most have little effect alone, though sulbactam has some activity against Acinetobacter.

manas.q: Name four beta-lactamase inhibitors.

children.note: Vancomycin and teicoplanin; teicoplanin's long half-life allows once-daily dosing after loading.

manas.q: What is the practical advantage of teicoplanin over vancomycin?

children.note: Both groups hit cell wall building, at different steps.
The beta-lactam ring resembles the D-Ala-D-Ala end of peptidoglycan and permanently acylates the PBP (transpeptidase) active site.

manas.q: Why can a beta-lactam ring inactivate penicillin-binding proteins?

children.note: Glycopeptides are too large to cross the Gram-negative outer membrane, so they act only on Gram-positives.

manas.q: Why is vancomycin inactive against Gram-negative bacteria?

children.note: Mycoplasma lacks a wall, and Chlamydia/Legionella are intracellular, so beta-lactams miss these 'atypicals'.

manas.q: Why do beta-lactams not treat Mycoplasma pneumonia?

children.note: Wall damage helps aminoglycoside entry; used together in enterococcal endocarditis.

manas.q: Why combine a cell-wall agent with an aminoglycoside in enterococcal endocarditis?

children.note: How exposure links to effect.
Effect tracks the share of the dosing interval that free drug stays above the MIC (fT>MIC), so frequent doses or extended infusions help.

manas.q: Which PK/PD index predicts beta-lactam efficacy?

children.note: Ceftriaxone is cleared by both bile and kidney; biliary sludge (pseudolithiasis) can occur.

manas.q: Which cephalosporin is excreted partly in bile?

children.note: Vancomycin effect is best predicted by the 24-hour AUC to MIC ratio.

manas.q: Which PK/PD index predicts vancomycin efficacy?

children.note: Four routes: destroy the drug, change the target, block entry, pump it out.
Enzymes that hydrolyse the beta-lactam ring; staphylococcal penicillinase is why most S. aureus resist penicillin.

manas.q: How do beta-lactamases cause resistance?

children.note: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases hydrolyse third-generation cephalosporins and aztreonam; carbapenems are preferred for serious ESBL infection.

manas.q: Which antibiotics do ESBLs inactivate?

children.note: KPC and OXA-48 (serine enzymes) and metallo-enzymes such as NDM, which need zinc; they inactivate carbapenems.

manas.q: Name three carbapenemase types.

children.note: The mecA gene encodes PBP2a, which binds beta-lactams poorly, so nearly all beta-lactams fail.

manas.q: What is the molecular basis of MRSA?

children.note: Penicillin-resistant pneumococci have altered PBPs, not beta-lactamases, so clavulanate does not help.

manas.q: Why does co-amoxiclav not overcome pneumococcal penicillin resistance?

children.note: Gram-negatives can lose porins (e.g. OprD loss gives Pseudomonas imipenem resistance) or pump drug out.

manas.q: How does Pseudomonas become resistant to imipenem without an enzyme?

children.note: vanA changes the precursor end to D-Ala-D-Lac, which vancomycin binds poorly; vanA resists vancomycin and teicoplanin.

manas.q: How does vanA cause vancomycin resistance?

children.note: Matching drug to bug (follow local guidance).
First choice in many guidelines for non-severe community pneumonia, otitis media and sinusitis; part of H. pylori regimens.

manas.q: Name common uses of amoxicillin.

children.note: Hospital-acquired infections, neutropenic sepsis and suspected Pseudomonas.

manas.q: When is piperacillin-tazobactam used?

children.note: Cephalosporins miss Listeria, so ampicillin/amoxicillin is added for meningitis in neonates, the elderly and immunosuppressed.

manas.q: Why is ampicillin added to ceftriaxone in some meningitis cases?

children.note: MRSA infection and serious Gram-positive infection in true beta-lactam allergy.

manas.q: When is IV vancomycin indicated?

children.note: Mostly safe, with key exceptions.
From rash and urticaria to IgE anaphylaxis; delayed severe forms include SJS/TEN and DRESS.

manas.q: Name immediate and delayed severe beta-lactam reactions.

children.note: Amoxicillin in glandular fever often gives a maculopapular rash that is usually not true allergy.

manas.q: Why do patients with glandular fever often get a rash on amoxicillin?

children.note: Broad-spectrum agents, notably cephalosporins and co-amoxiclav, disrupt gut flora and raise C. difficile risk.

manas.q: Which beta-lactams are most linked to C. difficile?

children.note: High doses, renal failure and imipenem raise seizure risk; cefepime can cause encephalopathy.

manas.q: Which factors raise seizure risk with beta-lactams?

children.note: Carbapenems sharply lower valproate levels, risking breakthrough seizures; avoid the combination.

manas.q: What is the interaction between carbapenems and valproate?

children.note: Co-amoxiclav and flucloxacillin can cause cholestatic hepatitis, sometimes weeks after the course.

manas.q: Which two penicillins cause cholestatic jaundice?

children.note: Fever, rigors and malaise hours after treating syphilis, from spirochaete lysis; not an allergy.

manas.q: What is the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction?

children.note: Rate-related histamine release: flushing of face, neck and upper body, itch, hypotension; slow the infusion. Not IgE allergy.

manas.q: What causes 'vancomycin flushing' and how is it prevented?

children.note: Risk rises with high exposure and other nephrotoxins (e.g. aminoglycosides); ototoxicity is rare.

manas.q: What raises the risk of vancomycin nephrotoxicity?

children.note: Benzathine penicillin is IM only; IV injection can be fatal.

manas.q: By which route must benzathine penicillin never be given?

children.note: Most labels are wrong; assess, don't assume.
Most patients labelled penicillin-allergic tolerate it on testing; wrong labels push broader antibiotics and resistance.

manas.q: What harm comes from a false penicillin allergy label?

children.note: What reaction, when, how soon after the dose, what treatment was needed, and any penicillin taken since.

manas.q: What details define a penicillin allergy history?

children.note: Isolated nausea or diarrhoea, or a family history only, are not allergy; other low-risk histories (e.g. old mild rash) may be de-labelled after a supervised oral challenge.

manas.q: Which histories suggest low risk of true penicillin allergy?

children.note: Skin prick then intradermal tests, then oral drug provocation, the reference test, in a supervised setting.

manas.q: What is the reference test to confirm or exclude penicillin allergy?

children.note: Cross-reactivity mostly reflects shared or similar R1 side chains, e.g. ampicillin with cefalexin and cefaclor; amoxicillin with cefadroxil (and similar to cefalexin).

manas.q: What mainly determines penicillin–cephalosporin cross-reactivity?

children.note: Carbapenem cross-reactivity is very low; aztreonam rarely cross-reacts with penicillins but shares a side chain with ceftazidime.

manas.q: Which cephalosporin shares a side chain with aztreonam?

children.note: Avoid penicillins; seek specialist advice before giving any other beta-lactam.

manas.q: How do you manage a patient with past penicillin anaphylaxis?

children.note: Measuring levels to balance cure and toxicity.
Narrow therapeutic window: too low fails and breeds resistance; too high harms kidneys.

manas.q: Why is vancomycin monitored?

children.note: Trough levels are poor stand-ins for AUC; 2020 US consensus favours AUC-guided dosing, target AUC/MIC 400–600 for MRSA.

manas.q: What vancomycin AUC/MIC target does the 2020 US consensus use for MRSA?

children.note: Use the narrowest effective drug for the shortest effective time.
WHO sorts antibiotics into Access (first/second choice), Watch (higher resistance risk) and Reserve (last resort).

manas.q: What do the WHO AWaRe groups mean?

children.note: Amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, benzylpenicillin, flucloxacillin, cefalexin and cefazolin.

manas.q: Name beta-lactams in the WHO Access group.

children.note: Ceftriaxone and other third-generation cephalosporins, piperacillin-tazobactam, carbapenems and vancomycin.

manas.q: Is ceftriaxone Access, Watch or Reserve?

children.note: Newer agents for multidrug resistance, e.g. ceftazidime-avibactam and cefiderocol.

manas.q: Name two Reserve-group beta-lactams.

children.note: WHO's 2019 target: at least 60% of national antibiotic use from the Access group; the 2024 UN political declaration on AMR raised this to 70% by 2030.

manas.q: What share of antibiotic use should come from the WHO Access group?

children.note: Check cultures and progress: stop, narrow (de-escalate), switch IV to oral, or set a stop date.

manas.q: What decisions are made at the 48–72 hour antibiotic review?

children.note: Quick wins.
Listeria, Atypicals, MRSA (except ceftaroline), Enterococci are not covered by cephalosporins.

manas.q: Which organisms do cephalosporins miss (LAME)?

children.note: Cilastatin blocks renal dehydropeptidase, which would otherwise break down imipenem.

manas.q: Why is imipenem given with cilastatin?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
The MoH Kenya Essential Medicines List 2023 (guidelines.health.go.ke) sets which antibiotics should be stocked; linked on the course bubble.

manas.q: Which Kenyan document lists the antibiotics facilities should stock?

children.note: Kenya runs a One Health national action plan on AMR, aligned with the WHO Global Action Plan (2015).

manas.q: How does Kenya organise its response to antimicrobial resistance?

children.note: Since 2017 the WHO Model EML groups antibiotics by AWaRe; the WHO AWaRe Antibiotic Book (2022) gives first and second choices.

manas.q: What does the WHO AWaRe Antibiotic Book provide?

children.note: ASHP, IDSA, PIDS and SIDP recommend AUC-guided vancomycin dosing over trough-only monitoring for serious MRSA.

manas.q: Which bodies issued the 2020 vancomycin AUC guidance?

children.note: BSACI (2022) guides non-allergists on de-labelling; NICE drug allergy guidance asks for precise recording of reactions.

manas.q: Which UK body published guidance for non-allergists on penicillin de-labelling?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-06.
BSACI gave UK non-allergists a checklist to spot low-risk penicillin labels and a framework for drug challenge, with adult and child sections.

manas.q: What two tools does the BSACI 2022 de-labelling guideline give non-allergists?

children.note: 174 studies, 28 countries: about 9.4% of adults carry a penicillin allergy label (9.9% high- vs 4.4% middle-income); African data scarce.

manas.q: What is the pooled global prevalence of reported penicillin allergy?

children.note: Meta-analysis of 57 studies, mostly adults: pooled nephrotoxicity 6.2% with AUC-guided vs 17.0% with trough-guided vancomycin monitoring (OR 0.53).

manas.q: How did AUC-guided vancomycin monitoring affect nephrotoxicity?

children.note: Meta-analysis of 11 studies (1463 critically ill): level-guided dosing was associated with better clinical and microbiological cure and target attainment, not lower mortality; RCTs needed.

manas.q: Did beta-lactam drug monitoring in ICU reduce mortality?

maps.title: HHP 300 · In depth: Histopathology specimen handling

nodeData.note: From theatre to report: labelling, fixation, processing, staining, special handling, artefacts, safety, reporting. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Most errors that spoil a biopsy happen before it reaches the lab.
Label the pot itself, not the lid, with at least two patient identifiers matching the request form: lids come off and can be swapped.

manas.q: Why label the specimen container rather than the lid?

children.note: Prior radiotherapy, chemotherapy, pregnancy or drugs change how tissue looks; omitting them risks misinterpretation.

manas.q: Why must treatments like radiotherapy be mentioned on the request form?

children.note: The surgeon marks edges with sutures or clips (e.g. short superior, long lateral) and records the key on the form.

manas.q: How does a surgeon show the orientation of an excision?

children.note: The lab paints surfaces with coloured inks that survive processing, so the slide shows exactly which margin a tumour reaches.

manas.q: Why are resection margins inked?

children.note: Time from removal of tissue from the patient to immersion in fixative; meanwhile autolysis degrades morphology, antigens and RNA.

manas.q: What is cold ischaemia time?

children.note: Stops decay and preserves structure.
Halt autolysis and putrefaction, preserve structure, harden tissue for cutting and inactivate most microbes.

manas.q: What are the aims of fixation?

children.note: Formaldehyde forms methylene bridges between proteins (mainly lysine side chains), locking structure in place.

manas.q: How does formaldehyde fix tissue?

children.note: Neutral buffering prevents acid formalin pigment (acid haematin) forming in bloody tissue.

manas.q: Why is formalin buffered to neutral pH?

children.note: Too little gives poor morphology and patchy IHC; too long masks epitopes and fragments nucleic acids.

manas.q: What problems follow under-fixation and over-fixation?

children.note: Ethanol or methanol fix by coagulating proteins; used for wet-fixed cytology smears such as Pap.

manas.q: How do alcohol fixatives work, and where are they used?

children.note: A picric acid fixative traditionally used for testicular biopsies; dry picric acid is explosive.

manas.q: Which fixative is traditionally used for testicular biopsies?

children.note: Glutaraldehyde cross-links rapidly and preserves fine structure for electron microscopy (e.g. renal biopsy).

manas.q: Which fixative is used for electron microscopy?

children.note: Urate crystals dissolve in aqueous formalin; send suspected gout tissue in absolute alcohol.

manas.q: How should tissue be sent if gout is suspected?

children.note: Some tests need living or unfixed tissue; plan before theatre.
No: tissue goes fresh and unfixed straight to the lab for intraoperative diagnosis; formalin would prevent freezing and cutting.

manas.q: Must frozen-section tissue be put in formalin?

children.note: Formalin kills organisms, so send a separate sterile unfixed sample (e.g. suspected TB) for culture.

manas.q: Why must tissue for culture never go in formalin?

children.note: Flow cytometry and cytogenetics need viable cells: send fresh tissue in saline or culture medium promptly.

manas.q: How should a lymph node be sent when lymphoma is suspected?

children.note: Renal biopsies need unfixed tissue for immunofluorescence; muscle biopsies are frozen for enzyme histochemistry.

manas.q: Which part of a renal biopsy must not be formalin-fixed?

children.note: The pathologist's naked-eye examination and sampling.
Measure, weigh where useful, describe and photograph; record lesion size and distance to each margin.

manas.q: What is recorded during macroscopic examination?

children.note: Slice serially and choose blocks of tumour, its closest margins, background tissue and lymph nodes.

manas.q: Which areas are sampled into blocks from a cancer resection?

children.note: Turning wet tissue into thin ribbons on glass.
Graded alcohols remove water, because paraffin wax will not mix with water.

manas.q: Why is tissue dehydrated before embedding?

children.note: Xylene (or a substitute) replaces alcohol; it mixes with both alcohol and wax and makes tissue translucent.

manas.q: What is the purpose of clearing with xylene?

children.note: Tissue is set in a wax block in the right plane, e.g. skin and gut wall on edge so all layers show.

manas.q: Why is skin embedded on edge?

children.note: Making cells and their contents visible.
Haematoxylin with a metal mordant binds acidic nucleic acids (basophilic); acidic eosin binds basic cytoplasmic proteins (eosinophilic).

manas.q: Why does haematoxylin stain nuclei?

children.note: Masson trichrome (collagen), reticulin (fibre framework), Alcian blue and mucicarmine (mucin), Gram (bacteria).

manas.q: Which special stain highlights collagen?

children.note: Diastase digests glycogen; PAS staining that remains after diastase points to mucin or fungi.

manas.q: What does diastase do in PAS-D staining?

children.note: Amyloid stains red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light.

manas.q: What does amyloid look like on Congo red under polarised light?

children.note: An antibody binds its target antigen; a linked enzyme (often peroxidase) turns a chromogen such as DAB brown where the antigen is.

manas.q: What is the principle of immunohistochemistry?

children.note: Heating sections in buffer partly reverses formalin cross-links, unmasking epitopes before IHC.

manas.q: Why is heat-induced antigen retrieval used?

children.note: ER, PR and HER2 in breast cancer decide therapy; HER2 equivocal on IHC is tested by in situ hybridisation.

manas.q: How is an equivocal HER2 IHC result resolved?

children.note: Fast, but with trade-offs.
Ice crystals distort cells; fatty tissue and bone cut poorly when frozen.

manas.q: Which tissues are hard to cut by frozen section?

children.note: The final diagnosis waits for permanent sections; deferral is acceptable when unsure.

manas.q: Is a frozen-section diagnosis final?

children.note: Capsular or vascular invasion needs full sampling, so frozen section rarely separates follicular adenoma from carcinoma.

manas.q: Why is frozen section poor for thyroid follicular lesions?

children.note: Avoid frozen section on suspected TB or other high-risk infection, which can contaminate the cryostat.

manas.q: Why avoid frozen section of suspected TB tissue?

children.note: Softening bone so it can be cut.
Bone and calcified tissue are fixed before decalcification, which itself damages unfixed tissue.

manas.q: Should bone be fixed before or after decalcification?

children.note: Strong acids are fast but harm nuclear staining, IHC and DNA; EDTA chelation is slow but preserves them.

manas.q: Which decalcifier is preferred when molecular tests are needed?

children.note: Cells versus tissue architecture.
Cytology looks at single cells and clusters; histology keeps architecture, so it can show invasion.

manas.q: What can histology show that cytology usually cannot?

children.note: Fine needle aspiration: quick and cheap for nodes, thyroid and breast lumps, but cannot always show invasion.

manas.q: What is a key limitation of fine needle aspiration cytology?

children.note: A core needle gives tissue architecture and enough material for receptors and IHC.

manas.q: Why is core biopsy preferred to FNA for breast cancer diagnosis?

children.note: Cervical smears are wet-fixed at once (alcohol or spray) or sent as liquid-based cytology; air-drying spoils Pap staining.

manas.q: Why must a Pap smear be fixed immediately?

children.note: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded blocks are a DNA/RNA archive.
Formalin fragments DNA and RNA and causes artefactual C>T changes through cytosine deamination.

manas.q: Which sequencing artefact does formalin cause?

children.note: The pathologist marks the tumour area and estimates tumour cell percentage; macrodissection enriches it.

manas.q: Why does the pathologist estimate tumour cellularity before molecular testing?

children.note: Things on the slide that are not disease.
Forceps squeeze cells into streaks; small cell carcinoma and lymphocytes are especially fragile.

manas.q: Which tumours are most prone to crush artefact?

children.note: Diathermy heat distorts and darkens cells at edges, which can make margins hard to assess.

manas.q: Why does diathermy artefact matter at margins?

children.note: Brown-black birefringent deposits in bloody tissue fixed in acidic formalin.

manas.q: What causes formalin pigment?

children.note: Chemical and biological hazards.
IARC lists formaldehyde as a human carcinogen (e.g. nasopharyngeal cancer); it also irritates eyes and airways and sensitises skin.

manas.q: Which cancer is formaldehyde exposure linked to?

children.note: Ventilated grossing benches and fume hoods, PPE, closed containers, spill kits and air monitoring.

manas.q: How is formaldehyde exposure reduced in the lab?

children.note: Flammable solvent and CNS depressant; less toxic substitutes are often used.

manas.q: What are the hazards of xylene?

children.note: Treat all fresh tissue as infectious; formalin does not reliably inactivate prions.

manas.q: Does formalin inactivate prions?

children.note: From slide to clinical decision.
Clinical details, macroscopy, microscopy and a clear diagnosis, with comments and any further tests.

manas.q: What are the main parts of a histopathology report?

children.note: Synoptic reports list type, grade, size, margins, lymphovascular invasion, nodes and pTNM stage.

manas.q: Which items does a synoptic cancer report include?

children.note: Unexpected or critical findings are phoned to the clinician, not left in the report queue.

manas.q: How should unexpected critical findings be communicated?

children.note: Glass slides as images.
Scanners digitise slides for screen reading, teaching and remote opinions (telepathology).

manas.q: What is whole-slide imaging?

children.note: Algorithms can flag cancer or count features on scanned slides, as aids for the pathologist.

manas.q: What role do AI tools currently play in pathology?

children.note: Quick wins.
Formalin suits routine histology and IHC; culture, flow cytometry and karyotyping need fresh tissue; immunofluorescence and EM work best on unfixed or glutaraldehyde-fixed tissue.

manas.q: Which tests need fresh or specially fixed tissue rather than formalin?

children.note: Label → fix → gross → process → embed → cut → stain → report.

manas.q: List the histology workflow from theatre to report in order.

children.note: Shared standards; Kenya first.
Kenyan medical labs can be accredited to ISO 15189 by KENAS; follow your hospital lab's SOPs for specimens.

manas.q: Which international standard covers medical laboratory quality?

children.note: ASCO/CAP: breast tissue for ER/PR/HER2 into 10% NBF within 1 h of removal and fixed 6–72 h.

manas.q: What fixation times do ASCO/CAP set for breast biomarker testing?

children.note: The WHO Classification of Tumours ('Blue Books') sets the diagnostic terms used worldwide.

manas.q: Which publication sets international tumour classification?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-06.
NCI study, kidney tumours, 24 IHC markers: staining shifted after ≥2 h delay to fixation; 72 h in formalin lowered CD44 and c-Met; supports ≤1 h delay and 12–24 h fixation.

manas.q: What delay to fixation did the NCI biospecimen study support?

children.note: 100 studies (48 pooled): mean sensitivity 96.3%, specificity 93.3%, but 99% had high or unclear risk of bias.

manas.q: What was the main weakness of AI digital pathology studies?

children.note: Review of 40 studies: FFPE and fresh-frozen breast cancer samples agreed well on DNA and RNA tests; excluding variants under 5% allele frequency was needed to overcome FFPE artefacts.

manas.q: How were FFPE artefacts handled in breast cancer sequencing?

children.note: In four Tehran pathology labs, 91% of exposures exceeded the NIOSH limit; technicians had the highest cancer risk.

manas.q: Who had the highest formaldehyde cancer risk in the Tehran lab study?

maps.title: HHP 301 · In depth: Sickle cell disease: clinical management

nodeData.note: From HbS biology to diagnosis, crises, transfusion, hydroxyurea and newer therapies. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What SCD is and how it is inherited.
Inherited red cell disorders in which HbS is co-inherited with a second HbS or another abnormal β-globin allele: e.g. HbSS, HbSC or HbS/β-thalassaemia.

manas.q: What is sickle cell disease?

children.note: A point mutation at codon 6 of the β-globin gene swaps glutamic acid for valine (Glu6Val), making haemoglobin S.

manas.q: What amino acid change produces HbS?

children.note: If both parents carry HbS, each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child and 1 in 2 of a carrier.

manas.q: What is the risk of an affected child when both parents have sickle cell trait?

children.note: HbSS and HbSβ0 are usually most severe; HbSC has milder anaemia but more proliferative retinopathy.

manas.q: Which SCD genotype is linked with more proliferative retinopathy?

children.note: Carriers are usually well; the renal medulla may sickle, causing painless haematuria and poor urine concentration.

manas.q: Which kidney problems can occur in sickle cell trait?

children.note: Polymerisation, vaso-occlusion and haemolysis.
When deoxygenated, HbS molecules stick together into long rigid fibres that bend red cells into sickle shapes.

manas.q: What happens to HbS when it is deoxygenated?

children.note: Hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration, cold, infection and exertion promote sickling; HbF blocks polymerisation.

manas.q: Name common triggers of sickling.

children.note: Rigid, sticky red cells, white cells and platelets cling to endothelium and block small vessels, causing ischaemia, infarction and pain.

manas.q: How does sickling cause pain and organ damage?

children.note: Sickled cells are destroyed early, giving anaemia, jaundice and pigment gallstones; free haemoglobin mops up nitric oxide.

manas.q: What are the consequences of chronic haemolysis in SCD?

children.note: Repeated splenic infarction in childhood leaves a small, non-working spleen and high risk from encapsulated bacteria.

manas.q: Why are people with HbSS prone to pneumococcal sepsis?

children.note: Finding SCD early and confirming the genotype.
Detects SCD before symptoms so penicillin, vaccines, parent teaching and clinic follow-up start early.

manas.q: Why screen newborns for SCD?

children.note: Separates and measures HbS, HbA, HbF, HbA2 and HbC to confirm the genotype; HPLC is common in screening labs.

manas.q: Which tests confirm the sickle genotype?

children.note: Cheap lateral-flow antibody tests can tell HbAA, HbAS and HbSS apart at the bedside, helping screening where labs are scarce.

manas.q: What can rapid point-of-care sickle tests distinguish?

children.note: Shows HbS is present but cannot separate trait from disease, and is unreliable in newborns with high HbF.

manas.q: Why is the sickle solubility test not enough for diagnosis?

children.note: Sickle cells, target cells, polychromasia and Howell-Jolly bodies (from hyposplenism); reticulocytes are raised.

manas.q: What does a blood film show in HbSS?

children.note: Recognise and act fast.
Assess pain score; paracetamol or NSAID for mild pain, add an opioid promptly for severe pain; reassess often; avoid pethidine.

manas.q: How is analgesia stepped up in a vaso-occlusive crisis?

children.note: Fluids (oral or IV), warmth, look for a trigger such as infection or malaria; incentive spirometry helps prevent chest syndrome.

manas.q: Why use incentive spirometry in a pain crisis?

children.note: Painful swelling of hands and feet from bone infarction in infants and toddlers; often the first sign of SCD.

manas.q: What is hand-foot syndrome?

children.note: Infection, fat embolism from infarcted marrow and lung infarction; often follows a pain crisis or surgery.

manas.q: What causes acute chest syndrome?

children.note: Oxygen, antibiotics covering atypical organisms, analgesia, spirometry, and transfusion (exchange if severe).

manas.q: How is acute chest syndrome treated?

children.note: Sudden weakness, speech or vision change; urgent imaging and exchange transfusion; then regular transfusion to prevent recurrence.

manas.q: What is the emergency treatment of stroke in SCD?

children.note: Trapped red cells return as the spleen shrinks, so give modest volumes; teach parents to feel the spleen.

manas.q: Why should transfusion volume be cautious in splenic sequestration?

children.note: Falling Hb with very low reticulocytes after parvovirus B19; usually self-limiting but may need transfusion.

manas.q: What causes aplastic crisis in SCD and what do reticulocytes show?

children.note: Urgent review, blood culture, malaria test and prompt empirical parenteral antibiotics, because sepsis can kill within hours.

manas.q: Why is fever in a child with SCD treated as an emergency?

children.note: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b and Neisseria meningitidis are the classic dangers with an absent spleen.

manas.q: Which bacteria threaten people with functional asplenia?

children.note: Salmonella is classic in SCD, with Staphylococcus aureus; hard to tell from bone infarction.

manas.q: Which organism is classically linked with osteomyelitis in SCD?

children.note: Triggers crises and severe anaemia and is a major killer of children with SCD in Africa; prevention is part of routine care.

manas.q: Why is malaria prevention vital in SCD?

children.note: Painful sustained erection from sickling; over four hours is a urological emergency needing aspiration and specialist care.

manas.q: When does priapism in SCD become an emergency?

children.note: Organ damage over years.
Bone death, most often of the femoral head; hip pain and limp; MRI detects early disease.

manas.q: Which bone is most often affected by avascular necrosis in SCD?

children.note: Chronic painful ulcers near the ankles, more common in HbSS and linked with haemolysis; slow to heal.

manas.q: Where do sickle leg ulcers usually occur?

children.note: Poor urine concentration (bedwetting, dehydration), haematuria from papillary necrosis, albuminuria and eventual kidney disease.

manas.q: Name the kidney effects of SCD.

children.note: Proliferative retinopathy can bleed into the vitreous or detach the retina; regular eye checks are advised.

manas.q: Why do people with SCD need eye screening?

children.note: Linked to haemolysis; screened with echocardiography (tricuspid jet velocity) and tied to higher mortality.

manas.q: How is pulmonary hypertension screened for in SCD?

children.note: Bilirubin stones from chronic haemolysis; cholecystectomy for symptomatic disease.

manas.q: What type of gallstones occur in SCD and why?

children.note: Small brain infarcts seen on MRI without stroke signs; linked to learning and memory problems.

manas.q: What are silent cerebral infarcts?

children.note: When and how to give blood.
Simple adds donor blood; exchange removes sickle blood while giving donor blood, lowering HbS% without raising viscosity much.

manas.q: How does exchange transfusion differ from simple transfusion?

children.note: A high Hb with much HbS makes blood thick (hyperviscosity) and may cause stroke; follow local target limits.

manas.q: Why must Hb not be raised too high in SCD transfusion?

children.note: Repeated transfusion causes red cell antibodies; extended phenotype matching (Rh and Kell) lowers the risk.

manas.q: How can alloimmunisation be reduced in SCD?

children.note: Days after transfusion, pain and dark urine with Hb falling below pre-transfusion level (hyperhaemolysis) can be life-threatening.

manas.q: What is hyperhaemolysis after transfusion in SCD?

children.note: Chronic transfusion loads liver, heart and glands with iron; monitor ferritin and liver iron and chelate (desferrioxamine, deferasirox).

manas.q: How is transfusional iron overload managed?

children.note: The main disease-modifying drug.
Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase; raises HbF (which blocks polymerisation) and lowers neutrophils and reticulocytes.

manas.q: How does hydroxyurea help in SCD?

children.note: Regular FBC for neutropenia and thrombocytopenia; rising MCV and HbF show response and adherence.

manas.q: What blood test monitors hydroxyurea safety?

children.note: Dose is raised in steps to the highest dose causing only mild, acceptable marrow suppression.

manas.q: What is the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) approach?

children.note: Teratogenic in animals; advise contraception and usually stop before conception and during pregnancy.

manas.q: What is the concern with hydroxyurea in pregnancy?

children.note: Beyond hydroxyurea and transfusion.
Amino acid that lowers oxidative stress in red cells; US FDA approved it in 2017 to reduce acute complications.

manas.q: How does L-glutamine act in SCD?

children.note: Anti-P-selectin antibody to reduce pain crises; the EU revoked its licence in 2023 after a trial showed no benefit.

manas.q: What is the target of crizanlizumab?

children.note: Raised Hb oxygen affinity to stop polymerisation; Pfizer withdrew it worldwide in September 2024 for safety reasons.

manas.q: What happened to voxelotor in 2024?

children.note: Exa-cel (CRISPR edit of the BCL11A erythroid enhancer, raising HbF) approved UK and US 2023; lovo-cel (added anti-sickling gene) US 2023. Both need myeloablative conditioning.

manas.q: How does exa-cel raise fetal haemoglobin?

children.note: Haematopoietic stem cell transplant can cure SCD; best with a matched sibling donor; risks include GVHD and infertility.

manas.q: Which treatment is currently curative for SCD?

children.note: Comprehensive clinic follow-up.
The 1986 PROPS trial showed daily oral penicillin cuts pneumococcal infection in young children with SCD.

manas.q: Which trial showed penicillin prophylaxis prevents pneumococcal infection in SCD?

children.note: Recognise fever, pallor, breathlessness, spleen enlargement and neurological signs, and come in at once.

manas.q: Which danger signs should parents of children with SCD know?

children.note: More crises and chest syndrome, pre-eclampsia, thrombosis, growth restriction, preterm birth and pregnancy loss.

manas.q: What risks does SCD add to pregnancy?

children.note: Joint obstetric and haematology care, folic acid, stop hydroxyurea, VTE assessment and close fetal growth monitoring.

manas.q: How is pregnancy in SCD managed?

children.note: Chronic pain, depression, school and work absence, stigma and costs; pain is often under-treated in emergency rooms.

manas.q: Name psychosocial burdens of SCD.

children.note: Quick wins.
Low reticulocytes: aplastic crisis; high reticulocytes with a big spleen: sequestration.

manas.q: What reticulocyte count suggests aplastic crisis?

children.note: Adults with HbSS usually have no palpable spleen (autosplenectomy); HbSC may keep a large spleen.

manas.q: Is splenomegaly expected in an adult with HbSS?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
Kenya's national guideline covers screening, prophylaxis, crisis care and follow-up; use it with your hospital protocol.

manas.q: Which Kenyan document guides SCD management?

children.note: The World Health Assembly recognised SCD as a public health problem in 2006; 19 June is World Sickle Cell Day.

manas.q: When is World Sickle Cell Day?

children.note: Expert panel: offer hydroxyurea to children with HbSS or HbSβ0 from 9 months regardless of severity; yearly TCD ages 2–16.

manas.q: From what age does NHLBI 2014 advise offering hydroxyurea in HbSS?

children.note: For an acute painful episode, NICE advises offering analgesia within 30 minutes of arrival.

manas.q: How quickly does NICE advise analgesia for a sickle pain crisis?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-06.
Nine RCTs (1104 people). Versus placebo in HbSS/Sβ0, hydroxyurea probably reduces pain crises and admissions, with fewer chest syndrome episodes and transfusions; no difference in deaths.

manas.q: What did the 2022 Cochrane review find for hydroxyurea in HbSS?

children.note: Open-label non-randomised trial (Kenya, Uganda, Angola, DRC): after escalation to MTD (mean 28.2 mg/kg/day) Hb and HbF rose and vaso-occlusive pain fell vs fixed dose, without more toxicity.

manas.q: What did REACH show about escalating hydroxyurea to MTD in African children?

children.note: In REACH, hydroxyurea at MTD was associated with about 50% less malaria; neutrophils below 3.0×10⁹/L were linked with lower malaria incidence (association; mechanism unclear).

manas.q: How was hydroxyurea at MTD associated with malaria in REACH?

children.note: Open-label phase 2 trial in Tanzania: 24% of children had raised TCD velocities; on hydroxyurea escalated to MTD, mean velocity fell from 182 to 149 cm/s by 12 months.

manas.q: What did SPHERE show about hydroxyurea and TCD velocity?

maps.title: HHP 302 · In depth: Immunity to infection

nodeData.note: Defence layers, pathogen patterns, evasion, immunopathology, vaccines and immunodeficiency. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Two arms working together.
Layered defence: barriers, then fast non-specific innate immunity, then slower specific adaptive immunity with memory.

manas.q: What are the layers of defence against infection?

children.note: The first line.
Intact skin, mucus, cilia, stomach acid, lysozyme in tears and saliva, and antimicrobial peptides such as defensins.

manas.q: Name physical and chemical barriers to infection.

children.note: Fast, germline-encoded recognition.
PRRs such as Toll-like receptors detect conserved microbial patterns (PAMPs) and danger signals from damaged cells (DAMPs).

manas.q: What do pattern recognition receptors detect?

children.note: TLR4 senses LPS, TLR5 flagellin, TLR3 double-stranded RNA, TLR7/8 single-stranded RNA, TLR9 unmethylated CpG DNA.

manas.q: Which Toll-like receptor recognises LPS?

children.note: Classical (antibody bound to antigen), lectin (mannose-binding lectin on microbial sugars) and alternative (spontaneous C3 on surfaces).

manas.q: What starts each complement pathway?

children.note: C3b opsonises, C3a and C5a cause inflammation and attract neutrophils, C5b–9 forms the membrane attack complex.

manas.q: What are the three main jobs of complement?

children.note: Neutrophils arrive first and form pus; macrophages engulf, present antigen and release cytokines; killing uses the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst.

manas.q: How do phagocytes kill ingested microbes?

children.note: Kill infected or tumour cells that lack MHC class I ('missing self'), make IFN-γ, and kill antibody-coated cells by ADCC via CD16.

manas.q: Which cells do NK cells kill?

children.note: IFN-α and IFN-β from infected cells put neighbouring cells into an antiviral state and boost MHC class I.

manas.q: What do type I interferons do?

children.note: Specific and with memory.
MHC class I shows internal (e.g. viral) peptides to CD8 T cells; MHC class II shows engulfed antigen to CD4 T cells.

manas.q: Which MHC class presents to CD8 T cells?

children.note: Driven by IL-12; make IFN-γ, which activates macrophages to kill intracellular microbes.

manas.q: Which cytokine drives Th1 cells?

children.note: Make IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13: IgE class switching, eosinophils and mucus; key against helminths.

manas.q: Which cytokines do Th2 cells make?

children.note: Make IL-17 and IL-22, recruiting neutrophils and strengthening mucosal barriers against extracellular bacteria and fungi.

manas.q: What is the role of Th17 cells?

children.note: Recognise peptide on MHC class I and kill infected cells with perforin and granzymes or Fas ligand.

manas.q: How do CD8 T cells kill infected cells?

children.note: Neutralisation, opsonisation, complement activation and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity.

manas.q: Name four functions of antibodies.

children.note: First antibody made; pentamer; strong complement activator; marks recent infection.

manas.q: Which antibody class is made first?

children.note: Main antibody of secondary responses; opsonin; crosses the placenta to protect the newborn.

manas.q: Which antibody crosses the placenta?

children.note: Secreted as a dimer on mucosal surfaces and in breast milk; blocks attachment.

manas.q: Which antibody protects mucosal surfaces?

children.note: Binds mast cells and basophils; important against helminths and in allergy.

manas.q: Which antibody class is key against helminths?

children.note: Which arm matters most.
Antibody, complement and neutrophils; opsonisation is vital against capsules, with the spleen clearing opsonised bacteria.

manas.q: Which immune mechanisms clear extracellular bacteria?

children.note: Macrophages make IL-12, Th1 cells make IFN-γ, macrophages are activated; inherited defects cause severe mycobacterial infection.

manas.q: Which cytokine axis controls intracellular bacteria such as TB?

children.note: TNF-α maintains granulomas; anti-TNF drugs can reactivate latent TB, so screen before starting them.

manas.q: Why screen for latent TB before anti-TNF therapy?

children.note: HIV enters CD4 T cells via CD4 plus CCR5 or CXCR4; steady CD4 loss leads to opportunistic infections such as PCP.

manas.q: Which co-receptors does HIV use to enter CD4 cells?

children.note: Neutrophils protect against Aspergillus and Candida; Th17 guards mucosa; T-cell defects, as in HIV, allow cryptococcus.

manas.q: Which immune defect predisposes to invasive aspergillosis?

children.note: Antibodies against merozoites and infected red cells reduce parasite numbers; the spleen removes infected cells.

manas.q: How do antibodies protect against blood-stage malaria?

children.note: Parasites switch among var genes encoding PfEMP1, which makes infected cells stick to vessel walls and dodges antibodies.

manas.q: What is PfEMP1 and why does it vary?

children.note: Immunity after repeated exposure that controls parasite density and severe disease but does not prevent infection.

manas.q: What is premunition in malaria?

children.note: IL-13 boosts mucus and gut smooth muscle contraction to expel worms; eosinophilia is a clue to tissue helminths.

manas.q: What is the 'weep and sweep' response to gut worms?

children.note: How pathogens survive.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis blocks phagosome–lysosome fusion and survives inside macrophages.

manas.q: How does M. tuberculosis survive inside macrophages?

children.note: High mutation rate, latent reservoir in resting CD4 cells, and Nef lowering MHC class I on infected cells.

manas.q: How does HIV escape the immune system?

children.note: Capsules resist phagocytosis; S. aureus protein A binds the Fc of IgG; IgA proteases cut mucosal antibody.

manas.q: How does S. aureus protein A help it evade immunity?

children.note: When the response causes harm.
LPS acting via TLR4 triggers excess TNF-α, IL-1 and IL-6: vasodilation, capillary leak, DIC and organ failure.

manas.q: Which cytokines drive septic shock?

children.note: Toxins such as TSST-1 link MHC class II to T-cell receptors outside the groove, activating many T cells: cytokine storm.

manas.q: How do superantigens cause toxic shock?

children.note: TB granulomas caseate and cavitate; schistosome egg granulomas in the liver cause periportal fibrosis.

manas.q: How do granulomas damage tissue?

children.note: Antibodies to group A streptococcal M protein cross-react with heart tissue: rheumatic fever.

manas.q: How does group A strep cause rheumatic fever?

children.note: IRIS is a paradoxical flare as ART restores immunity, usually within weeks to months; in cryptococcal meningitis ART is deferred 4–6 weeks after antifungals to cut deaths.

manas.q: Why is ART deferred in cryptococcal meningitis?

children.note: Innate memory.
Long-term epigenetic reprogramming of monocytes, macrophages or NK cells so they respond more strongly to later infections.

manas.q: What is trained immunity?

children.note: BCG can train innate cells, a proposed explanation for protection beyond TB.

manas.q: How might BCG protect against infections other than TB?

children.note: Types and examples.
BCG, measles-rubella, oral polio, rotavirus, yellow fever: strong lasting immunity; avoid in severe immunosuppression and pregnancy.

manas.q: Why avoid live vaccines in severe immunosuppression?

children.note: Killed whole organisms, e.g. inactivated polio (IPV) and rabies vaccine; often need boosters.

manas.q: Give examples of inactivated vaccines.

children.note: Hepatitis B and HPV use proteins; Hib and pneumococcal conjugates link sugar to protein so infants get T-cell help.

manas.q: Why are polysaccharide vaccines conjugated for infants?

children.note: Inactivated toxins (tetanus, diphtheria) induce antibodies that neutralise the toxin.

manas.q: What does a toxoid vaccine protect against?

children.note: mRNA in lipid nanoparticles makes cells produce the antigen, e.g. COVID-19 spike protein vaccines.

manas.q: How do mRNA vaccines work?

children.note: A harmless virus carries the antigen gene, e.g. ChAdOx1 COVID-19 vaccine and rVSV Ebola vaccine.

manas.q: Give an example of a viral vector vaccine.

children.note: RTS,S/AS01 (2021) and R21/Matrix-M (2023), recommended by WHO for children, target the sporozoite circumsporozoite protein.

manas.q: Which malaria vaccines does WHO recommend?

children.note: Which defect, which infection.
Recurrent sinus and chest infections with encapsulated bacteria, plus enteroviruses and Giardia (e.g. X-linked agammaglobulinaemia).

manas.q: Which infections suggest an antibody deficiency?

children.note: Viruses, fungi, Pneumocystis and intracellular organisms (e.g. SCID, DiGeorge, advanced HIV).

manas.q: Which infections suggest a T-cell defect?

children.note: Chronic granulomatous disease: catalase-positive organisms such as S. aureus and Aspergillus; neutropenia: bacteria and fungi.

manas.q: Which organisms infect people with chronic granulomatous disease?

children.note: Early components (C2, C4): lupus-like disease and pyogenic infection; terminal C5–C9: recurrent Neisseria.

manas.q: Which complement defect predisposes to recurrent Neisseria?

children.note: Overwhelming infection with pneumococcus, Hib and meningococcus; vaccinate and give prophylaxis.

manas.q: Which organisms threaten people without a spleen?

children.note: Tests that read the immune response.
Neutrophilia suggests bacteria, lymphocytosis viruses, eosinophilia helminths.

manas.q: What does eosinophilia suggest?

children.note: IgM suggests recent infection; IgG past infection or immunity; a rising titre in paired samples confirms recent infection.

manas.q: How do IgM and IgG results differ in meaning?

children.note: Detect T-cell memory to M. tuberculosis but cannot separate latent from active TB.

manas.q: Can an IGRA distinguish latent from active TB?

children.note: Quick wins.
Tuberculoid: strong Th1, few bacilli; lepromatous: weak cell-mediated immunity, many bacilli.

manas.q: How do tuberculoid and lepromatous leprosy differ immunologically?

children.note: Blocking C5 raises meningococcal risk; vaccinate before treatment.

manas.q: Why vaccinate against meningococcus before eculizumab?

children.note: Kenya first, then others.
BCG and oral polio at birth; pentavalent, pneumococcal, oral polio and rotavirus from 6 weeks; measles-rubella at 9 and 18 months.

manas.q: Which vaccines does KEPI give at birth?

children.note: The integrated guideline for TB, leprosy and lung disease covers diagnosis, treatment and TB preventive therapy.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers TB and leprosy care?

children.note: WHO advises one BCG dose at birth in countries with high TB burden; revaccination is not recommended.

manas.q: Does WHO recommend BCG revaccination?

children.note: The UK gives BCG only to infants at higher TB risk; the USA does not use BCG routinely.

manas.q: How does BCG policy in the UK and USA differ from Kenya?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-06.
M. tuberculosis both dodges and exploits host immunity, often reaching a balance of control and persistence, using protein and lipid effectors on macrophages.

manas.q: How does M. tuberculosis use the host immune response?

children.note: Most TB may come from reinfection of exposed people; old autopsy studies show primary and postprimary TB lesions look different, and postprimary lesions are poorly understood.

manas.q: Why does preexisting immunity matter for TB granulomas?

children.note: Training can reach bone marrow progenitors (central training), which may explain lasting vaccine protection; inappropriate training may drive SLE-type inflammation and is linked to transplant rejection.

manas.q: What is central trained immunity?

children.note: Antigen diversity, switching of targets and immune inhibition hinder malaria vaccines; conserved epitopes, multivalent vaccines and checkpoint blockade are being studied.

manas.q: What makes a sterilising malaria vaccine hard to achieve?

maps.title: HSU 404 · In depth: Anatomy of the ear

nodeData.topic: Anatomy of the ear in depth
nodeData.note: Applied anatomy of the outer, middle and inner ear, the facial nerve's path and why each relation matters. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Auricle and canal: shape, skin and nerves.
Elastic cartilage covered by tightly bound skin; the lobule has no cartilage, only fat and fibrous tissue.

manas.q: Which part of the auricle has no cartilage?

children.note: Auricular cartilage gets nutrients from its perichondrium; a haematoma lifts it off, the cartilage dies and a 'cauliflower ear' forms unless drained early.

manas.q: Why must an auricular haematoma be drained early?

children.note: The canal is about 2.5 cm long and S-shaped: outer third cartilage, inner two thirds bone.

manas.q: What fraction of the external acoustic meatus is cartilaginous?

children.note: Hair, sebaceous and wax (ceruminous) glands lie only in the cartilaginous part, so furuncles arise there, not in the bony canal.

manas.q: In which part of the ear canal does a furuncle arise, and why?

children.note: Auriculotemporal (V3), great auricular (C2–C3), lesser occipital (C2), the vagal auricular branch (Arnold's nerve) and a small facial nerve area.

manas.q: Name the nerves supplying the auricle and ear canal.

children.note: The eardrum beyond the cone of light.
Outer skin (continuous with canal), middle fibrous layer, inner mucosa (continuous with middle ear lining).

manas.q: What are the three layers of the tympanic membrane?

children.note: Pars tensa is the large taut part; pars flaccida lies above the lateral process of the malleus and lacks the firm fibrous layer, so it retracts more easily.

manas.q: Which part of the eardrum lacks a well-organised fibrous layer?

children.note: Lateral (short) process and handle of malleus, umbo at its tip, cone of light anteroinferiorly; the drum is divided into four quadrants by these lines.

manas.q: Name the landmarks seen on a normal eardrum.

children.note: Long process of incus, stapes and chorda tympani lie behind it, so myringotomy is done in the inferior half of the drum.

manas.q: Why is myringotomy avoided in the posterosuperior quadrant?

children.note: Outer surface: auriculotemporal and vagal auricular branch. Inner surface: glossopharyngeal via the tympanic plexus.

manas.q: Which nerve supplies the inner surface of the eardrum?

children.note: Think of an air-filled box with six walls.
Thin bone separating the middle ear from the middle cranial fossa and temporal lobe.

manas.q: What separates the middle ear from the middle cranial fossa?

children.note: Thin plate over the bulb of the internal jugular vein.

manas.q: Which vessel lies below the floor of the middle ear?

children.note: Internal carotid artery lies in front; the wall carries the Eustachian tube opening and the canal for tensor tympani.

manas.q: Which artery is related to the anterior wall of the middle ear?

children.note: Aditus to the mastoid antrum above, pyramidal eminence (stapedius tendon) and the descending facial canal.

manas.q: What opening is found on the posterior wall of the middle ear?

children.note: Promontory (basal turn of cochlea), oval window above-behind it, round window below-behind, with the facial canal and lateral canal bulge above.

manas.q: What forms the promontory on the medial wall of the middle ear?

children.note: Mainly the eardrum; above it the epitympanum (attic) holds the malleus head and incus body.

manas.q: Which ossicle parts sit in the attic?

children.note: The chain that matches air to fluid.
Sound passes from air to inner-ear fluid; the large drum focusing onto the small stapes footplate plus ossicular leverage boosts pressure.

manas.q: How does the middle ear overcome the air-to-fluid mismatch?

children.note: Inserts on the handle of malleus; supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).

manas.q: Which nerve supplies tensor tympani?

children.note: Inserts on the stapes neck; supplied by the facial nerve; damps loud sound, so paralysis gives hyperacusis.

manas.q: Why does facial nerve palsy above the stapedius branch cause hyperacusis?

children.note: Loud sound contracts stapedius; afferent limb is CN VIII, efferent limb CN VII; tested with tympanometry equipment.

manas.q: What are the afferent and efferent nerves of the stapedial reflex?

children.note: New bone fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window, giving a conductive hearing loss with a normal-looking drum.

manas.q: In otosclerosis, which ossicle becomes fixed?

children.note: Ventilates, drains and protects the middle ear.
Runs from the anterior middle-ear wall down, forward and medially to the nasopharynx; lateral third bony, medial two thirds cartilaginous.

manas.q: Which part of the Eustachian tube is bony?

children.note: Mainly tensor veli palatini, helped by levator veli palatini, on swallowing and yawning.

manas.q: Which muscle chiefly opens the Eustachian tube?

children.note: Equalises middle ear pressure with the atmosphere, drains secretions to the nasopharynx, and shields the ear from nasopharyngeal sound and secretions.

manas.q: List three functions of the Eustachian tube.

children.note: Large adenoids, cleft palate (weak tensor veli palatini), upper airway infection and nasopharyngeal masses cause negative pressure and effusion.

manas.q: Why do children with cleft palate get otitis media with effusion?

children.note: A new unilateral middle-ear effusion in an adult needs the nasopharynx examined to exclude a tumour blocking the tube.

manas.q: What must be excluded in an adult with a unilateral middle-ear effusion?

children.note: Air cells behind the middle ear.
The aditus links the attic to the mastoid antrum, which opens into mastoid air cells, so middle-ear infection reaches the mastoid.

manas.q: What links the epitympanum to the mastoid antrum?

children.note: Macewen's triangle, just above and behind the canal, is the surface marking of the mastoid antrum used in mastoid surgery.

manas.q: What is the surface marking of the mastoid antrum?

children.note: The mastoid process is undeveloped at birth, so the facial nerve exits superficially and is at risk from a standard postauricular incision.

manas.q: Why is the facial nerve vulnerable in infant ear surgery?

children.note: The longest bony course of any nerve.
Cerebellopontine angle → internal acoustic meatus → labyrinthine → geniculate ganglion → tympanic (horizontal) → mastoid (vertical) → stylomastoid foramen.

manas.q: List the segments of the facial nerve within the temporal bone in order.

children.note: The shortest and narrowest part of the canal, so swelling here is thought to compress the nerve, as in Bell's palsy.

manas.q: Which facial nerve segment has the narrowest bony canal?

children.note: Greater petrosal (tear and nasal glands), nerve to stapedius, and chorda tympani (taste to front two thirds of tongue, submandibular and sublingual glands).

manas.q: Name the three branches of the facial nerve given off in the temporal bone.

children.note: Loss of tearing, hyperacusis and taste loss together point to a lesion at or above the geniculate ganglion; only facial weakness suggests a lesion below the chorda.

manas.q: Which signs suggest a facial nerve lesion at the geniculate ganglion?

children.note: Varicella zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion: ear pain, vesicles on the auricle or canal and facial palsy, often with hearing loss or vertigo.

manas.q: What are the features of Ramsay Hunt syndrome?

children.note: Classic teaching: longitudinal (commoner) gives conductive loss; transverse more often hits facial nerve and inner ear. Newer: otic capsule-sparing vs -violating predicts outcome better.

manas.q: Which temporal bone fracture type more often causes facial palsy?

children.note: Labyrinths, fluids and receptors.
Bony labyrinth holds perilymph (sodium-rich, like extracellular fluid); membranous labyrinth holds endolymph (potassium-rich).

manas.q: Which inner-ear fluid is rich in potassium?

children.note: A spiral of about two and a half turns: scala vestibuli and scala tympani hold perilymph; scala media holds endolymph and the organ of Corti.

manas.q: Which cochlear compartment contains the organ of Corti?

children.note: The basal turn responds to high pitches and the apex to low pitches, so noise and ageing first damage high-frequency hearing.

manas.q: Which part of the cochlea detects high-frequency sound?

children.note: Inner hair cells send most signals to the brain; outer hair cells amplify, producing otoacoustic emissions used in newborn screening.

manas.q: Which hair cells produce otoacoustic emissions?

children.note: Utricle and saccule carry otoconia; loose crystals that drift into a canal, usually the posterior canal, cause positional vertigo (BPPV).

manas.q: Which semicircular canal is most often involved in BPPV?

children.note: Carries the facial nerve, nervus intermedius, cochlear and vestibular nerves and labyrinthine artery; a vestibular schwannoma grows here.

manas.q: What structures pass through the internal acoustic meatus?

children.note: Usually from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery; an end artery, so blockage can cause sudden hearing loss and vertigo.

manas.q: Why can a vascular blockage cause sudden sensorineural loss?

children.note: Why a normal ear can hurt.
Tympanic branch of CN IX: ear pain after tonsillectomy or from tonsil and tongue-base disease.

manas.q: Which nerve explains ear pain after tonsillectomy?

children.note: Vagal auricular branch: ear pain from larynx or hypopharynx lesions, including cancer.

manas.q: Ear pain from laryngeal cancer is referred via which nerve?

children.note: If the ear looks normal, examine teeth, TMJ, throat, larynx and neck; persistent pain in a smoker needs ENT endoscopy.

manas.q: What should you examine when otalgia occurs with a normal ear?

children.note: Explains linked malformations.
Six small hillocks from the first and second pharyngeal arches fuse to form the auricle; poor fusion leaves a preauricular sinus.

manas.q: What causes a preauricular sinus?

children.note: Canal from the first pharyngeal cleft; eardrum from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm).

manas.q: From which germ layers does the eardrum develop?

children.note: Tympanic cavity and Eustachian tube from the first pharyngeal pouch (tubotympanic recess).

manas.q: Which pharyngeal pouch forms the middle ear?

children.note: Malleus and incus from the first arch; stapes mainly from the second arch.

manas.q: From which pharyngeal arch does the stapes mainly develop?

children.note: Otic placode of surface ectoderm forms the otic vesicle; so microtia with a malformed middle ear can still have a working cochlea.

manas.q: Why can a child with microtia have a normal cochlea?

children.note: Anatomy that explains disease.
Up through tegmen to temporal lobe; back via mastoid to sigmoid sinus and cerebellum; medially to labyrinth; into a dehiscent facial canal.

manas.q: Through which bone can middle-ear infection reach the temporal lobe?

children.note: Petrous apex infection: ear discharge, deep facial or retro-orbital pain (CN V) and lateral rectus palsy (CN VI).

manas.q: What is Gradenigo's triad?

children.note: Keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear, usually from a pars flaccida (attic) retraction pocket; it erodes bone.

manas.q: Where do most acquired cholesteatomas start?

children.note: Ossicles (often the long process of incus), lateral semicircular canal (fistula), facial canal and tegmen.

manas.q: Which ossicle part is most often eroded in chronic ear disease?

children.note: Otitis media reaching a dehiscent canal, cholesteatoma, temporal bone fracture, mastoid or parotid surgery, and infant surgery with a shallow nerve.

manas.q: List ear-related causes of facial nerve palsy.

children.note: Quick wins.
Ear canal: outer third cartilage. Eustachian tube: lateral third bone. Examiners like this contrast.

manas.q: Contrast which third is cartilage in the ear canal and Eustachian tube.

children.note: Tensor tympani – V3 (first arch); stapedius – VII (second arch): nerve follows the arch.

manas.q: Match tensor tympani and stapedius to their nerves.

children.note: Central pars tensa perforation: tubotympanic, usually safe. Attic or marginal disease with cholesteatoma: atticoantral, unsafe.

manas.q: Which type of chronic ear disease is called 'unsafe'?

children.note: Brief context for hearing care.
WHO's 2021 report calls for ear and hearing care to be part of primary care and universal health coverage.

manas.q: What did WHO's 2021 World Report on Hearing call for?

children.note: US JCIH benchmarks: screen hearing by 1 month, confirm by 3 months, start intervention by 6 months; OAE or automated ABR are used.

manas.q: What do the 1-3-6 newborn hearing benchmarks mean?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-06.
European head and neck radiologists advise CT as the first scan before surgery: it maps the anatomy and shows bone erosion; MRI is for rare cases.

manas.q: Which scan is first-line before cholesteatoma surgery?

children.note: Non-echoplanar diffusion MRI detects leftover cholesteatoma well, so routine second-look surgery is no longer needed for follow-up.

manas.q: Which MRI sequence best finds residual cholesteatoma?

children.note: A review notes Eustachian tube dysfunction is a common middle-ear problem in children that can lower quality of life; it covers medical and surgical options.

manas.q: In which age group is Eustachian tube dysfunction especially common?

maps.title: Medicine as a Profession · In depth: Medical professionalism

nodeData.note: Where professionalism comes from, how it is learned, regulated and assessed, and how it breaks down. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What we mean by the word.
The values, behaviours and relationships that make the public able to trust doctors; it is shown in daily conduct, not only stated.

manas.q: In one line, what is medical professionalism?

children.note: A special body of knowledge, a service ethic, a code of conduct, and the privilege of self-regulation granted by society.

manas.q: List the features that mark medicine as a profession.

children.note: Law sets the enforceable minimum; ethics gives moral principles; professionalism is how those principles show in behaviour.

manas.q: How does professionalism differ from ethics and law?

children.note: Definitions vary across cultures and institutions, which is one reason teaching and assessing professionalism is hard.

manas.q: Why is professionalism hard to assess consistently?

children.note: From oath to charter.
