The phrase is linked to Hippocratic ideas but is not a literal line of the Oath; the Oath does promise to help and avoid injury.

manas.q: Does 'first do no harm' appear word for word in the Hippocratic Oath?

children.note: Written after the trials of Nazi doctors; made voluntary consent of research subjects essential.

manas.q: What principle did the Nuremberg Code make essential in research?

children.note: World Medical Association's code for research on human participants, first adopted in 1964 and revised many times since.

manas.q: Which WMA declaration governs research on humans?

children.note: The 2017 revision adds respect for patient autonomy and asks doctors to care for their own health so they can give good care.

manas.q: What did the 2017 Declaration of Geneva add about the doctor's own health?

children.note: The 2002 Physician Charter came from the ABIM Foundation, ACP–ASIM Foundation and European Federation of Internal Medicine.

manas.q: Which bodies produced the 2002 Physician Charter?

children.note: Competence, honesty, confidentiality, proper relations with patients, quality, access, fair use of resources, science, managing conflicts of interest, team duties.

manas.q: Name some of the Physician Charter's ten commitments.

children.note: Turning attributes into behaviour.
Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice (Beauchamp and Childress) give a framework for hard cases.

manas.q: What are the four principles of biomedical ethics?

children.note: Tell patients openly when something has gone wrong, apologise, explain and put it right where possible.

manas.q: What is the duty of candour?

children.note: Know your limits, ask for help, and keep learning; KMPDC requires CPD points for renewal of the annual practising licence.

manas.q: Why must Kenyan doctors keep doing CPD?

children.note: Gifts, sponsorship or financial ties can bias decisions; declare them and put the patient's interest first.

manas.q: How should a doctor handle a conflict of interest?

children.note: Teamwork, courtesy to every cadre and no bullying or harassment are part of professional behaviour.

manas.q: Is how you treat nurses and colleagues part of professionalism?

children.note: Becoming a doctor, not just acting like one.
The gradual process by which a learner comes to think, feel and act as a doctor, taking on the profession's values as their own.

manas.q: What is professional identity formation?

children.note: Role models, clinical experience, mentoring, feedback, reflection and belonging to a community of practice.

manas.q: Name influences on professional identity formation.

children.note: Students copy what seniors do more than what they say, so good and bad examples both shape identity.

manas.q: Why does role modelling matter so much in training?

children.note: Writing or talking through experiences helps turn them into learning and steady values.

manas.q: How does reflection support professional growth?

children.note: What the culture teaches without saying.
Lessons absorbed from institutional culture, habits and hierarchy rather than from the formal syllabus.

manas.q: What is the hidden curriculum?

children.note: Jokes about patients, ignoring consent for students, cutting corners when busy, and silence in the face of poor behaviour.

manas.q: Give examples of a negative hidden curriculum.

children.note: Exposure to cynicism and stress during training can wear down empathy and ideals if not countered.

manas.q: How can the hidden curriculum affect empathy?

children.note: Name what you see, reflect on it, seek good role models, and use safe channels to raise concerns.

manas.q: How can a student resist a negative hidden curriculum?

children.note: The regulator and its code.
KMPDC is set up under the Medical Practitioners and Dentists Act (Cap 253) as the statutory regulator.

manas.q: Under which Act is the KMPDC established?

children.note: Registers and licenses doctors and dentists, sets training and conduct standards, and hears complaints about practitioners.

manas.q: List the main functions of KMPDC.

children.note: KMPDC's Code of Professional Conduct and Discipline sets the expected standards; breaches can lead to disciplinary action.

manas.q: What does the KMPDC Code of Professional Conduct and Discipline do?

children.note: Society lets the profession regulate itself; failing to deal with misconduct risks losing that trust.

manas.q: Why is self-regulation called a privilege?

children.note: Basics every student must model.
Patient has capacity, gets enough information, and decides freely; consent can be withdrawn at any time.

manas.q: What makes consent valid?

children.note: Introduce yourself as a student and get the patient's agreement before history, examination or procedures.

manas.q: What must a student do before examining a patient?

children.note: Patient information stays private, shared within the team only as needed; exceptions include consent, law and serious risk to others.

manas.q: Name exceptions to medical confidentiality.

children.note: The Constitution protects privacy (Article 31) and the Data Protection Act 2019 treats health data as sensitive.

manas.q: Which Kenyan law treats health data as sensitive personal data?

children.note: Talking about patients in lifts or corridors, leaving notes open, or sharing details in chat groups.

manas.q: Give everyday examples of confidentiality breaches.

children.note: Keeping the relationship professional.
A sexual or romantic relationship with a current patient is never acceptable; the power imbalance makes true consent doubtful.

manas.q: Is a relationship with a current patient ever acceptable?

children.note: Offer a chaperone for intimate examinations and record the offer and who was present.

manas.q: When should a chaperone be offered?

children.note: Avoid it except in emergencies; objectivity, examination and record-keeping all suffer.

manas.q: Why should doctors avoid treating their own family?

children.note: Small thank-you tokens may be fine; refuse gifts that could influence care or create obligation.

manas.q: When should a doctor refuse a gift from a patient?

children.note: Beyond 'no patient photos'.
Posts can be copied and shared even after deletion; privacy settings do not guarantee privacy.

manas.q: Do privacy settings make posts safe?

children.note: Keep personal accounts separate; politely decline friend requests from patients and redirect care questions to proper channels.

manas.q: How should you respond to a friend request from a patient?

children.note: When you post as a doctor or student, stay accurate, evidence-based, and declare interests; avoid spreading misinformation.

manas.q: What standard applies to health advice you post online?

children.note: Wellbeing is a professional duty.
Emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation and reduced sense of accomplishment, often measured with the Maslach Burnout Inventory.

manas.q: What are the three dimensions of burnout?

children.note: ICD-11 lists burnout as an occupational phenomenon from unmanaged workplace stress, not as a medical condition.

manas.q: How does ICD-11 classify burnout?

children.note: Illness, substance use or exhaustion that affects safe practice; the doctor should seek help and not self-treat.

manas.q: What should an impaired doctor do?

children.note: Sleep, support, a personal doctor and early help-seeking protect patients as well as the doctor.

manas.q: Why is self-care part of professionalism?

children.note: When things go wrong.
Lateness, dishonesty, falsifying records or logbooks, plagiarism and disrespect to patients or staff.

manas.q: Give examples of unprofessional behaviour by students.

children.note: A US study (Papadakis, 2005) linked unprofessional behaviour in medical school with later disciplinary action by medical boards.

manas.q: What did Papadakis (2005) link with later disciplinary action?

children.note: Patient safety comes first: speak to a supervisor, then use institutional channels, then the regulator if needed.

manas.q: In what order should you escalate a patient-safety concern?

children.note: Report incidents, be open with patients and focus on learning and system fixes rather than blame.

manas.q: Why report errors rather than hide them?

children.note: Observing behaviour over time.
Professionalism Mini-Evaluation Exercise: an observer rates specific professional behaviours during a real encounter.

manas.q: What is the P-MEX?

children.note: Ratings from peers, nurses, other staff and patients (360°) give a wider view than one assessor.

manas.q: Who gives ratings in multi-source feedback?

children.note: Reflective writing and critical incident reports show how learners think about professional challenges.

manas.q: How do portfolios help assess professionalism?

children.note: Ratings are subjective and context-bound; repeated observations by many raters over time are more reliable.

manas.q: How can professionalism assessment be made more reliable?

children.note: High-yield points.
Patient welfare, patient autonomy, social justice — memorise these three.

manas.q: State the three principles of the Physician Charter.

children.note: Disciplinary complaints go to KMPDC, the regulator — not to KMPDU, which is a union.

manas.q: Which body handles complaints about a doctor's conduct in Kenya?

children.note: Examiners want observable actions: punctuality, consent, honesty, respect, escalation.

manas.q: Why do examiners stress observable behaviour?

children.note: Other codes; Kenya first.
Kenyan doctors follow the KMPDC Code of Professional Conduct and Discipline alongside Kenyan law.

manas.q: Which code sets conduct standards for Kenyan doctors?

children.note: The General Medical Council's Good Medical Practice sets UK standards; an updated version took effect in 2024.

manas.q: What is the UK GMC's core guidance called?

children.note: The ABIM Foundation-led charter is widely used in US training; the AMA also publishes a Code of Medical Ethics.

manas.q: Which professional ethics code does the AMA publish?

children.note: The WMA's Declaration of Geneva and International Code of Medical Ethics serve national medical associations worldwide.

manas.q: Name two WMA codes for doctors.

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-06.
A 2025 review of 29 studies in trainees found burnout mostly correlated with lower professionalism, empathy and patient care; it calls for wellbeing support and system change.

manas.q: How did burnout relate to professionalism in a 2025 review of trainees?

children.note: A scoping review of 16 student studies found a significant inverse association between empathy and burnout; compassion seemed to ease burnout. Cause and effect is unproven.

manas.q: What relationship did a 2023 review find between empathy and burnout?

children.note: A review of 72 papers found assessment mostly subjective; P-MEX is useful but hard to run, and longitudinal multi-source methods are more reliable.

manas.q: What did a 2025 scoping review say makes professionalism assessment more reliable?

children.note: An umbrella review of eight reviews: most reported better professionalism, empathy and compassion after teaching, but methods varied widely and long-term effects are poorly reported.

manas.q: What gap did a 2025 umbrella review find in professionalism teaching research?

maps.title: HBC 200 · In depth: Fatty acid oxidation

nodeData.note: From fat stores to acetyl-CoA and ketones: each step, its control, and the inherited defects. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Where and when fat is burned.
Stepwise breakdown of fatty acids to acetyl-CoA, mainly by β-oxidation in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing NADH and FADH2.

manas.q: What is fatty acid β-oxidation?

children.note: Liver, heart and resting skeletal muscle rely heavily on fatty acids, especially in fasting.

manas.q: Which tissues rely heavily on fatty acid oxidation?

children.note: Red cells lack mitochondria; the brain takes up little fatty acid, so it relies on glucose, then ketones in long fasts.

manas.q: Why can red cells not oxidise fatty acids?

children.note: Getting fatty acids out of adipose tissue.
Adipose triacylglycerol is split by lipases (ATGL, hormone-sensitive lipase, monoacylglycerol lipase) into glycerol and fatty acids.

manas.q: Which lipases break down adipose triacylglycerol?

children.note: Glucagon and adrenaline raise cAMP and activate PKA, which switches lipolysis on; insulin switches it off.

manas.q: Which hormone inhibits lipolysis?

children.note: Free fatty acids travel bound to albumin to tissues.

manas.q: How are free fatty acids carried in blood?

children.note: Glycerol goes to the liver, where glycerol kinase lets it enter gluconeogenesis; adipose tissue lacks this enzyme.

manas.q: Why can glycerol but not fatty acids form glucose?

children.note: Priming the fatty acid.
On the outer mitochondrial membrane, fatty acid + CoA + ATP form fatty acyl-CoA, AMP and pyrophosphate.

manas.q: What reaction does acyl-CoA synthetase catalyse?

children.note: ATP goes to AMP, so 2 high-energy bonds are used; pyrophosphate breakdown makes the reaction irreversible.

manas.q: How many high-energy bonds does fatty acid activation use?

children.note: Crossing the inner membrane.
The inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to long-chain acyl-CoA, so the acyl group is passed to carnitine.

manas.q: Why do long-chain fatty acids need carnitine?

children.note: CPT-I makes acylcarnitine; a translocase swaps it in for free carnitine; CPT-II on the inner membrane remakes acyl-CoA.

manas.q: What are the three steps of the carnitine shuttle?

children.note: Short and medium-chain fatty acids enter mitochondria without carnitine.

manas.q: Which fatty acids enter mitochondria without carnitine?

children.note: From the diet, especially meat, and made in the body from lysine and methionine.

manas.q: From which amino acids is carnitine made?

children.note: Four reactions repeat each cycle.
Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase forms a trans double bond between C2 and C3, reducing FAD to FADH2.

manas.q: Which coenzyme is reduced in the first step of β-oxidation?

children.note: Enoyl-CoA hydratase adds water across the double bond to give L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA.

manas.q: What does enoyl-CoA hydratase produce?

children.note: 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase oxidises the hydroxyl group to a ketone, reducing NAD+ to NADH.

manas.q: Which step of β-oxidation produces NADH?

children.note: Thiolase uses CoA to cut off acetyl-CoA, leaving an acyl-CoA two carbons shorter for the next cycle.

manas.q: What does thiolase release in each cycle?

children.note: Separate acyl-CoA dehydrogenases act on very long, long, medium and short chains (VLCAD, LCAD, MCAD, SCAD).

manas.q: Why are there several acyl-CoA dehydrogenases?

children.note: For long chains, one inner-membrane complex carries out steps 2–4, including long-chain hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD).

manas.q: Which enzyme activity of the trifunctional protein is LCHAD?

children.note: C16 palmitate needs 7 cycles, giving 8 acetyl-CoA, 7 FADH2 and 7 NADH.

manas.q: How many cycles of β-oxidation does palmitate need?

children.note: Need extra enzymes: an enoyl-CoA isomerase and, for many polyunsaturated ones, 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase using NADPH.

manas.q: Which extra enzymes oxidise unsaturated fatty acids?

children.note: Burn fat or make fat, not both.
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes malonyl-CoA in the fed state; malonyl-CoA blocks CPT-I, so new fat is not burned at once.

manas.q: How does malonyl-CoA prevent a futile cycle?

children.note: Insulin activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase (more malonyl-CoA, less oxidation); glucagon inhibits it (more oxidation).

manas.q: How does glucagon increase fatty acid oxidation?

children.note: When energy is low, AMP-activated kinase phosphorylates and inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase, lowering malonyl-CoA.

manas.q: How does AMPK increase fatty acid oxidation?

children.note: A nuclear receptor that switches on genes for fatty acid oxidation in fasting; fibrates act through it.

manas.q: Which nuclear receptor do fibrates activate?

children.note: Liver turns excess acetyl-CoA into fuel.
In fasting or uncontrolled diabetes, hepatic oxaloacetate goes to gluconeogenesis, so acetyl-CoA builds up and forms ketones.

manas.q: Why does acetyl-CoA form ketones in fasting?

children.note: Acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA (mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase, rate-limiting) → acetoacetate.

manas.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis?

children.note: Acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate (made from it using NADH) and acetone (formed spontaneously, breathed out).

manas.q: Name the three ketone bodies.

children.note: The liver lacks succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid CoA transferase (thiophorase), so it exports ketones to other tissues.

manas.q: Why can the liver not use ketone bodies?

children.note: Urine nitroprusside strips detect acetoacetate (and acetone) but not β-hydroxybutyrate, the main ketone in DKA.

manas.q: Which ketone body is not detected by nitroprusside strips?

children.note: Peroxisomes, ER and odd chains.
Peroxisomal acyl-CoA oxidase passes electrons straight to oxygen, making H2O2 instead of FADH2; shortened chains go to mitochondria.

manas.q: How does the first step of peroxisomal β-oxidation differ?

children.note: Branched phytanic acid is shortened by one carbon in peroxisomes; its failure causes Refsum disease.

manas.q: Which disease results from defective α-oxidation of phytanic acid?

children.note: In the endoplasmic reticulum, cytochrome P450 oxidises the far end, making dicarboxylic acids; it rises when β-oxidation fails.

manas.q: Where does ω-oxidation occur and what does it produce?

children.note: Lack of B12 blocks methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so methylmalonic acid rises: a useful test of B12 deficiency.

manas.q: Why does methylmalonic acid rise in B12 deficiency?

children.note: Beyond MCAD basics.
Illness or fasting brings hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, lethargy, liver enlargement and sometimes high ammonia.

manas.q: What is the typical metabolic picture of a fatty acid oxidation defect?

children.note: VLCAD, LCHAD and trifunctional protein defects can also cause cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis.

manas.q: Which extra features do long-chain oxidation defects cause?

children.note: A mother carrying an LCHAD-deficient fetus is at risk of acute fatty liver of pregnancy and HELLP syndrome.

manas.q: Which pregnancy complications are linked to fetal LCHAD deficiency?

children.note: The adult muscle form causes attacks of muscle pain and rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria after exercise or fasting.

manas.q: How does the adult form of CPT-II deficiency present?

children.note: Liver form: hypoketotic hypoglycaemia in infancy, with normal or high free carnitine.

manas.q: What happens to free carnitine in CPT-I deficiency?

children.note: Faulty OCTN2 carnitine transporter (SLC22A5) causes very low carnitine and cardiomyopathy; carnitine supplements treat it.

manas.q: Which transporter is defective in primary carnitine deficiency?

children.note: Low carnitine from other causes, e.g. valproate, dialysis or organic acidaemias.

manas.q: Name causes of secondary carnitine deficiency.

children.note: Hypoglycin A in unripe ackee fruit inhibits acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, causing severe hypoglycaemia.

manas.q: What causes Jamaican vomiting sickness?

children.note: Catch the sample during the attack.
Tandem mass spectrometry of blood shows which acylcarnitine builds up, e.g. octanoylcarnitine (C8) in MCAD deficiency.

manas.q: Which acylcarnitine is raised in MCAD deficiency?

children.note: Dicarboxylic aciduria with little ketone suggests a β-oxidation defect.

manas.q: What urine organic acid pattern suggests a β-oxidation defect?

children.note: During hypoglycaemia, before treatment if possible: glucose, ketones, free fatty acids, insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, lactate, ammonia and acylcarnitines (plus urine organic acids).

manas.q: Which tests make up the critical sample in hypoglycaemia?

children.note: Enzyme or gene testing confirms the defect; carnitine levels help separate primary from secondary deficiency.

manas.q: How is a fatty acid oxidation defect confirmed?

children.note: Prevent fasting, treat early.
Frequent feeds and a written emergency plan with glucose drinks or IV dextrose during illness.

manas.q: What is the key preventive measure in fatty acid oxidation defects?

children.note: In long-chain defects, a low long-chain fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides bypasses the block; avoid MCT in MCAD.

manas.q: Why are medium-chain triglycerides avoided in MCAD deficiency?

children.note: Carnitine supplements are the main treatment for primary carnitine deficiency.

manas.q: What treats primary carnitine deficiency?

children.note: Quick points examiners like.
Low glucose with low ketones means fat cannot be burned or ketones made: think fatty acid oxidation defect or hyperinsulinism.

manas.q: What two causes should hypoketotic hypoglycaemia suggest?

children.note: Even-chain fatty acids give acetyl-CoA, and pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible, so no net glucose forms.

manas.q: Why can even-chain fatty acids not make net glucose?

children.note: 8 acetyl-CoA × 10 + 7 NADH × 2.5 + 7 FADH2 × 1.5 = 108; minus 2 for activation = 106.

manas.q: How is the 106 ATP from palmitate calculated?

children.note: Acetyl-CoA from β-oxidation activates pyruvate carboxylase, supporting gluconeogenesis in fasting.

manas.q: Which enzyme does acetyl-CoA activate to support gluconeogenesis?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-09.
A review describes fasting liver fat oxidation and ketogenesis driven by hormones and rising fatty acids, acting through PPAR-α; women tend to have higher ketones.

manas.q: Which transcription factor mediates fasting hepatic fatty acid oxidation, per a 2024 review?

children.note: In 757 reported patients, cardiac problems (mainly cardiomyopathy, 23.8%) were the commonest feature; most screen-detected people stayed well, but rare sudden severe events occurred.

manas.q: What was the most common feature of primary carnitine deficiency in a 2022 review?

maps.title: HHP 303 · In depth: Thyroid function tests

nodeData.note: The thyroid axis, what each test measures, assay pitfalls, result patterns and monitoring. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What thyroid function tests are and why TSH leads.
Blood tests of the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis: mainly TSH and free T4, with free T3, antibodies and thyroglobulin in selected cases.

manas.q: Which tests make up a thyroid function panel?

children.note: TSH has a log-linear inverse relationship with free T4, so a small change in free T4 gives a large change in TSH — provided the pituitary works normally.

manas.q: Why is TSH a more sensitive marker of primary thyroid status than free T4?

children.note: How the hormones are made, carried and controlled.
Hypothalamic TRH stimulates pituitary TSH, which drives thyroid growth, iodine uptake and hormone release; T4 and T3 feed back to suppress TRH and TSH.

manas.q: Describe the feedback loop of the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis.

children.note: Iodide is trapped by the sodium–iodide symporter, then thyroid peroxidase oxidises it and attaches it to tyrosines on thyroglobulin, which are coupled into T4 and T3.

manas.q: Outline the steps of thyroid hormone synthesis.

children.note: The gland secretes mostly T4; most circulating T3 is made in tissues by removing an iodine from T4. T3 is the more active hormone at the receptor.

manas.q: Where does most circulating T3 come from?

children.note: Deiodinase enzymes either activate T4 to T3 or inactivate it to reverse T3; the balance shifts in illness, fasting and with some drugs.

manas.q: What do deiodinase enzymes do to T4?

children.note: Over 99% of T4 and T3 is bound, mainly to thyroxine-binding globulin, also transthyretin and albumin; only the free fraction acts on tissues.

manas.q: Which proteins carry thyroid hormones, and which fraction is active?

children.note: T4 has a long half-life (about a week) and TSH takes weeks to settle, so TFTs are rechecked weeks, not days, after a change in treatment.

manas.q: Why are TFTs not rechecked within days of a levothyroxine dose change?

children.note: What each test adds.
Measured by a sandwich (immunometric) immunoassay with two antibodies; modern assays detect very low levels, separating suppressed from low-normal TSH.

manas.q: What type of assay is used to measure TSH?

children.note: Confirms and grades thyroid dysfunction and is the key test when the pituitary is diseased or TSH is unreliable.

manas.q: When is free T4 the key thyroid test rather than TSH?

children.note: Added in suspected hyperthyroidism; detects T3 toxicosis, where free T3 is raised with a normal free T4. Little value in diagnosing hypothyroidism.

manas.q: What is T3 toxicosis?

children.note: Total T4 rises with more binding protein (pregnancy, oestrogen) while free T4 stays normal, so free hormone assays are preferred.

manas.q: Why does total T4 rise in pregnancy while the patient stays euthyroid?

children.note: Mark autoimmune thyroiditis and predict a higher chance that subclinical hypothyroidism will progress to overt disease.

manas.q: What does a positive anti-TPO antibody add in subclinical hypothyroidism?

children.note: They cross the placenta and can cause fetal or neonatal thyrotoxicosis, so they are checked in pregnant women with current or past Graves disease.

manas.q: Why measure TSH-receptor antibodies in a pregnant woman with past Graves disease?

children.note: A tumour marker after total thyroidectomy for differentiated thyroid cancer, not a test to diagnose cancer; anti-thyroglobulin antibodies interfere.

manas.q: What is serum thyroglobulin used for?

children.note: Made by parafollicular C cells; a marker for medullary thyroid carcinoma.

manas.q: Calcitonin is a tumour marker for which thyroid cancer?

children.note: Read TSH and free T4 together.
Primary thyrotoxicosis: Graves disease, toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis or excess thyroxine intake.

manas.q: List causes of a low TSH with a high free T4.

children.note: Subclinical hyperthyroidism, or a non-thyroid cause: acute non-thyroidal illness, glucocorticoids, dopamine or early pregnancy. Check free T3.

manas.q: Give causes of a low TSH with a normal free T4.

children.topic: Raised or normal TSH, high free T4
children.note: Rare: TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma or thyroid hormone resistance. First exclude assay interference, heparin and erratic thyroxine use.

manas.q: What should you exclude before diagnosing a TSH-secreting adenoma?

children.note: Tablets taken just before a clinic test can give a normal or high free T4 with a still-raised TSH, reflecting poor adherence over previous weeks.

manas.q: How does poor levothyroxine adherence show on TFTs?

children.note: When the result does not fit the patient.
High-dose biotin supplements disturb streptavidin–biotin immunoassays: falsely low TSH and high free T4/T3 can mimic Graves. Stop biotin before retesting.

manas.q: How can biotin supplements mimic Graves disease on TFTs?

children.note: Patient antibodies can bridge the two assay antibodies and falsely raise TSH; suspect when results do not fit, and retest on another platform.

manas.q: How do heterophile antibodies affect a TSH sandwich assay?

children.note: Heparin releases lipase, which frees fatty acids that displace T4 from binding proteins in the sample, falsely raising free T4.

manas.q: Why can heparin falsely raise measured free T4?

children.note: TSH bound to immunoglobulin forms a large, inactive complex that is measured but cleared slowly, giving a falsely high TSH; PEG precipitation reveals it.

manas.q: What is macro-TSH?

children.note: Glucocorticoids and dopamine suppress TSH; lithium can cause hypothyroidism and goitre.

manas.q: Name drugs that suppress TSH and one that causes hypothyroidism.

children.note: Where normal ranges change.
hCG weakly stimulates the TSH receptor, so TSH falls in the first trimester; use trimester-specific reference ranges.

manas.q: Why does TSH fall in the first trimester?

children.note: Requirements usually rise in pregnancy, so women on levothyroxine need early TFTs and often a dose increase once pregnant.

manas.q: What happens to levothyroxine requirements in pregnancy?

children.note: TSH tends to rise with age, but uniform adult ranges are used, so more older people are labelled subclinically hypothyroid.

manas.q: Why is subclinical hypothyroidism diagnosed more often in older people?

children.note: TSH surges briefly after birth, so screening samples taken too early can give false-positive results.

manas.q: Why does the timing of newborn TSH screening matter?

children.note: Subacute, painless and postpartum thyroiditis: a thyrotoxic phase with low isotope uptake, then often a hypothyroid phase, then usually recovery.

manas.q: Describe the phases of thyroiditis on TFTs.

children.note: Which test to follow.
Levothyroxine is titrated to TSH, rechecked about 6–8 weeks after each dose change.

manas.q: How is levothyroxine monitored in primary hypothyroidism?

children.note: TSH cannot guide treatment; titrate levothyroxine to free T4.

manas.q: Which test guides levothyroxine in central hypothyroidism?

children.note: TSH may stay suppressed for months after the patient improves, so free T4 and T3 guide antithyroid drugs early on.

manas.q: Why are free T4/T3, not TSH, used early in treating hyperthyroidism?

children.note: A suppressed TSH on levothyroxine raises the risk of atrial fibrillation and bone loss, especially in older people.

manas.q: What are the risks of a suppressed TSH from too much levothyroxine?

children.note: Quick points examiners like.
High uptake: Graves, toxic nodules. Low uptake: thyroiditis, exogenous thyroxine, iodine load.

manas.q: Which causes of thyrotoxicosis show low isotope uptake?

children.note: Exogenous thyroxine suppresses the gland, so thyroglobulin is low; in thyroiditis it is high.

manas.q: How does thyroglobulin separate factitious thyrotoxicosis from thyroiditis?

children.note: Thyroid storm and myxoedema coma are diagnosed clinically; send TFTs but start treatment without waiting.

manas.q: Should you wait for TFTs before treating thyroid storm?

children.note: Check the clinical picture, drugs (biotin, heparin), adherence and timing, then repeat on another assay before acting.

manas.q: What is the approach to discordant thyroid results?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
Follow MoH Kenya clinical guidance and use your laboratory's own reference ranges, which differ between assays.

manas.q: Why should TFTs be read against the local lab's reference range?

children.note: WHO supports universal salt iodisation and judges population iodine status by urinary iodine, not by individual TFTs.

manas.q: How does WHO assess iodine status in a population?

children.note: The European Thyroid Association guideline on subclinical hypothyroidism bases treatment on age, TSH level, symptoms and comorbidities.

manas.q: On what does the ETA base treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism?

children.note: The American Thyroid Association pregnancy guideline advises trimester-specific, population-based TSH reference ranges.

manas.q: What reference ranges does the ATA advise for TSH in pregnancy?

children.note: NICE guideline NG145 covers assessment and management of thyroid disease in adults and children in the UK.

manas.q: Which NICE guideline covers thyroid disease?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-09.
A narrative review found subclinical hypothyroidism linked with outcomes between euthyroid and overt disease, but little evidence that treatment helps; individual decisions remain.

manas.q: What did a 2023 review conclude about treating subclinical hypothyroidism?

children.note: In RCTs of women with subclinical hypothyroidism, levothyroxine before or in early pregnancy did not improve live birth or miscarriage; a possible preterm benefit when TSH >4.0 needs study.

manas.q: Did levothyroxine improve live birth in subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy RCTs?

children.note: In seven studies of over-65s with subclinical hypothyroidism, levothyroxine was not significantly associated with fewer cardiovascular events; bone outcomes could not be pooled.

manas.q: Was levothyroxine linked with fewer cardiovascular events in over-65s with subclinical hypothyroidism?

maps.title: HMM 300 · In depth: Herpesviruses

nodeData.note: Classification, latency, each virus's diseases, lab diagnosis, antivirals and prevention. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What a herpesvirus is and the three subfamilies.
Large enveloped viruses with a linear double-stranded DNA genome, an icosahedral capsid and a protein tegument between capsid and envelope.

manas.q: Describe the structure of a herpesvirus.

children.note: HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV: replicate fast, destroy the cells they infect and hide latent in sensory neurons.

manas.q: Which herpesviruses are alpha-herpesviruses and where do they go latent?

children.note: CMV, HHV-6 and HHV-7: replicate slowly, enlarge infected cells (cytomegaly) and stay latent in white blood cells.

manas.q: Which herpesviruses are beta-herpesviruses?

children.note: EBV and HHV-8: latent mainly in lymphocytes and able to drive cancers.

manas.q: Which herpesviruses are gamma-herpesviruses, and what is special about them?

children.note: Why infection is lifelong.
The genome is copied in the nucleus by a viral DNA polymerase — the target of most antivirals. Intranuclear inclusions (Cowdry type A) result.

manas.q: Which viral enzyme do most anti-herpes drugs target?

children.note: The genome persists as a circular episome with very limited gene expression, hidden from the immune system; drugs cannot clear it.

manas.q: Why can antivirals not cure herpesvirus infection?

children.note: Stress, fever, UV light, menstruation and weakened immunity can reactivate latent HSV.

manas.q: Name triggers that reactivate latent HSV.

children.note: Mostly close contact with saliva, secretions or lesions; VZV is also airborne; CMV also spreads by blood, transplants, breast milk and across the placenta.

manas.q: How is CMV transmitted?

children.note: HSV-1 and HSV-2 in practice.
Gingivostomatitis in young children, recurrent cold sores, keratitis with a dendritic corneal ulcer and encephalitis.

manas.q: What eye lesion is typical of HSV keratitis?

children.note: Painful recurrent genital ulcers, classically HSV-2, though HSV-1 now causes a growing share of first episodes.

manas.q: Which HSV types cause genital herpes?

children.note: Usually caught from maternal genital infection at birth; risk is highest with a first maternal infection near term, when caesarean birth is considered.

manas.q: When is the risk of neonatal herpes highest?

children.note: Herpetic whitlow on fingers; eczema herpeticum, a widespread infection over atopic eczema needing urgent antiviral treatment.

manas.q: What is eczema herpeticum?

children.note: Genital herpes ulcers raise the risk of acquiring and transmitting HIV.

manas.q: How does genital herpes affect HIV transmission?

children.note: Chickenpox and shingles.
Highly contagious, airborne; itchy crops of macules, papules, vesicles and crusts present together, mostly on the trunk.

manas.q: What is the typical rash pattern of chickenpox?

children.note: Secondary bacterial skin infection, pneumonia (worse in adults and pregnancy), cerebellar ataxia in children and encephalitis.

manas.q: List complications of varicella.

children.note: Reactivation in a ganglion gives pain then a vesicular rash in one dermatome that does not cross the midline.

manas.q: Describe the rash of herpes zoster.

children.note: Zoster of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve; vesicles on the nose tip (Hutchinson sign) warn of eye involvement.

manas.q: What is Hutchinson sign in herpes zoster?

children.note: Zoster of the geniculate ganglion: facial palsy with vesicles in the ear canal or on the auricle.

manas.q: What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome?

children.note: Herpes zoster is a WHO clinical stage 2 condition; a young adult with shingles should be offered an HIV test.

manas.q: What should you offer a young adult with herpes zoster in Kenya?

children.note: Early pregnancy infection can cause congenital varicella syndrome (skin scars, limb hypoplasia, eye and brain defects); rash near delivery risks severe neonatal varicella.

manas.q: What is congenital varicella syndrome?

children.note: Beyond glandular fever.
EBV infects B cells through CD21 (complement receptor 2); the atypical lymphocytes in the blood are reactive cytotoxic T cells.

manas.q: Which receptor does EBV use to enter B cells?

children.note: Fever, sore throat, posterior neck nodes and splenomegaly; amoxicillin often causes a rash. Avoid contact sports because of splenic rupture risk.

manas.q: Why should patients with infectious mononucleosis avoid contact sports?

children.note: Endemic form presents as a jaw or abdominal tumour in children in malaria areas, including Kenya's lake region; MYC translocation, classically t(8;14).

manas.q: Which translocation is classic for Burkitt lymphoma?

children.note: Some Hodgkin lymphomas, oral hairy leukoplakia in HIV, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.

manas.q: Name EBV-associated diseases besides Burkitt lymphoma.

children.note: Silent in most, serious in some.
Usually silent or a mononucleosis-like illness with a negative heterophile test.

manas.q: How does CMV mononucleosis differ from EBV on the heterophile test?

children.note: Enlarged cells with large intranuclear inclusions are the histological hallmark of CMV.

manas.q: What is the histological hallmark of CMV infection?

children.note: A major opportunistic infection after organ and stem cell transplants, causing pneumonitis, colitis and hepatitis.

manas.q: What CMV diseases occur after transplantation?

children.note: Besides retinitis, CMV causes colitis and oesophagitis in advanced HIV.

manas.q: Apart from retinitis, which CMV diseases occur in advanced HIV?

children.note: The less famous three.
HHV-6 (sometimes HHV-7): days of high fever in an infant, then a rash as the fever settles; febrile seizures may occur.

manas.q: What is the clinical pattern of roseola infantum?

children.note: Purple patches, plaques or nodules on skin, mouth (especially the palate) and internal organs; a vascular tumour driven by HHV-8.

manas.q: Where should you look for Kaposi sarcoma lesions?

children.note: In endemic African settings it spreads mainly through saliva, often in childhood; sexual spread also occurs.

manas.q: How is HHV-8 mainly spread in endemic Africa?

children.note: Choosing the right test.
Test of choice for CSF, swabs from lesions and blood viral loads (CMV, EBV) in transplant and HIV patients.

manas.q: What is the test of choice for herpesvirus DNA in CSF or lesions?

children.note: Monospot can be negative early and in young children; EBV-specific antibodies (VCA IgM) then help.

manas.q: When can the Monospot test be falsely negative?

children.note: Low-avidity IgG suggests a recent primary CMV infection, helping time maternal infection in pregnancy.

manas.q: What does low-avidity CMV IgG suggest?

children.note: CSF shows lymphocytes and raised protein; MRI shows temporal lobe change. A negative early PCR may need repeating if suspicion stays high.

manas.q: What MRI finding suggests HSV encephalitis?

children.note: Mechanisms and toxicities (no doses here).
Viral thymidine kinase phosphorylates it first, so it is activated mainly in infected cells; the triphosphate blocks viral DNA polymerase and ends the chain.

manas.q: Why is acyclovir selective for infected cells?

children.note: An oral prodrug of acyclovir with much better absorption.

manas.q: What is valaciclovir?

children.note: Intravenous acyclovir can crystallise in renal tubules; keep the patient well hydrated and adjust for kidney function.

manas.q: How is acyclovir kidney injury prevented?

children.note: CMV lacks thymidine kinase, so acyclovir works poorly; ganciclovir is activated by the CMV UL97 kinase. Main toxicity: bone marrow suppression.

manas.q: Why is ganciclovir, not acyclovir, used for CMV?

children.note: Acts directly on viral DNA polymerase without activation, so it works on kinase-mutant resistant virus; nephrotoxic and upsets electrolytes.

manas.q: Why does foscarnet work against acyclovir-resistant HSV?

children.note: Vaccines and post-exposure care.
Live attenuated; avoid in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression.

manas.q: In whom is varicella vaccine contraindicated?

children.note: Given after significant exposure to susceptible high-risk people: pregnant women, the immunosuppressed and some newborns.

manas.q: Who should receive varicella-zoster immunoglobulin after exposure?

children.note: A live attenuated vaccine and a recombinant adjuvanted glycoprotein E vaccine; only the recombinant one suits immunosuppressed people.

manas.q: Which zoster vaccine can be given to immunosuppressed patients?

children.note: No licensed vaccine; hygiene advice in pregnancy and CMV-safe (seronegative or leucodepleted) blood for at-risk patients.

manas.q: How is CMV transmission reduced in transfusion?

children.note: Quick points examiners like.
Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions: HSV and VZV. Owl's eye cells: CMV.

manas.q: Which inclusions are seen in HSV and VZV versus CMV?

children.note: Lesions beyond a few dermatomes or crossing the midline suggest disseminated zoster — think immunosuppression.

manas.q: What does zoster spreading beyond a few dermatomes or across the midline suggest?

children.note: Usually from thymidine kinase mutations, seen in immunosuppressed patients on long courses.

manas.q: What usually causes acyclovir resistance?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
Kenya's ARV guidelines use WHO clinical staging: herpes zoster is stage 2 and Kaposi sarcoma stage 4, both prompting HIV care and ART.

manas.q: What WHO stage are herpes zoster and Kaposi sarcoma?

children.note: WHO advises routine childhood varicella vaccination only where high, sustained coverage is possible, as low coverage can shift infection to older ages.

manas.q: Why does WHO link varicella vaccination to high coverage?

links.title: Kenya MoH

children.note: In the US the recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended for adults aged 50 and over and immunocompromised adults aged 19 and over.

manas.q: Who does ACIP recommend for recombinant zoster vaccine?

links.title: Kenya MoH

children.note: The UK National Screening Committee does not recommend routine antenatal CMV screening.

manas.q: Does the UK screen all pregnant women for CMV?

links.title: Kenya MoH

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-09.
A GRADE-based European consensus stresses early, accurate maternal diagnosis by serology, valaciclovir to prevent vertical transmission, and risk-based postnatal care.

manas.q: Which drug does the European consensus support to prevent vertical CMV transmission?

children.note: A review notes zoster rises with age and immunosuppression; postherpetic neuralgia is among the commonest complications; early antiviral therapy and pain control are central.

manas.q: What are the cornerstones of herpes zoster management?

children.note: Zoster vaccines make shingles preventable, but a review found access mostly limited to high-income countries, with few national schedules including them, mainly for cost-effectiveness reasons.

manas.q: Why do few countries include zoster vaccine in national schedules?

maps.title: HOG 300 · In depth: Female pelvic anatomy

nodeData.note: Bony pelvis, organs, supports, pelvic floor, vessels, nodes, nerves and clinical links. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: The bony ring and its obstetric meaning.
A ring of the two hip bones, sacrum and coccyx; the pelvic brim divides the false (greater) pelvis above from the true (lesser) pelvis below.

manas.q: What divides the false pelvis from the true pelvis?

children.note: Sacral promontory, sacral ala, arcuate and pectineal lines, pubic crest and the upper border of the symphysis pubis.

manas.q: Name the landmarks of the pelvic brim.

children.note: The female pelvis is wider and shallower, with a rounder inlet, wider subpubic angle and larger outlet — adapted for birth.

manas.q: How does the female pelvis differ from the male?

children.note: Gynaecoid (round inlet, most favourable for birth), android, anthropoid and platypelloid.

manas.q: Which pelvic shape is most favourable for vaginal birth?

children.note: Shortest front-to-back diameter of the inlet, from sacral promontory to the back of the symphysis; estimated clinically from the diagonal conjugate.

manas.q: What is the obstetric conjugate and how is it estimated?

children.note: Felt on vaginal examination; the level of the spines is station 0 when assessing descent of the fetal head.

manas.q: What landmark defines station 0 in labour?

children.note: Uterus, tubes, ovaries, vagina and pouches.
Fundus, body, isthmus and cervix; usually anteverted and anteflexed. The isthmus becomes the lower segment in pregnancy.

manas.q: Which part of the uterus forms the lower segment in pregnancy?

children.note: Endometrium (shed in menstruation), myometrium (smooth muscle) and perimetrium (peritoneal cover).

manas.q: Name the three layers of the uterine wall.

children.note: Fimbriated infundibulum, ampulla (usual site of fertilisation and commonest site of ectopic pregnancy), isthmus and intramural part.

manas.q: What is the commonest site of tubal ectopic pregnancy?

children.note: Held by the suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament carrying its vessels, the ovarian ligament to the uterus, and the mesovarium.

manas.q: Which ligament carries the ovarian vessels?

children.note: The ovary lies on the side wall near the obturator nerve, so ovarian disease can refer pain to the medial thigh.

manas.q: Why can ovarian disease cause medial thigh pain?

children.note: The rectouterine pouch is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when upright, so blood, pus or fluid collects there; it lies behind the posterior fornix.

manas.q: Where does free fluid collect in the female pelvis when upright?

children.note: What holds the organs up.
A double peritoneal fold from uterus to side wall containing the tube, round and ovarian ligaments, uterine vessels, and the ureter near its base.

manas.q: What does the broad ligament contain?

children.note: Runs through the inguinal canal to the labium majus, a remnant of the gubernaculum; helps keep anteversion but is not a main support.

manas.q: Where does the round ligament of the uterus end?

children.note: Level I: cardinal–uterosacral (apex). Level II: lateral vaginal attachment to the pelvic side wall. Level III: fusion with perineal body and membrane.

manas.q: What are DeLancey's three levels of vaginal support?

children.note: Muscles that close the pelvic outlet.
Levator ani (pubococcygeus, puborectalis, iliococcygeus) plus coccygeus, forming the muscular floor.

manas.q: Which muscles form the pelvic diaphragm?

children.note: The gap in levator ani through which urethra and vagina pass; a widened hiatus or levator avulsion predisposes to prolapse.

manas.q: What is the urogenital hiatus?

children.note: Fibromuscular centre between vagina and anus where perineal muscles, external anal sphincter and levator fibres meet; key to perineal strength.

manas.q: Which structures meet at the perineal body?

children.note: 1st: skin/vaginal lining. 2nd: perineal muscles. 3rd: anal sphincter (3a <50% of EAS, 3b >50% of EAS, 3c internal sphincter torn too). 4th: also anal lining.

manas.q: Classify perineal tears by degree.

children.note: Pea-sized glands beside the vaginal opening, roughly at 4 and 8 o'clock; a blocked duct gives a cyst or abscess.

manas.q: Where are the Bartholin glands?

children.note: Extending the uterine and ovarian arteries.
Gives uterine, vaginal, obturator, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal, middle rectal and umbilical (superior vesical) arteries.

manas.q: Name branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.

children.note: The uterine artery climbs the side of the uterus in the broad ligament and joins the ovarian artery near the tube.

manas.q: Where do the uterine and ovarian arteries anastomose?

children.note: Trophoblast remodels them into wide, low-resistance vessels in pregnancy; poor remodelling is linked to pre-eclampsia.

manas.q: What happens to spiral arteries in normal pregnancy?

children.note: Used for severe pelvic haemorrhage; it lowers pulse pressure while rich collaterals keep pelvic organs alive.

manas.q: Why do pelvic organs survive internal iliac artery ligation?

children.note: Key for cancer spread.
To parametrial, obturator and internal and external iliac nodes, then common iliac and para-aortic nodes.

manas.q: Describe lymphatic drainage of the cervix.

children.note: To superficial inguinal nodes.

manas.q: Which nodes drain the vulva?

children.note: Mainly with the ovarian vessels to para-aortic nodes; some along the round ligament to superficial inguinal nodes.

manas.q: How can fundal cancer reach the inguinal nodes?

children.note: Autonomic and somatic.
Sympathetic fibres from about T10–L1 via the hypogastric plexuses; parasympathetic from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4).

manas.q: Where does parasympathetic supply to the pelvic organs come from?

children.note: First-stage uterine pain travels with sympathetic fibres to T10–L1; second-stage perineal pain travels in the pudendal nerve (S2–S4).

manas.q: Which spinal segments carry first- and second-stage labour pain?

children.note: Mainly direct branches of the sacral nerves (S3–S4), with a contribution from the pudendal nerve.

manas.q: What nerves supply levator ani?

children.note: L2–L4 on the side wall; can be injured during pelvic node dissection, weakening thigh adduction.

manas.q: What weakness follows obturator nerve injury in pelvic surgery?

children.note: Where anatomy meets practice.
Crosses into the pelvis near the ovarian vessels, so it is at risk when the infundibulopelvic ligament is clamped.

manas.q: Why is the ureter at risk when clamping the infundibulopelvic ligament?

children.note: Failure of ligament and levator support lets bladder (cystocele), rectum (rectocele), uterus or vault descend.

manas.q: What causes pelvic organ prolapse?

children.note: A needle through the posterior fornix samples fluid in the pouch of Douglas — largely replaced by ultrasound.

manas.q: Through which fornix is culdocentesis done?

children.note: Angled away from the midline to reduce extension into the anal sphincter, compared with a midline cut.

manas.q: Why is mediolateral episiotomy preferred over midline?

children.note: The ovary twists on its ligaments, blocking venous then arterial flow; sudden pain needs urgent surgery to save it.

manas.q: What is the vascular sequence in ovarian torsion?

children.note: Applying the anatomy at the bedside.
Assesses uterine size, position and mobility, adnexal masses and cervical motion tenderness.

manas.q: What does a bimanual examination assess?

children.note: Cusco bivalve to see the cervix; Sims speculum to inspect vaginal walls for prolapse and fistula.

manas.q: Which speculum is used to assess prolapse?

children.note: Feel the sacral promontory, sacral curve, ischial spines and subpubic arch to judge pelvic capacity.

manas.q: What is assessed in clinical pelvimetry?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
The National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care guide intrapartum care, including perineal care, in Kenyan facilities.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers intrapartum and perineal care?

children.note: WHO recommends against routine or liberal episiotomy in spontaneous vaginal birth.

manas.q: What is WHO's position on routine episiotomy?

children.note: RCOG uses the Sultan classification, splitting third-degree tears into 3a, 3b and 3c.

manas.q: Which classification of perineal tears does RCOG use?

children.note: The International Continence Society's POP-Q system measures prolapse at set vaginal points relative to the hymen.

manas.q: What is the reference point in the POP-Q system?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-09.
A meta-analysis (27 studies, mostly Western) associated vaginal birth, parity, age, BMI and levator defects with prolapse; higher stage and younger age with recurrence after repair.

manas.q: Which anatomical defect was a strong risk factor for prolapse in the 2022 meta-analysis?

children.note: An expert review says levator tears come from overstretching at birth and are linked to forceps, long second stage and big babies; it urges antenatal counselling.

manas.q: What mechanism causes levator ani injury during vaginal birth?

children.note: In operative vaginal births, mediolateral/lateral episiotomy was associated with fewer anal sphincter injuries, mainly in first-time mothers; evidence was very low quality.

manas.q: Was mediolateral episiotomy linked with fewer sphincter injuries in operative births?

children.note: Reported prolapse prevalence varies widely with the method used, and data from low- and middle-income countries are scarce.

manas.q: Why is prolapse prevalence hard to compare across studies?

maps.title: HPD 300 · In depth: Paediatric history and examination

nodeData.topic: Paediatric history and examination in depth
nodeData.note: A child's history section by section, examination by system, and growth, development, feeding and vaccines. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: How a paediatric consultation differs.
Normal values, common illnesses and how a child shows illness all change with age, so judge every finding against the child's age.

manas.q: Why must paediatric findings be interpreted by age?

children.note: Greet child and caregiver, sit at the child's level, let a young child stay on the caregiver's lap and explain what you will do.

manas.q: How do you build rapport with a young child before examining?

children.note: The caregiver gives consent; also seek the child's agreement (assent) in words suited to their age and understanding.

manas.q: What is the difference between consent and assent in paediatrics?

children.note: Offer time alone, explain confidentiality and its limits (risk of harm), and screen psychosocially, e.g. with HEADSS.

manas.q: What should you offer an adolescent during the history?

children.note: Home, Education/employment, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression: a structured adolescent psychosocial history.

manas.q: What does HEADSS stand for?

children.note: Section by section, beyond the adult template.
Record the caregiver's own words, duration and sequence; ask about feeding, activity and urine output as clues to severity.

manas.q: Which questions help judge severity in a child's presenting illness?

children.note: Maternal illness, antenatal clinic attendance, HIV and syphilis results, medicines taken and any pregnancy complications.

manas.q: What should the antenatal part of a paediatric history cover?

children.note: Place and mode of delivery, gestation at birth, birth weight, whether the baby cried at once or needed resuscitation.

manas.q: What are the key points of a birth history?

children.note: Newborn unit admission, jaundice, breathing or feeding problems, infections and oxygen or phototherapy given.

manas.q: What neonatal events should be asked about?

children.note: Breastfeeding (exclusive? how long?), age complementary foods began, what and how often the child eats now, e.g. a 24-hour recall.

manas.q: What does a feeding history include?

children.note: Check the card or booklet against the national schedule and note missed or delayed doses, rather than relying on memory.

manas.q: How should immunisation status be confirmed?

children.note: Ask when milestones were reached in each domain and whether any skill has been lost; loss of skills is a red flag.

manas.q: Which developmental history finding is always a red flag?

children.note: Previous admissions, operations, blood transfusions and chronic illnesses such as sickle cell disease, asthma or epilepsy.

manas.q: What belongs in a child's past medical history?

children.note: Current and recent medicines, including herbal or over-the-counter remedies, and any drug or food allergy with the reaction.

manas.q: Why ask about herbal and over-the-counter medicines in children?

children.note: Health of parents and siblings, deaths in childhood, consanguinity, inherited disease (e.g. sickle cell), TB contacts, parental HIV status.

manas.q: Which family history points matter most in paediatrics?

children.note: Who cares for the child, caregivers' work, housing, water and sanitation, school or daycare, and financial or social stresses.

manas.q: What does a paediatric social history cover?

children.note: Brief screen of other systems so that problems the caregiver did not mention are not missed.

manas.q: Why do a systems review in a child's history?

children.note: Look before you touch.
Is the child alert, interacting and playing, or drowsy, floppy and uninterested? This first look often says how sick the child is.

manas.q: What does the end-of-bed look assess in a child?

children.note: Heart and breathing rates are highest in infants and fall with age; compare with an age chart rather than adult values.

manas.q: How do heart and respiratory rates change with age?

children.note: Lethargy, sunken eyes, slow skin pinch and drinking poorly or not at all point to dehydration; combine signs, do not rely on one.

manas.q: Which signs suggest dehydration in a child?

children.note: Look at palms, nail beds and conjunctivae; palmar pallor is the sign used in IMCI to flag anaemia.

manas.q: Which pallor sign does IMCI use to flag anaemia?

children.note: Bilateral pitting oedema of the feet in a child suggests severe acute malnutrition (kwashiorkor) until proven otherwise.

manas.q: What does bilateral pitting pedal oedema suggest in a child?

children.note: Note unusual face shape, eyes, ears, hands (e.g. single palmar crease) or limbs that may point to a syndrome.

manas.q: Why look for dysmorphic features?

children.note: By system, adapted to the child.
Lower chest wall indrawing, nasal flaring, grunting and head nodding show increased work of breathing.

manas.q: Name signs of increased work of breathing in a child.

children.note: Feel femoral pulses in infants; weak or absent femorals suggest coarctation of the aorta.

manas.q: Why feel femoral pulses in an infant?

children.note: Infants show heart failure as fast breathing, sweating or tiring at feeds, poor weight gain and an enlarged liver.

manas.q: How does heart failure present in an infant?

children.note: A soft liver edge can be felt in many healthy infants; palpate for the spleen starting from the right iliac fossa.

manas.q: Where should palpation for the spleen begin?

children.note: Check that testes are descended and look for hernias and hydroceles, with a chaperone and permission.

manas.q: What should be checked in the groins and genitalia?

children.note: Bulging anterior fontanelle in a calm, upright infant suggests raised pressure; sunken suggests dehydration. It usually closes by about 18 months.

manas.q: What does a bulging anterior fontanelle suggest?

children.note: Neck stiffness is unreliable under about 1 year; look for irritability, bulging fontanelle, poor feeding or convulsions.

manas.q: Why is neck stiffness unreliable in infants?

children.note: Watch spontaneous movement and posture, then tone, power, reflexes and gait suited to age.

manas.q: How is the neurological exam adapted for young children?

children.note: Done last because they upset the child; hold the child securely on the caregiver's lap.

manas.q: How should a young child be held for ear and throat examination?

children.note: Measure, plot and interpret.
Weight, length lying down under 2 years (height standing after), and head circumference in infants and young children.

manas.q: How is length measured in a child under 2 years?

children.note: Plot on WHO growth charts and follow the trend over time; one point says less than a line crossing centiles.

manas.q: Why is a growth trend more useful than one measurement?

children.note: Length or height-for-age below −2 SD (z-score): a sign of chronic undernutrition.

manas.q: How is stunting defined?

children.note: Weight-for-length/height below −2 SD; below −3 SD is severe wasting. Reflects recent or acute undernutrition.

manas.q: How is wasting defined?

children.note: Weight-for-age below −2 SD; mixes stunting and wasting, so it cannot tell them apart.

manas.q: Why does weight-for-age not separate stunting from wasting?

children.note: For children 6–59 months, MUAC below 11.5 cm means severe acute malnutrition; 11.5 to below 12.5 cm means moderate.

manas.q: What MUAC means severe acute malnutrition in a child aged 6–59 months?

children.note: Plot serially; a small or fast-growing head needs review (e.g. microcephaly, hydrocephalus).

manas.q: Why is head circumference plotted serially?

children.note: Four domains, key ages, red flags.
Gross motor; fine motor and vision; speech, language and hearing; social, emotional and behaviour.

manas.q: What are the four developmental domains?

children.note: Social smile about 6 weeks; sits unsupported about 6–8 months; walks alone about 12 months; joins two words about 2 years.

manas.q: At about what age does a baby walk alone?

children.note: Loss of skills, not walking by 18 months, no words by 18 months, and hand preference before 1 year all need assessment.

manas.q: Name developmental red flags.

children.note: For babies born preterm, subtract weeks born early from the age when judging milestones, usually until 2 years.

manas.q: How is development judged in a baby born preterm?

children.note: Use the child's booklet.
Kenya's booklet records pregnancy, birth, growth charts, vaccines and milestones; ask the caregiver for it at every visit.

manas.q: What does Kenya's Mother and Child Health Handbook record?

children.note: Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, then safe complementary foods while breastfeeding continues to 2 years or beyond.

manas.q: For how long is exclusive breastfeeding recommended?

children.note: Kenya Expanded Programme on Immunization: national free vaccine schedule, recorded in the child's booklet.

manas.q: What is KEPI?

children.note: BCG and a polio dose at birth; then doses at 6, 10 and 14 weeks; measles-rubella at 9 and 18 months.

manas.q: At what ages are measles-rubella vaccines given under KEPI?

children.note: Given every 6 months from 6 to 59 months; check the booklet for doses missed.

manas.q: How often is vitamin A given to children 6–59 months?

children.note: Spot the sick child first.
Unable to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargic or unconscious: any one needs urgent care.

manas.q: What are the IMCI general danger signs?

children.note: Before a full history, triage: emergency signs in airway/breathing, circulation, coma or convulsion, or severe dehydration get treated at once.

manas.q: What does ETAT+ check before a full history is taken?

children.note: Points examiners like.
Age, sex, main problem and duration, key findings, plus growth, development and vaccine status in one or two lines.

manas.q: What should a paediatric case summary include?

children.note: Weigh and plot every sick child; a missed fall in weight or centile is a common exam and ward error.

manas.q: Why plot every sick child's weight?

children.note: Much of the respiratory exam is done by watching a calm, exposed child before any hands-on step.

manas.q: Why observe a child before touching them?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
Kenya's Basic Paediatric Protocols (use the current edition) and the IMNCI chart booklet guide assessment, triage and treatment of children.

manas.q: Which Kenyan protocols guide paediatric assessment?

children.note: The WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children and IMCI set the assessment and danger-sign approach used in many countries.

manas.q: Which WHO book guides hospital care for children?

children.note: WHO Child Growth Standards (2006) describe how breastfed children grow in good conditions and are used widely.

manas.q: In which year were the WHO Child Growth Standards published?

children.note: The UK uses UK-WHO charts for young children; the US CDC advises WHO charts under 2 years and CDC charts from 2 years.

manas.q: Which growth charts does the US CDC advise under 2 years?

children.note: The American Academy of Pediatrics advises a formal developmental screening tool at the 9, 18 and 30 month visits.

manas.q: At which visits does the AAP advise formal developmental screening?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-09.
A meta-analysis of mostly before-after studies linked paediatric early warning systems with lower mortality (not significant without the one RCT) and fewer unplanned codes; arrests did not change.

manas.q: What were paediatric early warning systems associated with in a 2022 meta-analysis?

children.note: A Cochrane review of 6 LMIC studies found only very low to low certainty evidence that growth monitoring and promotion improves growth, feeding or service use.

manas.q: How certain is the evidence that growth monitoring and promotion helps under-fives?

children.note: The UNICEF/WHO package coaching caregivers to play, talk and respond to children was used in 54 LMICs; training, supervision and fidelity varied.

manas.q: What does the UNICEF/WHO Care for Child Development package teach caregivers?

children.topic: 📋 WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care

maps.title: HSU 305 · In depth: Introduction to anaesthesia

nodeData.note: Core ideas, history, drug classes, preop assessment, fasting, monitoring, regional versus general, and safety. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What the words mean.
A reversible, drug-induced loss of sensation; general anaesthesia adds reversible loss of consciousness.

manas.q: What is general anaesthesia?

children.note: Combining drugs that each give one part of the triad, so each is used at a lower dose with fewer side effects.

manas.q: What is balanced anaesthesia?

children.note: Minimal, moderate and deep sedation shade into general anaesthesia; airway and breathing support needs rise along the scale.

manas.q: What are the levels of the sedation continuum?

children.note: Induction, maintenance and emergence, followed by recovery in the post-anaesthesia care unit.

manas.q: What are the phases of a general anaesthetic?

children.note: Beyond Morton's 1846 ether demonstration.
Horace Wells, a dentist, used nitrous oxide for tooth extraction in 1844; his public demonstration in 1845 was judged a failure.

manas.q: Which dentist pioneered nitrous oxide for dental extraction?

children.note: James Young Simpson introduced chloroform in Edinburgh in 1847; John Snow gave it to Queen Victoria in childbirth in 1853.

manas.q: Who introduced chloroform anaesthesia in 1847?

children.note: Carl Koller used cocaine as a topical anaesthetic for eye surgery in 1884.

manas.q: Who first used cocaine for eye surgery?

children.note: August Bier performed spinal anaesthesia with cocaine in 1898.

manas.q: Who performed the first spinal anaesthetic?

children.note: Griffith and Johnson introduced curare into anaesthesia in 1942, allowing lighter anaesthesia with good relaxation.

manas.q: When was curare introduced into anaesthesia?

children.note: Main groups; no doses here.
Propofol, thiopental, ketamine and etomidate produce rapid loss of consciousness; propofol and thiopental lower blood pressure, etomidate is cardiostable and ketamine tends to raise it.

manas.q: Name four intravenous induction agents.

children.note: Sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane and nitrous oxide; volatiles are usually used to maintain anaesthesia.

manas.q: Name common inhalational anaesthetic agents.

children.note: Minimum alveolar concentration: the alveolar concentration that stops movement to a surgical incision in 50% of patients; a measure of potency.

manas.q: What is minimum alveolar concentration (MAC)?

children.note: It is not irritant to the airway and acts quickly, so it is the usual choice for inhalational induction, e.g. in children.

manas.q: Why is sevoflurane used for inhalational induction?

children.note: Fentanyl, morphine and similar drugs give analgesia and blunt responses to surgery; they can depress breathing and cause nausea.

manas.q: What is the main dangerous side effect of opioids in anaesthesia?

children.note: Depolarising (suxamethonium) or non-depolarising (rocuronium, atracurium, vecuronium); they paralyse but give no sleep or analgesia.

manas.q: What are the two classes of neuromuscular blockers?

children.note: Neostigmine (given with an anticholinergic) reverses non-depolarising block; sugammadex encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium.

manas.q: How does sugammadex reverse rocuronium?

children.note: Block voltage-gated sodium channels in nerves; amides (lidocaine, bupivacaine) and esters (e.g. procaine).

manas.q: How do local anaesthetics block nerve conduction?

children.note: Find and fix risk before theatre.
Previous anaesthetics and problems, family history of anaesthetic reactions, exercise tolerance, smoking, drugs and allergies.

manas.q: What should the anaesthetic history ask about?

children.note: Ask about malignant hyperthermia or prolonged paralysis after suxamethonium in relatives; both are inherited.

manas.q: Which inherited anaesthetic problems should be asked about in the family history?

children.note: Mouth opening, Mallampati class, teeth, thyromental distance, jaw movement and neck extension predict difficult airway.

manas.q: Which bedside findings predict a difficult airway?

children.note: Order tests because of the patient's illness and the surgery planned, not routinely for everyone.

manas.q: Should preoperative tests be routine for all patients?

children.note: Most regular medicines continue; anticoagulants, antiplatelets and diabetes drugs need a specific plan.

manas.q: Which drug groups need a specific preoperative plan?

children.note: Explain the anaesthetic plan, common side effects and serious risks, and alternatives, so the patient can decide.

manas.q: What should anaesthetic consent cover?

children.note: A grade of fitness, not of surgical risk alone.
I: a normal healthy patient. II: mild systemic disease without limitation.

manas.q: What do ASA I and ASA II mean?

children.note: III: severe systemic disease. IV: severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life.

manas.q: What do ASA III and ASA IV mean?

children.note: V: moribund, not expected to survive without the operation. VI: brain-dead organ donor.

manas.q: What do ASA V and ASA VI mean?

children.note: E is added for an emergency operation, e.g. ASA III E.

manas.q: What does the suffix E mean in ASA grading?

children.note: Reducing aspiration risk.
An empty stomach lowers the risk of regurgitation and aspiration once airway reflexes are lost.

manas.q: Why are patients fasted before anaesthesia?

children.note: Clear fluids up to 2 h, breast milk up to 4 h, and solids or formula up to 6 h before elective anaesthesia.

manas.q: What is the traditional 2-4-6 fasting rule?

children.note: Long fasts cause thirst, hunger, dehydration and, in children, distress and low blood sugar risk; aim for the shortest safe fast.

manas.q: What harms follow over-long preoperative fasting?

children.note: Emergencies, bowel obstruction, pregnancy and trauma may keep a full stomach despite fasting; plan an RSI.

manas.q: Which patients may have a full stomach despite fasting?

children.note: What every anaesthetic needs.
Pulse oximetry, non-invasive blood pressure, ECG and capnography, plus inspired oxygen and agent levels, and temperature where needed.

manas.q: What are the core monitors during general anaesthesia?

children.note: Waveform CO2 confirms the tube is in the trachea and shows ventilation, circulation and disconnection.

manas.q: What does waveform capnography confirm after intubation?

children.note: A trained anaesthetist must be present throughout; machines support, not replace, clinical watching.

manas.q: Who must be present throughout every anaesthetic?

children.note: Face mask, supraglottic airway (e.g. laryngeal mask) or tracheal tube, chosen by surgery, aspiration risk and access.

manas.q: What airway devices are used in general anaesthesia?

children.note: Choosing the technique.
Local anaesthetic into CSF in the subarachnoid space below the end of the cord: dense, fast block for lower body surgery.

manas.q: Where is local anaesthetic injected in a spinal anaesthetic?

children.note: Local anaesthetic into the epidural space, usually through a catheter: slower onset, can be topped up, used in labour.

manas.q: How does an epidural differ from a spinal?

children.note: Local anaesthetic around a nerve or plexus, often ultrasound-guided, for a limb or area.

manas.q: What is a peripheral nerve block?

children.note: Patient stays awake with own airway, good pain relief after surgery, less nausea; useful for caesarean section.

manas.q: What are the advantages of regional anaesthesia?

children.note: Sympathetic block dilates vessels and lowers blood pressure; treated with fluids and vasopressors.

manas.q: Why does a spinal anaesthetic lower blood pressure?

children.note: Headache worse when upright after the dura is punctured; finer, pencil-point needles reduce it.

manas.q: What is typical of a post-dural puncture headache?

children.note: Patient refusal, coagulopathy, infection at the site, uncorrected hypovolaemia and raised intracranial pressure.

manas.q: Name contraindications to spinal anaesthesia.

children.note: What can go wrong.
Nausea and vomiting, sore throat, shivering, drowsiness and minor dental or lip injury.

manas.q: Name common minor complications of general anaesthesia.

children.note: Sudden hypotension, bronchospasm or rash after a drug, often a relaxant or antibiotic; adrenaline is the key treatment.

manas.q: What is the key treatment for anaphylaxis under anaesthesia?

children.note: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity: perioral tingling, tinnitus, seizures, arrhythmias; stop injecting, support ABC, give lipid emulsion.

manas.q: What is the specific treatment for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity?

children.note: Anaesthesia impairs heat control; warm fluids and the patient and monitor temperature in long cases.

manas.q: Why do patients get cold under anaesthesia?

children.note: A 2010 European declaration on patient safety in anaesthesiology, endorsing the WHO checklist and safety protocols.

manas.q: What is the Helsinki Declaration in anaesthesia?

children.note: Quick points examiners like.
A paralysed patient may be awake; never give a relaxant without anaesthesia.

manas.q: Why must a muscle relaxant never be given without anaesthesia?

children.note: ASA grades the patient's illness; it ignores the operation, so it is only part of risk assessment.

manas.q: What does ASA physical status not account for?

children.note: A lower MAC means a more potent agent; MAC falls with age, pregnancy and opioids.

manas.q: What does a low MAC value mean?

children.note: How guidance compares; Kenya first.
Kenyan theatres follow MoH and hospital anaesthesia protocols and use the WHO surgical safety checklist.

manas.q: Which checklist is used in Kenyan theatres?

children.note: WHO and the World Federation of Societies of Anaesthesiologists issued international standards for safe anaesthesia practice in 2018.

manas.q: Which two bodies issued the 2018 international standards for safe anaesthesia?

children.note: The American Society of Anesthesiologists publishes the physical status classification and fasting guidance used worldwide.

manas.q: Which body publishes the ASA physical status classification?

children.note: A 2018 consensus of European paediatric anaesthesia societies allows clear fluids up to 1 hour before elective anaesthesia.

manas.q: How long before anaesthesia may children drink clear fluids in the 2018 European consensus?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-09.
ESAIC's 2025 update (55 recommendations) urges tailored assessment and choosing tests per patient using risk scores, not routine testing.

manas.q: What does the ESAIC 2025 guideline advise about preoperative tests?

children.note: A narrative review notes clear-fluid fasts were cut to 2 h, yet patients often still fast far longer for organisational reasons; trials are needed.

manas.q: Why do patients still fast too long, per a 2024 review?

children.note: A review of 300 studies found the safety checklist helped team outcomes more clearly than patient outcomes; how it is done matters.

manas.q: Which outcomes did the surgical safety checklist improve most clearly?

children.note: A review found prolonged fasting in children common and harmful; several paediatric societies have shortened clear-fluid times, others have not.

manas.q: What did a 2023 review say about prolonged fasting in children?

maps.title: HCP 200 · In depth: Drug development and nomenclature

nodeData.topic: Drug development and nomenclature in depth
nodeData.note: From a new molecule to a licensed, named medicine: discovery, trials, regulation and how drugs get their names. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: The big picture of how a medicine reaches patients.
Drug development is the staged process of discovering a compound, testing it in the lab and in people, licensing it and monitoring it after launch.

manas.q: What are the main stages of drug development?

children.note: Discovery → preclinical testing → clinical trial phases I–III → regulatory approval → phase IV post-marketing surveillance.

manas.q: Put the stages of drug development in order.

children.note: Most candidate compounds fail during development, mainly because of poor efficacy or unacceptable toxicity; the process is long and costly.

manas.q: Why do most candidate drugs never reach the market?

children.note: Where new drugs come from.
A molecular target linked to disease (receptor, enzyme, ion channel, transporter) is chosen, and compounds are screened against it.

manas.q: What is the first step in rational drug discovery?

children.note: A promising 'lead' compound is chemically modified to improve potency, selectivity and drug-like properties before testing.

manas.q: What is a lead compound?

children.note: Many drugs began as plant products, e.g. morphine from the opium poppy, digoxin from foxglove, quinine from cinchona bark.
