manas.q: Why does the knee flex in the opposite direction to the elbow?

children.note: At the ankle, dorsiflexion and plantarflexion replace flexion and extension because those words are ambiguous there.

manas.q: Why are dorsiflexion and plantarflexion used at the ankle?

children.note: Raising the arm above the head needs rotation of the scapula on the chest wall as well as movement at the shoulder joint itself.

manas.q: Which bone must rotate for full elevation of the arm?

children.note: Where the official words come from.
The international standard list of anatomical terms, in Latin with English equivalents; first published in 1998.

manas.q: What is Terminologia Anatomica?

children.note: Eponyms honour people but say nothing about the structure; e.g. Achilles tendon = calcaneal tendon, Eustachian tube = pharyngotympanic tube.

manas.q: What is the descriptive name for the Achilles tendon?

children.note: Many names describe shape or place: deltoid (triangular), brachium (arm), pollex (thumb), hallux (great toe).

manas.q: What do pollex and hallux mean?

children.note: Supra- means above, infra- below, inter- between, sub- beneath, peri- around.

manas.q: What do the prefixes supra-, infra- and inter- mean?

children.note: Turning terms into clear notes and safe practice.
State the body region, surface and side, the distance from a fixed landmark, then size and depth, so any reader can find it.

manas.q: What details locate a wound precisely in clinical notes?

children.note: Palpable bony points mark deeper structures; the sternal angle lies at the level of the 2nd costal cartilage.

manas.q: Which costal cartilage lies at the level of the sternal angle?

children.note: The common ankle sprain happens in inversion and stretches the lateral ligaments, most often the anterior talofibular ligament.

manas.q: Which ligament is most often injured in an inversion sprain?

children.note: Joint movement is recorded in degrees, starting from the anatomical position taken as zero (neutral-zero method).

manas.q: What is the starting point for measuring joint range?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-20.
Anatomists from FIPAT's gross anatomy group argue TA2 offers several names for one structure, unlike TA1, losing the goal of one agreed international standard.

manas.q: What criticism of TA2 did anatomists raise in 2024?

children.note: AnatomicalTerms.info is a free site linking each Terminologia Anatomica term to synonyms, eponyms and other-language terms, with short open definitions to ease learning.

manas.q: What does the AnatomicalTerms.info site offer students?

children.note: Quick wins.
Supination turns the palm up as if holding a bowl of soup; pronation turns it down.

manas.q: What memory aid helps recall supination?

children.note: Inversion = sole faces in (medially); eversion = sole faces out.

manas.q: Which way does the sole face in inversion?

children.note: Fingers abduct from the middle finger; toes from the second toe.

manas.q: What is the reference line for abduction of the toes?

children.note: In anatomical position the ulna is medial and the radius lateral (thumb side).

manas.q: Which forearm bone is lateral in the anatomical position?

children.note: Remember the rows: hypochondriac–epigastric, lumbar–umbilical, inguinal–hypogastric.

manas.q: List the nine abdominal regions row by row.

maps.title: HMP 100 · In depth: Homeostasis and body fluids

nodeData.topic: Homeostasis and body fluids in depth
nodeData.note: Feedback control, fluid compartments, osmolality, water shifts and basic regulation. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Keeping the internal environment steady.
Homeostasis is keeping the internal environment (the ECF bathing cells) relatively constant despite outside change; Walter Cannon coined the term.

manas.q: What is homeostasis and who coined the term?

children.note: A sensor detects the variable, a control centre compares it with the set point, and an effector corrects it, linked by afferent and efferent paths.

manas.q: Name the three parts of a homeostatic control system.

children.note: The set point is the value the system defends; the variable swings within a narrow range around it. Set points can reset, e.g. raised in fever.

manas.q: What happens to the temperature set point in fever?

children.note: How control systems respond to change.
A rise in blood pressure stretches baroreceptors, the brainstem cuts sympathetic and boosts vagal output, and heart rate and vessel tone fall.

manas.q: Outline the baroreceptor reflex response to a rise in BP.

children.note: Gain = correction achieved ÷ error that remains; the higher the gain, the more completely the disturbance is corrected.

manas.q: How is the gain of a control system calculated?

children.note: Positive feedback amplifies a change until an outside event stops it, e.g. delivery of the baby ends the oxytocin loop of labour.

manas.q: What ends the positive feedback loop of labour?

children.note: Positive feedback can be deadly: in severe haemorrhage, low pressure starves the heart muscle, the heart weakens and pressure falls further.

manas.q: Give an example of harmful positive feedback.

children.note: An anticipatory response before the variable changes, e.g. saliva and gastric acid secreted at the sight or smell of food.

manas.q: What is feedforward control? Give an example.

children.note: Where body water sits and what divides it.
Fat holds little water, so the fraction of body weight that is water falls with obesity; it is also lower in women and older adults.

manas.q: Why is total body water lower in obese people?

children.note: A small specialised part of ECF in epithelial-lined spaces: CSF, synovial, pleural, peritoneal and intraocular fluid, and gut secretions.

manas.q: Give examples of transcellular fluid.

children.note: About 7% of body weight, roughly 5 L in a 70 kg adult; plasma makes up a little over half of it.

manas.q: What is the normal blood volume of a 70 kg adult?

children.note: The capillary wall separates plasma from interstitial fluid; the cell membrane separates ECF from ICF.

manas.q: What barrier separates plasma from interstitial fluid?

children.note: The indicator-dilution method.
Volume = amount of indicator given (minus any excreted or metabolised) ÷ its concentration once evenly mixed.

manas.q: State the indicator-dilution formula for volume.

children.note: Spreads evenly only within the compartment measured, is not toxic or metabolised, and is easy to measure.

manas.q: List properties of an ideal indicator for volume.

children.note: ICF and interstitial fluid cannot be measured directly: ICF = TBW − ECF; interstitial = ECF − plasma volume.

manas.q: How are ICF and interstitial volumes obtained?

children.note: Blood volume = plasma volume ÷ (1 − haematocrit).

manas.q: How is blood volume calculated from plasma volume?

children.note: Different solutes inside and outside cells.
Chloride and bicarbonate are the main extracellular anions.

manas.q: What are the main anions of ECF?

children.note: Phosphates and proteins are the main intracellular anions; magnesium is an important intracellular cation after potassium.

manas.q: What are the main intracellular anions?

children.note: Ion levels are similar, but plasma has much more protein because capillary walls let little protein through.

manas.q: How does plasma differ from interstitial fluid?

children.note: Free calcium is far lower in the cytosol than in ECF, so calcium entry can act as a signal.

manas.q: Is free calcium higher inside or outside cells?

children.note: In every compartment total positive charges equal total negative charges.

manas.q: What is the principle of electroneutrality?

children.note: How solutes pull water.
Osmolality = osmoles per kg of water; osmolarity = per litre of solution. In dilute body fluids the two are almost the same.

manas.q: What is the difference between osmolality and osmolarity?

children.note: Measured minus calculated osmolality; a raised gap points to unmeasured osmoles such as ethanol, methanol or ethylene glycol.

manas.q: What does a raised osmolal gap suggest?

children.note: Only solutes that cannot cross the membrane move water. Urea crosses cells freely, so it adds to osmolality but not tonicity.

manas.q: Why does urea not contribute to tonicity?

children.note: A solution's effect on cell volume: in isotonic fluid cells keep their size, in hypotonic they swell, in hypertonic they shrink.

manas.q: What happens to red cells in a hypotonic solution?

children.note: 0.9% sodium chloride is about isotonic with plasma, so red cells keep their volume in it.

manas.q: Why is 0.9% sodium chloride called isotonic saline?

children.note: Predicting which compartment changes.
Water crosses cell membranes freely until ICF and ECF osmolality match; sodium stays mainly in the ECF.

manas.q: What determines water movement between ICF and ECF?

children.note: Adding or losing isotonic fluid changes ECF volume only; osmolality is unchanged so no water enters or leaves cells.

manas.q: What happens to ICF volume after isotonic fluid loss?

children.note: Extra water lowers ECF osmolality, water moves into cells, and both compartments expand; cells swell.

manas.q: What happens to cells after a large pure water load?

children.note: Raised ECF osmolality draws water out of cells: ECF expands and ICF shrinks.

manas.q: How does hypertonic saline change ICF and ECF volumes?

children.note: Fluid exchange across capillaries.
Capillary hydrostatic pressure and interstitial oncotic pressure push fluid out; plasma oncotic and interstitial hydrostatic pressure oppose it.

manas.q: Which Starling forces favour filtration out of capillaries?

children.note: Mostly due to albumin; a fall in plasma albumin lets more fluid stay in the tissues.

manas.q: Which plasma protein provides most oncotic pressure?

children.note: Lymph vessels return excess filtered fluid and leaked protein to the blood.

manas.q: What is the role of lymphatics in fluid balance?

children.note: Raised capillary pressure (heart failure), low albumin (nephrotic syndrome, liver disease, kwashiorkor), leaky capillaries (inflammation), blocked lymph (filariasis).

manas.q: List four mechanisms of oedema with examples.

children.note: Intake must match losses.
Drinks, water in food and a small amount of metabolic water from oxidation of nutrients.

manas.q: What are the sources of body water intake?

children.note: Urine (the largest route and the one adjusted to keep water balance), insensible loss from skin and lungs, sweat and faeces.

manas.q: Which route of water loss is adjusted to keep water balance?

children.note: Evaporation from skin and airways that we do not feel; it rises with fever, heat and fast breathing.

manas.q: What increases insensible water loss?

children.note: The basic hormonal controls.
Made in the hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary when osmolality rises or volume falls; adds aquaporin-2 channels in collecting ducts.

manas.q: How does ADH increase water reabsorption?

children.note: Driven by raised osmolality, low blood volume and angiotensin II acting on hypothalamic centres.

manas.q: What stimulates thirst?

children.note: Low renal perfusion releases renin; angiotensin II constricts vessels and triggers aldosterone, which makes the kidney retain sodium and water.

manas.q: Outline the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

children.note: ANP from atria and BNP from ventricles are released on stretch; they increase sodium and water excretion and oppose RAAS.

manas.q: What do natriuretic peptides do?

children.note: Total body sodium sets ECF volume; water balance sets the sodium concentration.

manas.q: Which controls ECF volume: sodium content or water?

children.note: Applying fluid physiology at the bedside.
Thirst, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, fast pulse and low urine output.

manas.q: List clinical signs of dehydration.

children.note: Serum sodium below 135 mmol/L, usually too much water for the sodium; brain cells swell, causing confusion or seizures.

manas.q: Why can hyponatraemia cause seizures?

children.note: Serum sodium above 145 mmol/L, usually a water deficit; cells, including brain cells, shrink.

manas.q: What happens to cells in hypernatraemia?

children.note: Isotonic crystalloid spreads through the ECF, so only about a quarter of it stays in the plasma.

manas.q: What fraction of infused isotonic saline stays in plasma?

children.note: The glucose is metabolised, leaving free water that spreads through all body water; little stays in plasma, so it is poor for resuscitation.

manas.q: Why is 5% dextrose poor for restoring blood volume?

children.note: Guidance on IV maintenance fluids in children.
A 2024 viewpoint found international guidelines agree that isotonic fluids are the standard for IV maintenance in ill children.

manas.q: What fluid type do guidelines agree on for paediatric maintenance?

children.note: ESPNIC (European paediatric intensive care) advises isotonic balanced fluid with glucose, restricted volumes in most children, and regular electrolyte and glucose checks.

manas.q: What did ESPNIC 2022 recommend for paediatric IV maintenance?

children.note: Per hour: 4 mL/kg for the first 10 kg, 2 mL/kg for the next 10 kg, 1 mL/kg for each kg above 20. Many guidelines now restrict volumes; follow local guidance.

manas.q: State the Holliday–Segar 4-2-1 rule for maintenance fluid.

links.title: Guidelines favour isotonic fluids
ESPNIC: balanced, glucose, restricted

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-20.
A systematic review gave 16 recommendations: isotonic balanced fluids providing glucose, restricted volumes for most children, and regular electrolyte, glucose and fluid checks.

manas.q: What were key ESPNIC 2022 maintenance fluid advice points?

children.note: A viewpoint says IV fluids need choice, rate, duration and de-escalation like drugs; most evidence is from rich countries, so fit for LMICs is uncertain.

manas.q: Why did a 2024 viewpoint urge caution applying fluid evidence to LMICs?

children.note: A review notes hospital AKI is common, with risks such as surgery, CKD and heart failure; IV fluid timing, type, amount and rate matter.

manas.q: Which patients are at higher risk of hospital-acquired AKI?

children.note: Quick wins.
TBW ≈ 60% of body weight, ICF ≈ 40%, ECF ≈ 20%.

manas.q: State the 60-40-20 rule.

children.note: 2[Na+] + glucose + urea, all in mmol/L; normal about 285–295 mOsm/kg.

manas.q: Give the formula for calculated plasma osmolality.

children.note: Labour (oxytocin), LH surge, clotting.

manas.q: Name three positive feedback loops.

children.note: ECF: inulin; plasma: Evans blue or labelled albumin; TBW: heavy water.

manas.q: Which marker measures plasma volume?

maps.title: HMP 200 · In depth: Glomerular filtration and clearance

nodeData.topic: Glomerular filtration and clearance in depth
nodeData.note: How the glomerulus filters plasma, how GFR is controlled, measured and estimated, and how it is used to stage CKD. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What GFR is and the sieve that makes the filtrate.
GFR is the volume of plasma filtered from all glomerular capillaries into Bowman's space per unit time, usually given in mL/min.

manas.q: What is the glomerular filtration rate?

children.note: Fenestrated capillary endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane, and podocyte foot processes joined by slit diaphragms.

manas.q: Name the three layers of the glomerular filtration barrier.

children.note: Small solutes pass freely; large molecules are held back. Negative charges in the barrier repel anionic proteins such as albumin.

manas.q: Why is albumin normally kept out of the filtrate?

children.note: Filtrate is almost protein-free plasma: water, ions, glucose, amino acids, urea and creatinine at roughly plasma concentrations.

manas.q: What is the composition of glomerular filtrate?

children.note: Pressures that push fluid out of, or pull it back into, glomerular capillaries.
The main force favouring filtration; about 60 mmHg in classic textbook figures, kept high because the efferent arteriole adds resistance downstream.

manas.q: What is the main force driving glomerular filtration?

children.note: Opposes filtration (about 18 mmHg in textbook figures); rises sharply if the urinary tract is obstructed.

manas.q: Which Starling force rises in urinary tract obstruction?

children.note: Plasma protein pull opposing filtration; it rises along the capillary as protein-free fluid leaves, so filtration falls toward the efferent end.

manas.q: Why does oncotic pressure rise along the glomerular capillary?

children.note: Close to zero, because the filtrate contains almost no protein.

manas.q: Why is oncotic pressure in Bowman's space near zero?

children.note: Net pressure = (PGC − PBS) − (πGC − πBS); with textbook figures this is roughly 10 mmHg.

manas.q: How is net filtration pressure across the glomerulus calculated?

children.note: GFR = Kf × net filtration pressure. Kf reflects permeability and surface area; it is very high in glomeruli and falls when glomeruli are lost or scarred.

manas.q: What two factors multiply to give GFR?

children.note: How afferent and efferent tone change GFR and plasma flow.
Lowers glomerular pressure and renal plasma flow, so GFR falls. Afferent dilation does the opposite.

manas.q: What does afferent arteriole constriction do to GFR?

children.note: Raises glomerular pressure so GFR rises modestly, while plasma flow falls; filtration fraction therefore rises.

manas.q: What happens to filtration fraction when the efferent arteriole constricts?

children.note: Low plasma protein lowers oncotic pressure and tends to raise GFR; high plasma protein tends to lower it.

manas.q: How does low plasma protein affect GFR?

children.note: Constricts efferent more than afferent arterioles at low levels, helping preserve GFR when renal perfusion falls.

manas.q: How does angiotensin II help preserve GFR in low perfusion?

children.note: Dilate the afferent arteriole, protecting GFR when perfusion is poor; NSAIDs block this.

manas.q: Which local mediators dilate the afferent arteriole?

children.note: Marked sympathetic activation (e.g. haemorrhage) constricts afferent arterioles and lowers renal blood flow and GFR.

manas.q: What does strong sympathetic activation do to GFR?

children.note: Keeps GFR and renal blood flow steady despite everyday blood pressure changes.
Raised pressure stretches the afferent arteriole wall; smooth muscle contracts in response, limiting the rise in glomerular pressure.

manas.q: How does the myogenic mechanism protect the glomerulus?

children.note: Macula densa cells sense NaCl reaching the end of the thick ascending limb; more NaCl triggers afferent constriction (adenosine is a key mediator), bringing GFR back down.

manas.q: What does the macula densa sense in tubuloglomerular feedback?

children.note: Macula densa, granular (juxtaglomerular) cells that release renin, and extraglomerular mesangial cells, sitting where the distal tubule meets its own glomerulus.

manas.q: What are the parts of the juxtaglomerular apparatus?

children.note: Below the autoregulatory range, GFR falls with blood pressure, so severe hypotension reduces urine output.

manas.q: Why does urine output fall in severe hypotension?

children.note: Turning urine and plasma measurements into kidney function numbers.
The volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute; it is a virtual volume, not a real one.

manas.q: What does renal clearance of a substance represent?

children.note: Urine creatinine 10 mmol/L, plasma 0.1 mmol/L, urine flow 1 mL/min: clearance = (10 × 1) ÷ 0.1 = 100 mL/min.

manas.q: Urine creatinine 10 mmol/L, plasma 0.1 mmol/L, flow 1 mL/min: what is the clearance?

children.note: Filtered load = GFR × plasma concentration of a freely filtered substance; compare it with excretion to see if the tubule reabsorbs or secretes.

manas.q: How do you calculate the filtered load of a substance?

children.note: Equal to GFR: filtered only (inulin). Less than GFR: net reabsorption (urea; glucose normally zero). More than GFR: net secretion (PAH).

manas.q: What does a clearance greater than GFR tell you?

children.note: FF = GFR ÷ renal plasma flow; normally about 20%, so most plasma leaves via the efferent arteriole unfiltered.

manas.q: How is filtration fraction calculated?

children.note: Renal blood flow = renal plasma flow ÷ (1 − haematocrit).

manas.q: How do you convert renal plasma flow to renal blood flow?

children.note: Proximal tubule glucose carriers saturate; above a plasma level of roughly 10 mmol/L glucose spills into urine (glycosuria).

manas.q: Why does glucose appear in urine when plasma glucose is high?

children.note: CH2O = urine flow − osmolar clearance. Positive when urine is dilute, negative when urine is concentrated.

manas.q: What does a positive free water clearance mean?

children.note: Substances used to measure or estimate GFR.
Freely filtered, not reabsorbed, secreted or metabolised by the tubule, not toxic, and easy to measure.

manas.q: List the properties of an ideal GFR marker.

children.note: Exogenous markers such as iohexol or radiolabelled agents (e.g. 51Cr-EDTA, 99mTc-DTPA) measure GFR when an estimate is not reliable enough.

manas.q: Name exogenous markers used to measure GFR.

children.note: Made from muscle creatine at a fairly steady rate; output depends on muscle mass, so sex, age, body build and diet affect serum levels.

manas.q: Why does serum creatinine depend on muscle mass?

children.note: The relation is inverse: halving GFR roughly doubles serum creatinine, so early GFR loss may leave creatinine within the normal range.

manas.q: Why can serum creatinine stay normal despite early loss of GFR?

children.note: Trimethoprim, cimetidine and dolutegravir reduce tubular creatinine secretion, raising serum creatinine slightly without a true fall in GFR.

manas.q: Which drugs raise serum creatinine without lowering true GFR?

children.note: A small protein made by all nucleated cells; less affected by muscle mass than creatinine, but influenced by thyroid status, steroids and inflammation.

manas.q: Why is cystatin C useful when muscle mass is unusual?

children.note: Poor GFR marker: partly reabsorbed and changed by protein intake, GI bleeding, catabolism and dehydration.

manas.q: Why is urea a poor marker of GFR?

children.note: Measures creatinine clearance from a timed urine collection; incomplete collections are a common source of error.

manas.q: What is the main pitfall of 24-hour urine creatinine clearance?

children.note: Formulas that estimate GFR from blood markers and patient factors.
Estimates creatinine clearance (mL/min) from age, weight, sex and serum creatinine; not indexed to body surface area.

manas.q: Which variables does the Cockcroft–Gault equation use?

children.note: Estimate GFR indexed to 1.73 m² body surface area; CKD-EPI is more accurate than MDRD at higher GFR values.

manas.q: What body surface area are MDRD and CKD-EPI results indexed to?

children.note: eGFR assumes stable creatinine; in acute kidney injury creatinine lags behind the real change, so eGFR misleads.

manas.q: Why is eGFR unreliable in acute kidney injury?

children.note: Less reliable at extremes of muscle mass or body size, after amputation, and in pregnancy.

manas.q: Name situations where creatinine-based eGFR is less reliable.

children.note: Staging chronic kidney disease by GFR and albuminuria.
Abnormal kidney structure or function lasting more than 3 months, with implications for health.

manas.q: How long must kidney abnormalities last to define CKD?
Give the GFR range for CKD stage G3b.

children.note: With GFR ≥60, CKD needs another marker of damage, such as albuminuria or structural change.

manas.q: What is needed to diagnose CKD when GFR is above 60?

children.note: By urine albumin:creatinine ratio: A1 <3, A2 3–30, A3 >30 mg/mmol.

manas.q: What albumin:creatinine ratio defines albuminuria category A3?

children.note: Where GFR physiology meets the ward.
Low renal perfusion (e.g. dehydration, haemorrhage) lowers GFR; at first the tubules still work and the change can reverse with restored perfusion.

manas.q: Why does GFR fall in dehydration or haemorrhage?

children.topic: ACE inhibitors and renal artery stenosis
children.note: With bilateral renal artery stenosis, GFR depends on angiotensin II efferent tone; ACE inhibitors can then cause a sharp fall in GFR.

manas.q: Why can ACE inhibitors drop GFR in bilateral renal artery stenosis?

children.note: Many renally cleared drugs need dose changes when GFR is low; check the drug's prescribing guidance.

manas.q: Why must renal function be checked before prescribing some drugs?

children.note: GFR rises by about 50% in normal pregnancy, so serum creatinine is normally lower than outside pregnancy.

manas.q: What happens to GFR in normal pregnancy?

children.note: Early diabetes can raise GFR above normal (hyperfiltration) before later decline; albuminuria is an early sign of diabetic kidney disease.

manas.q: What happens to GFR early in diabetic kidney disease?

children.note: GFR tends to fall with age, while low muscle mass in older people can hide this behind a normal creatinine.

manas.q: Why may older people have a normal creatinine despite low GFR?

children.note: How eGFR is reported and used in different places.
International KDIGO guidance stages CKD by cause, GFR category and albuminuria category together.

manas.q: Which three elements does KDIGO use to classify CKD?

children.note: The US NKF–ASN task force (2021) recommended the race-free CKD-EPI 2021 creatinine equation and wider use of cystatin C.

manas.q: Which eGFR equation did the US task force recommend in 2021?

children.note: The European Kidney Function Consortium equation is designed to work across ages from children to older adults, with creatinine or cystatin C.

manas.q: What is the EKFC equation?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-20.
A 2024 review covers how creatinine and cystatin C are measured, their pros and cons, age-related reference ranges and their use in eGFR equations, focusing on EKFC.

manas.q: Which two serum markers are most used to calculate eGFR?

children.note: After an NKF–ASN task force reviewed over 20 approaches, it backed the race-free CKD-EPI 2021 equation and more cystatin C testing; authors say this aids equity.

manas.q: What did the NKF–ASN task force recommend for eGFR?

children.note: A meta-analysis of 12 studies found race-corrected and creatinine-based equations tended to overestimate GFR in Black people; cystatin C-only equations showed small bias.

manas.q: Which eGFR equations tended to overestimate GFR in Black populations?

children.note: Quick wins.
Afferent constriction: GFR and flow both fall. Efferent constriction: GFR up, flow down, filtration fraction up.

manas.q: Contrast the effects of afferent and efferent constriction on GFR.

children.note: Glucose (≈0) < urea < inulin (= GFR) < PAH (≈ renal plasma flow).

manas.q: Rank glucose, urea, inulin and PAH by clearance.

children.note: Because some creatinine is secreted, its clearance runs slightly above true GFR.

manas.q: Why does creatinine clearance overestimate GFR?

children.note: Back-pressure raises Bowman's space pressure and opposes filtration.

manas.q: How does ureteric obstruction reduce GFR?

maps.title: HCH 500 · In depth: Health policy and legal framework

nodeData.note: How policy is made and analysed, the Constitution and laws behind Kenyan practice, and global legal tools. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Key words used in policy and law questions.
Decisions, plans and actions taken to reach defined health goals in a society, set by government and other actors.

manas.q: Define health policy.

children.note: Healthy public policy (Ottawa Charter, 1986) means policies in any sector, such as transport or housing, judged by their effect on health.

manas.q: What is healthy public policy?

children.note: Policy states direction; law binds and is enforced; a strategy plans how to act; guidelines advise practice and are usually not law.

manas.q: How does a policy differ from a law?

children.note: An Act is passed by Parliament or a county assembly; regulations (subsidiary legislation) are detailed rules made under an Act by a minister or body it names.

manas.q: What is subsidiary legislation?

children.note: Analysis of policy explains how and why a policy came about; analysis for policy gives evidence to shape a new one.

manas.q: Distinguish analysis of policy from analysis for policy.

children.note: The supreme law; any law inconsistent with it is void.
Article 43(1)(a): everyone has the right to the highest attainable standard of health, including reproductive health care.

manas.q: Which Article of Kenya's Constitution gives the right to health?

children.note: Every child has a right to basic nutrition, shelter and health care, and the child's best interests are paramount.

manas.q: Which Article protects children's right to health care in Kenya?

children.note: Every person has the right to a clean and healthy environment, which links law to sanitation and pollution control.

manas.q: Which Article gives the right to a clean and healthy environment?

children.note: Article 2(6): any treaty or convention Kenya ratifies forms part of Kenyan law, e.g. WHO tobacco convention.

manas.q: How do ratified treaties become part of Kenyan law?

children.note: National: health policy and national referral facilities. Counties: county health services, including facilities and pharmacies.

manas.q: How does the Fourth Schedule divide health functions?

children.note: Article 10 national values include participation of the people; they bind everyone who makes or implements laws or public policy decisions.

manas.q: Which Article lists participation of the people as a national value?

children.note: The Constitution defines an adult as a person aged 18 or over, relevant to consent for treatment and research.

manas.q: At what age is a person an adult under Kenya's Constitution?

children.note: Laws a doctor meets in practice, beyond those on the course map.
The Medical Practitioners and Dentists Act (Cap 253) sets up the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Council to register, license and discipline doctors and dentists.

manas.q: Which Act creates the KMPDC?

children.note: The Pharmacy and Poisons Board, under the Pharmacy and Poisons Act (Cap 244), regulates medicines, pharmacies and poisons.

manas.q: Which body regulates medicines in Kenya, and under which Act?

children.note: The Food, Drugs and Chemical Substances Act (Cap 254) controls safety, quality and labelling of food, drugs and chemicals, guarding against adulteration.

manas.q: What does Cap 254 regulate?

children.note: The Mental Health Act (Cap 248) governs admission, including involuntary admission, and treatment of people with mental illness; it has since been amended.

manas.q: Which Kenyan law governs involuntary psychiatric admission?

children.note: HIV and AIDS Prevention and Control Act: protects against discrimination, sets consent and confidentiality rules for testing, creates an HIV tribunal.

manas.q: What special body does the HIV and AIDS Prevention and Control Act create?

children.note: Regulates making, sale and advertising of alcohol; sale to people under 18 is prohibited.

manas.q: Which 2010 law controls alcohol sale in Kenya?

children.note: OSHA 2007 sets duties of employers to protect the safety, health and welfare of workers.

manas.q: Which law sets employer duties for worker safety in Kenya?

children.note: Defines sexual offences such as rape and defilement and sets their penalties; doctors often examine survivors and give evidence.

manas.q: Which Act governs sexual offences in Kenya?

children.note: Health data is sensitive personal data; collecting and sharing it needs a lawful basis and safeguards.

manas.q: How is health data classed under Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019?

children.note: Cap 149 requires registration of births and deaths; doctors certify cause of death.

manas.q: Which law requires registration of deaths in Kenya?

children.note: Who makes, passes, enforces and shapes health policy.
Sets national policy, standards and regulation, and runs national referral services; the Cabinet Secretary leads it.

manas.q: What are the Ministry of Health's main roles after devolution?

children.note: The National Assembly makes most national laws and approves the budget; the Senate protects county interests, considers Bills concerning counties and revenue sharing, including health.

manas.q: What role does the Senate play in health?

children.note: County executive (health CEC member) runs services; the county assembly passes county laws and budgets.

manas.q: Who passes county health laws?

children.note: Sets up forums for cooperation between national and county governments, including on shared functions like health.

manas.q: Which law creates forums for national–county cooperation?

children.note: KMPDC, Nursing Council of Kenya and Clinical Officers Council license practitioners and handle complaints.

manas.q: Name three Kenyan health professional councils.

children.note: KEMRI does health research; universities and ethics committees review studies; NACOSTI licenses research.

manas.q: Which body licenses research in Kenya?

children.note: Donors, NGOs, faith-based providers, professional unions, industry and the media all lobby and shape policy.

manas.q: Name non-state actors that influence health policy.

children.note: Models and steps beyond the policy cycle and triangle.
Publication, first reading, committee stage with public views, second reading, committee of whole House, third reading, Senate if it concerns counties, then presidential assent.

manas.q: List the stages of a Bill in Kenya's Parliament.

children.note: Rational model: weigh all options and pick the best. Incrementalism (Lindblom): small changes from the status quo, more realistic.

manas.q: Contrast rational and incremental models of policy-making.

children.note: Problem, policy and politics streams run separately; when they meet, a 'policy window' opens for change.

manas.q: Name the three streams in Kingdon's model.

children.note: Top-down: implement as designed centrally. Bottom-up: frontline workers and context reshape how policy works.

manas.q: Contrast top-down and bottom-up implementation.

children.note: Lipsky: nurses, doctors and clerks use discretion daily, so they in effect make policy as they deliver it.

manas.q: What is a street-level bureaucrat?

children.note: Evidence is one input; values, interests, money and timing often decide the outcome.

manas.q: Why does good evidence not always change policy?

children.note: Methods to study or plan a policy.
List actors, their position, power and interest; then plan how to engage, persuade or neutralise them.

manas.q: What does stakeholder analysis map?

children.note: High power, high interest: manage closely. High power, low interest: keep satisfied. Low power, high interest: keep informed.

manas.q: How should high-power, high-interest stakeholders be handled?

children.note: SWOT reviews internal strengths and weaknesses plus external opportunities and threats; PESTLE scans political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental context.

manas.q: What does PESTLE stand for?

children.note: Judges the likely health effects of a proposed policy or project before it is adopted.

manas.q: What is a health impact assessment?

children.note: Approach that builds health into decisions of every sector; promoted at WHO's 2013 Helsinki health promotion conference.

manas.q: Where was Health in All Policies promoted by WHO in 2013?

children.note: Legal duties every doctor needs.
Must be informed, voluntary and given by a person with capacity; for minors usually a parent or guardian, except in emergency.

manas.q: What three elements make consent valid?

children.note: Duty to keep patient information private; exceptions include consent, court order, legal notification and serious risk to others.

manas.q: Give exceptions to medical confidentiality.

children.note: Duty of care, breach of that duty, causation, and resulting harm must all be shown.

manas.q: What four elements prove clinical negligence?

children.note: Bolam (UK, 1957): standard is a responsible body of doctors. Montgomery (UK, 2015): disclose material risks the patient would want.

manas.q: What did the Montgomery case change about consent?

children.note: Global instruments and other countries' legal routes.
Binding WHO rules requiring countries to build core capacities and report public health emergencies of international concern.

manas.q: What do the International Health Regulations (2005) require?

children.note: The Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, adopted 2003 and in force 2005, was WHO's first treaty; Kenya is a party.

manas.q: What was WHO's first international health treaty?

children.note: Adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2025 to improve pandemic prevention, preparedness and response.

manas.q: When did the World Health Assembly adopt the Pandemic Agreement?

children.note: Created the National Health Service, funded by taxes and free at point of use, from 1948.

nodeData.note: Film anatomy, choosing X-ray, echo, CT or MRI, cardiac signs and mediastinal masses. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Widest heart diameter divided by widest internal chest diameter on a PA film; above 0.5 suggests cardiomegaly.

children.note: On an AP (often supine) film the heart is further from the detector and looks magnified, so do not call cardiomegaly on AP alone.

children.note: Central chest space between the two pleural sacs, from sternum to vertebral bodies and thoracic inlet to diaphragm.

manas.q: What are the boundaries of the mediastinum?

children.note: From above: SVC, then right atrium forming the right heart border.

children.note: From above: aortic knuckle, pulmonary trunk, left atrial appendage, then left ventricle.

manas.q: List the structures of the left mediastinal border from top to bottom.

children.note: Right ventricle lies behind the sternum (retrosternal space); left atrium and ventricle form the posterior heart border.

manas.q: Which chamber lies directly behind the sternum on a lateral film?

children.note: Classic X-ray split: anterior, middle, posterior. The ITMIG CT scheme names them prevascular, visceral and paravertebral.

manas.q: What are the three CT-based (ITMIG) mediastinal compartments?

children.note: Thin line of tissue beside the right trachea, normally only a few millimetres (about 4 mm or less); widening suggests nodes or a mass.

manas.q: What does widening of the right paratracheal stripe suggest?

children.note: Cheap, everywhere: heart size, oedema, effusions, mediastinal contour, calcification, lines and tubes.

manas.q: What can a chest X-ray show in cardiac disease?

children.note: First-line for chambers, ejection fraction, valves and pericardial effusion; bedside, no radiation.

manas.q: What is the first-line imaging test for heart structure and function?

children.note: Closer view of the back of the heart: left atrial appendage thrombus, vegetations, prosthetic valves, aortic dissection.

manas.q: Give three indications where TOE beats TTE.

children.note: Bedside POCUS in shock or arrest: effusion, tamponade, gross LV function, RV dilatation; the FAST scan includes a subxiphoid view.

manas.q: What can focused cardiac ultrasound answer in a shocked patient?

children.note: CT pulmonary angiography for pulmonary embolism; CT aortography for dissection; contrast CT to characterise mediastinal masses.

manas.q: Which CT test confirms suspected pulmonary embolism?

children.note: Reference standard for ventricular volumes and EF; tissue characterisation and late gadolinium enhancement for myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, pericardium.

manas.q: What does late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI show?

children.note: Myocardial perfusion scans show ischaemia; FDG PET-CT stages and follows lymphoma.

manas.q: Which nuclear test stages lymphoma?

children.note: Apex displaced down and to the left, e.g. aortic regurgitation, dilated cardiomyopathy.

manas.q: What does a left ventricular enlargement look like on a PA film?

children.note: Fills the retrosternal clear space on the lateral film; apex may look upturned on PA.

manas.q: Which lateral-film sign suggests right ventricular enlargement?

children.note: Enlarged central pulmonary arteries with rapid tapering (pruning) of peripheral vessels.

manas.q: What are the chest X-ray signs of pulmonary arterial hypertension?

children.note: Curvilinear calcium around the heart, best seen on lateral film or CT; suggests constrictive pericarditis, often after TB.

manas.q: What does pericardial calcification suggest, and what is a common cause in Kenya?

children.note: Calcified aortic or mitral valve or annulus is easier to place on the lateral film; it points to significant valve disease, confirmed by echo.

manas.q: What does valve calcification on a chest film prompt?

children.note: Air outlining mediastinal structures; continuous diaphragm sign; causes include asthma, vomiting (oesophageal rupture) and trauma.

manas.q: What is the continuous diaphragm sign?

children.note: Effusion with right atrial systolic and right ventricular diastolic collapse and a dilated IVC; tamponade remains a clinical diagnosis.

manas.q: Name echo signs of cardiac tamponade.

children.note: Echo-free space in diastole: under 10 mm small, 10–20 mm moderate, over 20 mm large.

manas.q: How is pericardial effusion size graded on echo?

children.note: Thickened leaflets, restricted posterior leaflet, 'hockey-stick' anterior leaflet in stenosis; World Heart Federation criteria standardise screening.

manas.q: What echo features suggest rheumatic mitral stenosis?

children.note: Dilated, poorly contracting LV with low EF; in Africa think also of peripartum and alcohol-related causes.

manas.q: What does dilated cardiomyopathy look like on echo?

children.note: Tropical restrictive disease: fibrosis obliterating ventricular apices with large atria.

manas.q: What is the typical echo finding in endomyocardial fibrosis?

children.note: Place the mass in front of, within, or behind the heart and trachea before naming a differential.

manas.q: What is the first step in assessing a mediastinal mass?

children.note: If hilar vessels are still seen through a mass, the mass is not hilar; it lies in front of or behind the hilum (classically anterior mediastinal).

manas.q: What does the hilum overlay sign tell you?

children.note: A mass with a sharp edge above the clavicles lies posteriorly; an anterior mass blurs at the clavicles.

manas.q: What does a sharp mass edge above the clavicles imply?

children.note: Lymph nodes (TB, lymphoma, metastases, sarcoidosis), foregut or bronchogenic cysts, aortic aneurysm, oesophageal lesions and hiatus hernia.

manas.q: List causes of a middle mediastinal mass.

children.note: Neurogenic tumours (nerve-sheath tumours in adults, neuroblastoma in children), TB spine paravertebral abscess, extramedullary haematopoiesis.

manas.q: Which tumours are typical in the posterior mediastinum?

children.note: Anterior mass mainly in adults over about 40; linked with myasthenia gravis.

manas.q: Which autoimmune disease is associated with thymoma?

children.note: Young adults, mostly men; teratoma may contain fat, fluid and calcium on CT; check AFP and beta-hCG.

manas.q: Which tumour markers are checked for a mediastinal germ cell tumour?

children.note: Bulky anterior or middle nodes in young adults; risk of airway and SVC compression; PET-CT for staging.

manas.q: Why is a bulky mediastinal lymphoma an anaesthetic risk?

children.note: Anterior mass continuous with the neck, often pushing the trachea aside.

manas.q: How does a retrosternal goitre usually present on a chest X-ray?

children.note: Face and arm swelling, distended chest veins; most often malignancy (lung cancer, lymphoma); CT venography shows cause and level.

manas.q: What is the commonest cause of superior vena cava obstruction?

children.note: Intimal flap with true and false lumens; Stanford A involves the ascending aorta (surgery), B does not (usually medical).

manas.q: How does the Stanford classification guide aortic dissection treatment?

children.note: After deceleration: widened mediastinum, lost aortic knuckle, trachea or NG tube pushed right, left apical cap; CT angiography confirms.

manas.q: List chest X-ray signs of traumatic aortic injury.

children.note: CXR is often normal (helps exclude other causes); CTPA shows filling defects; echo may show RV strain in massive PE.

manas.q: What is the role of the chest X-ray in suspected pulmonary embolism?

children.note: AP or supine film, poor inspiration, pectus excavatum and pericardial fat pads can all enlarge the heart shadow.

manas.q: Name causes of false cardiomegaly on a chest film.

children.note: Large thymus can look like a mass; the 'sail sign' is normal in babies.

manas.q: What is the thymic sail sign?

children.note: Dissection, PE and small effusions can all have a normal chest film; image further if suspicion is high.

manas.q: Which serious conditions can have a normal chest X-ray?

children.note: Before CT contrast check kidney function, prior reactions and pregnancy; weigh radiation dose, especially in the young.

manas.q: What should be checked before giving iodinated CT contrast?

children.note: Kenya MoH national cardiovascular disease guidelines are the local reference for heart failure and rheumatic heart disease work-up; use the current edition.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers cardiovascular disease management?

children.note: A 2018 World Health Assembly resolution called on countries to prevent and control rheumatic heart disease.

manas.q: What did the 2018 World Health Assembly resolution address?

children.note: ESC guidance makes echo first-line for suspected pericardial disease, with CT and CMR as second-level tests.

manas.q: What is the first-line imaging test for pericardial disease in ESC guidance?

children.note: NICE NG106 (2018): measure NT-proBNP first, then refer for echo, faster when the level is very high.

manas.q: In UK NICE heart failure guidance, what test comes before echo?

children.note: US scenario-based ratings, e.g. CT angiography as the usual test for suspected acute aortic syndrome.

manas.q: What do the ACR Appropriateness Criteria provide?

children.note: Review: one CMR scan shows pericardial thickening, effusion and inflammation; accurate for constriction, often avoiding catheterisation; enhancement may predict recurrence (small cohorts).

manas.q: What can cardiac MRI add in pericardial disease (2023 review)?

children.note: Review: these rare tumours of young adults differ from testicular ones; mediastinal non-seminomas have the poorest survival, while seminomas do about as well as testicular seminomas.

manas.q: Which mediastinal germ cell tumour type has the poorest prognosis?

children.note: Multi-society guideline on using CMR in children with congenital and acquired heart disease for diagnosis, planning interventions and follow-up.

manas.q: What does the 2022 multi-society guideline cover?

children.note: Papers read on 2026-11-23.
For any mediastinal mass: compartment first, then age, then CT features (fat, calcium, fluid, enhancement).

manas.q: What is the stepwise approach to a mediastinal mass?

children.note: Size, function, valves and effusion — echo is the usual next test after the chest film.

manas.q: What is usually the next test after a chest film in suspected heart disease?

children.note: Think TB pericarditis; echo confirms effusion and guides drainage.

maps.title: HHP 604 · In depth: Death and early post-mortem changes

nodeData.note: Confirming death; livor, rigor, algor mortis; timing death. Times are approximate; they vary with heat and body. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Irreversible loss of the person as a whole: circulation and breathing stop, or the brainstem has irreversibly failed.

manas.q: What is somatic death?

children.note: Cells die after somatic death at different speeds — brain within minutes, muscle over hours; this lag allows supravital reactions.

manas.q: Why do tissues die at different times after somatic death?

children.note: Life signs so faint they seem absent, e.g. hypothermia, cold-water drowning, sedative overdose, electrocution; resuscitate and re-examine.

manas.q: Name conditions that can mimic death (suspended animation).

children.note: Time since death; always given as a range, never a single hour.

manas.q: Why is the post-mortem interval given as a range?

children.note: No central pulse, heart sounds or breathing over a period of observation (UK practice: at least 5 minutes); ECG asystole supports it.

manas.q: How is death confirmed after cardiorespiratory arrest?

children.note: Known cause of irreversible brain damage; exclude sedatives, neuromuscular blockers, hypothermia and metabolic or endocrine causes first.

manas.q: What must be excluded before brainstem death tests?

children.note: Loss of corneal reflex, corneal clouding within hours, and segmentation ('trucking') of retinal blood columns soon after death.

manas.q: What retinal sign appears soon after death?

children.note: Brown-black band of drying sclera when the eyelids stay open after death; not an injury.

manas.q: What is tache noire?

children.note: A cold patient without signs of life is rewarmed before death is confirmed.

manas.q: Why is a hypothermic patient rewarmed before confirming death?

children.note: After circulation stops, gravity pools blood in dependent capillaries and venules, giving purple-red skin.

manas.q: What causes livor mortis?

children.note: Skin pressed on a firm surface stays pale (shoulder blades, buttocks when supine); tight clothing leaves pale marks.

manas.q: Why are pressure areas pale within lividity?

children.note: Early lividity blanches and shifts if the body is turned; it fixes after roughly 8–12 h (varies). Two patterns suggest the body was moved after partial fixing.

manas.q: What does a body with two lividity patterns suggest?

children.note: Cherry-pink: CO, cyanide, cold. Chocolate-brown: methaemoglobin (e.g. nitrites, chlorates). Colour points the way for toxicology.

manas.q: Which poisoning gives chocolate-brown lividity?

children.note: Cut the skin: lividity is blood within vessels and washes away; a bruise is blood in the tissue and does not.

manas.q: How is lividity told apart from a bruise at autopsy?

children.note: In a body suspended for hours, lividity collects in the legs, forearms and hands, sometimes with petechiae.

manas.q: Where does lividity collect in a hanging body?

children.note: Blood also pools in dependent organs, e.g. back of the lungs, which can mimic pneumonia or congestion.

manas.q: What lung finding can hypostasis mimic?

children.note: ATP runs out, so actin–myosin cross-bridges stay locked; rigor resolves as proteins break down in decomposition.

manas.q: What is the biochemical basis of rigor mortis?

children.note: Muscles relax right after death; jaw drops, sphincters may relax, pupils dilate.

manas.q: What happens to muscles immediately after death?

children.note: Usually seen first in small muscles (eyelids, jaw, neck), then limbs and trunk; all muscles start together but small ones show it sooner.

manas.q: Where is rigor mortis usually noticed first?

children.note: Faster onset and shorter course with heat, fever, exertion or convulsions before death; slower in cold. Textbook times assume temperate rooms.

manas.q: Which factors speed the onset of rigor mortis?

children.note: Once established rigor is forcibly broken, it does not come back in that joint.

manas.q: Does rigor return after it is broken?

children.note: High heat coagulates muscle protein; burnt bodies flex into the pugilistic attitude — not a sign of fighting.

manas.q: What causes the pugilistic attitude in burnt bodies?

children.note: Freezing hardens tissues; true rigor follows after thawing.

manas.q: What is cold stiffening?

children.note: Cadaveric spasm has no preceding flaccidity, affects one muscle group and follows sudden death in intense activity, e.g. clutching weeds when drowning.

manas.q: How does cadaveric spasm differ from rigor mortis?

children.note: Heat leaves by conduction, convection, radiation and evaporation until the body matches its surroundings.

manas.q: By which routes does a body lose heat after death?

children.note: Core temperature may hold for some hours before falling, so the cooling curve is S-shaped, not straight.

manas.q: Why is the post-mortem cooling curve sigmoid?

children.note: Rectal or other deep temperature with a long thermometer, repeated over time, plus ambient temperature at the scene.

manas.q: How is post-mortem core temperature measured?

children.note: Body size and fat, clothing, wind, wetness (water cools faster), ambient heat, and fever or hypothermia at death.

manas.q: List factors that change the rate of body cooling.

children.note: Uses rectal and ambient temperature and body weight, with correction factors for clothing and conditions; gives a range with error limits.

manas.q: What inputs does the Henssge nomogram use?

children.note: When ambient temperature is near body temperature, cooling is slight and of little use; the body may even gain heat.

manas.q: Why is algor mortis less useful in hot climates?

children.note: Rises after death as cells leak; used to estimate PMI but with wide error.

manas.q: Which vitreous chemical rises steadily after death?

children.note: Muscles can still contract to mechanical or electrical stimulation in the first hours.

manas.q: What are supravital reactions?

children.note: Pallor and loss of elasticity; lips and scrotum dry to a brown parchment look that can mimic abrasion.

manas.q: What can post-mortem drying of the lips mimic?

children.note: Show the last meal, but emptying time varies so widely that it is weak evidence of time.

manas.q: Why are stomach contents unreliable for timing death?

children.note: Warm and flaccid: under ~3 h; warm and stiff: ~3–8 h; cold and stiff: ~8–36 h; cold and flaccid: over ~36 h. Temperate figures; heat shortens them.

manas.q: Give the rough warm/cold, stiff/flaccid guide to time since death.

children.note: Use temperature, rigor, lividity and eye changes together, then check against scene evidence such as last sighting, mail and food.

manas.q: Why should several PMI methods be combined?

children.note: Once green abdominal discolouration and bloating begin, use the decomposition map's methods.

manas.q: Which signs mark the move from early changes to decomposition?

children.note: Fixed lividity that does not match the body's position shows it was moved after death.

manas.q: What does lividity inconsistent with position mean?

children.note: Cadaveric spasm gripping a weapon supports a self-inflicted act; it cannot be produced after death.

manas.q: Why is cadaveric spasm forensically valuable?

children.note: Unusual lividity colour prompts blood for carbon monoxide, cyanide or methaemoglobin testing.

manas.q: What does cherry-pink lividity prompt you to test for?

children.note: Mistaking lividity for injury can wrongly suggest assault; cut and look.

manas.q: What wrong conclusion can misreading lividity lead to?

children.note: Intense head and neck lividity with petechiae can mimic strangulation or asphyxia.

manas.q: What can lividity in a face-down body mimic?

children.note: No single sign gives an exact time of death; ranges overlap and depend on body and surroundings.

manas.q: Can one post-mortem sign give the exact time of death?

children.note: Warm conditions speed rigor and decay relative to temperate textbook tables; Kenyan legal steps are in the medicolegal map.

manas.q: Why must textbook post-mortem times be adjusted in Kenya?

children.note: WHO's international certificate: Part I is the chain of causes with the underlying cause on the lowest used line; Part II lists other contributing conditions.

manas.q: Where does the underlying cause go on the WHO death certificate?

children.note: The Academy of Medical Royal Colleges code accepts irreversible loss of brainstem function as death.

manas.q: Which brain death standard does the UK use?

children.note: The Uniform Determination of Death Act (1981) defines death as irreversible loss of circulation and breathing, or of all brain function including brainstem.

manas.q: How does the US define death under the Uniform Determination of Death Act?

children.note: A 2020 international consensus set minimum standards for determining brain death.

manas.q: What did the 2020 World Brain Death Project produce?

children.note: Review: for late intervals and skeletal remains only carbon-14 dating is well recognised; other methods give mixed results.

manas.q: What is the only well-recognised method for dating skeletal remains (2023 review)?

children.note: Systematic review of 18 studies: machine-learning models looked accurate but studies were small, selected and too varied to pool.

manas.q: What limited the 2022 review of machine learning for PMI?

children.note: Review of 14 papers: microbial communities around a decomposing body change in a predictable order, a possible future PMI tool.

manas.q: How might microbes help estimate time since death?

children.note: Papers read on 2026-11-23.
Lividity versus bruise is decided by incision, not by look.

manas.q: How do you decide lividity versus bruise?

children.note: Cadaveric spasm starts at the instant of death; rigor follows primary flaccidity.

manas.q: Which comes first, flaccidity or rigor?

children.note: Write the PMI as a range and state the factors that widen it.

manas.q: How should time since death be written in a report?

maps.title: HOG 500 · In depth: Antepartum haemorrhage

nodeData.note: Grading, praevia, accreta, abruption, vasa praevia, work-up, management and complications. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What counts as APH and how big the bleed is.
Kenyan teaching commonly uses bleeding after 28 weeks; RCOG (UK) uses from 24 weeks. Bleeding before the cut-off is treated as early pregnancy bleeding.

manas.q: From what gestation does the UK (RCOG) define antepartum haemorrhage?

children.note: RCOG grades: spotting; minor <50 mL; major 50–1000 mL without shock; massive >1000 mL and/or signs of shock.

manas.q: What blood loss defines massive APH in the RCOG grading?

children.note: Concealed bleeding in abruption means maternal shock may be far worse than the blood seen. Judge by pulse, BP, urine output.

manas.q: Why can visible blood loss mislead in placental abruption?

children.note: Placental: praevia, abruption, vasa praevia. Local: cervix or vagina. Others: uterine rupture, show, and unexplained.

manas.q: Name the three placental causes of APH.

children.note: When no cause is found, the pregnancy is still higher risk (preterm birth, growth restriction); many units add growth scans.

manas.q: Is unexplained APH a low-risk finding?

children.note: Beyond painless bleeding and 'no VE'.
Placenta implanted partly or wholly in the lower uterine segment, over or close to the internal cervical os.

manas.q: What is placenta praevia?

children.note: RCOG 2018: 'placenta praevia' = placenta lies directly over the os; 'low-lying' = edge less than 20 mm from the os on transvaginal scan.

manas.q: How does RCOG define a low-lying placenta?

children.note: I: lower segment, not reaching os; II: reaches os (marginal); III: partly covers os; IV: completely covers os.

manas.q: What is grade IV placenta praevia?

children.note: Previous caesarean, previous praevia, multiparity, older age, multiple pregnancy, IVF, smoking, prior uterine surgery.

manas.q: Give four risk factors for placenta praevia.

children.note: In the third trimester the lower segment forms and stretches; the attached placenta shears off, opening maternal sinuses.

manas.q: Why does placenta praevia bleed in late pregnancy?

children.note: TVS is safe in praevia and more accurate than abdominal scan for locating the placental edge.

manas.q: Is transvaginal ultrasound safe in suspected placenta praevia?

children.note: Most low placentas at the 20-week scan move away as the lower segment grows; re-scan around 32 weeks.

manas.q: When is a low placenta seen at 20 weeks usually re-scanned?

children.note: Placenta over the os: caesarean by a senior team, blood ready. Edge under 20 mm: caesarean more likely, labour only after senior discussion; 20 mm or more: labour usually possible.

manas.q: Which placental position needs caesarean delivery?

children.note: The lower segment contracts poorly over the placental bed, so postpartum haemorrhage is common after praevia.

manas.q: Why is PPH common after placenta praevia?

children.note: Abnormally adherent placenta: the hidden danger behind praevia.
Accreta: villi on myometrium; increta: into myometrium; percreta: through serosa, possibly into bladder.

manas.q: What distinguishes percreta from accreta?

children.note: Praevia over a previous caesarean scar carries the highest risk, rising with each extra caesarean.

manas.q: What combination gives the highest risk of placenta accreta spectrum?

children.note: Loss of the clear zone, placental lacunae, bladder wall interruption and increased vascularity; MRI can help.

manas.q: Name two ultrasound signs of placenta accreta spectrum.

children.note: Planned caesarean in a centre with blood bank and senior team; caesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ is often preferred, as pulling it off causes massive bleeding.

manas.q: Why should an accreta placenta not be pulled off?

children.note: Extends the course bubbles on signs, risks and DIC.
Premature separation of a normally sited placenta from the uterine wall before birth of the baby.

manas.q: Define placental abruption.

children.note: Blood may drain vaginally (revealed), stay trapped behind the placenta (concealed), or both (mixed).

manas.q: What is a concealed abruption?

children.note: Blood tracks into the myometrium, giving a bruised, purple uterus at caesarean; it usually still contracts.

manas.q: What is a Couvelaire uterus?

children.note: Scan misses many abruptions; diagnosis is clinical. A normal scan does not exclude it.

manas.q: Does a normal ultrasound exclude placental abruption?

children.note: Frequent contractions or a hypertonic uterus with fetal tachycardia, reduced variability, decelerations or bradycardia.

manas.q: What CTG and uterine findings suggest abruption?

children.note: Damaged placenta and decidua release tissue factor; clotting factors and fibrinogen are consumed. Low fibrinogen predicts heavy bleeding.

manas.q: Why does abruption cause DIC?

children.note: Resuscitate the mother and deliver urgently, usually by caesarean, unless vaginal birth is imminent.

manas.q: How is abruption with a live distressed fetus managed?

children.note: Vaginal birth is usually preferred (amniotomy, oxytocin) with blood and clotting support; caesarean only for maternal reasons.

manas.q: What is the preferred mode of birth after abruption with fetal death?

children.note: A previous abruption raises the risk substantially in later pregnancies; plan closer antenatal care.

manas.q: Does abruption recur?

children.note: Fetal, not maternal, bleeding — the baby can die in minutes.
Unprotected fetal vessels run in the membranes over or close to the internal os, not covered by cord or placenta.

manas.q: What is vasa praevia?

children.note: Type 1: velamentous cord insertion; type 2: vessels running between lobes of a bilobed or succenturiate placenta.

manas.q: What are the two types of vasa praevia?

children.note: Painless bleeding when membranes rupture, then sudden fetal bradycardia or death, while the mother stays stable.

manas.q: What is the classic presentation of vasa praevia?

children.note: The bleeding is fetal blood; a term baby has only a few hundred mL, so a small loss is catastrophic.

manas.q: Why is a small bleed from vasa praevia so dangerous?

children.note: Transvaginal scan with colour Doppler; suspect with low placenta, velamentous cord, bilobed placenta, IVF or twins.

manas.q: How is vasa praevia diagnosed before labour?

children.note: Deliver by planned caesarean before labour and membrane rupture; avoid amniotomy.

manas.q: How should known vasa praevia be delivered?

children.note: Not every APH is placental.
Cervical ectropion, polyp, cervicitis, cervical cancer, vaginal infection or trauma.

manas.q: Name three local causes of APH.

children.note: Gentle speculum exam is allowed to see the cervix; digital exam waits until praevia is excluded.

manas.q: Is speculum examination allowed before praevia is excluded?

children.note: Usually a scarred uterus in labour: pain, shock, abnormal CTG, loss of station, palpable fetal parts.

manas.q: Name features of uterine rupture.

children.note: Blood-stained mucus with contractions; small amount, but rule out other causes first.

manas.q: What is a 'show'?

children.note: Mother first, then baby, then the cause.
Assess airway, breathing, circulation; two large-bore cannulas; call senior obstetrician, anaesthetist and midwife.

manas.q: What is the first step in a heavy APH?

children.note: FBC, group and crossmatch, clotting screen with fibrinogen, urea, electrolytes; Kleihauer if Rh-negative.

manas.q: What bloods are sent in APH?

children.note: Where labs are slow, blood that fails to clot in a plain tube suggests coagulopathy.

manas.q: What bedside test screens for coagulopathy in APH?

children.note: Fetal heart by Doppler or CTG; fetal distress guides urgency of delivery.

manas.q: How is fetal wellbeing assessed in APH?

children.note: Locates the placenta, checks fetal life, growth and presentation; poor at excluding abruption.

manas.q: What is ultrasound best for in APH?

children.note: Praevia: painless, soft uterus, malpresentation. Abruption: pain, tender tense uterus, fetal distress, shock out of proportion.

manas.q: Contrast the uterus in praevia and abruption.

children.note: Stabilise, decide on timing, prepare for PPH.
Warmed fluids and early blood; activate massive haemorrhage protocol; tilt the undelivered woman left to relieve aortocaval compression by the uterus.

manas.q: Why tilt an undelivered pregnant woman to the left?

children.note: Preterm, minor bleeding, stable mother and fetus: admit, observe, steroids if early birth likely.

manas.q: When can APH be managed expectantly?

children.note: Give antenatal corticosteroids when preterm birth is likely within 7 days, usually up to 34 weeks (WHO: from 24 weeks), to mature fetal lungs.

manas.q: When are antenatal steroids given in APH?

children.note: Rh-negative woman: give anti-D within 72 hours of the bleed; Kleihauer test guides extra doses after 20 weeks.

manas.q: What does the Kleihauer test add for anti-D after APH?

children.note: Tocolytics are generally avoided in suspected abruption or heavy bleeding.

manas.q: Are tocolytics used in suspected abruption?

children.note: Active third stage with oxytocin; uterotonics and blood ready, especially after praevia or abruption.

manas.q: Why prepare for PPH after APH?

children.note: Mother and baby both at risk.
Shock, DIC, acute kidney injury, PPH, hysterectomy, transfusion reactions and death.

manas.q: List maternal complications of APH.

children.note: Pituitary necrosis after massive obstetric haemorrhage: failed lactation, amenorrhoea, later hypopituitarism.

manas.q: What is Sheehan syndrome?

children.note: Hypoxia, preterm birth, growth restriction, stillbirth; neonatal anaemia after vasa praevia.

manas.q: List fetal complications of APH.

children.note: Quick patterns examiners love.
Think placenta praevia — scan before any vaginal examination.

manas.q: Painless bleeding with breech at 34 weeks: what diagnosis first?

children.note: Think abruption, even with little visible blood; check clotting.

manas.q: Pain, tender uterus, little blood, shocked mother: diagnosis?

children.note: Bleeding with sudden fetal bradycardia at ROM = vasa praevia until proved otherwise.

manas.q: Fresh bleed at ROM with fetal bradycardia: diagnosis?

children.note: Always look for placenta accreta spectrum.

manas.q: What must you exclude with praevia over a caesarean scar?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then where others differ.
Kenyan clinical guidelines and teaching define APH from 28 weeks; no VE, resuscitate and refer to a unit with theatre and blood.

manas.q: From what gestation do Kenyan guidelines define APH?

children.note: WHO emergency obstetric care manuals: stabilise, no digital exam until praevia excluded, deliver if bleeding is heavy.

manas.q: What does WHO advise before vaginal examination in late-pregnancy bleeding?

children.note: APH from 24 weeks with volume grading; praevia and low-lying defined by the 20 mm rule on transvaginal scan.

manas.q: How does RCOG's APH definition differ from Kenya's?

children.note: ACOG suggests planned birth at 36+0 to 37+6 weeks for uncomplicated praevia, and 34+0 to 35+6 weeks for suspected accreta spectrum.

manas.q: When does ACOG suggest delivery for suspected accreta?

children.note: 2023 guideline gives dedicated advice on diagnosing and managing vasa praevia (see research).

manas.q: Which body published a 2023 vasa praevia guideline?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-23.
Abruption affects about 0.6–1.2% of pregnancies, nearly half at term; it mixes chronic vasculopathy with acute shear. Proposes a management algorithm.

manas.q: About what share of pregnancies are affected by abruption?

children.note: GRADE-based Canadian guideline: vasa praevia raises the risk of adverse outcomes, so fetal vessels near the cervix need careful scanning; it weighs hospital vs home care and caesarean timing.

manas.q: Why does vasa praevia need careful ultrasound characterisation?

children.note: Meta-analysis (7 studies): accreta without praevia linked more to IVF, prior D&C and myomectomy, less to caesarean; less often found antenatally; better maternal outcomes.

manas.q: Which risk factor is linked more with accreta without praevia?

maps.title: HPD 500 · In depth: Preterm and low birth weight

nodeData.topic: Preterm and low birth weight in depth
nodeData.note: Definitions, causes, immature physiology, signs, work-up, antenatal/newborn care, complications and prevention. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Beyond the course's weight and age cut-offs.
Moderate-to-late preterm is 32 to <37 weeks; late preterm is 34 to <37 weeks. Most preterm babies fall here.

manas.q: What gestation range is 'late preterm'?

children.note: Birth weight below the 10th centile for gestational age, at any gestation.

manas.q: How is small for gestational age defined?

children.note: A low birth weight baby may be preterm, small for gestational age (often from growth restriction), or both; each has different risks.

manas.q: Name the two ways a baby can be low birth weight.

children.note: Usually late placental insufficiency: head spared, abdomen and weight small.

manas.q: Which part is spared in asymmetric growth restriction?

children.note: Early insult (chromosomal, congenital infection, severe early insufficiency): head, length and weight all small.

manas.q: Give causes of symmetric growth restriction.

children.note: Best by first-trimester ultrasound; after birth, the New Ballard score uses neuromuscular and physical signs.

manas.q: What score estimates gestational age after birth?

children.note: About 1 in 10 babies is born preterm; prematurity complications are the leading cause of death in under-5s.

manas.q: What is the leading cause of death in children under 5?

children.note: Why babies arrive early or small.
Infection or chorioamnionitis, previous preterm birth, short cervix, twins, polyhydramnios, uterine anomaly, cervical surgery.

manas.q: Give four causes of spontaneous preterm labour.

children.note: PPROM: membranes rupture before 37 weeks and before labour; raises infection and preterm birth risk.

manas.q: What does PPROM stand for?

children.note: Early delivery for mother or baby: pre-eclampsia, APH, growth restriction, fetal distress.

manas.q: Name two reasons for provider-initiated preterm birth.

children.note: Teenage pregnancy, undernutrition, anaemia, malaria, HIV, urinary infection, smoking, short pregnancy interval.

manas.q: Name maternal factors that raise preterm and LBW risk.

children.note: Placental insufficiency, hypertension, malaria in pregnancy, smoking, congenital infection, chromosomal disorders, twins.

manas.q: Give three causes of fetal growth restriction.

children.note: Organ immaturity explains each complication.
Large surface area for weight, thin skin and little brown fat or subcutaneous fat.

manas.q: Why do preterm babies lose heat quickly?

children.note: Small glycogen and fat stores, poor feeding and high needs; SGA babies are also at risk.

manas.q: Why are preterm and SGA babies prone to hypoglycaemia?

children.note: Less maternal IgG crosses before term, skin barrier is weak, and invasive devices add risk.

manas.q: Why are preterm babies more prone to infection?

children.note: Immature liver conjugation and shorter red cell life; treat at lower bilirubin levels than term babies.

manas.q: Why are phototherapy thresholds lower in preterm babies?

children.note: Coordinated suck, swallow and breathing matures around 32–34 weeks; earlier babies need tube or cup feeds.

manas.q: Around what gestation does coordinated suck-swallow develop?

children.note: Look of a preterm baby.
Thin, shiny, red skin with visible veins; fine lanugo hair.

manas.q: Describe the skin of a preterm baby.

children.note: Soft flat ear cartilage, few sole creases, small or absent breast bud.

manas.q: Name three physical signs of prematurity.

children.note: Boys: testes undescended, few scrotal rugae. Girls: prominent clitoris and labia minora.

manas.q: What genital signs suggest prematurity?

children.note: Low tone with extended limbs ('frog-like'); weak cry and suck.

manas.q: What posture does a very preterm baby show?

children.note: Monitor, screen and look for complications.
Weigh every baby at birth and plot on a growth chart; score gestation.

manas.q: What must be recorded for every newborn?

children.note: Check blood glucose early and regularly in preterm, LBW and SGA babies, especially before feeds.

manas.q: Which babies need routine glucose checks?

children.note: FBC, CRP, blood culture; lumbar puncture if meningitis suspected.

manas.q: What tests make up a neonatal sepsis screen?

children.note: Measure when jaundice appears; use gestation-specific phototherapy charts.

manas.q: How is jaundice treatment decided in preterm babies?

children.note: Through the anterior fontanelle to detect bleeding or white matter injury in very preterm babies.

manas.q: How is IVH detected in preterm babies?

children.note: Ground-glass lungs with air bronchograms; low volumes.

manas.q: What does RDS look like on chest X-ray?

children.note: What helps before the baby is born.
Speed lung maturity; cut neonatal death, RDS and IVH. WHO: 24–34 weeks when birth is likely within 7 days.

manas.q: At what gestation does WHO recommend antenatal steroids?

children.note: Dexamethasone 6 mg IM 12-hourly ×4 doses, or betamethasone 12 mg IM 24-hourly ×2 doses.

manas.q: What is the dexamethasone regimen for fetal lung maturity?

children.note: Magnesium sulfate before very preterm birth lowers the risk of cerebral palsy.

manas.q: Why give magnesium sulfate before very preterm birth?

children.note: Give antibiotics (erythromycin often first choice); not routinely in preterm labour with intact membranes.

manas.q: Which preterm women should get routine antibiotics?

children.note: Short delay only, e.g. to finish steroids or transfer; no proven baby benefit on its own.

manas.q: What is the main purpose of tocolysis?

children.note: Transfer in utero to a unit with newborn care is safer than moving a sick baby after birth.

manas.q: Why is in-utero transfer preferred?

children.note: After stabilisation (resuscitation has its own map).
Wait at least 1 minute in babies not needing resuscitation; less transfusion and IVH in preterms.

manas.q: How long does WHO advise waiting before clamping the cord?

children.note: KMC, warm room, hat, incubator if needed; check temperature often.

manas.q: Name ways to keep a LBW baby warm.

children.note: Mother's own milk by breast, cup or nasogastric tube; donor milk if unavailable. Protects against NEC and infection.

manas.q: Why is breast milk vital for preterm babies?

children.note: Start early and increase daily as tolerated; IV fluids if too sick to feed.

manas.q: How are feeds given to a baby too immature to suck?

children.note: Give to all newborns to prevent haemorrhagic disease; smaller dose by local protocol in very small babies.

manas.q: What prevents haemorrhagic disease of the newborn?

children.note: Give enough oxygen but avoid excess; too much raises the risk of retinopathy of prematurity.

manas.q: Why avoid excess oxygen in preterm babies?

children.note: Feeding well, keeping warm, gaining weight, no active illness, and a confident mother.

manas.q: List criteria for discharging a LBW baby.

children.note: Mechanisms behind the course's list.
Fragile germinal matrix bleeds, mostly in the first 72 hours and in babies <32 weeks.

manas.q: When do most intraventricular haemorrhages occur?

children.note: White matter injury around the ventricles; leads to spastic diplegic cerebral palsy.

manas.q: Which cerebral palsy type follows periventricular leukomalacia?

children.note: Feed intolerance, distension, bloody stools; X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis. Nil by mouth, antibiotics, surgery if perforation.

manas.q: What is the classic X-ray sign of NEC?

children.note: Abnormal retinal vessel growth; can blind. Screen at-risk babies; treat with laser or anti-VEGF injection.

manas.q: How is severe retinopathy of prematurity treated?

children.note: Chronic lung disease: still needing oxygen at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age.

manas.q: How is bronchopulmonary dysplasia defined?

children.note: Commoner in preterms: murmur, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, heart failure.

manas.q: Name signs of a PDA in a preterm baby.

children.note: Low iron stores and frequent sampling cause anaemia; low calcium and phosphate cause metabolic bone disease.

manas.q: Why do preterm babies become anaemic?

children.note: Hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and polycythaemia.

manas.q: Name three problems typical of SGA babies.
