children.note: Higher risk of developmental delay, learning, vision and hearing problems; growth-restricted babies have more adult heart disease and diabetes.

manas.q: What adult diseases are linked to growth restriction?

children.note: Stopping preterm birth before it starts.
Treat urinary infection and anaemia, malaria prevention in pregnancy, nutrition, HIV care, birth spacing.

manas.q: Name antenatal measures that lower preterm and LBW births.

children.note: For singleton pregnancy with short cervix or previous spontaneous preterm birth (see research).

manas.q: Who benefits from vaginal progesterone to prevent preterm birth?

children.note: Stitch for selected women with a history of preterm loss or a short cervix.

manas.q: What is cervical cerclage?

children.note: Quick hits.
Assess development by corrected age (subtract weeks born early) until about 2 years.

manas.q: How is corrected age worked out?

children.note: Antenatal steroids are among the most effective single interventions for preterm survival.

manas.q: Which antenatal intervention most improves preterm survival?

children.note: Always state both gestation and weight centile; their problems and causes differ.

manas.q: Why record both gestation and weight centile?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then where others differ.
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols: KMC for small babies, bubble CPAP for respiratory distress, breast milk feeding; check the current edition for apnoea treatment.

manas.q: Which CPAP type do Kenyan protocols use for small babies?

children.note: KMC from birth for all preterm/LBW babies who are not critically ill; consider CPAP from birth under 32 weeks.

manas.q: Which preterm babies may get CPAP immediately after birth per WHO?

children.note: Steroids only when gestation is reliable, birth likely, no maternal infection and adequate newborn care exists.

manas.q: What conditions does WHO set for antenatal steroids?

children.note: ACOG allows a steroid course at 34–36 weeks for selected women; WHO does not routinely recommend after 34 weeks.

manas.q: Does WHO recommend antenatal steroids after 34 weeks?

children.note: UK screens babies born before 31 weeks or under 1501 g; US uses similar but slightly different cut-offs.

manas.q: Which babies does the UK screen for ROP?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-23.
WHO made 25 recommendations (11 new): KMC immediately after birth, caffeine for apnoea, family involvement in care and home visits after discharge.

manas.q: How many new recommendations did WHO make for preterm/LBW care?

children.note: 31 RCTs, 15,559 babies: KMC cut deaths by about a third vs usual care; starting within 24 h and ≥8 h/day worked best.

manas.q: How many hours a day of KMC gave greater benefit?

children.note: Network meta-analysis of 61 RCTs: vaginal progesterone should be considered first choice in singleton pregnancy at risk from previous spontaneous preterm birth or short cervix.

manas.q: Which treatment was favoured to prevent preterm birth in high-risk singletons?

maps.title: HPS 100 · In depth: Biopsychosocial Model of Health

nodeData.note: Engel's model in depth: roots, three domains, how they interact, clinical use, critiques. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What the model claims and the ideas it grew from.
Health and illness result from biological, psychological and social systems acting on each other at the same time, so all three must be assessed in every patient.

manas.q: What is the core claim of the biopsychosocial model?

children.note: Engel argued in Science (1977) that medicine needed a new model; the biomedical model left no room for the person or their life context.

manas.q: In which journal did Engel set out the biopsychosocial model in 1977?

children.note: Engel drew on systems theory: nature as a hierarchy of linked systems, from cells and organs to the person, family, community and society.

manas.q: Which theory underpins Engel's biopsychosocial model?

children.note: A change at one level (e.g. job loss) can travel up or down the hierarchy and alter others (mood, sleep, blood pressure).

manas.q: How does the hierarchy of systems explain illness in the biopsychosocial model?

children.note: Health is not simply present or absent; people move along a continuum as the three domains shift over time.

manas.q: Is health seen as a yes/no state in the biopsychosocial model?

children.note: The older model the BPS model was built to complete, not to discard.
Explains illness by reducing it to the smallest biological parts, such as cells, molecules or a single pathogen.

manas.q: What is reductionism in the biomedical model?

children.note: Treats mind and body as separate (traced to Descartes), so psychological complaints are seen as outside 'real' medicine.

manas.q: Which philosopher is linked to the mind–body dualism behind the biomedical model?

children.note: Great successes: germ theory, antibiotics, vaccines, surgery. The BPS model keeps biology and adds the person and context.

manas.q: Does the biopsychosocial model reject the biomedical model?

children.note: The biomedical approach puts the doctor as expert and patient as passive; BPS care moves towards shared, patient-centred decisions.

manas.q: How does the role of the patient differ between biomedical and BPS models?

children.note: Typical factors in each domain, used when building a full case formulation.
Genes, age, sex, pathogens, physiology, organ damage, nutrition, drug effects and comorbidities.

manas.q: List examples of biological factors in the BPS model.

children.note: Beliefs, emotions, mood, personality, coping style, cognition, health behaviours and past experiences of illness.

manas.q: List examples of psychological factors in the BPS model.

children.note: Family, social support, income, work, education, housing, culture, religion, stigma and access to services.

manas.q: List examples of social factors in the BPS model.

children.note: The 3 Ps grid crossed with the three domains: what made the person vulnerable, what triggered it, what keeps it going. Some add protective factors.

manas.q: What are the 3 Ps used in a biopsychosocial formulation?

children.note: Pathways that link mind, body and social world.
Perceived stress activates the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, raising cortisol; chronic activation affects immunity, metabolism and mood.

manas.q: Which hormonal axis links psychological stress to bodily change?

children.note: Acute stress triggers sympathetic activation and adrenaline release: raised heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose.

manas.q: What does sympathetic activation do during acute stress?

children.note: Study of how mind, nervous, endocrine and immune systems interact; e.g. chronic stress can slow wound healing.

manas.q: What does psychoneuroimmunology study?

children.note: Stress, mood and social setting shape behaviours (smoking, alcohol, diet, exercise, adherence) that then change biology.

manas.q: Give the behavioural pathway by which social factors affect disease.

children.note: Melzack and Wall (1965): spinal 'gates' modulate pain signals, and mood, attention and expectation can open or close them.

manas.q: Who proposed the gate control theory of pain and what does it show?

children.note: Expectation alone can improve (placebo) or worsen (nocebo) symptoms, showing belief has measurable bodily effects.

manas.q: What do placebo and nocebo effects show about mind and body?

children.note: Good social support is linked to better health and is thought to cushion the harmful effects of stress.

manas.q: What is the buffering effect of social support?

children.note: Turning the model into everyday practice.
Beyond symptoms, ask about mood, beliefs, work, family, money, culture and supports, then link them to the problem.

manas.q: What extra areas does a biopsychosocial history cover?

children.note: ICE = Ideas, Concerns, Expectations: asking about these reveals the patient's own view of the illness and helps agree a plan.

manas.q: What does ICE stand for in consultation skills?

children.note: The BPS model underlies patient-centred care: seeing the person, sharing power and building the relationship.

manas.q: Which care approach is built on the biopsychosocial model?

children.note: Doctors, nurses, psychologists, physiotherapists, social workers and community health workers each cover different domains.

manas.q: Why does BPS care often need a multidisciplinary team?

children.note: In back pain, psychosocial 'yellow flags' (fear-avoidance, low mood, poor recovery expectations) are linked to a higher risk of long-term disability.

manas.q: What are yellow flags in low back pain?

children.note: Control depends on biology plus understanding, mood, diet, cost of drugs and family support, not prescriptions alone.

manas.q: Why is the BPS model useful in diabetes care?

children.note: Viral suppression depends on drugs and on stigma, disclosure, food security, transport costs and support groups.

manas.q: How do social factors affect HIV treatment outcomes?

children.note: Depression is common in chronic illness and worsens adherence and outcomes, so screening for mood is part of good care.

manas.q: Why screen for depression in chronic physical illness?

children.note: Many Kenyans use traditional or faith healing alongside clinics; asking respectfully about this is part of the social domain.

manas.q: Why ask Kenyan patients about traditional or faith healing?

children.note: Why some call the model vague, and how it has been extended.
Critics say it lists factors without saying how they combine or which matters most for a given patient.

manas.q: What is the main theoretical criticism of the biopsychosocial model?

children.note: Wrongly blaming symptoms on stress can delay diagnosis of physical disease; biology must still be investigated properly.

manas.q: What is the danger of over-applying the psychological domain?

children.note: Full BPS assessment takes time, training and team support that busy clinics may lack.

manas.q: Name a practical barrier to using the BPS model.

children.note: Some add a spiritual domain (bio-psycho-social-spiritual), important in palliative care and in many Kenyan communities.

manas.q: What fourth domain do some add to the BPS model?

children.note: How the model shows up in global frameworks.
The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health uses a biopsychosocial approach: body, activity, participation and context.

manas.q: Which WHO classification uses a biopsychosocial approach to disability?

children.note: The medical model locates disability in the body; the social model in barriers in society. The ICF combines both.

manas.q: How does the ICF combine the medical and social models of disability?

children.note: WHO's Mental Health Gap Action Programme supports non-specialists in primary care to manage common mental disorders.

manas.q: What is the aim of WHO's mhGAP programme?

children.note: WHO health promotion charter: health is created and lived by people in the settings of everyday life, shaped by social conditions, so action goes beyond the health sector.

manas.q: What did the Ottawa Charter say about where health is created?

children.note: UK and other national guidelines advise assessing psychosocial factors and favour exercise and self-management over imaging for most low back pain.

manas.q: What do major low back pain guidelines advise beyond biology?

children.note: Recent papers on the model, from Europe PMC.
Authors propose rebuilding the model on general scientific theories (causation as regulation, dysfunction as dysregulation), citing psychotherapy and social epidemiology findings as support.

manas.q: What core idea does the 2023 'revitalized' BPS model use for dysfunction?

children.note: A narrative review in musculoskeletal pain finds the model is often used narrowly or reductively, in two parallel versions, 'humanistic' and 'causation'; an 'enactive' approach could unite them.

manas.q: What two versions of the BPS model did the 2023 review describe?

children.note: An umbrella review linked worse long-term outcome in acute–subacute back pain to high pain and disability, distress, negative expectations and heavy physical work.

manas.q: Which factors were linked to poor outcome in acute low back pain in the 2022 umbrella review?
manas.ref: Int J Environ Res Public Health 2022

children.note: Quick points examiners like.
For any case, draw a 3×3 grid: predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating against bio, psycho, social.

manas.q: How would you structure a biopsychosocial formulation in an exam?

children.note: Always state the model adds to, rather than replaces, biomedical diagnosis and treatment.

manas.q: Does the BPS model replace biomedical treatment?

children.note: Strong answers cite a pathway: HPA axis, gate control, behaviour, or social support buffering.

manas.q: Name two mechanisms that link psychological stress to disease.

children.note: Illustrate with HIV, diabetes or TB care where cost, stigma and support shape outcomes.

manas.q: Give a Kenyan example showing all three BPS domains.

maps.title: HME 600 · In depth: Cardiac arrhythmias and ECG

nodeData.topic: Cardiac arrhythmias and ECG in depth
nodeData.note: How to read a rhythm strip, sort brady- and tachyarrhythmias, and act on stable versus unstable patients. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: The words used for abnormal rhythms.
Any rhythm other than normal sinus rhythm, or a sinus rhythm at an abnormal rate: bradycardia below 60/min, tachycardia above 100/min.

manas.q: What heart rates define bradycardia and tachycardia in adults?

children.note: Rate 60–100/min, a P wave before every QRS, P upright in lead II, and a constant PR interval.

manas.q: What are the ECG features of normal sinus rhythm?

children.note: Where the impulse starts and how rhythms go wrong.
SA node, atria, AV node (where conduction is delayed), bundle of His, left and right bundle branches, then Purkinje fibres.

manas.q: List the normal cardiac conduction pathway in order.

children.note: If higher centres fail, the AV junction escapes at about 40–60/min and the ventricles at about 20–40/min.

manas.q: At what rates do junctional and ventricular escape rhythms run?

children.note: Abnormal automaticity, triggered activity (after-depolarisations, as in torsades) and re-entry.

manas.q: What are the three basic mechanisms of tachyarrhythmia?

children.note: Needs two pathways with different conduction and refractoriness plus one-way block; a circuit then loops. It underlies AVNRT, AVRT and atrial flutter.

manas.q: What conditions are needed for a re-entry circuit?

children.note: Use the same order every time.
Rate, rhythm, axis, P waves, PR interval, QRS width, ST segment, T waves, then QT interval.

manas.q: What is a systematic order for reading an ECG?

children.note: At 25 mm/s one small square is 0.04 s and one large square 0.2 s.

manas.q: At standard paper speed, how long is one large ECG square?

children.note: Regular rhythm: 300 divided by large squares between R waves. Irregular: count QRS complexes on a 10-second strip and multiply by 6.

manas.q: How do you calculate heart rate on an irregular ECG?

children.note: PR 0.12–0.20 s. QRS under 0.12 s is narrow; 0.12 s or more is broad.

manas.q: What are the normal PR interval and the cut-off for a broad QRS?

children.note: Correct for heart rate (QTc, e.g. Bazett: QT divided by the square root of RR). A QTc above 500 ms carries a high risk of torsades.

manas.q: Above what QTc value is torsades risk high?

children.note: The first question is always: is the patient unstable?
ABCDE, oxygen if hypoxic, cardiac monitor, IV access, 12-lead ECG, and look for causes such as electrolyte problems, ischaemia or drugs.

manas.q: What are the first steps for a patient with an arrhythmia?

children.note: Shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia and heart failure. Any one of these makes the arrhythmia unstable.

manas.q: What are the four adverse features in a peri-arrest arrhythmia?

children.note: Synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation or anaesthesia, up to three attempts; if it fails, give amiodarone and repeat the shock.

manas.q: How is an unstable tachycardia with a pulse treated?

children.note: Give IV atropine; if no response, other drugs or pacing (transcutaneous, then transvenous) with expert help.

manas.q: What is the first drug for unstable bradycardia?

children.note: Is the QRS narrow or broad? Is the rhythm regular or irregular? This gives four groups with different causes.

manas.q: Which two ECG questions sort a stable tachycardia?

children.note: Slow rhythms from the sinus node or the AV node.
Fit athletes, sleep, beta-blockers and other rate-slowing drugs, hypothyroidism, hypothermia, raised intracranial pressure and inferior MI.

manas.q: Give causes of sinus bradycardia.

children.note: Sinus node disease, often in older people: pauses, sinus arrest, or alternating slow and fast rhythms (tachy-brady).

manas.q: What is the tachy-brady syndrome?

children.note: PR above 0.20 s but every P wave is conducted; usually harmless.

manas.q: What defines first-degree heart block?

children.note: PR lengthens beat by beat until one P wave is not conducted; usually at the AV node and often benign.

manas.q: What is the ECG pattern of Mobitz type I block?

children.note: Fixed PR with sudden dropped beats; block is below the AV node and can progress to complete block, so pacing is usually needed.

manas.q: Why is Mobitz II more dangerous than Mobitz I?

children.note: Recent asystole, Mobitz II, complete block with broad QRS, or a pause over 3 s: plan pacing even if the patient seems stable now.

manas.q: Which bradycardia findings signal risk of asystole?

children.note: The right coronary artery supplies the AV node in most people, so inferior MI often causes AV block, frequently temporary.

manas.q: Why does inferior MI often cause AV block?

children.note: QRS under 0.12 s: the rhythm starts above the ventricles.
A response to fever, pain, bleeding, sepsis, hypoxia or thyrotoxicosis; treat the cause, never cardiovert it.

manas.q: How is sinus tachycardia treated?

children.note: Usually AVNRT (re-entry in the AV node) or AVRT (via an accessory pathway); sudden onset and end, P waves often hidden.

manas.q: What are the two commonest types of re-entrant SVT?

children.note: In a stable patient try a Valsalva manoeuvre; the modified version adds lying flat with legs raised straight after the strain.

manas.q: What is the first treatment for stable regular SVT?

children.note: Rapid IV bolus with a flush blocks the AV node briefly: it ends AVNRT and AVRT and unmasks flutter waves. Warn the patient of a brief awful feeling.

manas.q: How does adenosine help with a regular narrow tachycardia?

children.note: Accessory pathway: short PR and a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) in sinus rhythm.

manas.q: What are the resting ECG signs of WPW?

children.note: The commonest sustained arrhythmia; extends the AF bubbles on the course map.
Paroxysmal (ends by itself or with treatment within 7 days), persistent (over 7 days), long-standing persistent (over 1 year) and permanent (accepted, no further rhythm control).

manas.q: How is AF classified by duration?

children.note: Hypertension, heart failure, ischaemic and rheumatic valve disease, thyrotoxicosis, alcohol, sepsis and lung disease. Check thyroid function and an echo.

manas.q: List common causes of atrial fibrillation.

children.note: C: treat comorbidities and risk factors; A: avoid stroke; R: reduce symptoms (rate and rhythm control); E: evaluate and reassess over time.

manas.q: What does AF-CARE stand for in the 2024 ESC guideline?

children.note: The newest guidance changes the score shown on the course map.
ESC 2024 and the German 2025 guideline use CHA2DS2-VA: the same score as CHA2DS2-VASc but without the point for female sex.

manas.q: What is the difference between CHA2DS2-VA and CHA2DS2-VASc?

children.note: Female sex adds stroke risk mainly when other risk factors are present; it behaves as a risk modifier, not a risk factor on its own.

manas.q: Why was female sex dropped from the AF stroke score?

children.note: With CHA2DS2-VA, oral anticoagulation is advised at 2 or more and considered at 1, for women and men alike.

manas.q: At what CHA2DS2-VA score is anticoagulation recommended?

children.note: Older VASc thresholds were already one point higher for women, so most decisions stay the same. Learn both; use the one your exam and lecturer use.

manas.q: Do CHA2DS2-VA and CHA2DS2-VASc usually lead to the same decision?

children.note: Moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve: anticoagulate with warfarin whatever the score; DOACs are not used.

manas.q: When is the AF stroke score not used?

children.note: In AF without those valve problems, DOACs are preferred over warfarin where available; warfarin needs regular INR checks.

manas.q: Which anticoagulant class is preferred in non-valvular AF?

children.note: Fix what can be changed: high BP, alcohol, NSAIDs or antiplatelets, unstable INR. A high bleeding risk alone is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation.

manas.q: How should bleeding risk be used in AF anticoagulation decisions?

children.note: Beta-blocker or a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker (avoid the latter in reduced ejection fraction); digoxin helps in heart failure or inactive patients.

manas.q: Which drugs are used for rate control in AF?

children.note: Unless onset is clearly recent, anticoagulate for at least 3 weeks (or exclude clot by TOE) before elective cardioversion and continue for at least 4 weeks after.

manas.q: How long should anticoagulation precede elective cardioversion of AF?

children.note: Right atrial macro-re-entry: sawtooth flutter waves about 300/min, often 2:1 block giving a regular rate near 150. Anticoagulate as for AF; ablation often cures it.

manas.q: What ventricular rate suggests flutter with 2:1 block?

children.note: QRS 0.12 s or more: dangerous until proven otherwise.
A regular broad complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise, especially after MI or in structural heart disease.

manas.q: How should a regular broad complex tachycardia be treated until proven otherwise?

children.note: AV dissociation, capture and fusion beats, very broad QRS, extreme axis and the same QRS direction across all chest leads (concordance).

manas.q: Name ECG features that favour VT over SVT with aberrancy.

children.note: Amiodarone under monitoring with expert help; synchronised shock if the patient becomes unstable.

manas.q: What is the treatment for stable monomorphic VT?

children.note: AF with bundle branch block, pre-excited AF (WPW) or polymorphic VT.

manas.q: What are the causes of an irregular broad complex tachycardia?

children.note: Avoid AV node blockers (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, beta-blockers): they can push conduction down the accessory pathway and cause VF.

manas.q: Why are AV nodal blockers dangerous in pre-excited AF?

children.note: Polymorphic VT twisting around the baseline, linked to a long QT. Give IV magnesium, stop QT-prolonging drugs and correct potassium.

manas.q: What is the first drug for torsades de pointes?

children.note: Low potassium, magnesium or calcium; drugs such as macrolides, haloperidol, methadone, sotalol, amiodarone and bedaquiline; congenital long QT.

manas.q: Name drugs and electrolyte problems that prolong the QT.

children.note: Why arrhythmias matter.
Stroke and systemic emboli, heart failure from fast rates (tachycardia cardiomyopathy) and higher mortality and dementia risk.

manas.q: What are the main complications of AF?

children.note: Sudden collapse from a pause or very slow rhythm in heart block, with quick recovery and flushing.

manas.q: What is a Stokes–Adams attack?

children.note: VT and VF are the main causes; survivors without a reversible cause are usually offered an implantable defibrillator (ICD).

manas.q: What device is offered to VF survivors without a reversible cause?

children.note: High-yield points.
A regular narrow tachycardia near 150/min: look hard for flutter waves (e.g. in II and V1).

manas.q: Which arrhythmia should a regular rate of 150 make you suspect?

children.note: Tall peaked T waves, flat P waves, broad QRS, then a sine-wave pattern and arrest; give IV calcium to protect the heart.

manas.q: What are the ECG changes of hyperkalaemia?

children.note: Flat T waves, U waves and ST depression; it also makes digoxin toxicity and torsades more likely.

manas.q: What are the ECG changes of hypokalaemia?

children.note: Sagging ‘reverse tick’ ST depression shows the drug is present, not that it is toxic.

manas.q: What does reverse-tick ST depression indicate?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then where other guidance differs.
Kenya MoH national guidelines on cardiovascular disease are the local reference for AF and arrhythmia care; check their stroke score and drug lists with your lecturer.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guidance should you check for AF and arrhythmia care?

children.note: Rheumatic mitral valve disease is a common cause of AF in Kenya and the region; DOACs are not used in rheumatic mitral stenosis, so warfarin with INR checks stays central.

manas.q: Why does warfarin remain central for AF in Kenya?

children.note: The World Health Assembly passed a resolution on rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease in 2018 (WHA71.14), urging prevention and control.

manas.q: Which 2018 WHA resolution addressed rheumatic heart disease?

children.note: Introduced AF-CARE and CHA2DS2-VA, dropping sex from the stroke score.

manas.q: Which body introduced CHA2DS2-VA in 2024?

children.note: The ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline kept CHA2DS2-VASc and describes AF in stages, from being at risk through to permanent AF.

manas.q: Which stroke score did the 2023 US AF guideline keep?

children.note: European and US resuscitation algorithms share the core: look for adverse features, shock unstable tachycardia, atropine then pacing for unstable bradycardia.

manas.q: What core steps do peri-arrest arrhythmia algorithms share?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-25.
AWMF guideline: use CHA2DS2-VA, anticoagulate at 2 or more; in patients with CV risk factors early rhythm control cut CV events (3.9 vs 5.0 per 100 patient-years); no general screening.

manas.q: Which stroke score does the 2025 German AF guideline recommend?

children.note: Chinese cardiology societies propose a CHA2DS2-VASc-60 score tuned to Asian patients and stress early rhythm control and ablation. Built on Asian data; score details are not in the abstract.

manas.q: What stroke score did the 2024 Chinese AF guideline propose?

children.note: UK Kidney Association: DOAC trials excluded CrCl under 30 mL/min, so evidence is thin; guidance covers no anticoagulation, DOAC use, monitoring and left atrial appendage occlusion.

manas.q: Why is anticoagulation in AF with advanced CKD uncertain?

maps.title: HME 601 · In depth: Eczema and dermatitis

nodeData.note: Types of eczema, why skin flares, how it looks on African skin, and how to treat it step by step. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What eczema is and how it is grouped.
The two words are used for the same thing: itchy inflammation of the epidermis with ill-defined redness, scale and sometimes vesicles.

manas.q: Are eczema and dermatitis different conditions?

children.note: Endogenous (from within): atopic, seborrhoeic, discoid, pompholyx, venous, asteatotic. Exogenous (outside cause): irritant and allergic contact.

manas.q: Which eczemas are endogenous and which exogenous?

children.note: Acute: red, swollen, vesicles, weeping and crusting. Chronic: dry scale, fissures and lichenification (thick skin with exaggerated lines).

manas.q: How does acute eczema look different from chronic eczema?

children.note: Why the skin becomes inflamed and itchy.
The hallmark on histology: fluid between epidermal cells pushes them apart; severe spongiosis forms vesicles.

manas.q: What is the histological hallmark of eczema?

children.note: Atopic eczema is driven by Th2 cytokines, mainly IL-4 and IL-13, with IL-31 a key itch signal; this is the target of newer biologics.

manas.q: Which cytokines drive atopic eczema?

children.note: Scratching damages the barrier further, raising inflammation and itch; breaking the cycle is a goal of treatment.

manas.q: What is the itch–scratch cycle?

children.note: Most atopic skin carries S. aureus; it worsens flares and causes infected (impetiginised) eczema.

manas.q: Which bacterium commonly colonises atopic eczema?

children.note: Eczema in infancy often comes first, followed in some children by food allergy, asthma and allergic rhinitis.

manas.q: What is the atopic march?

children.note: How it presents at different ages.
Usually starts in infancy or early childhood, relapses and remits, and often improves with age; some continue into adult life.

manas.q: When does atopic eczema usually start?

children.note: Cheeks, scalp, trunk and outer limbs; the nappy area is usually spared.

manas.q: Which area is usually spared in infant atopic eczema?

children.note: Flexures, hands, face, neck and eyelids are common sites; sometimes widespread.

manas.q: Which sites are commonly involved in adult atopic eczema?

children.note: Itchy skin plus 3 or more: flexural involvement, personal asthma or hay fever, generally dry skin, visible flexural eczema, onset before age 2.

manas.q: What are the UK Working Party criteria for atopic eczema?

children.note: Extra skin fold under the lower eyelid (Dennie–Morgan), palmar hyperlinearity, keratosis pilaris and ichthyosis vulgaris.

manas.q: Name signs associated with atopic eczema.

children.note: EASI and SCORAD are scored by clinicians; POEM is a patient-reported score of symptoms over the past week.

manas.q: Name tools used to score eczema severity.

children.note: Standard patterns seen in darker skin.
Small itchy papules centred on hair follicles, often on the trunk, are common in Black African skin and may be the main sign.

manas.q: What is follicular eczema?

children.note: Lichenification and prurigo-like nodules from chronic rubbing are often prominent.

manas.q: Which chronic changes are prominent in eczema on darker skin?

children.note: Pale, slightly scaly patches on a child’s face, linked with atopy and more visible on dark skin; harmless and fades slowly.

manas.q: What is pityriasis alba?

children.note: Dark or pale patches after eczema are usually post-inflammatory, not steroid damage, and fade slowly over months; controlling flares is the best prevention.

manas.q: What usually causes dark or pale patches after eczema heals?

children.note: Patterns beyond atopic eczema.
Greasy yellow scale on scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, ears and central chest; cradle cap in infants. Treat with antifungal (e.g. ketoconazole) shampoo or cream.

manas.q: Where does seborrhoeic dermatitis typically affect adults?

children.note: Coin-shaped, very itchy plaques, often on the limbs; can mimic tinea, so scrape for fungus if unsure.

manas.q: Which fungal infection can discoid eczema mimic?

children.note: Deep, itchy vesicles on palms, soles and sides of the fingers.

manas.q: Where does pompholyx eczema occur?

children.note: Lower legs with venous hypertension: brown haemosiderin staining, oedema, often before leg ulcers; prone to contact allergy to applied creams.

manas.q: What skin change accompanies venous eczema of the legs?

children.note: Dry, cracked ‘crazy paving’ skin on the shins of older people, worse in dry weather and with frequent washing.

manas.q: What is asteatotic eczema?

children.note: A single thick, itchy plaque from repeated rubbing, e.g. on the neck or ankle.

manas.q: What causes lichen simplex chronicus?

children.note: Extends the irritant vs allergic bubble on the course map.
Wet work, soaps, detergents and solvents; hands of cleaners, health workers, hairdressers and mechanics are typical.

manas.q: Which jobs carry high risk of irritant hand dermatitis?

children.note: Nickel (jewellery, belt buckles), fragrances, preservatives, rubber chemicals in gloves, chromate in cement and PPD in hair dye.

manas.q: Name common causes of allergic contact dermatitis.

children.note: PPD in hair dye and ‘black henna’ tattoos can cause severe facial or scalp swelling.

manas.q: Which chemical in hair dye commonly causes allergic contact dermatitis?

children.note: Earlobes and umbilicus point to nickel; hairline and eyelids to dye or cosmetics; hands and wrists to gloves or cement.

manas.q: What does dermatitis at the earlobes and umbilicus suggest?

children.note: Allergic reactions usually appear 1–3 days after contact (sometimes longer), so patients may not link the cause.

manas.q: How long after contact does allergic contact dermatitis appear?

children.note: Mostly a clinical diagnosis; tests answer specific questions.
Allergens stay on the back for 48 hours; readings are taken at about day 2 and again at day 4.

manas.q: When are patch tests read?

children.note: Bacterial swab for infected eczema; viral swab (PCR) when eczema herpeticum is suspected.

manas.q: Which swab is taken if eczema herpeticum is suspected?

children.note: If a rash could be tinea, do a KOH scraping; steroids on tinea give ‘tinea incognito’, which looks atypical.

manas.q: What is tinea incognito?

children.note: Not used to diagnose eczema; reserve for suspected immediate food or other allergy.

manas.q: When are IgE or skin prick tests useful in eczema?

children.note: Extends the course bubble on emollients and steroids.
Apply often and generously, smoothing in the direction of hair growth; keep going when skin is clear. Ointments suit very dry skin.

manas.q: How should emollients be applied in eczema?

children.note: Emollient soaked into clothing, bandages or bedding makes them catch fire easily; warn patients to keep away from flames.

manas.q: What safety warning applies to emollients on fabric?

children.note: Contains sodium lauryl sulfate, which can sting and irritate; use only as a wash, not as a leave-on moisturiser.

manas.q: Why is aqueous cream a poor leave-on emollient?

children.note: Mild: hydrocortisone 1%. Moderate: clobetasone butyrate. Potent: betamethasone valerate 0.1%. Very potent: clobetasol propionate 0.05%.

manas.q: Give an example of a mild and a very potent topical steroid.

children.note: Mild on face, flexures and genitals; stronger on trunk and limbs; potent often needed on palms and soles.

manas.q: Which body sites need the mildest topical steroids?

children.note: Cream squeezed from the fingertip to the first crease (about 0.5 g) covers an area of two adult palms.

manas.q: What area does one fingertip unit cover?

children.note: After control, applying the steroid (or calcineurin inhibitor) twice a week to usual flare sites helps prevent relapse.

manas.q: What is proactive therapy in atopic eczema?

children.note: Tacrolimus or pimecrolimus: steroid-free, so no skin thinning; useful on face and eyelids; may burn briefly at first.

manas.q: What advantage do topical calcineurin inhibitors have over steroids?

children.note: Damp then dry tubular bandages over emollient or steroid calm severe flares, usually in children, under specialist advice.

manas.q: What are wet wraps used for?

children.note: Weeping, crusting or pustules suggest bacterial infection; treat with an antibiotic per local guideline and keep treating the eczema.

manas.q: What signs suggest infected eczema?

children.note: They do not treat eczema itself; a short course of a sedating one may help sleep during a bad flare.

manas.q: Do antihistamines treat atopic eczema?

children.note: Specialist options: narrowband UVB phototherapy, ciclosporin, methotrexate, azathioprine, biologics such as dupilumab, and JAK inhibitors. Oral steroids are not advised (rebound flares).

manas.q: Name systemic treatments for severe atopic eczema.

children.note: Identify and avoid the cause, protect hands (gloves with cotton liners), emollients and a topical steroid; consider job adjustments.

manas.q: How is contact dermatitis managed?

children.note: What can go wrong beyond flares.
Eczema covering most of the skin: risk of fluid loss, temperature instability and infection; needs urgent review.

manas.q: What is erythroderma?

children.note: Severe atopic eczema is linked with atopic keratoconjunctivitis and cataract; eyelid eczema is common.

manas.q: Which eye problems are linked with atopic eczema?

children.note: Night itch disturbs the whole family; eczema is linked to poor sleep, low mood, anxiety and missed school or work.

manas.q: How does atopic eczema affect quality of life?

children.note: Fear of steroids leads to undertreatment; explain that correct use, with fingertip units, is safe.

manas.q: Why does steroid fear matter in eczema care?

children.note: High-yield points.
Eczema itches; a rash without itch should make you reconsider the diagnosis.

manas.q: What should a non-itchy ‘eczema’ prompt?

children.note: Itch in several family members, worse at night, with finger-web or genital lesions suggests scabies rather than eczema.

manas.q: Which features suggest scabies instead of eczema?

children.note: Skin-lightening products may contain potent steroids; ask about them in facial rashes, thinning or steroid acne.

manas.q: Why ask about skin-lightening creams in a facial rash?

children.note: Kenya first, then where other guidance differs.
The MoH Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions, written by facility level, include common skin conditions; follow them for local first-line care.

manas.q: Which Kenyan MoH guidelines cover common skin conditions?

children.note: Check which emollients and steroid strengths are on the national list before prescribing at each facility level.

manas.q: Where can you check which topical steroids are on Kenya’s national list?

children.note: NICE guidance for children under 12 (CG57, 2007) uses a stepped approach, matching steroid potency to severity with emollients always.

manas.q: What approach does NICE use for childhood eczema?

children.note: American guidelines rate newer creams, biologics and JAK inhibitors, and advise against oral steroids (see research).

manas.q: What does the AAD advise about systemic steroids in eczema?

children.note: Japanese guidance includes local topicals such as delgocitinib and difamilast ointments (see research).

manas.q: Which topical drugs feature in Japan’s eczema guideline?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-25.
27 GRADE recommendations: strong for moisturisers, topical steroids and calcineurin inhibitors, newer creams, biologics and JAK inhibitors; strongly against oral steroids. Trials mostly short.

manas.q: What did the 2026 AAD paediatric guideline say about systemic steroids?

children.note: Four new strong recommendations: tapinarof cream, roflumilast cream, lebrikizumab, and nemolizumab with topical therapy. Short trials limit long-term comparisons.

manas.q: Which four therapies got new strong AAD recommendations for adults in 2025?

children.note: Topical steroids, tacrolimus, delgocitinib and difamilast first; for refractory moderate-to-severe disease add ciclosporin, biologics, JAK inhibitors or phototherapy. Five new drugs added.

manas.q: Which treatments does Japan’s 2024 guideline add for refractory eczema?

maps.title: HME 602 · In depth: Therapeutic drug monitoring

nodeData.note: Kinetics behind a level, when and how to sample, reading results, and spotting toxicity. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What TDM is and what it is not.
Measuring a drug concentration (usually in blood) and using it, with the clinical picture, to adjust the dose for one patient.

manas.q: What is therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)?

children.note: A range where most patients benefit with little toxicity; some respond below it and some are toxic within it.

manas.q: Why is a drug level within range not proof the patient is safe?

children.note: When a clear effect can be measured (INR, blood pressure, glucose), follow the effect; levels help most when no such marker exists.

manas.q: When is measuring drug effect preferred over measuring drug levels?

children.note: The kinetics that explain a level.
Highest concentration after a dose, once absorption or infusion and distribution are complete.

manas.q: What does a peak (Cmax) level represent?

children.note: Lowest concentration, taken just before the next dose; rising troughs warn of accumulation.

manas.q: When is a trough (Cmin) level taken, and what does it warn of?

children.note: Area under the concentration–time curve: total drug exposure over a period, usually 24 hours (AUC24).

manas.q: What does the area under the curve (AUC) measure?

children.note: t½ ≈ 0.693 × Vd ÷ clearance: a bigger volume or lower clearance lengthens half-life.

manas.q: How do volume of distribution and clearance determine half-life?

children.note: Routine levels are only meaningful at steady state (about 4–5 half-lives); a loading dose shortens the wait.

manas.q: Why should routine drug levels be taken at steady state?

children.note: When elimination saturates, a fixed amount is removed per hour; a small dose rise can cause a large level rise. Phenytoin is the classic example.

manas.q: Why can a small phenytoin dose increase cause toxicity?

children.note: Only unbound (free) drug acts and is cleared; most assays report the total (bound + free) concentration.

manas.q: Which fraction of a protein-bound drug is active, and which does the lab usually report?

children.note: Criteria and the main drugs.
Gentamicin, amikacin: killing depends on peak; kidney and ear toxicity relate to sustained exposure (high troughs).

manas.q: Why are aminoglycoside levels monitored?

children.note: Narrow window between under-treating serious MRSA infection and kidney injury; exposure varies with renal function.

manas.q: Why is vancomycin monitored?

children.note: Phenytoin (saturable kinetics, high protein binding) and carbamazepine (induces its own metabolism over weeks).

manas.q: Why do phenytoin and carbamazepine levels behave unpredictably?

children.note: Ciclosporin and tacrolimus after transplant: trough levels on whole blood, as both rejection and toxicity are serious.

manas.q: Which sample is used to monitor ciclosporin and tacrolimus?

children.note: Lithium, digoxin, theophylline; high-dose methotrexate levels guide folinic acid rescue.

manas.q: What do methotrexate levels guide after high-dose therapy?

children.note: Checking adherence, suspected toxicity, poor response, new interacting drugs, changing kidney function, pregnancy.

manas.q: Apart from routine dosing, when else is a drug level helpful?

children.note: A level is only as good as its timing.
Write the exact time of the last dose and of the sample on the request; without them the result cannot be read.

manas.q: Which two times must be recorded with every TDM sample?

children.note: Take it just before the next dose is due.

manas.q: When should a trough level be drawn?

children.note: After distribution is complete, not during the infusion; timing depends on drug and route — follow the local protocol.

manas.q: Why should a peak level not be drawn during the infusion?

children.note: Never sample from a line or arm used to give the drug; contamination gives falsely high levels.

manas.q: Why must a level not be drawn from the infusion line?

children.note: Do not use a lithium heparin tube for a lithium level — it gives a falsely high result.

manas.q: Which blood tube must never be used for a lithium level?

children.note: If toxicity is suspected, take a level at once whatever the dose timing, and record the time; a digoxin level under 6 h after a dose reads falsely high.

manas.q: When toxicity is suspected, when should the level be taken?

children.note: Treat the patient, not the number.
Correct timing? At steady state? Taking it as prescribed? Interacting drugs? Kidney and liver function?

manas.q: What should you check before changing a dose because of a level?

children.note: Low albumin (or uraemia) raises the free fraction: a low or normal total level can hide a toxic free level. Measure free phenytoin.

manas.q: Why can a normal total phenytoin level be toxic in hypoalbuminaemia?

children.note: The Sheiner–Tozer equation estimates phenytoin corrected for albumin but is imprecise; a measured free level is better.

manas.q: What is the limitation of albumin-corrected phenytoin formulas?

children.note: Total phenytoin usually 10–20 mg/L in adults with normal albumin; confirm the local lab range.

manas.q: What is the usual total phenytoin target range in adults?

children.note: For lithium, digoxin and others use the local laboratory range and the indication; targets differ by use.

manas.q: Which reference range should guide lithium and digoxin levels?

children.note: Low potassium or magnesium and high calcium raise toxicity risk even with a normal level.

manas.q: Which electrolyte changes increase digoxin toxicity?

children.note: A change in practice.
Troughs were used for decades but track AUC poorly; high trough targets were linked with more kidney injury.

manas.q: Why are vancomycin troughs a poor guide to exposure?

children.note: For serious MRSA infection, US consensus (2020) targets AUC24/MIC 400–600, estimated from two levels or Bayesian software.

manas.q: What AUC24/MIC target is recommended for vancomycin in serious MRSA infection?

children.note: Trough-guided dosing remains common where AUC tools are unavailable; follow the local protocol.

manas.q: When might trough-guided vancomycin dosing still be used?

children.note: What to look for on the ward.
Nausea, vomiting, confusion, blurred or yellow-green vision and any arrhythmia, especially with AV block. Severe cases: digoxin-specific antibody fragments.

manas.q: List clinical features of digoxin toxicity.

children.note: Vomiting, diarrhoea, coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, seizures. Triggers: dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides.

manas.q: Which drugs and states precipitate lithium toxicity?

children.note: Monitor kidney function, thyroid function and calcium: lithium causes hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and hypercalcaemia.

manas.q: Which tests are monitored long term on lithium, and why?

children.note: Nystagmus, ataxia, slurred speech, drowsiness and confusion.

manas.q: What are the signs of phenytoin toxicity?

children.note: Kidney injury (often reversible) and cochlear or vestibular damage (often permanent); loop diuretics add ear risk.

manas.q: Which aminoglycoside toxicity is often permanent?

children.note: Vomiting, tachyarrhythmias, hypokalaemia and seizures; ciprofloxacin and macrolides raise levels, smoking lowers them.

manas.q: What are features of theophylline toxicity?

children.note: High-yield points.
An untimed level is close to useless: no dose time, no interpretation.

manas.q: What makes a drug level uninterpretable?

children.note: Always read a total phenytoin level alongside the albumin.

manas.q: Which result must you read with a total phenytoin level?

children.note: Levels fall over the first weeks as it induces its own metabolism; doses are built up gradually.

manas.q: Why do carbamazepine levels fall in the first weeks of treatment?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then where others differ.
Assay access varies between hospitals; check what your lab measures and its turnaround. Without levels, monitor clinical signs and kidney function.

manas.q: How should you monitor a narrow-margin drug when levels are unavailable?

children.note: Gentamicin (Access) and vancomycin (Watch) are on the WHO Model List, as are lithium, digoxin and phenytoin.

manas.q: In which AWaRe groups are gentamicin and vancomycin?

links.title: Kenya

children.note: The 2020 ASHP/IDSA-led consensus moved vancomycin monitoring from troughs to AUC for serious MRSA infection.

manas.q: Which guidance shifted vancomycin monitoring to AUC?

links.title: Kenya

children.note: Once-daily gentamicin is often adjusted with a nomogram (e.g. Hartford) from one timed level; local charts differ.

manas.q: How are once-daily gentamicin levels often interpreted?

links.title: Kenya

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-25.
Meta-analysis of 57 mostly adult studies: nephrotoxicity 6.2% with AUC-guided vs 17.0% with trough-guided TDM (OR 0.53). Studies 2009–2021; designs not stated in abstract.

manas.q: How did AUC-guided vancomycin TDM affect nephrotoxicity in the 2023 meta-analysis?

children.note: Meta-analysis of 63 studies: pharmacist input lowered acute kidney injury (RR 0.67) and helped standardise TDM. Abstract truncated; study designs and other results not shown.

manas.q: What effect did pharmacist intervention have on vancomycin-related AKI?

children.note: Review of 12 studies in deep-seated infection: 11 poor quality, one with a control group (no outcome difference). TDM often led to dose reductions.

manas.q: What did the 2026 review conclude about beta-lactam TDM in deep infections?

maps.title: HOS 600 · In depth: Polytrauma and pelvic fractures

nodeData.topic: Polytrauma and pelvic fractures in depth
nodeData.note: Primary survey, pelvic ring patterns, bleeding control, urological injury and resuscitation. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Key terms.
Serious injury (AIS ≥3) in two or more body regions plus at least one: SBP ≤90 mmHg, GCS ≤8, base excess ≤ −6, INR ≥1.4 or PTT ≥40 s, age ≥70.

manas.q: What does the Berlin definition of polytrauma require?

children.note: Sacrum and two innominate bones joined by the symphysis and sacroiliac joints; a ring rarely breaks in only one place.

manas.q: Why should one pelvic ring break prompt a search for a second?

children.note: Mechanically unstable (ring can displace) and haemodynamically unstable (bleeding shock); they often but not always go together.

manas.q: What are the two meanings of an "unstable" pelvic fracture?

children.note: Why the pelvis bleeds and what else it damages.
Strong posterior sacroiliac ligaments give most stability; their disruption makes the ring vertically unstable.

manas.q: Which ligaments give the pelvic ring most of its stability?

children.note: Opening the ring increases pelvic volume, so blood collects without the tamponade a closed ring gives.

manas.q: Why does an open-book pelvic injury bleed so much?

children.note: In males, pelvic fracture injures the posterior (membranous) urethra; straddle falls injure the anterior (bulbar) urethra.

manas.q: Which part of the male urethra is injured in pelvic fracture?

children.note: Extraperitoneal rupture usually accompanies pelvic fracture; intraperitoneal follows a blow to a full bladder.

manas.q: Which bladder rupture type usually accompanies pelvic fracture?

children.note: Bone fragments can tear rectum or vagina (an open fracture); the lumbosacral plexus is at risk in posterior injuries.

manas.q: Which structures besides the bladder and urethra are at risk in pelvic fracture?

children.note: Two systems to know.
Grouped by force: anteroposterior compression (APC), lateral compression (LC), vertical shear (VS) and combined mechanism.

manas.q: Name the four Young–Burgess pelvic injury groups.

children.note: I: slight symphysis widening, ligaments intact. II: wider, anterior SI ligaments torn (open book). III: full SI disruption.

manas.q: How do APC I, II and III pelvic injuries differ?

children.note: I: sacral compression on the side of impact. II: plus iliac wing (crescent) fracture. III: plus opposite-side open book ("windswept").

manas.q: What is a "windswept pelvis" in Young–Burgess terms?

children.note: Hemipelvis displaced upwards through the ring, often from a fall from height landing on one leg.

manas.q: What mechanism typically causes a vertical shear pelvic injury?

children.note: A: stable. B: rotationally unstable, vertically stable (e.g. open book, lateral compression). C: rotationally and vertically unstable.

manas.q: What do Tile A, B and C pelvic fractures mean?

children.topic: APC II–III and VS bleed most
children.note: Ring-opening and shear patterns carry more haemorrhage risk than LC I.

manas.q: Which pelvic injury patterns carry the highest bleeding risk?

children.note: ABCDE order with catastrophic bleeding first, treating as you go.
Stop exsanguinating external bleeding first: direct pressure, packing, tourniquet for limbs.

manas.q: What does the <C> in <C>ABCDE stand for?

children.note: Open and secure the airway while protecting the cervical spine.

manas.q: What is protected while managing the airway in trauma?

children.note: Find and treat tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax and flail chest.

manas.q: Which chest injuries must be found in the B of the primary survey?

children.note: Two large-bore cannulas, bloods and crossmatch; look for bleeding on the floor and in chest, abdomen, pelvis and long bones.

manas.q: Where are the five sites of major blood loss in trauma?

children.note: Disability: GCS, pupils, glucose. Exposure: full log-roll check, then keep warm.

manas.q: What is assessed in D and E of the primary survey?

children.note: Look for perineal bruising, leg shortening or rotation, blood at the meatus. Do not repeatedly spring the pelvis.

manas.q: Why should the pelvis not be repeatedly sprung?

children.note: With a high-energy mechanism and shock, apply a binder before imaging confirms a fracture.

manas.q: When should a pelvic binder be applied in trauma?

children.note: In the resuscitation room and beyond.
Chest and pelvic films in the resus room quickly show major ring disruption and chest bleeding.

manas.q: Which X-rays are taken in the trauma resuscitation room?

children.note: Detects free fluid in abdomen, pericardium and chest, but is poor at detecting retroperitoneal pelvic bleeding.

manas.q: Which bleeding source is FAST scanning poor at detecting?

children.note: CT with contrast defines fractures and organ injury; a contrast blush shows active arterial bleeding.

manas.q: What does a contrast blush on trauma CT mean?

children.note: If blood at the meatus, image the urethra before any urethral catheter.

manas.q: Which test excludes urethral injury before catheterisation?

children.note: Crossmatch, FBC, coagulation, lactate and base deficit (shock), and a pregnancy test in women of childbearing age.

manas.q: Which blood results indicate the severity of shock?

children.note: Resuscitate while bleeding is stopped.
Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy feed each other and raise mortality; prevent all three from the start.

manas.q: What is the lethal triad of trauma?

children.note: Accept a lower blood pressure until bleeding is controlled; not in head injury, where brain perfusion needs a higher pressure.

manas.q: In which patients is permissive hypotension avoided?

children.note: Limit crystalloid; give blood products in balanced ratios (red cells, plasma, platelets) via a massive transfusion protocol.

manas.q: Why is large-volume crystalloid avoided in bleeding trauma?

children.note: CRASH-2 (2010): 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h, cut death from bleeding when started within 3 h; started after 3 h it appeared harmful.

manas.q: Within how many hours of injury should tranexamic acid be started?

children.note: Short operation to stop bleeding and contamination, then ICU to correct physiology, then planned definitive surgery.

manas.q: What are the stages of damage control surgery?

children.note: Options after the binder.
Check skin; remove or loosen once the pelvis is fixed, as prolonged pressure causes sores. An improvised sheet works if none.

manas.q: What is a risk of leaving a pelvic binder on too long?

children.note: Packs placed beside the bladder through a low incision tamponade venous and bone bleeding; fast, needs no radiology.

manas.q: Which pelvic bleeding sources does preperitoneal packing control?

children.note: Interventional radiology blocks bleeding arteries, often after a CT blush; needs a radiology suite and team.

manas.q: What finding often prompts pelvic angioembolisation?

children.note: An anterior frame (or posterior C-clamp) restores ring volume and stability as part of damage control.

manas.q: How does external fixation reduce pelvic bleeding?

children.note: A balloon in the aorta (zone III for pelvic bleeding, above the bifurcation) temporarily stops inflow; a bridge to definitive control. Benefit is unproven.

manas.q: Which aortic zone is used for REBOA in pelvic bleeding?

children.note: Do not make it worse.
No urethral catheter until urethral injury is excluded; a blind catheter can complete a partial tear.

manas.q: What must you not do when there is blood at the urethral meatus?

children.note: Inability to void, perineal or scrotal haematoma; a high-riding prostate is an unreliable sign.

manas.q: Which signs suggest urethral injury after pelvic fracture?

children.note: If urethral injury is confirmed and drainage is needed, use a suprapubic catheter.

manas.q: How is the bladder drained when the urethra is injured?

children.note: Extraperitoneal rupture: usually catheter drainage. Intraperitoneal rupture: surgical repair.

manas.q: Which type of bladder rupture needs surgical repair?

children.note: Early and late.
Pelvic and polytrauma patients are high risk; start thromboprophylaxis once bleeding is controlled.

manas.q: When is thromboprophylaxis started after pelvic trauma?

children.note: Wounds into perineum, rectum or vagina mean high mortality and sepsis risk; a diverting colostomy may be needed.

manas.q: Why may a colostomy be needed in open pelvic fracture?

children.note: Closed degloving: fluid collects between skin and fascia, often over the greater trochanter; risks infection near incisions.

manas.q: What is a Morel-Lavallée lesion?

children.note: Urethral stricture, erectile dysfunction, nerve injury, chronic sacroiliac pain, limp and leg-length difference.

manas.q: List late complications of pelvic ring injury.

children.note: High-yield points.
Assume pelvic bleeding once chest and abdomen are cleared; bind and call for bleeding control.

manas.q: In a shocked patient with a pelvic fracture, what is assumed?

children.note: Look for bone or blood in rectum or vagina — it turns the injury into an open fracture.

manas.q: Why is rectal and vaginal examination done in pelvic fracture?

children.note: Low-energy lateral compression fractures are common in older people and can still bleed.

manas.q: What pelvic fracture pattern is typical after a low fall in older people?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then where others differ.
Motorcycle taxi crashes are a major source of pelvic and multiple injury; riders and passengers both get hurt.

manas.q: Which vehicle type drives much road trauma in Kenya?

children.note: Without angioembolisation or CT, binder, packing and external fixation are the main tools; refer once stable enough.

manas.q: Which pelvic bleeding controls need no interventional radiology?

links.title: Kenya: boda boda crashes

children.note: Road traffic injury is the leading cause of death for people aged 5–29. WHO Basic Emergency Care teaches the ABCDE approach; TXA is on the EML.

manas.q: According to WHO, which age group dies most from road traffic injury?

links.title: Kenya: boda boda crashes

children.note: The American College of Surgeons trauma course teaching the ABCDE primary survey internationally; recent editions put control of exsanguinating bleeding first.

manas.q: Which organisation runs ATLS?

links.title: Kenya: boda boda crashes

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-25.
Review of 10 studies: similar in-hospital death; packing was quicker with less early transfusion; REBOA a bridge. Mostly retrospective, no RCTs.

manas.q: How did pelvic packing compare with angioembolisation in the 2026 review?

children.note: Meta-analysis of 7 retrospective cohorts (837 patients): REBOA linked to higher in-hospital (RR 1.44) and 24 h death. Retrospective data only; limited certainty.

manas.q: What did the 2026 meta-analysis find about zone III REBOA in pelvic fracture?

children.note: Scoping review of 27 case patients: most had combined front-and-back ring disruption and all had urinary, genital or perineal injury. Case reports only.

manas.q: Which injuries accompanied motorcycle fuel-tank pelvic fractures?

maps.title: HPS 600 · In depth: Treatment-resistant illness and ECT

nodeData.topic: Treatment-resistant illness and ECT in depth
nodeData.note: Rule out pseudo-resistance, then step up: switch, augment, combine, clozapine and ECT. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Words to use precisely before calling an illness resistant.
Usually: depression that has not responded to at least two adequate antidepressant trials (right dose, long enough, taken) in the current episode.

manas.q: How is treatment-resistant depression usually defined?

children.note: Response: a large fall (commonly 50% or more) in a depression rating score. Remission: symptoms reduced to minimal, below a set cut-off. Remission is the real goal.

manas.q: What is the difference between response and remission?

children.note: A therapeutic dose taken for at least about 6 weeks, with adherence confirmed, before judging an antipsychotic to have failed.

manas.q: How long is an adequate antipsychotic trial?

children.note: A therapeutic dose for about 4–6 weeks; little or no improvement by then suggests a change is needed.

manas.q: How long should an antidepressant be tried before judging it?

children.note: How to check each item before escalating treatment.
Ask without blame, count tablets, involve family, and use drug levels where available (e.g. clozapine, lithium). Partial adherence is a very common cause of apparent failure.

manas.q: Which very common cause of apparent treatment failure is checked first?

children.note: Unipolar depression may really be bipolar; psychosis may be organic. Revisit history, collateral and course before escalating.

manas.q: Which diagnostic error commonly hides behind resistant depression?

children.note: Screen for hypothyroidism, anaemia, HIV-related brain disease and other medical illness, and review medicines that worsen mood (e.g. corticosteroids).

manas.q: Which medical causes should be screened in resistant depression?

children.note: Alcohol and cannabis use, anxiety disorders, personality difficulties and ongoing stressors (poverty, violence, grief) all blunt treatment response.

manas.q: Which comorbidities commonly blunt treatment response?

children.note: Tobacco smoke induces CYP1A2, lowering clozapine and olanzapine levels; stopping smoking (e.g. on admission) can raise levels sharply and cause toxicity.

manas.q: Why does stopping smoking matter for a patient on clozapine?

children.note: Steps after the first failed antidepressants.
If partly helped and well tolerated, raise the dose within the usual range before switching.

manas.q: What is the first step if an antidepressant has partly helped?

children.note: Change to another SSRI or to a different class, e.g. an SNRI (venlafaxine), mirtazapine or a tricyclic. Cross-taper carefully to avoid interactions.

manas.q: What switching options exist in resistant depression?

children.note: Adding lithium to an antidepressant is a well-established augmentation; needs level, renal and thyroid monitoring and counselling about toxicity.

manas.q: Which mood stabiliser is a classic antidepressant augmenter?

children.note: Second-generation antipsychotics such as aripiprazole or quetiapine can be added; watch weight, glucose, sedation and akathisia.

manas.q: Which antipsychotics are used to augment antidepressants?

children.note: Adding mirtazapine to an SSRI or SNRI is a common combination; monitor for serotonin toxicity.

manas.q: Name a common antidepressant combination strategy.

children.note: Combining medicine with a structured therapy such as CBT helps more than either alone in many patients.

manas.q: Which non-drug treatment should be added in resistant depression?

children.note: An antidepressant alone can trigger mania or rapid cycling; treat bipolar depression with a mood stabiliser-based plan.

manas.q: Why avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar depression?

children.note: Consider ECT early when depression is severe, psychotic, life-threatening (not eating, high suicide risk) or after several failed strategies.

manas.q: When should ECT be considered in depression?

children.note: The one drug with proven superiority in TRS.
Clozapine is more effective than other antipsychotics in TRS and reduces suicidal behaviour in schizophrenia; delay in starting it worsens outcome.

manas.q: Which antipsychotic is best for treatment-resistant schizophrenia?

children.note: Before starting: FBC with neutrophil count, weight, BP, pulse, glucose, lipids and an ECG; record smoking status and other drugs.

manas.q: What baseline tests are needed before clozapine?

children.note: Start low and increase gradually to limit hypotension, sedation and seizures. If doses are missed for more than 48 h, re-titrate from the start.

manas.q: What should happen if clozapine doses are missed for over 48 hours?

children.note: Rare but potentially fatal, risk highest in the first months. Any sore throat or fever needs an urgent FBC; stop clozapine if neutrophils fall below the scheme’s threshold.

manas.q: What symptom needs an urgent FBC in a patient on clozapine?

children.note: Typical scheme (e.g. UK): FBC weekly for the first 18 weeks, then every 2 weeks to one year, then monthly while on treatment.

manas.q: What is a typical FBC monitoring schedule for clozapine?

children.note: Many people of African descent have a naturally lower neutrophil count (linked to the Duffy-null type); this needs adjusted thresholds and haematology advice, not automatic refusal.

manas.q: Why may baseline neutrophils be low in some African patients?

children.note: Mostly in the first weeks: fever, tachycardia, chest pain, breathlessness, flu-like illness. Many protocols check troponin and CRP early; stop clozapine if confirmed.

manas.q: When does clozapine myocarditis usually occur and how does it present?

children.note: Clozapine slows the gut; ileus, obstruction and aspiration can be fatal. Ask about bowels at every visit and treat early with softener and stimulant laxatives.

manas.q: Why is clozapine constipation dangerous?

children.note: Dose- and level-related; risk rises with high doses and fast titration. An anticonvulsant (e.g. valproate) may be added if seizures occur.

manas.q: What raises the risk of seizures on clozapine?

children.note: Common, worse at night; a towel on the pillow, dose review and an anticholinergic such as hyoscine hydrobromide can help.

manas.q: How is clozapine-induced hypersalivation managed?

children.note: Sedation, weight gain and metabolic syndrome, tachycardia, postural hypotension, early benign fever and nocturnal enuresis.

manas.q: List other common side effects of clozapine.

children.note: Levels guide dosing in non-response or toxicity; a common response threshold is about 0.35 mg/L, taken as a trough level.

manas.q: What clozapine plasma level is commonly used as a response threshold?

children.note: Exact mechanism is unknown; a generalised seizure is needed.
Benefit depends on a generalised cerebral seizure; a stimulus that fails to cause one is not effective.

manas.q: What must happen for an ECT treatment to be effective?

children.note: Repeated seizures change monoamine signalling (serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine) and raise GABA activity.

manas.q: Which neurotransmitter changes are proposed for ECT?

children.note: The seizure threshold rises over an ECT course; this inhibitory, anticonvulsant effect may be part of how it helps.

manas.q: What happens to seizure threshold over an ECT course?

children.note: Seizures release hypothalamic and pituitary hormones, which may correct mood-related neuroendocrine changes.

manas.q: What is the neuroendocrine theory of ECT?

children.note: ECT raises BDNF and is linked with hippocampal growth on imaging, suggesting repair of brain networks.

manas.q: Which neuroplastic changes are linked with ECT?

children.note: Valid consent and legal safeguards.
Needs capacity, full information (benefits, risks including memory effects, alternatives), free choice and a signature; it can be withdrawn at any time.

manas.q: What makes consent for ECT valid?

children.note: The Act sets the rights of people with mental illness and safeguards for treatment, including involuntary patients; follow it and hospital policy for ECT decisions.

manas.q: Which Kenyan law sets safeguards for treatment such as ECT?

children.note: If a severely ill patient lacks capacity, ECT may proceed only through the legal route the Act and hospital policy set, with documentation and review.

manas.q: How is ECT approached when a patient lacks capacity?

children.note: Few absolute bars; weigh risks against a dangerous illness.
Modern guidance lists no absolute contraindications; raised ICP is the one usually treated as near-absolute, as ECT raises cerebral blood flow and ICP, risking herniation.

manas.q: Which condition is usually treated as a near-absolute contraindication to ECT?

children.note: Recent myocardial infarction or stroke, cerebral aneurysm or vascular malformation, unstable heart disease and high anaesthetic risk.

manas.q: List relative contraindications to ECT.

children.note: Pregnancy and old age are not contraindications; ECT can be safer than drugs in some pregnant or elderly patients.

manas.q: Are pregnancy and old age contraindications to ECT?

children.note: Modified ECT: anaesthesia, relaxant, monitoring.
Physical exam, anaesthetic review, basic bloods and ECG as indicated, fasting, and review of drugs that change seizure threshold.

manas.q: What work-up is done before ECT?

children.note: Benzodiazepines and anticonvulsants raise seizure threshold and may blunt ECT; reduce or time them with the team.

manas.q: Which drugs raise seizure threshold during ECT?

children.note: A short-acting IV anaesthetic plus a muscle relaxant (usually suxamethonium) with oxygen and a bite block; the relaxant prevents fractures and injury.

manas.q: Why is a muscle relaxant given during ECT?

children.note: ECG, oxygen saturation, BP and EEG; seizure duration is timed and recorded each session.

manas.q: What is monitored during ECT?

children.note: Electrodes on both temples: works faster and more reliably, but causes more memory and cognitive effects.

manas.q: What are the pros and cons of bilateral ECT?

children.note: Over the non-dominant (right) hemisphere: fewer memory effects, but needs a dose well above seizure threshold to work.

manas.q: What are the pros and cons of right unilateral ECT?

children.note: Dose set by seizure-threshold titration or a formula; treatments usually 2–3 times a week, typically a course of about 6–12.

manas.q: How often is ECT given and how long is a usual course?

children.note: Beyond the common early effects.
Brief vagal bradycardia, then a surge of tachycardia and hypertension during the seizure; arrhythmia is possible, hence cardiac caution.

manas.q: What cardiovascular changes occur during ECT?

children.note: Gaps for events around the course (autobiographical memory) are most typical; new learning usually recovers within weeks, but some report lasting gaps.

manas.q: Which type of memory is most affected by ECT?

children.note: Muscle aches (suxamethonium), nausea, dental or tongue injury, prolonged seizure, and switch into mania in bipolar illness.

manas.q: List other adverse effects of ECT.

children.note: Relapse after a good ECT response is common without follow-on treatment: continue antidepressant (often with lithium) or plan maintenance ECT.

manas.q: How is relapse prevented after successful ECT?

children.note: High-yield points.
Fever or sore throat on clozapine = urgent FBC for agranulocytosis.

manas.q: What must you do when a patient on clozapine has a sore throat?

children.note: Bilateral: speed and efficacy. Right unilateral: fewer memory effects. Choose by urgency and patient priorities.

manas.q: What is the key trade-off between unilateral and bilateral ECT?

children.note: Both TRD and TRS start from two adequate failed trials — but only after pseudo-resistance is excluded.

manas.q: How many adequate trials define treatment resistance?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then where other guidance differs.
The National Clinical Guidelines for Management of Common Mental Disorders are the local reference; drug choices follow the Kenya Essential Medicines List.

manas.q: Which Kenyan documents guide resistant illness treatment?

children.note: WHO guidance opposes unmodified ECT (without anaesthesia and muscle relaxant) and stresses informed consent and human rights.

manas.q: What form of ECT does WHO guidance oppose?

links.title: Kenya MoH

children.note: International working group criteria define TRS by at least two failed adequate antipsychotic trials, with adherence checked and symptoms rated.

manas.q: What did the TRRIP consensus define?

links.title: Kenya MoH

children.note: UK advice: offer clozapine after two adequate antipsychotic trials, at least one a non-clozapine second-generation drug.

manas.q: When does NICE CG178 advise offering clozapine?

links.title: Kenya MoH

children.note: The US FDA approved esketamine nasal spray in 2019 with an oral antidepressant for treatment-resistant depression (use alone approved 2025); given under supervision in certified settings.

manas.q: Which newer drug is approved in the USA for resistant depression?

links.title: Kenya MoH

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-25.
Meta-analysis (6 studies, 676 people): no significant difference in response, remission, relapse or adverse events; heterogeneity high for response and remission, so authors call for validation.

manas.q: How did ketamine compare with ECT for resistant depression in a 2026 meta-analysis?

children.note: Review (12 studies, 837 people): within a month delayed recall and autobiographical memory fell while self-rated memory improved; later recall improved but autobiographical memory stayed lower. Heterogeneous.

manas.q: Which memory type stayed lower beyond a month after ECT in a 2026 review?

children.note: Review (16 studies): no clear rise in confusion or cognitive test decline with lithium during ECT, but one analysis method suggested more confusion; evidence inconclusive.

manas.q: Does continuing lithium during ECT clearly worsen cognition, per a 2026 review?

maps.title: HSU 600 · In depth: Acute appendicitis

nodeData.note: Anatomy, why it happens, scores, imaging, special groups, operation and complications. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What appendicitis is and how it is classed.
Acute inflammation of the vermiform appendix; commonest in older children, teenagers and young adults, but seen at every age.

manas.q: Which age group most often gets acute appendicitis?

children.note: Uncomplicated: inflamed, intact appendix. Complicated: gangrene, perforation, abscess or phlegmon/mass. The split drives treatment.

manas.q: What makes appendicitis complicated?

children.note: Where to find it and how it is supplied.
A blind tube arising from the posteromedial caecum below the ileocaecal junction; its length varies widely.

manas.q: Where does the appendix arise?

children.note: The base is constant: the three taeniae coli converge on it, so surgeons follow a taenia down the caecum to find it.

manas.q: How does a surgeon find the base of the appendix?

children.note: The tip varies: retrocaecal is commonest, pelvic next; also subcaecal, pre-ileal, post-ileal and paracaecal.

manas.q: What is the commonest position of the appendix?

children.note: A branch of the ileocolic artery (from the superior mesenteric), running in the free edge of the mesoappendix.

manas.q: From which artery does the appendicular artery arise?

children.note: The appendicular artery has no useful collaterals, so swelling or thrombosis quickly leads to gangrene and perforation.

manas.q: Why does the inflamed appendix become gangrenous quickly?

children.note: A small triangular fold of peritoneum from the mesentery of the terminal ileum, carrying the appendicular vessels.

manas.q: What is the mesoappendix and what does it carry?

children.note: The wall is rich in lymphoid follicles, most abundant in youth and shrinking with age — fitting the age pattern of appendicitis.

manas.q: How does appendiceal lymphoid tissue relate to the age of patients?

children.note: From a blocked lumen to perforation.
The usual trigger: the lumen is blocked, mucus builds up and pressure rises inside a closed loop.

manas.q: What usually starts acute appendicitis?

children.note: A hard faecal stone (appendicolith) is a common cause in adults and is linked with a higher risk of perforation.

manas.q: What obstructs the appendix most often in adults?

children.note: Swollen lymphoid follicles, often after a viral or gut infection, are a common cause in children.

manas.q: What obstructs the appendix most often in children?

children.note: Worms (Ascaris, Enterobius), foreign bodies and tumours (neuroendocrine tumour of the appendix, caecal cancer in older adults).

manas.q: List less common causes of appendiceal obstruction.

children.note: Distension → venous congestion → arterial ischaemia → bacterial invasion of the wall → gangrene → perforation.

manas.q: Describe the sequence from obstruction to perforation.

children.note: Mixed gut flora, mainly Gram-negative rods (E. coli) and anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis).

manas.q: Which organisms are involved in appendicitis?

children.note: The omentum and loops may wall off a perforation (mass or abscess); in young children the short omentum often fails, giving generalised peritonitis.

manas.q: Why do young children more often get generalised peritonitis?

children.note: The position of the tip changes the picture.
Flank or loin pain, few anterior signs, a positive psoas sign; may cause a few red or white cells in urine.

manas.q: How does a retrocaecal appendicitis present?

children.note: Suprapubic pain, diarrhoea or urinary frequency, little abdominal tenderness but tenderness on rectal or vaginal examination.

manas.q: How does a pelvic appendicitis present?

children.note: Vomiting and diarrhoea with poorly localised pain; easily mistaken for gastroenteritis.

manas.q: Which appendix position mimics gastroenteritis?

children.note: Low-grade fever is typical; high fever suggests perforation or another diagnosis.

manas.q: What does a high fever suggest in suspected appendicitis?
