children.note: Mesenteric adenitis, gastroenteritis, Meckel’s diverticulitis, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian cyst or torsion, PID, ureteric colic, UTI and terminal ileitis.

manas.q: List the main differential diagnoses of appendicitis.

children.note: Tests, scores and imaging.
Every woman of childbearing age with RIF pain needs a pregnancy test to exclude ectopic pregnancy.

manas.q: Which test is mandatory in a woman of childbearing age with RIF pain?

children.note: Helps exclude UTI and stones, but mild pyuria or haematuria can occur when the appendix lies near the ureter or bladder.

manas.q: Does pyuria exclude appendicitis?

children.note: Raised white count and CRP support the diagnosis; when both are normal, appendicitis is less likely.

manas.q: Which blood tests support the diagnosis of appendicitis?

children.note: Better at ruling out (low score) than ruling in; a high score still benefits from imaging or senior review.

manas.q: Is the Alvarado score better for ruling in or ruling out appendicitis?

children.note: Appendicitis Inflammatory Response score: vomiting, RIF pain, graded rebound/guarding, fever, WBC, neutrophil % and CRP. 0–4 low, 5–8 intermediate, 9–12 high risk.

manas.q: What does the AIR score include, and what are its risk bands?

children.note: A child-specific score that includes pain on coughing, percussion or hopping, plus migration, anorexia, fever, nausea and blood counts.

manas.q: Which score is designed for children with suspected appendicitis?

children.note: First imaging in children, pregnancy and slim young women. Graded compression: a non-compressible, blind-ending tube over 6 mm wide suggests appendicitis.

manas.q: What ultrasound finding suggests appendicitis?

children.note: Contrast CT is the most accurate test in adults when the diagnosis is unclear; it also shows perforation, abscess and other causes.

manas.q: What is the most accurate imaging test for appendicitis in adults?

children.note: If ultrasound is inconclusive in pregnancy, MRI without contrast avoids radiation.

manas.q: What imaging follows an inconclusive ultrasound in pregnancy?

children.note: When doubt remains after assessment and imaging, laparoscopy both diagnoses and treats.

manas.q: What can be done when the diagnosis remains uncertain?

children.note: Who is easy to miss.
Vague history, rapid progression and high perforation rates, especially under 5; mesenteric adenitis after a sore throat is a key mimic.

manas.q: Why is appendicitis dangerous in young children?

children.note: The commonest non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy; pain may sit higher as the uterus displaces the caecum. Perforation threatens the fetus.

manas.q: What is the commonest non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy?

children.note: Do not delay operation; laparoscopic appendicectomy can be done in pregnancy with obstetric input and fetal monitoring.

children.note: Signs are muted and perforation is more common at presentation; CT helps, and caecal cancer and diverticulitis must be considered.

manas.q: Which diagnoses must be considered alongside appendicitis in older adults?

children.note: Ileocaecal TB (weight loss, night sweats, RIF mass, ascites), typhoid with ileal perforation, amoebic colitis/amoeboma, and in advanced HIV CMV colitis and lymphoma.

manas.q: Which conditions mimic appendicitis in people with HIV in Kenya?

children.note: In neutropenic patients (e.g. on chemotherapy) RIF pain may be typhlitis of the caecum, usually managed medically first.

manas.q: What is typhlitis and who gets it?

children.note: From ward to theatre.
Nil by mouth, IV fluids, analgesia, and IV antibiotics before surgery; resuscitate fully if septic or peritonitic.

manas.q: What are the pre-operative steps in appendicitis?

children.note: Cover Gram-negatives and anaerobes, e.g. a cephalosporin with metronidazole, following local guidelines.

manas.q: Which organisms must antibiotics for appendicitis cover?

children.note: Appendicectomy; antibiotics after surgery are usually not needed for an uncomplicated case.

manas.q: Are postoperative antibiotics needed after simple appendicectomy?

children.note: Appendicectomy with washout of pus and a short postoperative antibiotic course; generalised peritonitis may need laparotomy.

manas.q: How is perforated appendicitis managed?

children.note: Less wound infection and pain, faster recovery, and a view of the whole abdomen — useful in women and obese patients.

manas.q: What are the advantages of laparoscopic appendicectomy?

children.note: Safe and effective; still the main option where laparoscopy is unavailable.

manas.q: Is open appendicectomy still acceptable?

children.note: Oblique incision through McBurney’s point at right angles to the spino-umbilical line; each muscle layer is split along its fibres.

manas.q: Describe the gridiron incision.

children.note: A transverse skin-crease incision in the RIF, centred near the midclavicular line; better cosmetically, deeper layers split as for gridiron.

manas.q: How does the Lanz incision differ from the gridiron incision?

children.note: Deliver the caecum, follow a taenia to the base, ligate the mesoappendix (appendicular artery), ligate and divide the base, remove the appendix.

manas.q: What are the key steps of appendicectomy?

children.note: Every specimen goes to histology: an unexpected neuroendocrine tumour or other neoplasm may be found.

manas.q: Why is every appendix sent for histology?

children.note: Search for another cause: Meckel’s diverticulum, terminal ileum, ovaries and tubes, and mesenteric nodes.

manas.q: What should you look for if the appendix is normal at operation?

children.note: Not routine for everyone after a treated mass or abscess; older adults need follow-up imaging or colonoscopy to exclude a tumour.

manas.q: Is interval appendicectomy routine after an appendix mass?

children.note: During and after the illness.
More likely with delay, faecoliths, young children and older adults.

manas.q: Which factors raise the risk of perforation?

children.note: Swinging fever, diarrhoea with mucus and a tender boggy mass on rectal examination; drained radiologically or via the rectum.

manas.q: How does a pelvic abscess after appendicitis present?

children.note: The commonest complication after appendicectomy, more so after perforation.

manas.q: What is the commonest complication after appendicectomy?

children.note: Intra-abdominal abscess, ileus, later adhesive obstruction, faecal fistula, stump appendicitis and port-site hernia.

manas.q: List other complications after appendicectomy.

children.note: Rare septic thrombosis of the portal vein: rigors, high fever and jaundice, sometimes with liver abscesses.

manas.q: What is pylephlebitis?

children.note: High-yield points.
The base is where the taeniae coli meet — the tip may be anywhere.

manas.q: Where is the base of the appendix always found?

children.note: On ultrasound, a non-compressible appendix wider than 6 mm suggests appendicitis.

manas.q: What diameter on ultrasound suggests appendicitis?

children.note: In Kenya, chronic RIF pain with weight loss, or fever with perforation, should prompt TB and typhoid before calling it appendicitis.

manas.q: Which two infections must Kenyan doctors consider in RIF disease?

children.note: Kenya first, then how guidance compares.
Follow the MoH Clinical Guidelines for Level 4–6 hospitals and your local surgical protocol for appendicitis.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers hospital care of appendicitis?

children.note: WHO’s checklist (sign in, time out, sign out) applies to every appendicectomy and reduces avoidable errors.

manas.q: Which WHO tool applies to every appendicectomy?

links.title: Kenya MoH

children.note: The World Society of Emergency Surgery appendicitis guideline (updated 2020) uses scores and imaging to stratify risk and favours laparoscopy where available.

manas.q: How do the WSES Jerusalem guidelines approach diagnosis?

links.title: Kenya MoH

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-25.
Expert panel (GRADE, review of 2010–2022): conditional advice favouring operative management of uncomplicated and complicated appendicitis, delayed (>12 h) or immediate. Abstract truncated.

manas.q: What did the 2024 SAGES guideline conditionally advise for appendicitis?

children.note: GRADE-based national guidance for adults and children aiming at uniform, safe, cost-efficient care amid wide practice variation (shown by a national survey). Abstract gives no specific advice.

manas.q: Why were Swedish national appendicitis guidelines written?

children.note: Meta-analysis of RCTs (1333 children): complication-free success at 30 days favoured appendicectomy (moderate certainty); 6–24% recurred within a year after antibiotics.

manas.q: In children, what did a 2026 meta-analysis find for antibiotics versus appendicectomy?

maps.title: HCH 400 · In depth: Primary Health Care

nodeData.note: History, Astana's three parts, the 4 Cs, UHC, Kenya's levels, laws and funding, and how PHC is measured. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Where PHC came from and what it means.
Essential care, based on sound and acceptable methods, made universally reachable for families through their full participation, at a cost community and country can afford.

manas.q: How did Alma-Ata define primary health care?

children.note: Held in Alma-Ata (now Almaty, Kazakhstan) in September 1978, called by WHO and UNICEF; Halfdan Mahler was WHO Director-General.

manas.q: Which two agencies convened the Alma-Ata conference?

children.note: Inspired by community-based models such as China's barefoot doctors and village health worker schemes that reached rural people cheaply.

manas.q: Which Chinese scheme helped inspire the PHC idea?

children.note: The goal, set at the 1977 World Health Assembly and carried into Alma-Ata, of a level of health letting everyone lead socially and economically productive lives.

manas.q: What did 'Health for All' aim at?

children.note: Global Conference on PHC in Astana, Kazakhstan, October 2018, 40 years after Alma-Ata; called PHC the cornerstone of UHC and the SDGs.

manas.q: What did the Astana Declaration call PHC?

children.note: The WHO/UNICEF 2018 vision describes PHC as three linked parts.
Primary care plus essential public health functions at the core of integrated services across a person's life.

manas.q: What sits at the core of PHC's first component?

children.note: Acting on wider determinants (water, food, housing, education, income) through all sectors, not health alone.

manas.q: What is PHC's multisectoral component about?

children.note: People and communities as co-producers of health: informed, involved in decisions and in self-care.

manas.q: What is the third component of PHC per Astana?

children.note: Two terms often confused.
The first-level clinical service: a clinician or team seeing individuals for most of their health needs.

manas.q: Is primary care the same as primary health care?

children.note: A whole-of-society approach: primary care plus public health functions, multisectoral action and community empowerment.

manas.q: What does PHC include beyond primary care?

children.note: What the classic principles look like on the ground.
Put services where the poor and remote live; remove fees for basic care; track gaps by wealth, gender and place.

manas.q: Give a practical example of equity in PHC.

children.note: Community health committees and health facility management committees plan, oversee and help fund local services.

manas.q: Name a structure for community participation in PHC.

children.note: Health works with water, agriculture, education and roads, e.g. school health and latrine campaigns.

manas.q: Give an example of intersectoral action for health.

children.note: Simple, affordable, acceptable tools: ORS, malaria RDTs, partographs, growth charts.

manas.q: Give three examples of appropriate technology in PHC.

children.note: Barbara Starfield's core functions of strong primary care.
The usual entry point for new problems; access must be easy in time, distance and cost.

manas.q: What does 'first contact' mean in primary care?

children.note: A lasting relationship with one clinician or team over time (longitudinality), not one-off visits.

manas.q: What is longitudinality?

children.note: Handles most needs across ages and conditions, from prevention to chronic care, referring the rest.

manas.q: What does comprehensiveness mean in primary care?

children.note: Primary care links the patient's care across specialists, hospitals and services and keeps the record whole.

manas.q: Which C means primary care links care across services?

children.note: Starfield added family-centredness, community orientation and cultural competence.

manas.q: Name Starfield's derived features of primary care.

children.note: Her work linked stronger primary care with better population health, fairer outcomes and lower costs.

manas.q: What did Starfield link strong primary care with?

children.note: The debate after Alma-Ata.
Argued in NEJM that full PHC was unaffordable and proposed selective PHC: a few cheap, high-impact interventions.

manas.q: Who proposed selective primary health care?

children.note: Fast, measurable gains in child survival; easy to fund and monitor.

manas.q: What is the main argument for selective PHC?

children.note: Vertical programmes fragment services, ignore determinants and community voice, and weaken the system.

manas.q: Why do critics oppose selective PHC?

children.note: Use disease programmes to build shared system parts (staff, supply, data) that serve all.

manas.q: What is the diagonal approach?

children.note: How PHC delivers universal health coverage.
Everyone gets the quality services they need without financial hardship (SDG target 3.8).

manas.q: Which SDG target is universal health coverage?

children.note: Who is covered, which services are covered, and how much of the cost is covered.

manas.q: What are the three dimensions of UHC coverage?

children.note: SDG 3.8.2 counts households spending over 10% or 25% of their budget on health out of pocket.

manas.q: Which thresholds define catastrophic health spending in SDG 3.8.2?

children.note: WHO/UNICEF framework turning Astana into action: 14 levers.
Political commitment and leadership; governance and policy; funding and resource allocation; engaging communities and stakeholders.

manas.q: Name the four strategic levers of the 2020 PHC framework.

children.note: Models of care, workforce, infrastructure, medicines and products, private sector, purchasing, digital health, quality, research, monitoring.

manas.q: How many operational levers does the 2020 PHC framework list?

children.note: How Kenya organises PHC.
The Kenya Essential Package for Health groups services by level.
Community: community health units run by community health promoters.

manas.q: What is KEPH level 1?

children.note: Level 2 dispensaries and clinics; level 3 health centres and maternity or nursing homes.

manas.q: Which facilities are KEPH levels 2 and 3?

children.note: Primary (sub-county) hospitals: first-referral care.

manas.q: What is a level 4 facility?

children.note: Level 5 county referral (secondary) hospitals; level 6 national referral (tertiary) hospitals.

manas.q: What are KEPH levels 5 and 6?

children.note: Kenya Health Policy 2014–2030 groups the six levels into community, primary care, county referral and national referral tiers.

manas.q: What are Kenya's four tiers of care?

children.note: Usually about 5,000 people (about 1,000 households); CHPs supervised by a community health assistant/officer and linked to a nearby facility.

manas.q: Roughly how many people does a community health unit serve?

children.note: Renamed from community health volunteers in 2023; visit homes, teach, screen, refer and report through the eCHIS.

manas.q: What were community health promoters previously called?

children.note: Puts primary health care and community health services into law, giving Primary Care Networks (already in national policy) a legal basis.

manas.q: Which 2023 Kenyan law gives Primary Care Networks a legal basis?

children.note: A hub (usually a level 4 hospital) linked to spokes (levels 2–3 and CHUs) with a shared multidisciplinary team.

manas.q: What is the hub of a Primary Care Network?

children.note: Paying for PHC in Kenya.
In October 2023 Kenya passed the PHC, Social Health Insurance, Digital Health and Facility Improvement Financing Acts.

manas.q: Name the four health Acts Kenya passed in 2023.

children.note: The SHA replaced NHIF under the Social Health Insurance Act 2023.

manas.q: Which body replaced NHIF?

children.note: Primary Healthcare Fund; Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF); Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund.

manas.q: Name the three funds under the Social Health Authority.

children.note: Pays for primary care services at the primary level, funded mainly by government money.

manas.q: What does the Primary Healthcare Fund pay for?

children.note: African Union states pledged in 2001 to give at least 15% of government budgets to health; most countries still fall short.

manas.q: What share of budget did the Abuja Declaration pledge for health?

children.note: High out-of-pocket spending pushes families into poverty and delays care; pooled prepayment protects them.

manas.q: Why is out-of-pocket payment bad for PHC?

children.note: People who deliver PHC.
Clinical officers, nurses, midwives, doctors, public health officers, pharmacists and CHPs share PHC work.

manas.q: Who forms a PHC team in Kenya?

children.note: WHO's 2016 HRH strategy uses 4.45 doctors, nurses and midwives per 1,000 people as an SDG marker.

manas.q: What health-worker density does WHO link to UHC?

children.note: Why PHC falls short.
Budgets favour hospitals; primary levels get too little for drugs, staff and upkeep.

manas.q: Why are primary facilities often underfunded?

children.note: Patients skip weak dispensaries for hospitals, crowding referral care and wasting resources.

manas.q: What is bypassing of primary facilities?

children.note: Missing drugs, tests and staff erode trust in primary facilities.

manas.q: How do stock-outs harm PHC?

children.note: Systems built for maternal-child and infectious care must add chronic disease and mental health.

manas.q: Which disease shift strains PHC systems?

children.note: Tracking whether PHC works.
Primary Health Care Performance Initiative (2015): a partnership that publishes country Vital Signs Profiles on PHC.

manas.q: What does PHCPI publish for countries?

children.note: Follows system → inputs → service delivery → outputs → outcomes, so gaps can be traced to their cause.

manas.q: What chain does the PHCPI framework follow?

children.note: Immunisation coverage, skilled birth attendance, ANC visits, hypertension control and TB treatment success.

manas.q: Name tracer indicators of PHC performance.

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then other models.
PHC via KEPH levels, community health units, PCNs and the SHA's Primary Healthcare Fund.

manas.q: How does Kenya deliver PHC?

children.note: Leads Astana follow-up with UNICEF and the 2020 Operational Framework; monitors UHC with the World Bank.

manas.q: Which agency co-leads PHC with WHO?

children.note: Health Extension Programme: salaried, mostly female health extension workers at village health posts.

manas.q: What is Ethiopia's PHC programme called?

children.note: Family Health Strategy: teams with community health agents assigned to defined populations.

manas.q: What is Brazil's PHC model called?

children.note: NHS general practitioners act as gatekeepers: most specialist care needs a GP referral.

manas.q: How does UK primary care act as gatekeeper?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-27 (Europe PMC).
Mixed-methods study, 7 counties: PCN success went with strong county leadership, prioritised PHC funding, intersectoral work and joint planning; staff gaps meant sub-county teams served as MDTs.

manas.q: What made Primary Care Networks work in a 2025 study of seven Kenyan counties?

children.note: Realist synthesis of a scoping review: key features were community-set priorities and ongoing two-way communication; context, power, representation and culture shaped impact.

manas.q: What decides whether community engagement in PHC succeeds?

children.note: Scoping review (74 studies): governance shapes PHC through policy and plans, levers like decentralisation, regulation and supply chains, use of evidence, accountability and coordination.

manas.q: Which governance functions shape PHC delivery, per a 2025 scoping review?

maps.title: HDR 400 · In depth: Radiation protection

nodeData.note: Types, units, cell damage, thresholds, ICRP limits, pregnancy, children, dose-saving and staff safety. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What ionising radiation is.
Radiation with enough energy to knock electrons off atoms, creating ions that damage molecules such as DNA.

manas.q: What makes radiation 'ionising'?

children.note: Photons: penetrating, stopped by lead or concrete. X-rays come from machines and stop when switched off.

manas.q: Does an X-ray room stay radioactive after the machine is off?

children.note: Electrons; travel millimetres in tissue and are stopped by plastic or thin aluminium.

manas.q: What stops beta particles?

children.note: Two protons and two neutrons; stopped by paper or skin but very damaging if taken inside the body.

manas.q: When are alpha particles most dangerous?

children.note: How dose is measured.
Absorbed dose: 1 joule of energy per kilogram of tissue. Old unit: 1 Gy = 100 rad.

manas.q: What does one gray measure?

children.note: Absorbed dose × radiation weighting factor: 1 for photons and electrons, 20 for alpha.

manas.q: What is the radiation weighting factor for alpha particles?

children.note: Sum of organ equivalent doses × tissue weighting factors; e.g. breast 0.12, gonads 0.08 (ICRP 103).

manas.q: What is the ICRP 103 tissue weighting factor for gonads?

children.note: For comparing exams and setting limits in populations, not for estimating one patient's own risk.

manas.q: Should effective dose be used for an individual's cancer risk?

children.note: Worldwide average about 2.4 mSv a year (UNSCEAR); radon is the largest single part.

manas.q: What is the largest source of natural background radiation?

children.note: Mechanisms of damage.
Radiation ionises DNA itself; dominant for high-LET radiation such as alpha particles.

manas.q: Which radiation acts mainly by direct action?

children.note: Radiation splits water, forming free radicals (especially hydroxyl) that attack DNA; main route for X-rays.

manas.q: How do X-rays mostly damage DNA?

children.note: The most harmful lesion; misrepair causes cell death, mutations or chromosome aberrations.

manas.q: Which DNA lesion is most harmful?

children.note: Oxygen fixes radical damage, so well-oxygenated cells are more sensitive than hypoxic ones.

manas.q: Are hypoxic cells more or less radiosensitive?

children.note: 1906 law: sensitivity is greatest in cells that divide often, have long dividing futures and are poorly differentiated.

manas.q: What does the Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau state?

children.note: Bone marrow, lymphoid tissue, gonads, gut lining and lens; lymphocytes are sensitive despite not dividing.

manas.q: Which blood cell is an exception to Bergonié–Tribondeau?

children.note: Tissue reactions with a threshold.
ICRP (2011) lowered the cataract threshold to about 0.5 Gy, prompting the lower lens limit.

manas.q: What is the ICRP threshold dose for cataract?

children.note: Transient skin reddening from about 2 Gy; a risk in long fluoroscopy-guided procedures.

manas.q: From about what skin dose does transient erythema start?

children.note: Temporary epilation from about 3 Gy; higher doses can cause permanent loss and ulceration.

manas.q: At about what dose does temporary hair loss occur?

children.note: Whole-body doses above about 1 Gy: marrow, then gut, then neurovascular syndromes as dose rises.

manas.q: Above roughly what whole-body dose does acute radiation syndrome start?

children.note: Chance effects with no threshold.
Probability rises with dose; severity does not.

manas.q: Does severity of a stochastic effect depend on dose?

children.note: Linear no-threshold: risk assumed proportional to dose down to zero; a cautious basis for protection.

manas.q: What does the LNT model assume?

children.note: ICRP 103 uses about 5.5% per sievert (detriment-adjusted cancer risk, whole population) for protection planning, not to predict one person's risk.

manas.q: About what nominal cancer risk per sievert does ICRP 103 use?

children.note: Shown in animals but not proven in humans, including atomic bomb survivors' children.

manas.q: Have heritable radiation effects been proven in humans?

children.note: The framework behind all rules.
ICRP 103 (2007): planned, emergency and existing exposure situations.

manas.q: What are ICRP's three exposure situations?

children.note: Occupational (workers), medical (patients, carers, research volunteers) and public.

manas.q: What are ICRP's three exposure categories?

children.note: Dose limits do not apply to medical exposure; justification and optimisation protect patients.

manas.q: Do dose limits apply to patients?

children.note: Set by ICRP 103 for planned exposures.
20 mSv a year averaged over 5 years, with no more than 50 mSv in any one year.

manas.q: What is the ICRP occupational effective dose limit?

children.note: 1 mSv a year effective dose.

manas.q: What is the public dose limit?

children.note: Occupational 20 mSv a year averaged over 5 years (no year over 50); public 15 mSv a year.

manas.q: What is the occupational eye lens dose limit?

children.note: After she declares pregnancy, keep the fetal dose to about 1 mSv for the rest of the pregnancy.

manas.q: What fetal dose limit applies for a pregnant worker?

children.note: Imaging a pregnant or possibly pregnant woman.
Fetal doses from most diagnostic exams are well below about 100 mGy, the level below which tissue effects are not expected.

manas.q: Do most diagnostic exams reach fetal threshold doses?

children.note: All-or-none period: a high dose either ends the pregnancy or causes no effect.

manas.q: What is the all-or-none period?

children.note: Weeks 3–8 after conception: organogenesis (malformation risk); weeks 8–15: most CNS-sensitive. Effects are not expected below about 100 mGy.

manas.q: Which weeks are most sensitive for fetal brain effects?

children.note: ICRP 84: fetal doses under 100 mGy are not a reason to end a pregnancy.

manas.q: Below what fetal dose does ICRP say termination is not justified?

children.note: UK practice: ask about pregnancy within a 28-day cycle; for high-dose pelvic exams book within 10 days of period start.

manas.q: What is the 10-day rule used for?

children.note: Why children need extra care.
Pearce and colleagues (Lancet 2012) linked higher cumulative childhood CT dose with raised relative risk of leukaemia and brain tumours; absolute risks were small.

manas.q: What did the 2012 Lancet paediatric CT study show?

children.note: US Alliance for Radiation Safety in Pediatric Imaging campaign: child-size the technique, scan only when needed, scan once and only the area needed.

manas.q: What does the Image Gently campaign promote?

children.note: Is this test needed?
Evidence-based lists showing the best first test for each clinical question.

manas.q: What do imaging referral guidelines tell you?

children.note: UK Royal College of Radiologists' referral guidance.

manas.q: Which body publishes iRefer?

children.note: American College of Radiology ratings of how suitable each test is for a scenario.

manas.q: What do ACR Appropriateness Criteria rate?

children.note: Lowest dose for a useful image.
Diagnostic reference levels: typical doses (often the 75th percentile nationally) to flag high practice. Not limits.

manas.q: Are diagnostic reference levels dose limits?

children.note: Higher kVp with lower mAs usually lowers patient dose, at some cost to contrast.

manas.q: How can kVp and mAs be adjusted to lower dose?

children.note: Restrict the beam to the area of interest; cuts patient dose and scatter and improves image contrast.

manas.q: How does collimation help?

children.note: Automatic exposure control and CT tube current modulation match exposure to body size.

manas.q: What does automatic exposure control do?

children.note: CT reconstruction that reduces noise, allowing lower-dose scans.

manas.q: How does iterative reconstruction allow lower CT doses?

children.note: Pulsed mode, last-image hold, short screening time, detector close to the patient, tube under the table.

manas.q: Name ways to lower dose in fluoroscopy.

children.note: Beyond time, distance, shielding.
Most staff dose comes from radiation scattered by the patient.

manas.q: What is the main source of staff dose?

children.note: With a horizontal C-arm beam, scatter is highest on the tube side; stand on the detector side.

manas.q: Which side of a C-arm should staff stand?

children.note: Usually 0.25–0.5 mm lead equivalent; block most scatter. Store hung, check for cracks.

manas.q: What lead equivalence do aprons usually have?

children.note: Protect the thyroid and eye lens, especially in interventional work.

manas.q: Which organs do collars and lead glasses protect?

children.note: Ceiling-suspended screens and table skirts shield the operator's head and legs.

manas.q: What does a ceiling-suspended screen protect?

children.note: TLD, OSL, film or electronic badges; worn under the apron at chest or waist, with a second outside the apron at the collar for heavy users.

manas.q: Where should a personal dosimeter be worn?

children.note: Gonad and fetal shields.
The AAPM advised stopping routine gonadal and fetal shielding in diagnostic imaging.

manas.q: What did AAPM advise in 2019 about patient shielding?

children.note: Small benefit; can hide anatomy, trigger AEC to raise dose, and is often misplaced.

manas.q: Why is routine contact shielding no longer advised?

children.note: Common failures.
Poor positioning or wrong settings double the dose for no gain.

manas.q: Why are repeat films a protection problem?

children.note: CT requests without a clear clinical question are a major source of avoidable dose.

manas.q: What is a leading cause of avoidable patient dose?

children.note: Kenya and global bodies, then others.
The Nuclear Regulatory Act 2019 set up the Kenya Nuclear Regulatory Authority, replacing the Radiation Protection Board.

manas.q: Which body did KNRA replace?

children.note: IAEA Basic Safety Standards (GSR Part 3, 2014), co-sponsored by WHO; WHO and IAEA's 2012 Bonn Call for Action.

manas.q: What are the IAEA Basic Safety Standards called?

children.note: Current ICRP general recommendations: the exposure situations, categories and limits most countries adopt.

manas.q: Which ICRP publication holds the current main recommendations?

children.note: EU directive that put the 20 mSv occupational lens limit into law for member states.

manas.q: Which EU directive set the 20 mSv lens limit?

children.note: NCRP advises; federal rules keep a 50 mSv annual occupational limit rather than ICRP's 20 mSv average.

manas.q: How does the US occupational limit differ from ICRP's?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-27 (Europe PMC).
Eur Radiol 2026 review: in plain films and interventional work, patient shielding offers minimal benefit and may raise dose (AEC interference) or force repeats; CT is unclear. Decide case by case.

manas.q: Why is routine patient contact shielding now questioned?

children.note: Systematic review (12 articles): only about 19% of African countries had published studies on paediatric CT DRLs, and values varied; standard child CT protocols are needed.

manas.q: What share of African countries had published paediatric CT DRLs in a 2025 review?
