nodeData.note: Artery and vein occlusions and hypertensive retinopathy: blood supply, signs, tests, treatment and traps. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: The three main conditions and how they are split.
Blocked central retinal artery (CRAO) or one branch (BRAO), infarcting the inner retina. An emergency: the eye's version of an ischaemic stroke.

manas.q: Why is retinal artery occlusion called an eye stroke?

children.note: Clot in the central retinal vein (CRVO), near the lamina cribrosa, or in a branch (BRVO), usually where an artery crosses it.

manas.q: Where do CRVO and BRVO clots usually form?

children.note: Non-ischaemic (commoner): retina still perfused, milder. Ischaemic: wide capillary dropout, poor vision, high new-vessel risk.

manas.q: What separates ischaemic from non-ischaemic CRVO?

children.note: Retinal arteriole damage from raised BP: slow sclerotic change in chronic hypertension; leaky, ischaemic change in malignant hypertension.

manas.q: What two patterns does hypertensive retinopathy take?

children.note: Why the retina behaves as it does when vessels fail.
Inner retina: central retinal artery (from ophthalmic, from internal carotid). Outer retina and photoreceptors: choroid via posterior ciliary arteries.

manas.q: Which vessels supply the inner and the outer retina?

children.note: The fovea has no inner retina, so the normal choroid glows through it while the swollen, pale ischaemic retina around it looks white.

manas.q: Why does CRAO give a cherry-red spot?

children.note: Some people have a cilioretinal artery from the ciliary circulation; in CRAO it can keep a strip of retina, and sometimes central vision, alive.

manas.q: How can a cilioretinal artery save vision in CRAO?

children.note: Inner retinal neurons die within hours of total artery block, so any useful treatment window is very short.

manas.q: Why is CRAO time-critical?

children.note: At arteriovenous crossings the artery and vein share a sheath; a stiff, thick artery squeezes the vein, causing turbulence and clot (BRVO).

manas.q: Why do branch vein occlusions start at AV crossings?

children.note: Non-perfused retina releases VEGF, which makes vessels leak (macular oedema) and grow new fragile vessels on retina, disc, iris and angle.

manas.q: What does VEGF from ischaemic retina cause?

children.note: What the patient reports and what you see.
Sudden painless severe loss in one eye, often counting fingers or worse; dense RAPD; white retina, cherry-red spot, thin arteries.

manas.q: What vision and pupil findings suggest CRAO?

children.note: Broken-up blood columns ('box-cars') in retinal arteries and veins show very slow or stopped flow, as in acute CRAO.

manas.q: What does box-carring of retinal vessels show?

children.note: Cholesterol (Hollenhorst): shiny, at branch points, from carotid. Platelet-fibrin: white, plug-like. Calcific: white, chunky, from heart valves.

manas.q: What is a Hollenhorst plaque and where does it come from?

children.note: Age over 50 with headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, aching shoulders, weight loss and high ESR/CRP. Ask in every older CRAO.

manas.q: Which symptoms point to giant cell arteritis in CRAO?

children.note: Sudden painless loss of part of the field; a sector of white retina along one artery, often with a visible embolus.

manas.q: How does BRAO present?

children.note: Mild to moderate blur; scattered haemorrhages in all four quadrants, dilated veins; little or no RAPD. Some cases later turn ischaemic.

manas.q: What are the features of non-ischaemic CRVO?

children.note: Severe loss, marked RAPD, dense haemorrhages, many cotton-wool spots; on angiography wide non-perfusion (classically 10 or more disc areas).

manas.q: What signs suggest ischaemic CRVO?

children.note: Sector of haemorrhages beyond an AV crossing, most often superotemporal. Blur if the macula is involved; may go unnoticed if not.

manas.q: Which retinal quadrant does BRVO most often affect?

children.note: Thick walls change the light reflex: copper wiring, then silver wiring. At crossings: AV nipping, vein tapering (Gunn) and deflection (Salus).

manas.q: What do copper and silver wiring mean?

children.note: Flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, macular star of hard exudates, disc swelling; choroidal infarcts may show as Elschnig spots.

manas.q: What are Elschnig spots?

children.note: Two common systems.
1: mild arteriolar narrowing. 2: marked narrowing, AV nipping. 3: plus haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, exudates. 4: plus papilloedema.

manas.q: What defines Keith–Wagener–Barker grade 4?

children.note: Mild: narrowing, nipping. Moderate: haemorrhages, microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots, exudates. Malignant: moderate plus disc swelling.

manas.q: What three grades does the Wong–Mitchell system use?

children.note: Mostly the same as for heart attack and stroke.
Age, hypertension (the leading risk for RVO), diabetes, high lipids, smoking. Carotid disease, AF and valve disease add embolic risk for CRAO.

manas.q: What is the leading systemic risk factor for retinal vein occlusion?

children.note: Raised eye pressure and open-angle glaucoma raise the risk of CRVO, so check pressure in both eyes.

manas.q: Which eye disease increases the risk of CRVO?

children.note: Look for hyperviscosity (myeloma, Waldenström, polycythaemia), thrombophilia, vasculitis (Behçet, sarcoid), oestrogen pills and sickle disease.

manas.q: What should you look for in a young patient with retinal vein occlusion?

children.note: Eye tests plus a full vascular work-up.
Acuity, RAPD, eye pressure in both eyes, dilated fundoscopy; gonioscopy and iris check for new vessels at CRVO follow-up.

manas.q: Why look at the iris and angle during CRVO follow-up?

children.note: Measures macular oedema in RVO and guides anti-VEGF timing. In acute CRAO it shows a thick, bright inner retina that later thins.

manas.q: What does OCT show in RVO and in acute CRAO?

children.note: CRAO: delayed artery filling. RVO: maps capillary non-perfusion to call it ischaemic, and shows leakage and new vessels.

manas.q: What does fluorescein angiography add in vein occlusion?

children.note: In anyone over 50 with CRAO, check ESR and CRP the same day to catch giant cell arteritis before the other eye goes.

manas.q: Which bloods are urgent in CRAO over age 50?

children.note: FBC, glucose or HbA1c, lipids, renal function; in young or bilateral cases add protein electrophoresis, viscosity and thrombophilia screen.

manas.q: Which extra bloods suit a young patient with bilateral RVO?

children.note: BP, ECG or rhythm monitoring for AF, carotid duplex, echocardiogram; brain imaging, as silent brain infarcts are found in some patients with CRAO.

manas.q: Which tests look for an embolic source after CRAO?

children.note: Repeated BP, urine dipstick, creatinine, ECG; look for secondary causes in the young, and treat retinopathy as target-organ damage.

manas.q: Which tests suit a patient with hypertensive retinopathy?

children.note: Eye treatment plus control of the cause.
Send at once to an emergency or stroke unit, as for a brain stroke; old eye measures (massage, paracentesis, pressure drops) are not proven.

manas.q: What is the first step in acute CRAO?

children.note: Not yet standard: thrombolysis in the stroke window is under trial and offered in some stroke centres; evidence is uncertain and bleeding risk real. Follow local protocol.

manas.q: Is thrombolysis standard for CRAO?

children.note: If GCA is likely, start high-dose steroids immediately; do not wait for temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound.

manas.q: Should steroids wait for biopsy when GCA is suspected?

children.note: Antiplatelet or anticoagulation (for AF), statin, BP and sugar control, stop smoking; carotid surgery for significant symptomatic stenosis.

manas.q: How is stroke risk reduced after retinal artery occlusion?

children.note: Control BP, diabetes, lipids and eye pressure. Routine anticoagulation is not used just for the eye.

manas.q: Is anticoagulation routine for retinal vein occlusion?

children.note: Repeated intravitreal anti-VEGF injections are first line for RVO macular oedema; steroid implants are an option in some patients.

manas.q: What is first-line treatment for macular oedema in RVO?

children.note: Grid laser helped BRVO macular oedema in older trials and is now second line; in CRVO it reduced oedema but did not improve vision.

manas.q: Does grid laser improve vision in CRVO macular oedema?

children.note: Pan-retinal photocoagulation when new vessels appear (iris, angle, disc, retina); in BRVO, laser to the ischaemic sector. Watch ischaemic CRVO closely.

manas.q: When is pan-retinal photocoagulation given in vein occlusion?

children.note: PRP plus anti-VEGF to regress vessels, and pressure-lowering drops; drainage tube or cyclodiode laser if pressure stays high.

manas.q: How is neovascular glaucoma treated?

children.note: Admit; lower BP in a controlled, gradual way, as too fast a fall can cause optic nerve or brain ischaemia. Retinal signs fade over weeks.

manas.q: Why lower BP gradually in malignant hypertension?

children.note: What follows the acute event.
Most eyes keep poor vision; optic atrophy follows. Some develop iris new vessels. Risk of stroke and heart attack is raised afterwards.

manas.q: What is the usual visual outcome after CRAO?

children.note: Macular oedema, neovascular glaucoma (ischaemic type, around 3 months), vitreous haemorrhage; the other eye also carries risk.

manas.q: When does neovascular glaucoma classically follow ischaemic CRVO?

children.note: Generally better than CRVO; problems are macular oedema, new vessels and vitreous haemorrhage.

manas.q: How does BRVO prognosis compare with CRVO?

children.note: Retinopathy signals damage elsewhere: higher risk of stroke, heart and kidney disease. Malignant changes can reverse with BP control.

manas.q: What does hypertensive retinopathy say about systemic risk?

children.note: Two other vascular patterns seen in Kenya.
Peripheral artery blocks lead to 'sea-fan' new vessels; proliferative disease is commoner in HbSC than HbSS.

manas.q: Which sickle genotype gets proliferative retinopathy most?

children.note: Cotton-wool spots and small haemorrhages, usually without symptoms; distinguish from CMV retinitis, which needs urgent treatment.

manas.q: What does HIV microvasculopathy look like?

children.note: High-yield points.
CRAO, CRVO, vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment, ischaemic optic neuropathy, wet macular degeneration.

manas.q: Name causes of sudden painless monocular vision loss.

children.note: Also seen in lipid storage diseases such as Tay–Sachs and Niemann–Pick, from lipid-laden ganglion cells around the fovea.

manas.q: Which childhood diseases also give a cherry-red spot?

children.note: Brief one-eye 'curtain' loss is a TIA: same-day stroke work-up including carotid imaging; check ESR/CRP if over 50 to exclude GCA.

manas.q: How should amaurosis fugax be handled?

children.note: Flame (nerve fibre layer) haemorrhages and AV nipping suggest hypertension; dot-blot and microaneurysms suggest diabetes.

manas.q: Which haemorrhage type points to hypertension rather than diabetes?

children.note: Local guidance first, then how others differ.
Hypertension and CVD care follows the Kenya MoH national cardiovascular disease guidelines (use the current edition); retinopathy counts as target-organ damage.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers hypertension and cardiovascular risk?

children.note: The WHO World Report on Vision (2019) asks countries to build integrated, people-centred eye care into primary care and UHC.

manas.q: Which 2019 WHO report sets the eye care agenda?

children.note: An American Heart Association scientific statement (2021) treats CRAO as a stroke: same-day stroke-centre assessment and vascular work-up.

manas.q: How does the AHA advise CRAO be handled?

children.note: The Royal College of Ophthalmologists' RVO guidance sets anti-VEGF or steroid implant choices and new-vessel monitoring.

manas.q: Which UK body issues retinal vein occlusion guidance?

children.note: Where cost limits care, bevacizumab is widely used off-label as the cheaper anti-VEGF; access and follow-up visits shape outcomes.

manas.q: Which anti-VEGF is commonly used where cost is a barrier?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-27 (Europe PMC).
A 2024 review: CRAO needs emergency care like a brain stroke; vision rarely recovers on its own, heart and stroke risk is raised, and no treatment is yet officially recommended.

manas.q: Why does a 2024 review call CRAO a stroke of the eye?

children.note: Pooled patient data (771 people, 72 publications): vision improved in about 74% given IV tPA within 4.5 h; earlier treatment was linked to better vision. No controlled proof yet.

manas.q: What did a 2024 pooled analysis find for early IV thrombolysis in CRAO?

children.note: Six small trials (223 people): no treatment clearly beat observation or simple measures; tPA brought more serious side effects. Evidence low certainty — bigger trials needed.

manas.q: What did the 2023 Cochrane review conclude about CRAO treatments?

children.note: A review of five RVO guidelines: anti-VEGF injections are first choice for macular oedema, with no clear advice on which drug; most were of low method quality (US PPP 2019 scored best).

manas.q: What first-line treatment for RVO macular oedema do guidelines agree on?

maps.title: HSU 604 · In depth: Otosclerosis and conductive loss

nodeData.topic: Otosclerosis and conductive loss in depth
nodeData.note: Causes of conductive deafness, how to test for it, otosclerosis in detail, and the ear operations that fix it. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What conductive loss means.
Sound is blocked in the outer or middle ear before reaching a normal cochlea: bone conduction is normal, air conduction is worse.

manas.q: In conductive loss, which conduction stays normal?

children.note: Pure conductive loss tops out around 60 dB, because sound can still reach the cochlea through the skull. More means a nerve component.

manas.q: Roughly how severe can pure conductive loss get?

children.note: Conductive and sensorineural loss together: bone thresholds are raised and there is still an air–bone gap.

manas.q: What audiogram defines mixed hearing loss?

children.note: How the middle ear amplifies sound.
The large drum over small footplate (about 17:1) and ossicular lever (about 1.3:1) boost pressure, roughly 25–30 dB of gain.

manas.q: How does the middle ear boost sound pressure?

children.note: Otosclerosis is abnormal remodelling of the dense otic capsule: active spongy vascular bone (otospongiosis) later turns hard and sclerotic.

manas.q: What bone disorder underlies otosclerosis?

children.note: The commonest site is just in front of the oval window; new bone spreads to the footplate and fixes the stapes.

manas.q: Where does otosclerosis most often start?

children.note: Foci reaching the cochlear lining add sensorineural loss, giving mixed loss; surgery can close the conductive part but cannot fix the nerve part.

manas.q: Why can otosclerosis cause sensorineural loss?

children.note: Work from outside inwards.
Wax impaction, otitis externa (swollen canal), foreign body, exostoses in cold-water swimmers, canal stenosis.

manas.q: Name outer-ear causes of conductive loss.

children.note: Glue ear: fluid behind an intact drum; the commonest cause of hearing loss in children. Adult one-sided OME needs a postnasal space check.

manas.q: Why examine the postnasal space in adult one-sided glue ear?

children.note: Loss depends on size and site of the hole and ossicle damage; chronic discharge with perforation is CSOM.

manas.q: What decides how much hearing a perforation costs?

children.note: Skin in the middle ear that erodes bone, often the incus long process, causing loss and foul discharge; an 'unsafe' ear.

manas.q: Which ossicle part does cholesteatoma often erode?

children.note: From head injury, erosion or surgery; with an intact drum it gives a large gap and a hypermobile (Ad) tympanogram.

manas.q: What tympanogram suits ossicular discontinuity with an intact drum?

children.note: Chalky scarring of the drum and middle ear after infection; can stiffen the ossicles.

manas.q: What is tympanosclerosis?

children.note: Microtia and canal atresia, ossicle malformations, and congenital cholesteatoma (white mass behind an intact drum).

manas.q: How does congenital cholesteatoma look on otoscopy?

children.note: Who gets it and how it shows.
Young adults, often starting age 20–40, women more than men; most cases bilateral. Less common in people of African descent.

manas.q: Which age group typically develops otosclerosis?

children.note: Often familial, autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance; measles virus has been linked to the disease.

manas.q: How is otosclerosis inherited?

children.note: Older texts say pregnancy and the pill worsen it; a 2023 Brazilian task force found no increased risk. Not settled fact — do not tell patients it is.

manas.q: Do pregnancy or the pill worsen otosclerosis?

children.note: Slowly worsening hearing, tinnitus; soft speech (own voice heard loudly by bone); hears better in noise (paracusis Willisii).

manas.q: Why do people with otosclerosis often speak softly?

children.note: The drum usually looks normal, which is the key clue in a young adult with conductive loss.

manas.q: What does the drum look like in otosclerosis?

children.note: A pink-red blush on the promontory seen through the drum, from active vascular otospongiosis; present in a minority.

manas.q: What is Schwartze sign?

children.note: 512 Hz fork: good balance of decay and feel.
Lower forks are felt as vibration and higher ones fade fast; 512 Hz gives the most reliable result.

manas.q: Which tuning fork frequency is standard for Rinne and Weber?

children.note: Air louder than bone (positive) is normal or sensorineural; bone louder (negative) means conductive loss, usually a gap of about 20 dB or more.

manas.q: What does a negative Rinne test mean?

children.note: In a dead or severely deaf ear, bone sound crosses to the good cochlea and seems louder; mask the good ear (Bárány box).

manas.q: What causes a false-negative Rinne?

children.note: Fork on the forehead: sound goes to the conductive-loss ear, or away from a sensorineural-loss ear; central if normal or equal.

manas.q: Which way does Weber lateralise in conductive loss?

children.note: Weber to left and Rinne negative on left: left conductive loss. Weber to left and Rinne positive both sides: right sensorineural loss.

manas.q: Weber to the left, Rinne positive both sides: what loss?

children.note: Objective confirmation.
On pure-tone audiometry, a gap of more than 10 dB between air and bone thresholds, with normal bone thresholds, means conductive loss.

manas.q: What audiogram finding shows conductive loss?

children.note: The 2 kHz bone dip is a mechanical effect of stapes fixation, not true cochlear damage; it often recovers after stapes surgery.

manas.q: Why can the Carhart notch improve after surgery?

children.note: When ears differ, the better ear must be masked so it does not answer for the tested ear.

manas.q: Why is masking used in audiometry?

children.note: Normal peak near 0 daPa with normal compliance: normal middle ear (seen in sensorineural loss).

manas.q: What does a type A tympanogram mean?

children.note: Shallow peak at normal pressure: stiff system, as in otosclerosis or tympanosclerosis.

manas.q: Which tympanogram type suits otosclerosis?

children.note: Very tall peak: floppy system, as in ossicular discontinuity or a thin scarred drum.

manas.q: What does a type Ad tympanogram suggest?

children.note: Flat: fluid (OME) with normal canal volume; perforation or open grommet with large volume; wax with small volume.

manas.q: How does canal volume help read a flat tympanogram?

children.note: Peak at negative pressure: Eustachian tube dysfunction or early or resolving glue ear.

manas.q: What does a type C tympanogram show?

children.note: Absent in otosclerosis because the fixed stapes cannot move; present reflexes argue against it.

manas.q: Is the stapedial reflex present in otosclerosis?

children.note: Used selectively.
Shows a lucent focus in front of the oval window; cochlear disease may show a lucent ring around the cochlea. Useful before surgery or if atypical.

manas.q: What does HRCT show in otosclerosis?

children.note: A thin or missing bone over the superior canal can mimic conductive loss, with very good bone thresholds and present reflexes; HRCT shows it.

manas.q: Which inner-ear condition can mimic otosclerosis?

children.note: Diffusion-weighted (non-EPI) MRI detects residual or recurrent cholesteatoma and can avoid a second-look operation.

manas.q: Which scan detects recurrent cholesteatoma?

children.note: Choice between aids and surgery.
Effective with no surgical risk; a good first choice and the safe option for anyone unfit for or unwilling to have surgery.

manas.q: What is the no-risk treatment for otosclerosis?

children.note: Clear air–bone gap with negative Rinne at 512 Hz, good speech discrimination, healthy middle ear; operate on the worse ear first.

manas.q: Which ear is operated on first in otosclerosis?

children.note: A small hole is made in the fixed footplate and a piston prosthesis hung from the incus; fewer inner-ear problems than removing the whole footplate.

manas.q: What is done in a stapedotomy?

children.note: Removal of all or most of the footplate with a prosthesis; largely replaced by stapedotomy.

manas.q: How does stapedectomy differ from stapedotomy?

children.note: About 9 in 10 operations close the air–bone gap well; cochlear loss is not reversed.

manas.q: How often does stapes surgery close the air–bone gap?

children.note: Avoid surgery on an only-hearing ear (a dead ear would leave total deafness), with active infection or perforation, or with active Ménière's disease.

manas.q: Why not operate on an only-hearing ear?

children.note: Some centres use it to slow cochlear otosclerosis; evidence is limited.

manas.q: What is sodium fluoride used for in otosclerosis?

children.note: Consent points.
Sensorineural loss, rarely total ('dead ear'), occurs in about 1% or less; the reason the only-hearing ear is avoided.

manas.q: How common is a dead ear after stapes surgery?

children.note: The taste nerve crosses the middle ear and may be stretched or cut: altered or metallic taste on that side of the tongue.

manas.q: Which nerve injury causes taste change after ear surgery?

children.note: Dizziness is common for a few days; lasting vertigo suggests perilymph leak or a long prosthesis.

manas.q: What does persistent vertigo after stapedotomy suggest?

children.note: Tinnitus, drum perforation, prosthesis slipping or incus erosion (late loss), and rarely facial nerve injury.

manas.q: What can cause late hearing loss after stapes surgery?

children.note: Avoid straining, heavy lifting and forceful nose-blowing early on, to protect the new seal at the oval window.

manas.q: Why avoid nose-blowing after stapes surgery?

children.note: Fixing drum and ossicles.
I: drum repair, ossicles intact. II: graft on incus. III: graft on stapes head. IV: graft on mobile footplate, round window shielded. V: fixed footplate (fenestration).

manas.q: What is a type I tympanoplasty?

children.note: Temporalis fascia is the usual graft; cartilage (tragal or conchal) resists retraction and suits high-risk or revision ears.

manas.q: When is cartilage preferred to fascia for a drum graft?

children.note: Partial prosthesis sits on the stapes head; total prosthesis goes to the footplate. A cartilage cap under the drum reduces extrusion.

manas.q: What is the difference between a PORP and a TORP?

children.note: Sends sound through the skull to the cochlea; suits canal atresia and chronically discharging ears that cannot take ordinary aids.

manas.q: Who suits a bone-anchored hearing aid?

children.note: Wax: drops, then microsuction; avoid irrigation with a known perforation. Persistent glue ear with hearing loss: grommets.

manas.q: When should ear irrigation be avoided?

children.note: Longer view.
Slowly progressive; may become mixed loss and later affect the other ear. Surgery treats the stapes, not the disease.

manas.q: Does stapes surgery stop otosclerosis?

children.note: Unrecognised loss in children delays speech and language and harms school progress; test any child with concerns.

manas.q: Why does conductive loss in children matter?

children.note: High-yield points.
Young adult (often a woman), slowly worsening hearing, family history, normal drum, negative Rinne, As tympanogram, absent stapedial reflex: otosclerosis.

manas.q: Name the classic otosclerosis case pattern.

children.note: Think superior canal dehiscence before stapes surgery; operating on the stapes will not help.

manas.q: What should present reflexes with a conductive gap make you think of?

children.note: Local guidance first, then how others differ.
Use the Kenya MoH clinical guidelines for level 4–6 hospitals for ear care, and refer surgical conductive loss to ENT.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers hospital ear care?

children.note: WHO World Report on Hearing (2021): about 1.5 billion people live with some hearing loss; it urges ear and hearing care in primary care.

manas.q: About how many people did WHO's 2021 report say have hearing loss?

children.note: NICE's adult hearing loss guideline covers referral and supports earwax removal in primary or community care.

manas.q: Which NICE guideline covers adult hearing loss?

children.note: The American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery cerumen guideline (updated 2017) advises treating wax when it causes symptoms or blocks an ear exam.

manas.q: When does the US earwax guideline advise removing wax?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-27 (Europe PMC).
Expert task force: contraceptives and pregnancy did not raise the risk of worsening; drugs showed little benefit; hearing aids if stapedotomy is declined; cochlear implant for profound loss.

manas.q: Did a 2023 task force find that pregnancy worsens otosclerosis?

children.note: Systematic review: 6+ months of sodium fluoride or bisphosphonates was reported to stabilise or improve hearing; newer drugs too little used to judge. A 2023 task force judged drug benefit small.

manas.q: Which drugs have been tried to slow otosclerosis, and how strong is the evidence?

children.note: Meta-analysis (2602 patients): redo surgery is mostly for returning conductive loss; prosthesis problems and incus necrosis are the commonest causes; most gaps close within 20 dB, dead-ear risk low.

manas.q: What usually causes failure needing revision stapes surgery?

maps.title: HSU 605 · In depth: Difficult airway management

nodeData.note: Definitions, anatomy, prediction, preparation, the A–D ladder, neck access, special groups and extubation. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: The words used when an airway goes wrong.
A trained person cannot keep the patient oxygenated with a face mask, even with adjuncts and help, because of poor seal or obstruction.

manas.q: What is difficult mask ventilation?

children.note: No part of the vocal cords can be seen with a conventional laryngoscope despite best effort (Cormack–Lehane grade 3 or 4).

manas.q: Which Cormack–Lehane grades count as difficult laryngoscopy?

children.note: Passing the tube needs repeated attempts, an adjunct, an operator change or a different device.

manas.q: When is tracheal intubation called difficult?

children.note: Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate: tube, SGA and face mask have all failed and saturation is falling. It is an emergency for front-of-neck access.

manas.q: What does CICO mean?

children.note: Many difficult airways are not predicted, so every induction needs a backup plan, not just the predicted-difficult ones.

manas.q: Why must every induction have a backup airway plan?

children.note: What you must find in the neck in seconds.
Lies in the midline between the lower border of the thyroid cartilage and the upper border of the cricoid; few large vessels lie over it.

manas.q: Between which cartilages does the cricothyroid membrane lie?

children.note: Non-dominant hand grips the larynx: thumb and finger on the thyroid laminae, slide down to the cricoid, index finger rests on the membrane.

manas.q: What is the laryngeal handshake for?

children.note: Finding the membrane by touch is unreliable in obesity, women and neck swelling; mark it, or ultrasound it, before induction when difficulty is expected.

manas.q: How can you find the cricothyroid membrane before induction if hard to feel?

children.note: Bedside tests help, but none is reliable alone; combine them and still plan for failure.
Look outside; Evaluate 3-3-2; Mallampati; Obstruction or obesity; Neck mobility.

manas.q: What does LEMON stand for?

children.note: Three fingers mouth opening, three fingers hyoid to chin, two fingers hyoid to thyroid notch; less suggests a difficult view.

manas.q: What is the 3-3-2 rule?

children.note: Seated, mouth open, tongue out. I: pillars and uvula seen; II: uvula seen; III: only soft palate and uvula base; IV: hard palate only.

manas.q: What is seen in Mallampati class IV?

children.note: Thyroid notch to chin tip with neck extended; under about 6 cm suggests a small mandibular space and hard view.

manas.q: What thyromental distance suggests difficulty?

children.note: Mask seal poor (beard, facial trauma), Obesity or obstruction, Age over 55, No teeth, Stiff lungs or snoring.

manas.q: What does MOANS predict?

children.note: Restricted mouth opening, Obstruction at or below larynx, Distorted airway, Stiff lungs or cervical spine.

manas.q: What does RODS predict?

children.note: Surgery or scar, Haematoma, Obesity, Radiation, Tumour: each makes front-of-neck access harder.

manas.q: What does SHORT predict?

children.note: Ask about previous difficult airway, alert cards, snoring and sleep apnoea, stridor, neck surgery or radiotherapy; read old anaesthetic charts.

manas.q: Which history items point to a difficult airway?

children.note: Buy time and share the plan before you start.
Tight-fitting mask with high-flow oxygen until end-tidal oxygen is about 90%; fills the lungs with an oxygen store.

manas.q: What end-tidal oxygen shows good preoxygenation?

children.note: Oxygen by nasal cannula or high-flow nasal oxygen during apnoea keeps oxygen flowing to alveoli and lengthens safe apnoea time.

manas.q: How does apnoeic oxygenation help?

children.note: Pad shoulders and head so ear canal lines up with sternal notch; head-up tilt improves preoxygenation, especially in obesity.

manas.q: What landmark alignment does ramping aim for?

children.note: Checked, standard layout: videolaryngoscope, bougies, SGAs, scalpel kit, tubes of several sizes, capnography; everyone knows where it is.

manas.q: Why should the difficult airway trolley have a standard layout?

children.note: Brief the team on Plans A to D, who does what, and the trigger for each switch; assign someone to call out saturation and time.

manas.q: What should the pre-induction team brief cover?

children.note: Devices that rescue the view, the tube or oxygenation.
Camera near the blade tip gives a view without lining up mouth and larynx; improves first-pass success when the view is hard.

manas.q: What advantage does a videolaryngoscope give?

children.note: Clicks as the tip runs over tracheal rings, and holdup at small bronchi; railroad the tube over it with a quarter turn anticlockwise.

manas.q: Which bougie signs suggest tracheal placement?

children.note: Has a gastric drain channel and higher seal pressure, so it protects better against aspiration; preferred for rescue.

manas.q: What makes an SGA 'second generation'?

children.note: Steerable scope used for awake intubation and to intubate through an SGA; needs skill and a clear, dry airway.

manas.q: When is a flexible bronchoscope most useful?

children.note: A stepwise ladder; the goal is oxygenation, not the tube.
Each laryngoscopy swells and bloodies the airway; keep attempts few, change something each time, then stop.

manas.q: Why limit laryngoscopy attempts?

children.note: Say 'failed intubation' aloud and move to the next plan; saying it ends fixation and alerts the team.

manas.q: Why should failed intubation be declared aloud?

children.note: Place a second-generation SGA; if oxygenating, stop and think: wake, intubate through SGA, continue surgery on SGA, or neck access.

manas.q: What are the options once an SGA rescues oxygenation?

children.note: Two-person mask technique with oral or nasal airway and full relaxation; if oxygenation works, usually wake the patient.

manas.q: What is the aim of Plan C?

children.note: When mask and SGA both fail and saturation falls, declare CICO and cut; delay causes brain injury and death.

manas.q: What triggers Plan D?

children.note: Scalpel–bougie–tube cricothyroidotomy in adults.
Extend the neck (pillow under shoulders), laryngeal handshake, index finger on the membrane.

manas.q: What is the first step of scalpel cricothyroidotomy?

children.note: Wide (size 10) blade transversely through skin and membrane, then turn the blade so the sharp edge points to the feet.

manas.q: Which way does the scalpel edge face after rotating?

children.note: Slide a bougie along the blade into the trachea, then railroad a small cuffed tube (about 6.0) and inflate.

manas.q: What size tube is railroaded in scalpel cricothyroidotomy?

children.note: Make a vertical midline skin cut, blunt-dissect with fingers to feel the larynx, then proceed as above.

manas.q: What do you do if the cricothyroid membrane is impalpable?

children.note: For predicted difficult airways where losing spontaneous breathing is unsafe.
The patient keeps breathing and airway tone while the tube is placed; safest choice when both mask and intubation look hard.

manas.q: Why intubate a predicted difficult airway awake?

children.note: sedation (light, optional), Topicalisation of the airway with local anaesthetic, Oxygenation throughout, Performance of the procedure.

manas.q: What does sTOP stand for in awake intubation?

children.note: Needs a cooperative patient; severe stridor or a near-obstructed airway may need awake tracheostomy under local instead.

manas.q: When may awake tracheostomy be chosen over awake intubation?

children.note: Where airway risk rises.
Failed intubation is more frequent; airway swelling, full stomach, fast desaturation. Decide early whether to wake or proceed on SGA.

manas.q: What key decision follows failed intubation at caesarean?

children.note: Small oxygen reserve (low FRC) means fast desaturation; ramp, preoxygenate head-up, use HFNO, mark the neck beforehand.

manas.q: Why do obese patients desaturate quickly?

children.note: Big occiput, large tongue, small airway and high oxygen use; in young children the membrane is tiny, so ENT tracheostomy or needle techniques are favoured.

manas.q: Why is scalpel cricothyroidotomy avoided in young children?

children.note: Manual in-line stabilisation, open the front of the collar; a videolaryngoscope reduces neck movement needs.

manas.q: How is the neck protected during intubation in C-spine injury?

children.note: Blood or vomit blocks the camera; use a rigid wide-bore suction first and a direct view may beat the video view.

manas.q: What helps when the airway is soiled with blood or vomit?

children.note: Deep neck abscess or epiglottitis: avoid lying flat or upsetting the patient; secure in theatre with ENT scrubbed for a surgical airway.

manas.q: Where should a swollen infected airway be secured?

children.note: Many airway disasters happen at the end, not the start.
At-risk: known difficult intubation, airway swelling, restricted access (wired jaw, halo), full stomach, unstable patient.

manas.q: Which patients are 'at-risk' at extubation?

children.note: Plan extubation as carefully as intubation, prepare patient and team, perform it, then give post-extubation care; most at-risk patients are extubated awake.

manas.q: What are the four steps of extubation planning?

children.note: Awake extubation, airway exchange catheter left in place, delaying extubation, or elective tracheostomy.

manas.q: What options exist for an at-risk extubation?

children.note: Most airway harm comes from people and systems, not anatomy.
Repeated attempts at the tube while saturation falls; a team member must say 'we are in CICO'.

manas.q: What is task fixation in airway crises?

children.note: Closed-loop communication, clear leader, any member can call for help or the next plan.

manas.q: How does closed-loop communication help in a crisis?

children.note: The single most important check of tube position.
A square waveform over several breaths confirms tracheal placement; chest movement and auscultation can mislead.

manas.q: What confirms tracheal tube placement?

children.note: Assume oesophageal intubation until proven otherwise; remove or check the tube, even in cardiac arrest where good CPR still gives a trace.

manas.q: What should a flat capnography trace make you assume?

children.note: What failed or rushed airway management causes.
Prolonged desaturation leads to cardiac arrest, brain damage or death — the main reason for early front-of-neck access.

manas.q: What is the most serious outcome of a failed airway?

children.note: Bleeding, false passage, surgical emphysema, pneumothorax; later subglottic stenosis.

manas.q: What are complications of cricothyroidotomy?

children.note: Quick points examiners like.
Ensure full neuromuscular block before declaring CICO; it can make mask or SGA work.

manas.q: What should be ensured before declaring CICO?

children.note: After a difficult airway, record what worked, tell the patient, give an alert letter and inform their usual doctor.

manas.q: What should follow a difficult airway event?

children.note: How guidance differs between bodies.
No national Kenyan difficult-airway algorithm is cited here; follow your hospital's protocol. International aids such as DAS or Vortex are common models.

manas.q: What should guide difficult airway care in a Kenyan hospital?

children.note: Sign-in asks 'difficult airway or aspiration risk?' and whether equipment and help are available.

manas.q: Which WHO checklist item covers the airway?

children.note: DAS publishes adult guidance on unanticipated difficult intubation (Plans A–D, updated 2025), obstetrics (with OAA), extubation and awake intubation.

manas.q: What does the UK Difficult Airway Society publish?

children.note: National audit of major airway complications; showed harm in ICU and ED and failures to use capnography.

manas.q: What did the NAP4 audit highlight?

children.note: American Society of Anesthesiologists practice guideline; broader, covers awake vs asleep choices and both adults and children.

manas.q: Which US body issues difficult airway practice guidelines?

children.note: Australian cognitive aid: three lifelines (mask, SGA, tube); if none gives oxygenation, move to front-of-neck access.

manas.q: What are the three lifelines in the Vortex approach?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-27 (Europe PMC).
Keeps plans A–D. Priorities: oxygen delivery all through, best chance of success at the first attempt, waveform capnography, moving on when a plan fails, and teamwork.

manas.q: What do the DAS 2025 guidelines prioritise?

children.note: Meta-analysis (227 articles, no obvious airway problems): modified Mallampati caught about 39% of difficult intubations (specificity 86%); no single test clearly best — combine.

manas.q: How sensitive is the modified Mallampati test for difficult intubation?

children.note: Meta-analysis (60 studies): ultrasound finds the cricothyroid membrane better than palpation and skin-to-epiglottis depth helps predict difficult intubation.

manas.q: How does ultrasound compare with palpation for finding the cricothyroid membrane?

maps.title: HSU 606 · In depth: Dental caries

nodeData.note: Biofilm and acid, lesion types, risk, progression to abscess, detection, prevention and minimal-intervention care. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What caries is.
A biofilm-driven, sugar-dependent disease in which repeated acid attacks cause net mineral loss from enamel, dentine or cementum.

manas.q: How is dental caries defined today?

children.note: Loss and gain of mineral alternate many times a day; a lesion forms only when loss wins over time.

manas.q: Why is caries called a dynamic process?

children.note: Erosion is acid loss without bacteria (gastric reflux, acidic drinks); caries needs the plaque biofilm.

manas.q: How does dental erosion differ from caries?

children.note: How plaque turns sugar into a hole.
Salivary pellicle coats enamel; early colonisers attach, then others join in a sticky polysaccharide matrix.

manas.q: What first coats a clean tooth surface?

children.note: Bacterial glucosyltransferases build sticky glucans from sucrose, helping plaque stick and hold acid on the tooth.

manas.q: Why is sucrose more cariogenic than other sugars?

children.note: Frequent sugar and low pH favour acid-making, acid-tolerant species; the balance shifts. Caries is dysbiosis, not one invading germ.

manas.q: What does the ecological plaque hypothesis propose?

children.note: Plaque pH falls within minutes of sugar, stays below critical pH for a while, then saliva brings it back over roughly half an hour or more.

manas.q: What does the Stephan curve show?

children.note: Each sugar intake starts a new acid attack, so many small snacks harm more than the same sugar at one meal.

manas.q: Why does sugar frequency matter more than amount?

children.note: Dentine and cementum dissolve at a higher pH than enamel (around 6.2–6.7), so exposed roots decay faster.

manas.q: Why are exposed roots more caries-prone than enamel?

children.note: Fluorapatite starts dissolving only around pH 4.5, giving more protection than hydroxyapatite.

manas.q: At about what pH does fluorapatite dissolve?

children.note: Flushes sugar, buffers acid with bicarbonate, supplies calcium and phosphate, and carries antibacterial proteins (lysozyme, lactoferrin, IgA).

manas.q: How does saliva protect teeth?

children.note: Earliest visible lesion: chalky subsurface mineral loss under an intact surface layer; can remineralise.

manas.q: Is an early white spot lesion reversible?

children.note: Tubules sclerose and the pulp lays down tertiary dentine; outer infected dentine is soft, inner affected dentine can remineralise.

manas.q: How does dentine respond to advancing caries?

children.note: Ways to describe a lesion.
Pit and fissure (occlusal molars, common in children), smooth surface (just below contact points), and root (older adults with gum recession).

manas.q: Where do pit and fissure caries occur?

children.note: Primary is on an untouched surface; secondary (recurrent) caries forms at the edge of an existing filling.

manas.q: What is secondary caries?

children.note: Active: chalky, matt, rough, plaque-covered. Arrested: hard, shiny, often dark brown or black.

manas.q: How does an arrested lesion look?

children.note: Visual scale 0–6: 0 sound; 1–2 enamel colour change; 3 enamel breakdown; 4 dentine shadow; 5–6 cavity into dentine.

manas.q: What does ICDAS code 4 describe?

children.note: I pits/fissures; II posterior proximal; III anterior proximal, incisal angle spared; IV anterior proximal with incisal angle; V cervical third.

manas.q: What is a Black's class II lesion?

children.note: Caries in any primary tooth under age 6; severe forms destroy many teeth early.

manas.q: What defines early childhood caries?

children.note: Who gets caries and why.
Sweet tea, sodas, sweets and sugary snacks between meals are the main driver.

manas.q: What is the main dietary driver of caries?

children.note: Low saliva removes the main defence: Sjögren's, head and neck radiotherapy, dehydration, mouth breathing.

manas.q: Which conditions reduce saliva and raise caries risk?

children.note: Anticholinergics, tricyclics, antihistamines and many others dry the mouth; sugar-based syrups add sugar, especially in children.

manas.q: How do medicines raise caries risk?

children.note: HIV-related salivary gland disease and dry mouth raise risk; oral care belongs in HIV clinic reviews.

manas.q: How does HIV raise caries risk?

children.note: Orthodontic brackets, partial dentures, crowding and poor fillings hold plaque.

manas.q: Why do orthodontic patients get white spots?

children.note: Low income, poor access to dentists and cheap sugary foods cluster caries in poorer groups.

manas.q: How do social factors affect caries?

children.note: Previous caries experience is the strongest single predictor of new lesions.

manas.q: What is the best predictor of future caries?

children.note: From silent spot to spreading infection.
Painless; seen as white or brown spot. Patients rarely notice it.

manas.q: Is an early caries lesion painful?

children.note: Brief sensitivity to sweet or cold; a cavity or dark shadow may be seen.

manas.q: What symptom suggests caries has reached dentine?

children.note: Spontaneous, lingering, poorly localised pain, often at night; heat may worsen it.

manas.q: Which pain features suggest irreversible pulpitis?

children.note: Pain may stop as the pulp dies; the tooth may darken and does not respond to cold.

manas.q: Why may toothache stop before an abscess forms?

children.note: Pain on biting, tender to tapping, swelling of gum or face, sometimes a draining sinus.

manas.q: What signs suggest a periapical abscess?

children.note: Lower molar infection can spread to submandibular and neck spaces; upper teeth may spread towards the orbit.

manas.q: Where can lower molar infection spread?

children.note: Trismus, difficulty swallowing or breathing, raised floor of mouth, eye swelling, fever: refer to hospital urgently.

manas.q: Which features of dental infection need urgent hospital care?

children.note: Seeing caries early.
Remove plaque, dry the tooth and use good light; white spots appear only on dried enamel.

manas.q: Why dry teeth before examining for caries?

children.note: Use a ball-ended probe gently; a sharp explorer pushed into a soft lesion can break the surface.

manas.q: Why avoid a sharp probe on early lesions?

children.note: Show proximal caries between back teeth and depth into dentine, which eyes miss.

manas.q: Which radiograph shows proximal caries best?

children.note: Cold or electric test: no response suggests pulp necrosis.

manas.q: What does a negative cold test suggest?

children.note: Count of decayed, missing and filled teeth (dmft in primary teeth); WHO's standard survey measure.

manas.q: What does DMFT measure?

children.note: Cheapest, most effective care.
WHO advises free sugars below 10% of energy, ideally below 5%; keep sweet foods to meal times.

manas.q: What free-sugar limit does WHO advise?

children.note: Twice daily with 1000–1500 ppm toothpaste for most people; spit, do not rinse; a smear for babies, pea-size from age 3.

manas.q: What toothpaste fluoride strength suits most people?

children.note: Painted on by a health worker a few times a year; useful in high-risk children.

manas.q: Who benefits most from fluoride varnish?

children.note: Resin or glass ionomer coating seals deep fissures of permanent molars soon after eruption.

manas.q: Which teeth receive fissure sealants?

children.note: Community fluoridation now gives only a small, low-certainty extra benefit where fluoride toothpaste is used; not used where natural fluoride is already high, as in parts of the Kenyan Rift Valley.

manas.q: Why is water fluoridation unsuitable in parts of Kenya?

children.note: Before radiotherapy, chemotherapy, valve surgery or antiresorptives, get a dental check and treat sources of infection.

manas.q: Which patients need dental review before treatment?

children.note: Minimal intervention: arrest, keep tooth, restore when needed.
Detect early, remineralise non-cavitated lesions, remove only what must go, and keep as much tooth as possible.

manas.q: What is minimal intervention dentistry?

children.note: In deep lesions, leave affected dentine over the pulp and seal it, avoiding pulp exposure.

manas.q: Why leave some dentine in deep cavities?

children.note: Painted on to arrest cavitated lesions; cheap and painless but stains the lesion black.

manas.q: What is the main drawback of silver diamine fluoride?

children.note: Atraumatic restorative treatment: hand tools remove soft caries, then high-viscosity glass ionomer fills; no drill or power needed.

manas.q: What material is used in ART?

children.note: Glass ionomer releases fluoride; composite bonds and looks natural; amalgam is being phased down worldwide.

manas.q: Why is glass ionomer useful in caries-prone mouths?

children.note: Preformed metal crown cemented over a carious primary molar without removing decay, sealing bacteria in.

manas.q: What is the Hall technique?

children.note: Root canal treatment saves a permanent tooth; pulpotomy is common in primary molars; otherwise extract.

manas.q: How is an irreversibly inflamed permanent pulp treated?

children.note: Drain via the tooth, extraction or incision; antibiotics only for spreading infection or systemic signs, not plain toothache.

manas.q: When are antibiotics needed for dental pain?

children.note: Why untreated caries matters.
Pain disturbs eating, sleep and school; severe early caries has been linked to poor growth.

manas.q: How does severe caries affect children?

children.note: Ludwig's angina and other neck-space infections can block the airway.

manas.q: Which odontogenic infection threatens the airway?

children.note: Rare spread of upper tooth infection via facial and ophthalmic veins.

manas.q: Which rare intracranial complication follows upper tooth infection?

children.note: Oral viridans streptococci are a classic cause; good oral health matters in valve disease.

manas.q: Which oral bacteria classically cause endocarditis?

children.note: Extractions in people on bisphosphonates or denosumab risk osteonecrosis of the jaw; treat teeth early.

manas.q: Why treat teeth before starting bisphosphonates?

children.note: How bodies approach caries.
Prevention through fluoride toothpaste and sugar advice; ART and extraction fit primary care where dentists are few; avoid fluoride supplements in high-fluoride areas.

manas.q: Why avoid fluoride supplements in parts of Kenya?

children.note: Global Oral Health Status Report: oral diseases affect about 3.5 billion people; untreated caries of permanent teeth is the commonest condition.

manas.q: About how many people have oral diseases, per WHO 2022?

children.note: Fluoride toothpaste, glass ionomer cement and silver diamine fluoride were added to the WHO model list.

manas.q: Which caries products joined the WHO essential list in 2021?

children.note: International treaty on mercury that includes phasing down dental amalgam.

manas.q: Which treaty phases down dental amalgam?

children.note: NICE recall guidance sets dental check-up intervals by individual risk rather than a fixed six months.

manas.q: How does NICE set dental recall intervals?

children.note: Advises a first dental visit by the first birthday or within six months of the first tooth.

manas.q: When does AAPD advise a child's first dental visit?

children.note: FDI World Dental Federation promotes minimal intervention dentistry and runs World Oral Health Day on 20 March.

manas.q: When is World Oral Health Day?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-27 (Europe PMC).
Cochrane 2024 (non-randomised studies): since 1975, starting fluoridation may cut dmft by only ~0.25 tooth (low certainty; may be none). At 0.7 ppm ~12% had fluorosis of aesthetic concern.

manas.q: What did the 2024 Cochrane review find on modern water fluoridation?

children.note: WHO-commissioned systematic review (37 studies): unhealthy foods and drinks in children up to 10 years appear to raise caries risk; no included studies came from low-income countries.

manas.q: What did a WHO-commissioned review find on unhealthy foods and caries in young children?

children.note: A 2023 narrative review: modern care rests on risk assessment, early detection and minimally invasive restorations that save healthy tooth tissue and keep the pulp alive.

manas.q: What principles guide modern caries management?
